html:
George throws a ball at a target 15 times.
Each time George throws the ball, the probability of the ball hitting the target is 0.48

The random variable X represents the number of times George hits the target in 15 throws.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html: Find P(X = 3)
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html: Find P(X ≥ 5)
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: 0.920 — P(X ≥ 5) = 1 − P(X ≤ 4) = 1 − 0.07987… = 0.9201…

lead: George now throws the ball at the target 250 times.
html: Use a normal approximation to calculate the probability that he will hit the target more than 110 times.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: 0.885 — Y ~ B(250, 0.48) is approximated by N(120, 7.8992), since np = 120 and np(1 − p) = 62.4. With a continuity correction, P(Y > 110) ≈ P(W > 110.5) = 0.8854…

html:
A manufacturer uses a machine to make metal rods.

The length of a metal rod, L cm, is normally distributed with

  • a mean of 8 cm
  • a standard deviation of x cm

Given that the proportion of metal rods less than 7.902 cm in length is 2.5%
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html: show that x = 0.05 to 2 decimal places.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: Shown: x = 0.05 — P(L < 7.902) = 0.025 so 7.902 − 8⁄x = −1.96, giving x = 0.098 ÷ 1.96 = 0.05.

html: Calculate the proportion of metal rods that are between 7.94 cm and 8.09 cm in length.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

lead:
The cost of producing a single metal rod is 20p

A metal rod

  • where L < 7.94 is sold for scrap for 5p
  • where 7.94 ⩽ L ⩽ 8.09 is sold for 50p
  • where L > 8.09 is shortened for an extra cost of 10p and then sold for 50p
html:
Calculate the expected profit per 500 of the metal rods.
Give your answer to the nearest pound.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: £122 — P(L < 7.94) = 0.11507, P(middle) = 0.84900, P(L > 8.09) = 0.03593. Profit per rod: −15p, +30p and +20p (50 − 20 − 10). Expected profit per rod = −15(0.11507) + 30(0.84900) + 20(0.03593) = 24.46p, so per 500 rods = 12 231p ≈ £122.

lead:
The same manufacturer makes metal hinges in large batches.

The hinges each have a probability of 0.015 of having a fault.

A random sample of 200 hinges is taken from each batch and the batch is accepted if fewer than 6 hinges are faulty.

The manufacturer's aim is for 95% of batches to be accepted.
html: Explain whether the manufacturer is likely to achieve its aim.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: No — only about 91.8% of batches are accepted — the number of faulty hinges F ~ B(200, 0.015); a batch is accepted if F ≤ 5, and P(F ≤ 5) = 0.9176…, which is less than 0.95, so the aim is not likely to be achieved.

html: Dian uses the large data set to investigate the Daily Total Rainfall, r mm, for Camborne.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html: Write down how a value of 0 < r ⩽ 0.05 is recorded in the large data set.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: tr (trace) — amounts of 0.05 mm or less are recorded as “tr” in the large data set.

lead:
Dian uses the data for the 31 days of August 2015 for Camborne and calculates the following statistics

n = 31    Σr = 174.9    Σr2 = 3523.283
html: Use these statistics to calculate the mean of the Daily Total Rainfall in Camborne for August 2015.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: 5.64 mm — mean = Σr ÷ n = 174.9 ÷ 31 = 5.6419…

html: Use the same statistics (n = 31, Σr = 174.9, Σr2 = 3523.283) to calculate the standard deviation of the Daily Total Rainfall in Camborne for August 2015.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: 9.05 mm — s.d. = √(3523.283 ÷ 31 − 5.6419…2) = 9.0456… (9.20, from the n − 1 divisor, is also accepted).

lead:
Dian believes that the mean Daily Total Rainfall in August is less in the South of the UK than in the North of the UK.
The mean Daily Total Rainfall in Leuchars for August 2015 is 1.72 mm to 2 decimal places.
html: State, giving a reason, whether this provides evidence to support Dian's belief.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: No — Camborne (South) has a mean of 5.64 mm in August 2015, which is greater than Leuchars’ (North) 1.72 mm, so it does not support Dian’s belief (and it is only one month at one place in each).

lead: Dian uses the large data set to estimate the proportion of days with no rain in Camborne for 1987 to be 0.27 to 2 decimal places.
html: Explain why the distribution B(14, 0.27) might not be a reasonable model for the number of days without rain for a 14-day summer event.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: The days are not independent — rain on one day makes rain the next day more likely (weather comes in spells), and the probability of a dry day is not constant through the summer; also 0.27 comes from 1987 data.

html:
A dentist knows from past records that 10% of customers arrive late for their appointment.

A new manager believes that there has been a change in the proportion of customers who arrive late for their appointment.

A random sample of 50 of the dentist's customers is taken.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Write down

  • a null hypothesis corresponding to no change in the proportion of customers who arrive late
  • an alternative hypothesis corresponding to the manager's belief
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: H0: p = 0.1   H1: p ≠ 0.1 — p is the proportion of customers who arrive late.

html:
Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for a two-tailed test of the null hypothesis in (a)
You should state the probability of rejection in each tail, which should be less than 0.025
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: X = 0 or X ≥ 10 — X ~ B(50, 0.1). Lower tail: P(X = 0) = 0.0052 (P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0338 is too big). Upper tail: P(X ≥ 10) = 0.0245 (P(X ≥ 9) = 0.0579 is too big).

html: Find the actual level of significance of the test based on your critical region from part (b)
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

lead: The manager observes that 15 of the 50 customers arrived late for their appointment.
html: With reference to part (b), comment on the manager's belief.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: 15 is in the critical region, so reject H0 — there is evidence that the proportion of customers arriving late has changed, which supports the manager’s belief.

html:
Anna is investigating the relationship between exercise and resting heart rate.

  • the number of minutes, m, spent exercising each week

Her results are shown on the scatter diagram.
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths

html: Interpret the nature of the relationship between h and m
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: As the time spent exercising increases, resting heart rate decreases — a negative (non-linear) relationship between h and m.

lead:
Anna codes the data using the formulae

x = log10 m
y = log10 h

The product moment correlation coefficient between x and y is −0.897

Test whether or not there is significant evidence of a negative correlation between x and y
You should

  • state your hypotheses clearly
  • use a 5% level of significance
  • state the critical value used
name: Paper 31: Statistics — June 2022
subject: Maths
answer: Reject H0: significant evidence of negative correlation — H0: ρ = 0, H1: ρ < 0. Critical value for n = 19 at 5% (one-tailed) is −0.3887; −0.897 < −0.3887, so reject H0.

html: Examine Hick’s soul making theodicy and how it influences attitudes to evil and suffering.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
An accurate, detailed account of Hick's Irenaean soul-making theodicy and how it shapes responses to evil and suffering —

AO1 — knowledge and understanding (10 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Accurate, relevant and detailed (9–10 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Accurate and relevant, mostly detailed (7–8 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Generally accurate, some detail (5–6 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, partly relevant (3–4 marks)
  5. Level 1 — Very limited (1–2 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • Irenaeus: humans made in God's image, growing into his likeness; Hick develops this in Evil and the God of Love.
  • Epistemic distance: God creates at a distance so that faith and love are free; a world without suffering could not make souls.
  • The world is a 'vale of soul-making': evil and suffering are the conditions for virtues such as compassion, courage and forgiveness.
  • Universal salvation / eschatological fulfilment: all will eventually reach the likeness of God, which justifies the suffering on the way.
  • Influence on attitudes: suffering seen as purposeful and growth-producing; encourages compassionate response; but may seem to excuse or instrumentalise suffering (e.g. dysteleological suffering).

Examine asks for knowledge and understanding only — evaluation earns nothing here. Marks come from accurate detail, correct use of scholars and terms, and examples.

lead: ‘The ontological argument proves the existence of God.’
html: Evaluate this claim.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
A sustained evaluation of whether the ontological argument proves God's existence, reaching a justified conclusion —

AO2 — analysis and evaluation (15 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Thorough, sustained argument; justified conclusion (13–15 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Clear, reasoned evaluation of different views (10–12 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Some analysis; a view with some support (7–9 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, largely one-sided (4–6 marks)
  5. Level 1 — A view with little support (1–3 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • For: Anselm's Proslogion 2 and 3 (that than which nothing greater can be conceived; necessary existence); Descartes' supremely perfect being; Malcolm and Plantinga's modal versions.
  • Against: Gaunilo's perfect island; Kant — existence is not a real predicate (100 thalers); Russell/Frege — existence is a second-order predicate; Hume — any being can be conceived not to exist.
  • Replies: Anselm's answer to Gaunilo (islands are contingent); Plantinga's maximal greatness.
  • Possible conclusions: it shows what God would have to be like if God exists, but cannot move from concept to reality; or it succeeds for those who already believe (faith seeking understanding).

Evaluate asks for an argument: weigh the claim against the strongest counter-arguments and reach a conclusion that follows from them. Description on its own stays in the bottom levels.

html:

  • Religious language is analogical.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
An accurate, detailed explanation of religious language as symbolic and as analogical —

AO1 — knowledge and understanding (10 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Accurate, relevant and detailed (9–10 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Accurate and relevant, mostly detailed (7–8 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Generally accurate, some detail (5–6 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, partly relevant (3–4 marks)
  5. Level 1 — Very limited (1–2 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • Symbolic: Tillich — symbols participate in what they point to, open up levels of reality, grow and die; God as 'Ground of Being'; e.g. the cross, 'God is a rock'.
  • Randall: symbols arouse emotion, bind communities, communicate experiences that literal language cannot.
  • Analogical: Aquinas — language about God is neither univocal nor equivocal; analogy of attribution (e.g. the bull's urine/healthy) and analogy of proportion ('God is good' in proportion to God's nature).
  • Ramsey: models and qualifiers ('infinitely good'); Hick's analogy of proper proportionality.
  • Each idea should be explained with examples; the question requires BOTH.

lead: ‘Religion has no satisfactory response to the challenge of the verification principle.’
html: Evaluate this claim.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
A sustained evaluation of whether religion can answer the verification principle, reaching a justified conclusion —

AO2 — analysis and evaluation (15 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Thorough, sustained argument; justified conclusion (13–15 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Clear, reasoned evaluation of different views (10–12 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Some analysis; a view with some support (7–9 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, largely one-sided (4–6 marks)
  5. Level 1 — A view with little support (1–3 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • The challenge: Ayer and the Logical Positivists — a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable; religious statements are neither, so meaningless.
  • Religious responses: Hick's eschatological verification (Celestial City); Swinburne's toys-in-the-cupboard; religious language as non-cognitive (Braithwaite, Wittgenstein's language games, Tillich's symbols).
  • Weaknesses of the principle itself: it is self-refuting (cannot be verified); weak verification still excludes much of science and history.
  • Counter: eschatological verification is unfalsifiable now; non-cognitive accounts may give up what believers mean.
  • Conclusion should weigh whether any response is 'satisfactory' and to whom.

Evaluate asks for an argument: weigh the claim against the strongest counter-arguments and reach a conclusion that follows from them. Description on its own stays in the bottom levels.

html: Examine the approach taken to moral decision making by virtue ethics. You must illustrate your answer with reference to the issue of lying.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
An accurate, detailed account of virtue ethics' approach to moral decisions, applied to lying —

AO1 — knowledge and understanding (10 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Accurate, relevant and detailed (9–10 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Accurate and relevant, mostly detailed (7–8 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Generally accurate, some detail (5–6 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, partly relevant (3–4 marks)
  5. Level 1 — Very limited (1–2 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • Aristotle: eudaimonia as the goal; virtues as the mean between excess and deficiency (truthfulness between boastfulness and false modesty).
  • Virtues acquired by habit and imitation of the virtuous person; phronesis (practical wisdom) decides what the virtuous person would do.
  • Moral decisions ask 'what would a virtuous person do?' rather than following rules or calculating outcomes.
  • Lying: the truthful person generally does not lie; but practical wisdom might allow tact or deception in rare cases (e.g. to protect someone) — the agent's character and motive are key.
  • Credit modern virtue ethicists (Anscombe, MacIntyre, Foot) where used accurately.

Examine asks for knowledge and understanding only — evaluation earns nothing here. Marks come from accurate detail, correct use of scholars and terms, and examples.

lead: ‘Virtue ethics provides no clear guidance for moral decision making.’
html: Evaluate this claim.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
A sustained evaluation of whether virtue ethics gives clear guidance in moral decisions, with a justified conclusion —

AO2 — analysis and evaluation (15 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Thorough, sustained argument; justified conclusion (13–15 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Clear, reasoned evaluation of different views (10–12 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Some analysis; a view with some support (7–9 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, largely one-sided (4–6 marks)
  5. Level 1 — A view with little support (1–3 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • For the claim: 'what would the virtuous person do?' does not say what to do in a dilemma (Louden); virtues can conflict; the mean is vague; who counts as virtuous is circular.
  • Against: phronesis lets the agent respond to particulars; virtue ethics guides character over a lifetime rather than single acts; Hursthouse's v-rules ('do what is honest').
  • Comparison with rule-based theories, which give clearer but sometimes harsher guidance.
  • Conclusion may distinguish clear guidance for ordinary life from unclear guidance in hard cases.

Evaluate asks for an argument: weigh the claim against the strongest counter-arguments and reach a conclusion that follows from them. Description on its own stays in the bottom levels.

html:
Examine the meaning of right and wrong in:

  • Divine Command Theory
  • Intuitionism.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
An accurate, detailed explanation of what makes an action right or wrong in Divine Command Theory and in Intuitionism —

AO1 — knowledge and understanding (10 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Accurate, relevant and detailed (9–10 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Accurate and relevant, mostly detailed (7–8 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Generally accurate, some detail (5–6 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, partly relevant (3–4 marks)
  5. Level 1 — Very limited (1–2 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • Divine Command Theory: right = commanded by God, wrong = forbidden by God; morality depends on God's will (e.g. Ten Commandments); Adams' modified DCT ties commands to God's loving nature.
  • The Euthyphro dilemma as a way of explaining the theory's claim (not as evaluation).
  • Intuitionism: right and wrong are real, objective, non-natural properties known directly by intuition (Moore — 'good' is indefinable; naturalistic fallacy).
  • Prichard: obligations are recognised immediately; Ross: prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence).
  • Both parts required for the higher levels.

lead: ‘Humanity has no moral responsibility for its actions.’
html: Evaluate this claim.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2018
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
A sustained evaluation of whether humans are morally responsible, with a justified conclusion —

AO2 — analysis and evaluation (15 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Thorough, sustained argument; justified conclusion (13–15 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Clear, reasoned evaluation of different views (10–12 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Some analysis; a view with some support (7–9 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, largely one-sided (4–6 marks)
  5. Level 1 — A view with little support (1–3 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • For the claim: hard determinism — physical (Laplace), psychological (Freud, Pavlov), genetic determinism; theological determinism / predestination (Calvin); Libet's experiments.
  • Against: libertarianism — sense of freedom, moral experience, deliberation; Sartre's radical freedom; compatibilism (Hume, Locke's locked room) — responsibility needs only that the act flows from the agent's desires.
  • Implications: praise, blame and punishment; religious ideas of judgement require responsibility (Pelagius vs Augustine).
  • A reasoned conclusion on whether some, full or no responsibility follows.

html: Examine different understandings of the relationship between the body and the soul.
name: Paper 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics — June 2024
subject: Religious Studies
answer:
An accurate, detailed account of different understandings of the relationship between body and soul —

AO1 — knowledge and understanding (10 marks)

  1. Level 5 — Accurate, relevant and detailed (9–10 marks)
  2. Level 4 — Accurate and relevant, mostly detailed (7–8 marks)
  3. Level 3 — Generally accurate, some detail (5–6 marks)
  4. Level 2 — Limited, partly relevant (3–4 marks)
  5. Level 1 — Very limited (1–2 marks)

Indicative content (any relevant, accurate material is credited)

  • Plato: substance dualism; soul immortal, imprisoned in the body; the charioteer; Forms.
  • Aristotle: the soul as the form of the body (wax and impression); not separable.
  • Descartes: mind and body distinct substances, interacting via the pineal gland.

html:
Here are the first four terms of an arithmetic sequence.

1   5   9   13

Find an expression, in terms of n, for the nth term of this sequence.
answer: 4n − 3 — B2, oe. The terms go up by 4 each time, so the nth term starts 4n; then 4 × 1 = 4 against a first term of 1, so subtract 3. Any equivalent form counts and any letter counts — 4x − 3 is accepted, and so are un = 4n − 3 and T = 4n − 3. B1 only for 4n + k where k is wrong or absent, provided it is unambiguously shown, so a bare 4n still banks one mark. B1 only, too, for n = 4n − 3 or “4nth − 3” — the right expression spoiled by writing it as something it is not, which is worth pointing out because it looks like a full answer. The step that actually goes wrong is jumping from the common difference straight to 4n + 1 off the first term; test the expression at n = 1 every time.

Against that, decimals get no credit at all unless they lead to a correct fraction. html:
Petra is going to cover the floor with paint.

Petra has 3 tins of paint. There are 2.5 litres of paint in each tin. Petra thinks 1 litre of paint will cover 10 m2 of floor.

Assuming Petra is correct, does she have enough paint to cover the floor?
You must show all your working.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Yes: the floor is 68 m2 and 3 tins cover 75 m2 — the floor is 68 m2 and 3 tins cover 75 m2, so she has enough. Four marks and three of them are the route. P1 for the area of any one piece: 10 × 8 (= 80), 10 × 5 (= 50), 8 × 6 (= 48), (10 − 6) × 5 (= 20), (10 − 6) × (8 − 5) (= 12), 6 × (8 − 5) (= 18) or 5 × 6 (= 30) — but the scheme withholds it if they go on to multiply by a third length, which is the commonest way this mark is lost. P1 for a complete area: cut it off a rectangle, “80” − “12”, or split it, “50” + “18” or “48” + “20” — all three give 68. P1 for comparing on any one of three scales: 3 × 2.5 × 10 (= 75 m2 covered), or “68” ÷ 10 (= 6.8 litres needed), or “68” ÷ 10 ÷ 2.5 (= 2.72 tins needed) — and it follows through on whatever area they believe they have. A1 for Yes supported by a matching pair of figures: 68 and 75, or 6.8 and 7.5, or 68 and 2.72. The decision on its own is not the mark; the numbers have to be on the page beside it. A wrong statement about how much paint is left over is ignored provided the correct figures are there. The hard step is the side nobody gives you: the plan prints 10, 6, 8 and 5, and the missing piece is (10 − 6) by (8 − 5).

lead: Actually, 1 litre of paint will cover 11 m2 of floor.
html:
Does this affect your answer to part (a)?
You must give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No effect: she still has enough paint, as each litre now covers more floor, so she needs less — she still has enough. One mark, C1, and it follows through from part (a), so there has to be a decision in (a) for it to follow through from. The mark is for a decision plus a reason together. The scheme’s acceptable answers are “no effect, she will need less paint”, “it won’t change, she will still have enough”, “no, she will have more paint left over”, and “no, as this will cover 82.5 m<sup>2</sup>” (7.5 litres × 11). It also prints the near misses, and they are the thing to point out: “Petra will need less paint” and “she will have more paint left over” are refused — both are true, and both leave the decision off. “She won’t have enough paint” and “she will need more paint” are refused as wrong. Any figures written into the statement must be correct for the area claimed in (a). So the sentence needs the word yes, no or “no effect” in it, and covering more per litre can only help.

html: Work out an estimate for the total amount that Sophie pays.
answer: 40 euros — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8, rounding both numbers to 1 significant figure first. The answer column says “estimated value” rather than a number on purpose: the A1 follows through whatever rounding the student chose, so 40.8 (from 510) and 40.5 (from 500 × 0.81) are each worth full marks. P1 for a 1sf value actually used in a calculation — 500 ÷ 10, or 500 × 0.8, or 510 × 0.8, or 513 × 0.8, or 500 × 0.81. The rounding may come after a correct step: 513 ÷ 10 = 51.3 → 50, then 50 × 0.81 scores both process marks, as does 51 × 0.8. P1 for a full process to the total — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40), or 510 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40.8), or 500 ÷ 10 × 0.81 (= 40.5), or in general [distance] ÷ 10 × [amount]; the unrounded 513 ÷ 10 × 0.81 is accepted for this mark too. A1 for the answer their own rounded values give. Two tolerances the scheme states outright: 0.81 rounded to 0.80 is accepted, and 0.81 rounded to 1 is condoned for the process marks but loses the A1. The step that is actually hard is the ÷ 10 — 0.81 euros buys 10 kilometres, not one, so 500 × 0.8 = 400 euros is the answer to watch for.

The reason must be about the estimating — the rounding done at the start — and not about rounding the final answer at the end. lead: M is a different straight line with equation y = 5x
html: Write down the equation of a straight line parallel to M.
answer: Any equation of the form y = 5x + c with c ≠ 0 — eg y = 5x + 1. B1. The answer column just says “equation” because there is no single right one. Parallel means the same gradient, so the 5 must survive untouched; the only thing that may change is the intercept. c ≠ 0 is the condition students fall over: y = 5x is M itself, and the question asks for a line parallel to M, which means a different line. Any equivalent form is accepted, so 5x − y + 1 = 0 or y − 1 = 5x also score.

html:
Kasim has some small jars, some medium jars and some large jars. He has a total of 400 jars.

3⁄8 of the 400 jars are empty.

For the empty jars,
number of small jars : number of medium jars = 3 : 4
number of medium jars : number of large jars = 1 : 2

Work out the percentage of Kasim’s jars that are empty small jars.
answer: 7.5% — that is 7.5%, and the scheme takes 71⁄2 or any equivalent. Five marks, four of them process. P1 for the number of empty jars: 3⁄8 × 400 = 150. P1 for the start of the ratio work, and this is the step the question is really testing — 3 : 4 and 1 : 2 do not join up until the mediums agree, so scale the second to 4 : 8 and chain them into small : medium : large = 3 : 4 : 8. P1 for the empty small jars: 3⁄3 + 4 + 8 × “150” = 30, or writing the whole split out as 30 : 40 : 80. P1 for turning that into a percentage: 30 ÷ 400 × 100. A1 for 7.5. The scheme prints a second route worth the same five marks and it is shorter if a student can see it: chain to 3 : 4 : 8, so small jars are 3⁄15 = 1⁄5 of the empty ones, then 3⁄8 × 1⁄5 = 3⁄40 of all the jars, and 3⁄40 × 100 = 7.5 — the 400 is never needed at all. Two wrong answers to watch for: 30, which is the count of jars offered as if it were the percentage, and 20%, from dividing 30 by the 150 empty jars instead of by all 400.

html:
Triangle A is translated by the vector (6−4) to give triangle B.

Triangle B is rotated 90° clockwise about the point (1, 2) to give triangle C.

Describe fully the single transformation that maps triangle A onto triangle C.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Translations, Rotations, Describing a Single Transformation
answer: Rotation 90° clockwise about (−4, 1) — a translation followed by a rotation is a single rotation through the same angle, so only the centre has to be found. Translating by (6, −4) sends A(−3, 2), (−2, 2), (−2, 4) to B(3, −2), (4, −2), (4, 0); turning B 90° clockwise about (1, 2) gives C(−3, 0), (−3, −1), (−1, −1). The point that does not move under the combined map is (−4, 1): it translates to (2, −3), and (2, −3) turned 90° clockwise about (1, 2) lands back on (−4, 1). 270° anticlockwise about (−4, 1) is the same transformation.

html:
ABC and DAB are similar isosceles triangles.

AB = AC
AD = BD

BC : CD = 4 : 21

Find the ratio AB : AD
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 : 5 — B, C and D lie on one line, which is what BC : CD measures, so call BC = 4k and CD = 21k: then BD = 25k, and AD = BD = 25k. The triangles share the base angle at B, so A matches D, B matches A and C matches B, and AB⁄AD = BC⁄AB. So AB2 = BC × AD = 4k × 25k = 100k2, AB = 10k, and AB : AD = 10k : 25k = 2 : 5.

html: Write the number 18 475 correct to the nearest thousand.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 18 000 — B1, cao, and nothing else scores. The two thousands either side are 18 000 and 19 000, with the halfway point at 18 500; 18 475 sits below it, so it rounds down. The one digit that decides it is the hundreds digit, 4 — once that is below 5 the 7 and the 5 behind it play no part at all. The slip to name is reading “475, nearly 500” and rounding up to 19 000; the other common wrong answer is 18 500, which is 18 475 to the nearest hundred rather than the nearest thousand.

html: Write 0.3 as a percentage.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 30% — that is 30%, and the scheme prints the bare number, B1 cao. A percentage is a number out of 100, so take the decimal to hundredths and read the top: 0.3 = 3⁄10 = 30⁄100 = 30%, which is the same move as × 100. The wrong answer to watch for is 3% — it comes from reading 0.3 as “three” rather than as three tenths. 0.03 is the one that is 3%.

html: Write down the mathematical name for the type of angle marked y.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: reflex — B1 cao, and the scheme wants the word rather than a size. A reflex angle is anything bigger than 180° and smaller than 360°, so the arc marked y goes the long way round the point rather than the short way. Worth having ready as a set: acute under 90°, right angle exactly 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight line 180°, reflex over 180°. “Acute” is the answer to head off — the two lines on the paper make a small angle of well under 90°, and naming that one instead of the angle the label is actually attached to is the slip.

html:
Write these numbers in order of size. Start with the smallest number.

0.21   0.2   0.03   0.1   0.16
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 0.03, 0.1, 0.16, 0.2, 0.21 — B1 for the complete list, and the scheme also accepts the reverse order, 0.21, 0.2, 0.16, 0.1, 0.03, even though the question asks for the smallest first. Pad every number to the same number of decimal places before comparing — 0.21, 0.20, 0.03, 0.10, 0.16 — and then they sort on the digits after the point as if those were whole numbers: 03, 10, 16, 20, 21. The trap is doing that comparison without padding, which makes 0.16 look bigger than 0.2 because 16 > 2. The mark is all-or-nothing, so writing the list out fresh is safer than numbering the printed ones.

html: Find the square root of 64
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — B1, and the scheme says accept 8 or −8, so a student who has met the negative root is not penalised for giving it. The square root of 64 is the number that multiplies by itself to make 64: 8 × 8 = 64, and (−8) × (−8) = 64 as well, which is exactly why both are allowed. The wrong answer to watch for is 32 — halving instead of finding the number that squares to it.

html:
Ryan buys

  • 4 cakes at £1.30 each
  • 2 identical tins of soup.

Ryan pays with a £10 note.
He gets £1.80 change.

How much does Ryan pay for each tin of soup?
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £1.50 — the bracket is the scheme’s: 1.50 and 1.5 both count, and it condones the answer written £1.5(0)p. Four marks, and three of them are for the route, so the working has to be on the page. P1 for either starting step — 4 × £1.30 = £5.2(0), or £10 − £1.80 = £8.2(0). P1 for putting the two together: £10 − £1.80 − “£5.20” = £3, or equivalent — the quotation marks are the scheme saying it follows through on whatever the student got for the four cakes. P1 for “£3” ÷ 2. A1 for 1.5(0) cao. Working entirely in pence is accepted throughout. The hard step is the second one: the £1.80 change has to come off as well as the cakes. A student who does £10 − £5.20 = £4.80 and halves it reaches £2.4(0), which reads like a finished answer — the scheme gives that a special case 2 marks and no more.

WednesdayThursdayFridaySaturday
Lena6986

html: On the grid, draw a suitable diagram or chart for this information.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A fully labelled dual bar chart, scale from 0: Lena 6, 9, 8, 6 and Pavel 7, 6, 5, 6 hours, Wednesday to Saturday — and the scheme accepts a vertical line graph, a multiple or composite bar chart, or a frequency polygon for all four marks, so the kind of chart is not what is being tested. M1 for a key, or labels, that tell Lena and Pavel apart — unambiguous abbreviations such as L and P are accepted. M1 for 3 or 4 of the days labelled, or a linear scale present — the scale need not start at 0 for this mark, but it must be marked on the grid lines rather than in the spaces. M1 for bars, lines or points correctly showing the data for at least one person or two days, unambiguously right for whatever scale is drawn; for this mark the scheme also allows the four daily totals — 13, 15, 13, 12 — charted instead of the two people separately. C1 for a fully correct chart: days of the week labelled, vertical axis correctly scaled and labelled, and a key or labels for Lena and Pavel. For that last mark the scale must start at 0 and be linear across the range plotted. Condoned: “frequency” in place of “number of hours”, bars of unequal width, and no gaps or inconsistent gaps between them; the horizontal axis does not need an overall “day” label. The step that costs the fourth mark is the scale — deciding what one square is worth, and starting it at 0, before any bar is drawn.

html: Work out the size of the angle marked x.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles at a Point & on a Line
answer: 50° — M1 for 360 − 220 − 90 or equivalent, A1 for 50 cao. The three lines all meet at O, so the angles round that point fill one complete turn and add to 360°: 220 + 90 = 310, and 360 − 310 = 50. The hard step is seeing that this is a point and not a straight line — reaching for 180 is the usual wrong turn. There is a second route the scheme explicitly allows for, extending one of AO, OC or BO and working with angles on a straight line; it is worth knowing about here because it changes which reason earns the mark in part (ii).

html: Give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles at a Point & on a Line
answer: Angles at a point add up to 360° — C1, and the scheme underlines angles at a point and 360, so both halves have to appear: the rule and the number. It also accepts “a full turn adds up to 360” and “full rotation is 360”. The list of what is not accepted is the more useful half, because every entry on it looks close enough to pass: “angles in a circle add to 360”, “a whole circle adds up to 360”, “it must add up to 360 degrees”, the arithmetic on its own (220 + 90 = 310, 360 − 310), “angles at a point add up to 180”, and “angles on a straight line add to 180”. One exception: if part (i) was worked by extending AO, OC or BO, then “angles on a straight line add to 180” does earn the mark, because it is the reason for that method. This is where reason marks go — a student with the right number who writes the sum out again instead of naming the rule scores nothing.

html: Work out the output when the input is 13
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 16 — run 13 through the boxes in the printed order: 13 × 2 = 26, then 26 − 10 = 16. B1, cao, and there is no method mark here, so the number is the whole of it. Two slips collect wrong answers: doing the boxes in the other order (13 − 10 = 3, then 3 × 2 = 6), and running the machine backwards.

html: Work out the input when the output is 28
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 19 — go back through the machine undoing each box: 28 + 10 = 38, then 38 ÷ 2 = 19. M1 for starting that inverse — the scheme wants 28 + 10 (= 38), or simply the sight of +10 and ÷2, and it says those two may be shown in a reversed flow diagram, or written next to the number machine printed in the question; A1 for 19, cao. Check forwards: 19 × 2 = 38, 38 − 10 = 28. The hard step is the order of the inverses — the LAST box is undone FIRST, so it is +10 then ÷2. Doing it the other way round (28 ÷ 2 = 14, 14 + 10 = 24) is the common wrong answer.

html: Show that there is a number for which the output is the same as the input.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 10: 10 × 2 = 20 and 20 − 10 = 10, so an input of 10 gives an output of 10 — 10 × 2 = 20, and 20 − 10 = 10, so output equals input. M1 for carrying out at least one trial (any value at all, as long as it is evaluated correctly), or for forming a suitable equation such as 2x − 10 = x, or just for identifying 10; C1 for actually showing that 10 goes in and 10 comes out. The scheme allows the single line 10 × 2 = 20 − 10 = 10 for M1 and C1 together, and it accepts a correct inverse-function trial too. If the trial is written on the number machine printed in the question it must be a value other than the 13 of part (a) or the 28 of part (b). Algebraically, 2x − 10 = x gives x = 10. The hard step is that this is a “show that”: writing 10 on its own earns the M1 and not the C1 — the arithmetic has to be on the page.

html:
There are 24 cows and 36 sheep on a farm.

Write as a ratio the number of cows to the number of sheep. Give your ratio in its simplest form.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 : 3 — divide both numbers by 12, the highest common factor of 24 and 36: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3. M1 for any start — writing 24 : 36, or the reversed 3 : 2, or 1.5 : 1; A1 for 2 : 3, and the scheme also accepts 1 : 1.5, which is worth knowing because it is not whole numbers and still scores. Order is what gets lost: cows are named first, so it is 2 : 3 and not 3 : 2. And the scheme says do not ISW from 2 : 3 — subsequent working is not ignored here, so once 2 : 3 is written, carrying on and turning it into something else can throw the mark away. Stop at the simplified ratio.

html: Work out −12 ÷ −4
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — a negative divided by a negative is positive, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. B1, cao. The only thing being tested is the sign rule, and the answer it collects when that is missed is −3.

html: Find the value of 25
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 32 — 25 means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which doubles up 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. B1, cao. The scheme settles which power the paper printed: 52 would be 25, and the answer given is 32, so the question is 2 to the fifth. The slip is multiplying the two numbers instead of repeating the multiplication — 2 × 5 = 10.
examiner_note: The index did not come out of the PDF text layer. It is 2 to the power 5 — the mark scheme answers 32, and 5 squared would be 25, so the index is on the 2.

html:
Write one pair of brackets in this calculation so that the answer is correct.

30 ÷ 3 + 2 − 4 = 2
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 30 ÷ (3 + 2) − 4 — the brackets go round 3 + 2, so the division is by 5 instead of by 3: 30 ÷ 5 = 6, and 6 − 4 = 2. B1 for brackets correctly placed. Left alone, the order of operations does the division first and gives 10 + 2 − 4 = 8, so the whole job of the brackets is to push the addition in front of the division. One pair only, and it has to sit exactly there — 30 ÷ (3 + 2 − 4) is 30 ÷ 1 = 30, and (30 ÷ 3) + 2 − 4 is 8.

lead: The diagram shows a triangle and a rectangle.
html:
The perimeter of the rectangle is a quarter of the perimeter of the triangle.

Work out the length of the rectangle.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 6 cm — three process marks and an accuracy mark, and the scheme walks it in this order. P1 for the perimeter of the triangle, 14 + 30 + 36 (= 80). P1 for a quarter of that, 80 ÷ 4 (= 20) — and the scheme explicitly gives BOTH of those marks for quartering each side instead and adding, 36 ÷ 4 + 14 ÷ 4 + 30 ÷ 4 (= 20). P1 for a complete process back to the length, (20 − 4 − 4) ÷ 2 or 20 ÷ 2 − 4. A1 for 6, cao. The hard step is the last one: a rectangle perimeter of 20 contains the 4 cm width twice, so 8 comes off and the remaining 12 is halved. Halving first gets there too — 20 ÷ 2 = 10 is one length plus one width, so 10 − 4 = 6. Subtracting a single 4 and halving gives 8, which is the wrong answer this question is built to collect.

lead:
There are only £10 notes and £20 notes in a wallet.
Ali takes at random a note from the wallet.
html: Write down the probability that Ali takes a note with a value of more than £5
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — there are only £10 notes and £20 notes in the wallet and both are worth more than £5, so the event is certain and a certainty has probability 1. B1. The scheme also allows 100%, and any fraction of the form k⁄k such as 2⁄2. It does not accept a bare 100 (without the per-cent sign), and it does not accept the word certain — the question asks for a probability, which has to be written as a number on the 0-to-1 scale or as a percentage.

html:
There are only 1p coins and 2p coins in a bag. The total value of the coins in the bag is 40p. The total value of the 1p coins is the same as the total value of the 2p coins.

Simon takes at random a coin from the bag.

Find the probability that Simon takes a 1p coin.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄3 — the 1p coins and the 2p coins are worth 20p each, so there are 20 one-penny coins and only 10 two-penny coins: 30 coins in the bag, 20 of which are 1p, and 20⁄30 = 2⁄3. P1 for any start on the proportions, and the scheme lists four routes that all earn it: writing a correct ratio such as 1p : 2p = 2 : 1; working out the counts, 40 ÷ 2 (= 20) and (40 ÷ 2) ÷ 2 (= 10); assigning any numbers in the right proportion, such as 6 one-penny coins and 3 two-penny coins; or finding the probability of a 2p instead, 1⁄3. A1 for 2⁄3 oe — any equivalent fraction, or decimal form 0.66(6…) or 0.67, or percentage form 66(.6…)% or 67%. The hard step is that equal VALUE is not equal NUMBER: 20p made of 1p coins is twice as many coins as 20p made of 2p coins, which is why the answer is 2⁄3 and not 1⁄2.

html: Work out 273 × 54
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 14742 — M1 for a complete correct method with the place value right: both lines of the long method (13650 and 1092), or the internal numbers of a grid, or a complete partitioning structure; M1, dependent on the first, for adding all the appropriate parts together; A1 for 14742, cao. By the grid the six parts are 200 × 50 = 10000, 70 × 50 = 3500, 3 × 50 = 150, 200 × 4 = 800, 70 × 4 = 280 and 3 × 4 = 12, and 10000 + 3500 + 150 + 800 + 280 + 12 = 14742. Place value is the whole of the first mark: the second line of the long method is 273 × 50 = 13650, not 1365, and in the grid the top-left cell is 10000 rather than 1000. And because the second M1 is dependent, adding up correctly on top of misplaced parts scores nothing at all.

html:
Tessa recorded the times that 15 adults took to complete a run.
She showed her results in a stem and leaf diagram.

StemLeaf
45 9
53 7 8
61 2 4 5 7 7
72 6 7
81

Key: 4 | 5 represents 45 minutes
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The stem and leaf diagram is a table rather than a picture, so it is set as one here — the transcription had it as a sentence, which is fifteen values a reader has to re-pair by counting along two lists.

html: Find the median.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 64 minutes — there are 15 times, so the median is the 8th, at position (15 + 1) ÷ 2 = 8, and a stem and leaf diagram already has them in order. Count the leaves along: 45, 49 (2 so far), 53, 57, 58 (5), 61, 62, 64 — the 8th is the third leaf on the 6 row, which the key reads as 64 minutes. B1, cao. Two slips: pointing at the middle of the DIAGRAM rather than the middle of the list (the 6 row is the longest, so it draws the eye), and giving the leaf 4 instead of the value 64.

html: Find the range.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 36 minutes — largest minus smallest, 81 − 45. M1 for identifying 81 and 45 as the two numbers that matter, shown as 81 − 45, or 45 − 81, or 45 to 81; A1 for 36, cao. The scheme is strict on two points. Marking them on the diagram is insufficient for the M1 — circling the leaves, or writing 1 and 5, does not count; the full values have to be written out. And an answer of −36 scores M1 A0: the range is a size, so it is never negative, however the subtraction was set down.

html:
Tessa also recorded the times that 15 children took to complete the run. For the children, the median was 75 minutes.

Compare the times that the adults took with the times that the children took.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: The adults were faster: their median, 64 minutes, is lower than the children's 75 — their median of 64 minutes is lower than the children's 75, 11 minutes lower. C1 for one correct comparison of the medians, and it follows through from part (a), so it is marked against whatever median was found there. Statements the scheme names as acceptable: the adults were faster because they have the smaller median; the adults were 11 minutes faster on average; the adults were faster; the adults took less time; the children were slower; the children took more time; children took 11 minutes more on average; children had a larger median than the adults. Statements it refuses: the children were faster; the adults' median was 64, the children's median was 75; 11 minutes difference; the children had more time to run than the adults. The hard step is the one those refusals share — quoting the two medians side by side, or the gap between them, is not yet a comparison, because neither sentence says which group was quicker. Figures are not required, but if they appear they must be correct for the median found in (a), and the statement must be entirely true and not self-contradictory.

html:
Batteries are sold in packs of 4, in packs of 8 and in packs of 12

A pack of 4 batteries costs £1.80
A pack of 8 batteries costs £3.20
A pack of 12 batteries costs £6.00

Which pack gives the best value for money?
You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
The pack of 8: 40p a battery, against 45p for the pack of 4 and 50p for the pack of 12 — at 40p a battery against 45p for the pack of 4 and 50p for the pack of 12. "Supported" in the scheme's answer column is not decoration: correct answer with no supportive working scores 0 marks, so naming the right pack on its own earns nothing at all of the three.

P1 for a process of price ÷ quantity on at least two packs — at least two of 180 ÷ 4 (= 45), 320 ÷ 8 (= 40), 600 ÷ 12 (= 50). Pounds or pence both count. Any other route that lets two packs be compared also takes it, e.g. 180 × 2 (= 360) set against 320, or 320 ÷ 8 (= 40) then "40" × 12 (= 480) set against 600.

P1 for a complete process giving values that compare all three — the three unit prices together, or 3.20 ÷ 8 (= 0.40) then "0.40" × 4 (= 1.60) and "0.40" × 12 (= 4.80), or scaling everything to 24 batteries: 1.80 × 6 (= 10.80), 3.20 × 3 (= 9.60), 6.00 × 2 (= 12.00).

A1 for "pack of 8" with correct values covering all three packs.

The step that is actually hard is the one students think they have finished: comparing two pairs is not always enough. The scheme spells out which pairings settle it — 4 vs 8 together with 8 vs 12 works, and 4 vs 8 together with 4 vs 12 works, but 4 vs 12 together with 8 vs 12 does not, because the 4 and the 8 have then never been put side by side. Units matter too: the A mark is refused where inconsistent units would prevent the comparison, so "0.40p" written beside "45p" loses it even though the numbers are right.
examiner_note: The paper prints three packs of batteries over their prices. The three sentences under that picture give every price in full, so the picture adds nothing a student needs and is not drawn.

html: Solve 2(4x − 5) = 18
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
x = 3.5 — and 31⁄2 or 7⁄2 are accepted equally (oe).

M1 for the first step, either way round: expand the bracket to 8x − 10 (= 18), or divide throughout by 2 first to get 4x − 5 = 9.

M1 for isolating the x term — 8x = 18 + 10, or 4x = 9 + 5 — and this mark follows through from their own equation of the form ax ± b = c, so a slip in the first step does not cost the second mark as well.

A1 for 3.5.

The thing to say out loud to a student: the scheme insists the step is carried out, not just intended. Writing "÷ 2" down both sides of 2(4x − 5) = 18 in the margin scores nothing on its own — the line 4x − 5 = k has to actually appear, with k anything other than 18 or 36 (18 is the right-hand side left untouched, 36 is it doubled instead of halved). Same for the second mark: 8x = k must be written, with k not 8 and not 18. The commonest wrong answer is 4.5, from expanding to 8x − 10 and then adding 10 to only one side.

html: Write down the value of 100
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
1 — B1, cao, the whole mark in one line with no method to show.

100 = 1, and so is any non-zero number raised to the power 0. The reason, if a student wants one: am ÷ an = am−n, so 103 ÷ 103 is both 100 and, obviously, 1. Or read the powers of ten downwards — 1000, 100, 10 — each one a tenth of the one before, so the next is 1.

cao means nothing else scores. The two answers students give here are 0 (reading the index as "ten lots of nothing") and 10 (reading the power 0 as leaving the number alone), and neither earns anything.

Note on this row: the library text lost the index — the question is printed as a power and the row records only that it was 10 to the power 0. The mark scheme's answer of 1 is consistent with that, though on its own it cannot confirm the base, since every non-zero base to the power 0 gives 1.
examiner_note: The index did not come out of the PDF text layer. It is 10 to the power 0 — the scheme answers 1, which is what any non-zero number to the power 0 is.

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps triangle A onto triangle B.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Translation by the column vector ( 5−4) — 5 to the right and 4 down, written stacked in one pair of brackets. Two independent B1s: one for the word translation, one for the vector, so a student who names the transformation and gets the vector wrong still has a mark. The scheme will not take the vector in words — it says outright “do not accept 5 across, 4 down or 5 right, 4 down” — and will not take it written as a coordinate, (5, −4). It does condone the brackets being left off altogether, so a bare stacked 5 over −4 is fine. The trap is the last line of the scheme: no marks at all if more than one transformation is given, so “translation and reflection” scores zero even with the right vector — “describe fully the single transformation” means name one thing. Sitting beside a student, the step to slow down on is the sign: read across first, then up or down, and down is negative.

html:
Here are the first four terms of an arithmetic sequence.

1   5   9   13

Find an expression, in terms of n, for the nth term of this sequence.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: nth Term of a Linear Sequence
answer: 4n − 3 — B2, oe. The terms go up by 4 each time, so the nth term starts 4n; then 4 × 1 = 4 against a first term of 1, so subtract 3. Any equivalent form counts and any letter counts — 4x − 3 is accepted, and so are un = 4n − 3 and T = 4n − 3. B1 only for 4n + k where k is wrong or absent, provided it is unambiguously shown, so a bare 4n still banks one mark. B1 only, too, for n = 4n − 3 or “4nth − 3” — the right expression spoiled by writing it as something it is not, which is worth pointing out because it looks like a full answer. The step that actually goes wrong is jumping from the common difference straight to 4n + 1 off the first term; test the expression at n = 1 every time.

html: Work out 34⁄5 − 12⁄3
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 22⁄15, or 32⁄15 — oe, both count. M1 for a subtraction over a common denominator with at least one fraction converted correctly, then A1 for the value. Either route earns the M1 on its own: improper first, 34⁄5 − 12⁄3 = 19⁄5 − 5⁄3 = 57⁄15 − 25⁄15; or keep the whole numbers, (3)12⁄15 − (1)10⁄15. Two tolerances worth knowing, because they change what a student should do after they have the answer: 32⁄15 left improper is full marks, and the scheme says ISW — a wrong conversion to a mixed number after a correct 32⁄15, or a botched simplification of it, is ignored rather than penalised. Against that, decimals get no credit at all unless they lead to a correct fraction. The step to name is the common denominator itself: fifteenths for both, and only one of the two needs to be right to bank the method mark.

lead:
Kevin was asked to work out  213 × 58

Here is his working and his answer.

213 × 58 = 73 × 58

= 3524

= 1924
html:
Kevin’s answer is wrong.

What mistake has Kevin made?
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Kevin did not convert 35⁄24 correctly: it is 111⁄24, not 19⁄24 — 35⁄24 is 111⁄24, not 19⁄24 — C1 for explaining that, and only that; the multiplication itself, 7⁄3 × 5⁄8 = 35⁄24, is right. The scheme accepts “the 9 should be 11”, “in his answer 9⁄24 should have been 11⁄24”, “he has not got the numerator right in his final answer”, “he simplified into the mixed number incorrectly”, “he has not put the remainder as the numerator”, and either arithmetic version — 19⁄24 would give 33⁄24, or 35⁄24 = 111⁄24. It explicitly refuses the vague ones, and that is the whole difficulty of this mark: “he converted the fraction wrongly” scores nothing, and neither do “he should have used a common denominator”, “he has not simplified his answer”, “he should have done keep, flip, change” or “the answer should be 110⁄24”. Naming the number — 11, not 9 — is what earns it. Figures written in the question space count towards the explanation.

html:
Petra is going to cover the floor with paint.

Petra has 3 tins of paint. There are 2.5 litres of paint in each tin. Petra thinks 1 litre of paint will cover 10 m2 of floor.

Assuming Petra is correct, does she have enough paint to cover the floor?
You must show all your working.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Yes: the floor is 68 m2 and 3 tins cover 75 m2 — the floor is 68 m2 and 3 tins cover 75 m2, so she has enough. Four marks and three of them are the route. P1 for the area of any one piece: 10 × 8 (= 80), 10 × 5 (= 50), 8 × 6 (= 48), (10 − 6) × 5 (= 20), (10 − 6) × (8 − 5) (= 12), 6 × (8 − 5) (= 18) or 5 × 6 (= 30) — but the scheme withholds it if they go on to multiply by a third length, which is the commonest way this mark is lost. P1 for a complete area: cut it off a rectangle, “80” − “12”, or split it, “50” + “18” or “48” + “20” — all three give 68. P1 for comparing on any one of three scales: 3 × 2.5 × 10 (= 75 m2 covered), or “68” ÷ 10 (= 6.8 litres needed), or “68” ÷ 10 ÷ 2.5 (= 2.72 tins needed) — and it follows through on whatever area they believe they have. A1 for Yes supported by a matching pair of figures: 68 and 75, or 6.8 and 7.5, or 68 and 2.72. The decision on its own is not the mark; the numbers have to be on the page beside it. A wrong statement about how much paint is left over is ignored provided the correct figures are there. The hard step is the side nobody gives you: the plan prints 10, 6, 8 and 5, and the missing piece is (10 − 6) by (8 − 5).

lead: Actually, 1 litre of paint will cover 11 m2 of floor.
html:
Does this affect your answer to part (a)?
You must give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No effect: she still has enough paint, as each litre now covers more floor, so she needs less — she still has enough. One mark, C1, and it follows through from part (a), so there has to be a decision in (a) for it to follow through from. The mark is for a decision plus a reason together. The scheme’s acceptable answers are “no effect, she will need less paint”, “it won’t change, she will still have enough”, “no, she will have more paint left over”, and “no, as this will cover 82.5 m<sup>2</sup>” (7.5 litres × 11). It also prints the near misses, and they are the thing to point out: “Petra will need less paint” and “she will have more paint left over” are refused — both are true, and both leave the decision off. “She won’t have enough paint” and “she will need more paint” are refused as wrong. Any figures written into the statement must be correct for the area claimed in (a). So the sentence needs the word yes, no or “no effect” in it, and covering more per litre can only help.

html: Write down the numbers that are in set P′
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17 — B1, cao, so it is the whole list or nothing. P′ is everything in the universal set that is NOT inside circle P: the two numbers in Q alone (10 and 14) plus the four outside both circles (11, 13, 16, 17). P itself is 12, 15 and 18, and 18 is the one students lose — it sits in the overlap, so it is in P and must be left out of P′ even though it is in Q as well.

html:
A number is chosen at random from the universal set, E

Find the probability that this number is in the set P ∪ Q
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Venn Diagrams & Set Notation, Basic Probability
answer: 5⁄9 — five of the nine numbers in the universal set lie inside one circle or the other. M1 for identifying that set: 10, 12, 14, 15, 18. P ∪ Q is everything in either circle, and the number they share is counted once, not twice. The scheme also gives the M1 for work that shows the right half of the fraction without the other: a⁄9 with a a whole number from 1 to 8, or 5⁄b with b a whole number above 5, or the right numbers in the wrong form, eg 5 : 9. A1 is “oe” and generous with it: any equivalent fraction, or the decimal 0.55(5…) or 0.56, or the percentage 55(.5…)% or 56%. Two things cost the marks — reading ∪ (union, either circle) as ∩ (intersection, the overlap only), and double-counting the overlap to get 6⁄9. Reading the diagram: the overlap holds 18, so P ∪ Q is 12 and 15 from P, 10 and 14 from Q, and 18 from the middle.

html:
Sophie drives a distance of 513 kilometres on a motorway in France.
She pays 0.81 euros for every 10 kilometres she drives.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths

html: Work out an estimate for the total amount that Sophie pays.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 40 euros — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8, rounding both numbers to 1 significant figure first. The answer column says “estimated value” rather than a number on purpose: the A1 follows through whatever rounding the student chose, so 40.8 (from 510) and 40.5 (from 500 × 0.81) are each worth full marks. P1 for a 1sf value actually used in a calculation — 500 ÷ 10, or 500 × 0.8, or 510 × 0.8, or 513 × 0.8, or 500 × 0.81. The rounding may come after a correct step: 513 ÷ 10 = 51.3 → 50, then 50 × 0.81 scores both process marks, as does 51 × 0.8. P1 for a full process to the total — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40), or 510 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40.8), or 500 ÷ 10 × 0.81 (= 40.5), or in general [distance] ÷ 10 × [amount]; the unrounded 513 ÷ 10 × 0.81 is accepted for this mark too. A1 for the answer their own rounded values give. Two tolerances the scheme states outright: 0.81 rounded to 0.80 is accepted, and 0.81 rounded to 1 is condoned for the process marks but loses the A1. The step that is actually hard is the ÷ 10 — 0.81 euros buys 10 kilometres, not one, so 500 × 0.8 = 400 euros is the answer to watch for.

html:
Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate?
Give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: An underestimate: both 513 km and 0.81 euros were rounded down — because both numbers were rounded down: 513 km down to 500 km and 0.81 euros down to 0.80, so the estimate is less than the true cost. C1, following through from part (a). The scheme puts two conditions on it. The reason must be about the estimating — the rounding done at the start — and not about rounding the final answer at the end. And there must be a final answer in (a) for this to follow through from, so a student who abandoned (a) cannot pick the mark up here. A bare “underestimate” with no reason does not score; the word “down” is doing the work.

html: Find an equation for L.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Equation of a Line, Straight Line Graphs
answer: y = 3⁄2x + 3 — or y = 1.5x + 3, and “oe”, so 2y = 3x + 6 is equally full marks. The line crosses the y-axis at 3 and climbs 3 for every 2 across. M1 for a correct method for the gradient: (6 − 3) ÷ (2 − 0) = 3⁄2 off two points on the line, or identifying 3 as the intercept in words or in a partial equation, or writing y = 3⁄2x + c, or y − b = 3⁄2(x − a) for a correct point (a, b). The scheme is specific that just circling the 3 on the grid is not enough, and that the c has to appear as a letter or a number. M1 for assembling it — y = 3⁄2x (+ c), or their own gradient with the 3 in place, or y − y1 = 3⁄2(x − x1); earning this one implies the first. A1 for any correct equation, in any form. The mark that goes missing is the gradient: it is rise over run, so 2⁄3 is the classic inversion, and a grid whose squares are not one unit each will punish counting squares without checking the scale.

lead: M is a different straight line with equation y = 5x
html: Write down the equation of a straight line parallel to M.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Any equation of the form y = 5x + c with c ≠ 0 — eg y = 5x + 1. B1. The answer column just says “equation” because there is no single right one. Parallel means the same gradient, so the 5 must survive untouched; the only thing that may change is the intercept. c ≠ 0 is the condition students fall over: y = 5x is M itself, and the question asks for a line parallel to M, which means a different line. Any equivalent form is accepted, so 5x − y + 1 = 0 or y − 1 = 5x also score.

html:
Kasim has some small jars, some medium jars and some large jars. He has a total of 400 jars.

3⁄8 of the 400 jars are empty.

For the empty jars,
number of small jars : number of medium jars = 3 : 4
number of medium jars : number of large jars = 1 : 2

Work out the percentage of Kasim’s jars that are empty small jars.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Fractions of an Amount, Sharing in a Ratio, Percentage of an Amount
answer: 7.5% — that is 7.5%, and the scheme takes 71⁄2 or any equivalent. Five marks, four of them process. P1 for the number of empty jars: 3⁄8 × 400 = 150. P1 for the start of the ratio work, and this is the step the question is really testing — 3 : 4 and 1 : 2 do not join up until the mediums agree, so scale the second to 4 : 8 and chain them into small : medium : large = 3 : 4 : 8. P1 for the empty small jars: 3⁄3 + 4 + 8 × “150” = 30, or writing the whole split out as 30 : 40 : 80. P1 for turning that into a percentage: 30 ÷ 400 × 100. A1 for 7.5. The scheme prints a second route worth the same five marks and it is shorter if a student can see it: chain to 3 : 4 : 8, so small jars are 3⁄15 = 1⁄5 of the empty ones, then 3⁄8 × 1⁄5 = 3⁄40 of all the jars, and 3⁄40 × 100 = 7.5 — the 400 is never needed at all. Two wrong answers to watch for: 30, which is the count of jars offered as if it were the percentage, and 20%, from dividing 30 by the 150 empty jars instead of by all 400.

html:
In a sale, normal prices are reduced by 30%

The sale price of a TV is £280

Work out the normal price of the TV.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £400 — M1 for 280 ÷ 0.7 oe, A1 cao. A 30% reduction leaves 70%, so the £280 sale price IS 70% of the normal price — and you get back to the whole by dividing, not by adding 30% on. 280 ÷ 0.7 = 400. Check it forwards: 30% of 400 is 120, and 400 − 120 = 280. The wrong answer to head off is 364: that is 280 + 30% of 280, which takes the percentage of the wrong number — the reduction was 30% of 400, not of 280.

html: Solve x + 11 ≤ 5 − 1⁄2x
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: x ≤ −4 — M1 for a correct first step, M1 for a full method or for the critical value −4, A1 for x ≤ −4 oe. Clear the half first by doubling everything: 2x + 22 ≤ 10 − x. Then add x to both sides, 3x + 22 ≤ 10, and take 22 off: 3x ≤ −12, so x ≤ −4. The scheme gives 2 of the 3 marks for −4 written with an = or the wrong inequality sign, so the final mark is the sign itself — and because nothing here was multiplied or divided by a negative, the sign never flips.
examiner_note: The inequality sign did not come out of the PDF text layer. It is less-than-or-equal: the scheme answers x ≤ −4, and x + 11 = 5 − ½x exactly at −4, so the boundary is included rather than excluded.

html: Work out the length of CB. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths

The side CA, opposite the right angle, is 19 cm and the side AB is 10 cm."><polygon points="273.7,20.0 273.7,137.0 44.0,137.0" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3"/><polyline points="264.7,137.0 264.7,128.0 273.7,128.0" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="279.7" y="16.0" class="num" style="text-anchor:middle"><tspan class="lbl">A</tspan></text><text x="282.7" y="150.0" class="num" style="text-anchor:middle"><tspan class="lbl">B</tspan></text><text x="35.0" y="142.0" class="num" style="text-anchor:middle"><tspan class="lbl">C</tspan></text><text x="144.9" y="70.5" class="num" style="text-anchor:middle">19 cm</text><text x="281.7" y="82.5" class="num" style="text-anchor:start">10 cm</text></svg>
answer: 16.2 cm — M1 A1, anything from 16.1 to 16.2 accepted. The right angle is at B, so the side opposite it, CA = 19 cm, is the hypotenuse, and this is Pythagoras backwards: CB2 = 192 − 102 = 361 − 100 = 261, and √261 = 16.155…, which is 16.2 to 3 significant figures. Adding instead of subtracting gives 21.5 and no marks.
examiner_note: The lead used to say AB = 19 cm and AC = 10 cm. The paper prints 19 cm on CA and 10 cm on AB, with the right angle at B, which is what the scheme’s own working (19² = 10² + BC²) uses.

html: Write 90 as a product of its prime factors.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 — M1 A1, and 2 × 32 × 5 is accepted. Split 90 until only primes are left: 90 = 9 × 10 = 3 × 3 × 2 × 5. Check by multiplying back.

html:
A = 22 × 3, B = 2 × 32

Write down the lowest common multiple (LCM) of A and B.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 36 — B1, and 22 × 32 is accepted. A = 22 × 3 = 12 and B = 2 × 32 = 18. For the LOWEST common multiple take the HIGHEST power of each prime that appears: 22 and 32, so 4 × 9 = 36. Taking the lowest powers gives 6, which is the HCF.

html:
The number of hours, H, that some machines take to make 5000 bottles is given by H = 72⁄n where n is the number of machines.

On Monday, 6 machines made 5000 bottles.
On Tuesday, 9 machines made 5000 bottles.

The machines took more time to make the bottles on Monday than on Tuesday.

How much more time?
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 4 hours — M1 A1 cao. Put each number of machines into H = 72 ÷ n: Monday 72 ÷ 6 = 12 hours, Tuesday 72 ÷ 9 = 8 hours. The question asks how much MORE time, so subtract: 12 − 8 = 4. More machines means fewer hours, which is why the answer is a difference and not a total.

html:
There are only red discs, blue discs and yellow discs in a bag. There are 24 yellow discs in the bag.

Mel is going to take at random a disc from the bag. The probability that the disc will be yellow is 0.16

the number of red discs : the number of blue discs = 5 : 4

Work out the number of red discs in the bag.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Basic Probability, Sharing in a Ratio
answer: 70 — P1 P1 P1 A1. The 24 yellow discs are 0.16 of the bag, so the bag holds 24 ÷ 0.16 = 150 discs. That leaves 150 − 24 = 126 red and blue together, shared 5 : 4 — nine parts, so 126 ÷ 9 = 14 per part and red is 5 × 14 = 70. Blue is 56, and the scheme insists that if you find both you must say which one is the answer.

html:
Complete the table of values for y = x2 − x

x−2−10123
y6(i)0(ii)2(iii)

Work out the value of y = x2 − x when x = −1
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — (−1)2 − (−1) = 1 + 1: squaring a negative gives a positive, and subtracting a negative adds.

html: Work out the value of y = x2 − x when x = 1
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 0 — 12 − 1 = 1 − 1.

html: Work out the value of y = x2 − x when x = 3
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — 32 − 3 = 9 − 3.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for the whole table: B2 for all three values, 2, 0 and 6, correct (B1 for one or two of them).

html: On the grid, draw the graph of y = x2 − x for values of x from −2 to 3
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A smooth curve through (−2, 6), (−1, 2), (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 2), (3, 6) — B2, or B1 for plotting at least five of your own points correctly. It is a parabola with its lowest point half way between x = 0 and x = 1. A curve drawn free-hand is fine; joining the points with straight line segments is not.
examiner_note: The grid is the paper’s: x from −2 to 3 and y from −4 to 8, large squares 0.5 across and 1 up, five small squares in each.

html: Use your graph to find estimates for the solutions of the equation x2 − x = 4
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: −1.6 and 2.6 — M1 A1, anything in −1.7 to −1.5 and 2.5 to 2.7 accepted. Draw the line y = 4 across your curve and read off where they cross. The scheme gives zero for solving it algebraically — the question says use your graph, so the graph is the method being marked.

html:
Andy, Luke and Tina share some sweets in the ratio 1 : 6 : 14

Tina gives 3⁄7 of her sweets to Andy. Tina then gives 12½% of the rest of her sweets to Luke.

Tina says, “Now all three of us have the same number of sweets.”

Is Tina correct? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Sharing in a Ratio, Fractions of an Amount, Percentage of an Amount
answer: Yes: in parts, Andy 1 + 6 = 7, Luke 6 + 1 = 7, Tina 14 − 6 − 1 = 7 — P1 P1 P1 C1, and the figures have to be shown. Work in parts: the ratio 1 : 6 : 14 is 21 parts, so Andy 1, Luke 6, Tina 14. Tina gives 3⁄7 of her 14 = 6 to Andy, so Andy has 1 + 6 = 7 and Tina has 14 − 6 = 8 left. She then gives 12½% — an eighth — of those 8 to Luke, which is 1, so Luke has 6 + 1 = 7 and Tina keeps 8 − 1 = 7. All three have 7 parts, so Tina is right. The scheme is explicit: accurate figures with no supporting working score 0.

answer: Shown: x = 25, so the angles are 65°, 115°, 108°, 72°; 65 + 115 = 180, so AD is parallel to BC — M1 M1 A1 C1. The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360, so (2x + 15) + (4x + 15) + (4x + 8) + (3x − 3) = 360, which is 13x + 35 = 360, so 13x = 325 and x = 25. The angles are then 65°, 115°, 108° and 72°. Now 65 + 115 = 180, and co-interior angles that add to 180 mean those two sides are parallel — so ABCD has a pair of parallel sides and is a trapezium. The other pair, 65 + 72 = 137, is NOT 180, which is what stops it being a parallelogram. The last mark is for SAYING that: “co-interior angles sum to 180, so the lines are parallel”.

name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 10 — B1 cao. One symbol is 4 houses, and January shows two whole symbols and a half, so 4 + 4 + 2 = 10.

lead: In April, Ben sold 11 houses.
html: Show this information on the pictogram.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 full squares and 3 quarters of a square — B1. 11 houses at 4 to a symbol is 11 ÷ 4 = 2¾ symbols. The scheme allows the three quarters drawn as eleven separate quarter-squares, or as a half plus a quarter.

html:
Ben sold a total of 60 houses in the first five months of last year.

Work out the number of houses Ben sold in May.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 18 — P1 P1 A1. Read the first three months off the pictogram: January 10 (from part (a)), February 4 + 4 + 1 = 9, March 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. April is the 11 you drew. That is 10 + 9 + 12 + 11 = 42, so May is 60 − 42 = 18. The scheme wants 18 written down for full marks — drawing the squares for May alone earns P2, not A1.

html:
Anil has a job as a driver.
He is paid for each mile he drives.
He is also paid expenses.

One week Anil writes down the distance readings from his car.

Start of week:47241miles
End of week:47879miles

For this week, Anil is paid 47p for each mile he drives.
He is also paid expenses of £80

Work out the total amount that Anil is paid.
Give your answer in pounds.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £379.86 — P1 P1 B1 A1. The miles driven are the difference between the two readings: 47879 − 47241 = 638. At 47p each that is 638 × 47 = 29986p, which is £299.86, and the expenses go on top: 299.86 + 80 = 379.86. One of the four marks is for converting between pence and pounds at all, which is where this question is usually lost — an answer of 30066 is the same work with the units left in pence.

html:

List all the possible outcomes.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths

Three coins with two faces each is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes, so if you have not got eight you have missed one. Listing them in a fixed order — all the H-firsts, then all the T-firsts — is what stops that. M1 alone for any three correct.

lead: Majid has a spinner.
html:

name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No: the sections are not the same size; section 2 is a quarter of the circle, so the probability is 1⁄4 — C1. The three sections are not the same size, so they are not equally likely and you cannot just divide 1 by 3. Section 2 is the right angle, a quarter of the circle, so its probability is 1⁄4. The scheme accepts any of: the sections are different sizes; 1 and 3 are more likely than 2; 2 should be a quarter; 2 is less than a third. It specifically REFUSES “2 has a 90° angle” on its own — that is an observation, not a reason.

The mark is for the FIGURES, not the word — and 5.25 hours is 5 hours 15 minutes, not 5 hours 25, which is the decimal-time trap this question is built on.

The number of hours, H, that some machines take to make 5000 bottles is given by H = 72⁄n where n is the number of machines.

subject: Maths
answer: 4 hours — M1 A1 cao. Put each number of machines into H = 72 ÷ n: Monday 72 ÷ 6 = 12 hours, Tuesday 72 ÷ 9 = 8 hours. The question asks how much MORE time, so subtract: 12 − 8 = 4. More machines means fewer hours, which is why the answer is a difference and not a total.

subject: Maths
topics: Basic Probability, Sharing in a Ratio

That leaves 150 − 24 = 126 red and blue together, shared 5 : 4 — nine parts, so 126 ÷ 9 = 14 per part and red is 5 × 14 = 70. Blue is 56, and the scheme insists that if you find both you must say which one is the answer.

html:
Andy, Luke and Tina share some sweets in the ratio 1 : 6 : 14

Tina gives 3⁄7 of her sweets to Andy. Tina then gives 12½% of the rest of her sweets to Luke.

Tina says, “Now all three of us have the same number of sweets.”

Is Tina correct? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Sharing in a Ratio, Fractions of an Amount, Percentage of an Amount
answer: Yes: in parts, Andy 1 + 6 = 7, Luke 6 + 1 = 7, Tina 14 − 6 − 1 = 7 — P1 P1 P1 C1, and the figures have to be shown. Work in parts: the ratio 1 : 6 : 14 is 21 parts, so Andy 1, Luke 6, Tina 14. Tina gives 3⁄7 of her 14 = 6 to Andy, so Andy has 1 + 6 = 7 and Tina has 14 − 6 = 8 left. She then gives 12½% — an eighth — of those 8 to Luke, which is 1, so Luke has 6 + 1 = 7 and Tina keeps 8 − 1 = 7. All three have 7 parts, so Tina is right. The scheme is explicit: accurate figures with no supporting working score 0.

lead: ABCD is a quadrilateral.
html:
All angles are measured in degrees.

Show that ABCD is a trapezium.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles in Triangles & Quadrilaterals, Angles in Parallel Lines, Linear Equations
answer: Shown: x = 25, so the angles are 65°, 115°, 108°, 72°; 65 + 115 = 180, so AD is parallel to BC — M1 M1 A1 C1. The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360, so (2x + 15) + (4x + 15) + (4x + 8) + (3x − 3) = 360, which is 13x + 35 = 360, so 13x = 325 and x = 25. The angles are then 65°, 115°, 108° and 72°. Now 65 + 115 = 180, and co-interior angles that add to 180 mean those two sides are parallel — so ABCD has a pair of parallel sides and is a trapezium. The other pair, 65 + 72 = 137, is NOT 180, which is what stops it being a parallelogram. The last mark is for SAYING that: “co-interior angles sum to 180, so the lines are parallel”.

html: More students walk to school than cycle to school. How many more?
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths

html:
Aisha was born in 1993. There was an election in the year of Aisha’s 18th birthday. There is an election every 5 years.

Will there be an election in 2030? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No: Aisha was 18 in 2011, so elections fall in 2011, 2016, 2021, 2026, 2031; not 2030 — P1 P1 A1. Aisha turned 18 in 1993 + 18 = 2011, and that was an election year. Elections are every 5 years, so they fall in 2011, 2016, 2021, 2026, 2031 — 2030 is not one of them. The scheme also takes the shorter argument: election years from 2011 end in 1 or 6, and 2030 ends in 0.

html:
