html: Work out an estimate for the number of students who scored more than 70% in the test.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html:
The histogram shows information about the speed of 30 vehicles travelling on a road.

The speed limit on the road is 60 mph.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html: Work out the percentage of the vehicles that were exceeding the speed limit.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 20% — the 60–70 bar is 0.6 × 10 = 6 vehicles, and 6 ÷ 30 × 100 = 20%.

html: Work out an estimate for the mean speed of the 30 vehicles.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 45 mph — the frequencies are 6, 8, 10, 6; midpoints give 15×6 + 40×8 + 55×10 + 65×6 = 1350, and 1350 ÷ 30 = 45.

html: The histogram shows information about the times spent waiting at an emergency department.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html: Work out an estimate for the median time spent waiting.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 45 minutes — frequencies 20, 16, 9, 3 (total 48); the median is the 24th, 4 into the 16 in 40–60, so 40 + 4⁄16 × 20 = 45.

html: Work out an estimate for the interquartile range of the times spent waiting.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 36 minutes — frequencies 20, 16, 9, 3 (total 48); LQ (12th) = 12⁄20 × 40 = 24 and UQ (36th) = 60, so 60 − 24 = 36.

html: The histogram shows information about the masses of some apples growing in a garden.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html: Work out an estimate for the median mass of the apples.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 66 grams — frequencies 60, 150, 50, 40 (total 300); median (150th) = 30 + 90⁄150 × 60 = 66.

html: Work out an estimate for the interquartile range of the masses of the apples.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 57 grams — frequencies 60, 150, 50, 40 (total 300); LQ (75th) = 30 + 15⁄150 × 60 = 36; UQ (225th) = 90 + 15⁄50 × 10 = 93; 93 − 36 = 57.

html:
The histogram shows information about the weekly pay of 600 workers at a company.

One of the employees makes the following claim:

“60% of the workers at the company earn less than the mean weekly pay”
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html: By working out an estimate for the mean, show that the employee could be correct.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: Mean ≈ £120, and about 360 of 600 (60%) earn less — frequencies 330, 150, 65, 40, 15; 50×330 + 150×150 + 225×65 + 300×40 + 425×15 = 72 000, ÷ 600 = 120; below £120 is 330 + 1.5 × 20 = 360, which is 60%.

html: Explain why your answer to part (a) does not guarantee that the employee is correct.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: The mean is only an estimate — the midpoints assume where the pay lies in each class, so the true mean could be higher or lower.

html: The histogram shows information about the finish times of some runners at a 5 km race.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html:
Runners who ran faster than the qualifying time win entry to the next race.

10% of the runners ran faster than the qualifying time.

Use the histogram to work out an estimate for the qualifying time.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 17.5 minutes — frequencies 80, 110, 190, 180, 40 (total 600); 10% is 60 runners, 60⁄80 × 10 = 7.5 into the first bar, 10 + 7.5 = 17.5.

html:
Sam was the 102nd person to complete the race.

Use the histogram to work out an estimate for Sam’s average speed in metres per second.

Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 3.97 m/s — 80 runners finish by 20 minutes, so the 102nd is 22 into the 110 in 20–25: 22⁄110 × 5 = 1, so 21 minutes = 1260 s, and 5000 ÷ 1260 = 3.968…

html: The histogram shows information about the amount of fizzy drink consumed per day by some Year 9 students in a particular city.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html:
50 students consumed between 0 and 200 ml of fizzy drinks per day.

34 students consumed between 600 and 800 ml of fizzy drinks per day.

No students consumed more than 1000 ml of fizzy drinks per day.

Complete the histogram.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: A bar from 600 to 800 at frequency density 0.17 — 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 is the first bar’s height, so each small square is 0.01, and 34 ÷ 200 = 0.17.

html:
In the city there are 12,000 Year 9 students.

Use the histogram to estimate how many of the students in the city consume more than 800 ml of fizzy drink per day.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 1728 — the frequencies are 50, 90, 40, 34, 36 (total 250), and 36⁄250 × 12 000 = 1728.

html:
The histogram shows information about the heights of 200 trees in a park.

The histogram is incomplete.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html:
40 of the trees were between 15 metres and 25 metres in height.

None of the trees had a height of more than 50 metres.

Complete the histogram.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: A bar from 15 to 25, 4 large squares high — the other bars cover 32 large squares (15 + 14 + 3) for 160 trees, so one square is 5 trees and 40 trees is 8 squares over a width of 2.

html: Work out an estimate for the median height of the 200 trees.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 21.25 m — the 100th tree is 25 into the 40 in 15–25 (75 trees lie below 15 m), so 15 + 25⁄40 × 10 = 21.25.

html:
Trees that are taller than 40 metres are deemed to be too tall.

The park ranger arranges for the trees taller than 40 metres to be trimmed so that they are exactly 35 metres tall.

How does the trimming of these trees affect your answer to part (b)?
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: No change — the median is still 21.25 m — trimming only moves trees that were already above the median, and they stay above it.

html: The histogram shows information about the masses of some eggs produced on a farm during a year.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths

html:
30% of the eggs produced had a mass between 55g and 60g.

None of the eggs produced had a mass greater than 70g or less than 45g.

Complete the histogram.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: A bar from 60 to 62.5 at frequency density 380 — 55–60 holds 300 × 5 = 1500 eggs, which is 30%, so there are 5000; the other bars hold 150 + 750 + 1500 + 1650 = 4050, leaving 950 for 60–62.5, and 950 ÷ 2.5 = 380.

html:
Eggs that have a mass of between 60g and 70g are sold at a market.

Work out the percentage of the eggs produced on the farm that were sold at the market.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: 52% — 60–70 holds 950 + 1650 = 2600 of the 5000 eggs, and 2600 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 52%.

html:
Steve tested two different types of mobile phone battery to see how long they lasted on one charge.

He tested 240 batteries from Company A and 240 batteries from Company B.

The histogram shows information about the batteries from Company A.

The box plot shows information about the batteries from Company B.

Compare the distribution of battery lives from Company A and Company B.
name: Interpreting Histograms
subject: Maths
answer: B lasted longer on average (higher median) and was more consistent (lower IQR) — for A the frequencies are 30, 120, 40, 50: LQ (60th) = 3.5, median (120th) = 4.5, UQ (180th) = 5.75, IQR 2.25; for B the box plot gives LQ 4, median 4.8, UQ 5.6, IQR 1.6. So B’s median 4.8 h beats A’s 4.5 h, and B’s IQR 1.6 h is smaller than A’s 2.25 h.

html: Construct a locus of points that are the same distance from points A and B.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: The perpendicular bisector of AB — with the compasses set to more than half of AB (more than 4.7 cm), draw arcs from A and from B above and below the line, then join the two crossing points. It is a vertical line through the midpoint of AB; leave the arcs showing.

html: Construct a locus of points that are the same distance from lines AC and BC.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: The bisector of angle ACB — with the point on C, draw an arc cutting both lines; from those two crossing points draw two equal arcs that meet inside the angle, and rule a line from C through where they meet. subject: Maths

html: Construct the locus of points that are exactly 3 cm away from the line AB.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: Lines 3 cm either side of AB, joined by semicircles of radius 3 cm round A and B — a “running track” shape. beside the line the closest point is straight across, so the locus is parallel to AB; beyond each end the closest point is the end itself, so the locus is a semicircle round it.

 less than 4 cm from A

and less than 5 cm from B

and less than 6 cm from C

Show, by shading, the region R.
name: Loci
subject: Maths

The region R consists of all points that are

 inside the quadrilateral ABCD

and closer to point B than to point C

and closer to line CD than to line AD

Show, by shading, the region R.

subject: Maths

and more than 5 cm away from the point A

and closer to line AC than to line BC

Here is a map of a park showing two trees at points A and B and a footpath.

1 cm represents 2 metres.

A new tree is to be planted in that park that is

 an equal distance away from the two trees at points A and B

and exactly 6 m away from the edge of the footpath.

Using a ruler and a pair of compasses, identify the two possible locations for the new tree.

Label the locations P and Q.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: Where the perpendicular bisector of AB crosses lines 3 cm above and below the footpath — 6 m at 1 cm to 2 m is 3 cm. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB (it slopes down to the right) and rule lines parallel to the footpath 3 cm above its top edge and 3 cm below its bottom edge. P is about 7 cm and Q about 9.3 cm from the left edge of the park.

 within 100 m of picnic bench

and at least 80 m from the waste bins

and at least 200 m from the toilets.

Show, by shading, the region that the camper can pitch their tent.

Label the region R.

Here is a map of an island.

1 cm represents 3 kilometres.

Treasure is buried on the island so that it is

 less than 12 km away from the Shipwreck

and closer to Skull Rock than the Palm Tree

Show, by shading, the region where the treasure could be.

Label the region R.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: Land within 4 cm of the Shipwreck, on Skull Rock’s side of the bisector of Palm Tree–Skull Rock — 12 km at 1 cm to 3 km is 4 cm. Draw the circle, construct the perpendicular bisector of the line from the Palm Tree to Skull Rock, and shade the part of the circle to the right of it that is on the island (not the sea in the bay).

For security reasons visitors are not allowed to stand

 within 6 m of Painting 1 or Painting 2

or within 5 m of Painting 3

Show, by shading, the region where visitors are allowed to stand.

Label the region R.

html:
Here is a map showing a ship, S and a port, P.

A fishing boat located in the water that is

 closer to the port than the ship

and between a bearing of 020° and 045° from the ship

Show, by shading, the region where the fishing boat could be located.

Label the region R.
name: Loci
subject: Maths
answer: R is the sea between the lines on bearings 020° and 045° from S, on P’s side of the perpendicular bisector of SP — draw a north line at S, measure 20° and 45° clockwise from it and rule both lines; construct the perpendicular bisector of SP. Shade between the two bearing lines, beyond the bisector, up to the coast (not on the land).

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

y = x² − 3x − 4

y = 2x − 10
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 2, y = −6 and x = 3, y = −4 — x² − 3x − 4 = 2x − 10 gives x² − 5x + 6 = 0, so (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0; then y = 2x − 10.

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

y = x² + 5x − 8

y − 4x = 4
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 3, y = 16 and x = −4, y = −12 — y = 4x + 4, so x² + 5x − 8 = 4x + 4 gives x² + x − 12 = 0, (x − 3)(x + 4) = 0.

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

y = 3x² + 2x − 8

y = 9x − 10
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 1⁄3, y = −7 and x = 2, y = 8 — 3x² + 2x − 8 = 9x − 10 gives 3x² − 7x + 2 = 0, (3x − 1)(x − 2) = 0; then y = 9x − 10.

html:
C is a graph with equation  y = x² − 5x + 10

L is a straight line with equation  y = 3x − 6

Using algebra, find the coordinates of the point of intersection of C and L.

You must show all your working.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: (4, 6) — x² − 5x + 10 = 3x − 6 gives x² − 8x + 16 = 0, (x − 4)² = 0, so x = 4 and y = 3 × 4 − 6 = 6 (the line is a tangent).

html:
C is a graph with equation  y = 5x² − x − 15

L is a straight line with equation  y = 10x − 3

Using algebra, find the coordinates of the points of intersection of C and L.

You must show all your working.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: (3, 27) and (−0.8, −11) — 5x² − x − 15 = 10x − 3 gives 5x² − 11x − 12 = 0, (5x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3 or −4⁄5; then y = 10x − 3.

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

y = x² + x + 1

y = x + 3

Give your answers as exact values.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = √2, y = 3 + √2 and x = −√2, y = 3 − √2 — x² + x + 1 = x + 3 gives x² = 2, so x = ±√2; then y = x + 3.

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

x² + y² = 100

y = x − 2
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 8, y = 6 and x = −6, y = −8 — x² + (x − 2)² = 100 gives 2x² − 4x − 96 = 0, x² − 2x − 48 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 6) = 0; then y = x − 2.

html:
Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

x² + y² = 200

y = 2x − 10
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 10, y = 10 and x = −2, y = −14 — x² + (2x − 10)² = 200 gives 5x² − 40x − 100 = 0, x² − 8x − 20 = 0, (x − 10)(x + 2) = 0; then y = 2x − 10.

html:
C is a graph with equation  x² + y² = 65

L is a straight line with equation  2y = 10 − x

Using algebra, find the coordinates of the point of intersection of C and L.

You must show all your working.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: (8, 1) and (−4, 7) — x = 10 − 2y, so (10 − 2y)² + y² = 65 gives 5y² − 40y + 35 = 0, y² − 8y + 7 = 0, (y − 1)(y − 7) = 0; then x = 10 − 2y.

html:

You must show all your working.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: (6, 7) and (9, −2) — y = 25 − 3x, so x² + (25 − 3x)² = 85 gives 10x² − 150x + 540 = 0, x² − 15x + 54 = 0, (x − 6)(x − 9) = 0.

html:

x² − 2y² = 7

2y = x + 1
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: x = 5, y = 3 and x = −3, y = −1 — x = 2y − 1, so (2y − 1)² − 2y² = 7 gives 2y² − 4y − 6 = 0, y² − 2y − 3 = 0, (y − 3)(y + 1) = 0.

html:
C is a graph with equation  2x² − 3y² = 15

L is a straight line with equation  y = x − 2

Using algebra, find the coordinates of the points of intersection of C and L.

You must show all your working.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: (3, 1) and (9, 7) — 2x² − 3(x − 2)² = 15 gives −x² + 12x − 27 = 0, x² − 12x + 27 = 0, (x − 3)(x − 9) = 0; then y = x − 2.

html:
C is a graph with equation  x² − 8y² = k   where k is a positive integer.

L is a straight line with equation  4y = x − 1

L and C intersect at points A and B.

The x-coordinate of point A is −7.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths

html: Work out the value of k.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: k = 17 — at A, 4y = −7 − 1 = −8 so y = −2, and k = (−7)² − 8 × (−2)² = 49 − 32 = 17.

html: Work out the coordinates of point B.
name: Non Linear Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: B = (5, 1) — substituting x = 4y + 1 into x² − 8y² = 17 gives 8y² + 8y − 16 = 0, (y + 2)(y − 1) = 0; y = −2 is A, so y = 1 and x = 5.

The equation of line L1 is  y = 3x + 4

The equation of line L2 is  2y − 6x = 20

Show that these two lines are parallel.
name: Parallel Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Both gradients are 3 — L1 is already y = mx + c with gradient 3. Rearranging L2: 2y = 6x + 20, so y = 3x + 10, gradient 3. Both lines have the same gradient, so they are parallel.

name: Parallel Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Both gradients are 4 — L1 is already y = mx + c with gradient 4. Rearranging L2: 3y = 12x + 6, so y = 4x + 2, gradient 4. Both lines have the same gradient, so they are parallel.

subject: Maths

subject: Maths

html:

subject: Maths

html:

subject: Maths
answer: the gradients are 3⁄4 and −4⁄3, and 3⁄4 × −4⁄3 = −1 — L2: 6y = −8x + 30, so y = −4⁄3x + 5. The product is −1, so they are perpendicular.

html:
The equation of line L1 is  2y = 3x − 4

The equation of line L2 is  8y − 12x − 40 = 0

Show that these two lines are not perpendicular.
name: Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths
answer: both gradients are 3⁄2, and 3⁄2 × 3⁄2 = 9⁄4, not −1 — L1: y = 3⁄2x − 2. L2: 8y = 12x + 40, so y = 3⁄2x + 5. The lines are in fact parallel.

answer: k = 6 — L2: y = −1⁄3x + 6, so L1 needs gradient 3. L1 is y = k⁄2x − 1, so k⁄2 = 3.

answer: k = 12⁄5 — L1 has gradient −2⁄5. L2 is y = 6⁄kx + 20⁄k, gradient 6⁄k. Perpendicular: −2⁄5 × 6⁄k = −1, so −12 = −5k and k = 12⁄5.

subject: Maths
answer: 45 units² — L2 has gradient −1⁄2; through (−8, 11): 11 = 4 + c, so y = −1⁄2x + 7. They meet where 2x + 2 = −1⁄2x + 7, so x = 2 and P = (2, 6). Q = (−1, 0) and R = (14, 0), so the base QR is 15 and the height is 6: ½ × 15 × 6 = 45.

name: Probability Tree Diagrams
subject: Maths
answer: Win 1⁄9, Lose 8⁄9 on every pair — the Win sector is 40° of 360°, so P(Win) = 1⁄9 and P(Lose) = 8⁄9.

html:
The table below shows the prizes that the player can win.

Spins2 × Win1 × Win0 × win
Prize£10£3£0

To play the game players must pay £2.50

During one week 405 players play the game.

Work out an estimate for the amount of profit the game organiser made this week.
name: Probability Tree Diagrams
subject: Maths
answer: £722.50 — P(2 wins) = 1⁄81 and P(1 win) = 2 × 1⁄9 × 8⁄9 = 16⁄81. Of 405 players, expect 5 to win twice (£50 in prizes) and 80 to win once (£240). They pay 405 × £2.50 = £1012.50, so the profit is £1012.50 − £290 = £722.50.

html: Solve   x² + 7x + 10 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −5 < x < −2 — (x + 2)(x + 5) < 0, so the critical values are −5 and −2. The curve is ∪-shaped, so it is below zero between them.

html: Solve   x² − 9x + 20 > 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: x < 4 or x > 5 — (x − 4)(x − 5) > 0, critical values 4 and 5. The ∪-shaped curve is above zero outside them.
accept: x < 4 or x > 5 | x > 5 or x < 4

html: Solve   x² + 2x − 15 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −5 < x < 3 — (x + 5)(x − 3) < 0, critical values −5 and 3; below zero between them.

html: Solve   x² + x − 12 > 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: x < −4 or x > 3 — (x + 4)(x − 3) > 0, critical values −4 and 3; above zero outside them.
accept: x < -4 or x > 3 | x > 3 or x < -4

html: Solve   x² − 2x − 24 ≤ 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −4 ≤ x ≤ 6 — (x + 4)(x − 6) ≤ 0, critical values −4 and 6; on or below zero between them, ends included.

html: Solve   x² − 17x + 30 ≥ 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: x ≤ 2 or x ≥ 15 — (x − 2)(x − 15) ≥ 0, critical values 2 and 15; on or above zero outside them, ends included.
accept: x ≤ 2 or x ≥ 15 | x ≥ 15 or x ≤ 2

html: Solve   x² − 25 ≤ 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −5 ≤ x ≤ 5 — (x + 5)(x − 5) ≤ 0 (or x² ≤ 25), critical values ±5; between them, ends included.

html: Solve   2x² − 7x − 15 > 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: x < −3⁄2 or x > 5 — (2x + 3)(x − 5) > 0, critical values −1.5 and 5; above zero outside them.

html: Solve   3x² + 17x − 6 ≤ 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths

html: Solve   5x² − 13x + 6 ≥ 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: x ≤ 3⁄5 or x ≥ 2 — (5x − 3)(x − 2) ≥ 0, critical values 0.6 and 2; outside them, ends included.

html: Solve   2x² + 15x + 24 < 3 − 2x
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −7 < x < −3⁄2 — Rearrange: 2x² + 17x + 21 < 0, so (2x + 3)(x + 7) < 0, critical values −7 and −1.5; between them.

name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −2 < x < 4 — (x + 2)(x − 4) < 0, critical values −2 and 4; below zero between them.

html:
Find a set of possible values of x for which

4x − 5 < 19     and     x² − 8x − 20 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: −2 < x < 6 — 4x < 24 gives x < 6; (x − 10)(x + 2) < 0 gives −2 < x < 10. Both hold for −2 < x < 6.

html:
Find a set of possible values of x for which

6x + 1 > 16     and     x² − 8x + 12 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄2 < x < 6 — 6x > 15 gives x > 2.5; (x − 2)(x − 6) < 0 gives 2 < x < 6. Both hold for 2.5 < x < 6.

html:
Find a set of possible values of x for which

x² − 11x + 10 < 0     and     2x² + 3x − 20 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: 1 < x < 5⁄2 — (x − 1)(x − 10) < 0 gives 1 < x < 10; (2x − 5)(x + 4) < 0 gives −4 < x < 2.5. Both hold for 1 < x < 2.5.

html:
Find a set of possible values of x for which

x² − 9 ≥ 0     and     2x² − 13x + 15 < 0
name: Quadratic Inequalities
subject: Maths
answer: 3 ≤ x < 5 — x² ≥ 9 gives x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 3; (2x − 3)(x − 5) < 0 gives 1.5 < x < 5. Both hold for 3 ≤ x < 5.

name: Reflections
subject: Maths

subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the line y = −4 — the edges at y = −1 and y = −7 are each 3 from y = −4, and those at −2 and −6 are each 2 from it.

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape A onto shape B.
name: Reflections
subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the y-axis (x = 0) — each corner (x, y) of A goes to (−x, y). Because A is symmetrical, a translation by (7, 0) would also land on B, but this is a sheet on reflections and the reflection is the expected answer.

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape C onto shape D.
name: Reflections
subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the line x = −1 — the shape is flipped: C’s point (−3, −3) is 2 left of x = −1 and D’s matching point (1, −3) is 2 right of it; every corner pairs up the same way (x becomes −2 − x).

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape C onto shape D.
name: Reflections
subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the line y = −3 — C and D share the edge along y = −3, and C’s corners 2 above it, at (−3, −1) and (−5, −1), go to D’s corners 2 below it, at (−3, −5) and (−5, −5).

name: Reflections
subject: Maths

name: Reflections
subject: Maths

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape A onto shape B.
name: Reflections
subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the line y = −x — each corner (x, y) of A goes to (−y, −x): (−6, 3) → (−3, 6), (−4, 1) → (−1, 4), (−3, 1) → (−1, 3), and (−3, 3), on the line, stays.

html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape C onto shape D.
name: Reflections
subject: Maths
answer: Reflection in the line y = −4 — C’s edge at y = −3 and D’s at y = −5 are each 1 from y = −4; C’s top corners at y = −1 go to D’s bottom corners at y = −7 (y becomes −8 − y).

html:
Seven positive numbers have a mean of 5.

Six of the numbers are

2     2     3     5     7     10

Work out the other number.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — 7 × 5 = 35 altogether; the six add to 2 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 10 = 29, and 35 − 29 = 6.

html:
Six positive numbers have a mean of 20.

Five of the numbers are

13     14     20     20     35

Work out the median of all six numbers.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 19 — 6 × 20 = 120 and the five add to 102, so the sixth is 18. In order: 13, 14, 18, 20, 20, 35, and the median is halfway between 18 and 20.

html:
Pamai completes tests in Maths, English, Science, History, Geography and Spanish.

The table below shows Pamai’s test scores in five of her subjects.

SubjectMathsEnglishScienceHistoryGeography
Test Score (%)8257846377

For all six subjects Pamai’s mean score is 72%

Work out Pamai’s test score in Spanish.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 69% — 6 × 72 = 432 altogether; the five add to 363, and 432 − 363 = 69.

html:
A football team recorded how many goals they scored in their first 8 matches of a season.

The table below shows the number of goals scored for the first 7 of those games.

Game Number1234567
Goals Scored3110102

The mean number of goals scored for all 8 games was 1.5

Work out the number of goals scored in the 8th game.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 4 — 8 × 1.5 = 12 goals altogether; the first 7 games add to 8, so 12 − 8 = 4.

html:
The mean age of 9 members at a running club is 25 years.

A new member joins the club and the mean age increases to 26 years.

Work out the age of the new member of the running club.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 35 years — 9 × 25 = 225 before, 10 × 26 = 260 after, and 260 − 225 = 35.

html:
The mean weekly pay of 4 workers at a company is £600.

A new worker joins the company and is paid £700 per week.

Work out the new mean pay of all workers at the company.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: £620 — 4 × 600 = 2400, plus 700 is 3100, shared between 5 workers is 620.

html:
Six positive numbers have

a mean of 29

a range of 21

Four of the numbers are

19     21     35     37

Work out the other two numbers.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 22 and 40 — 6 × 29 = 174 and the four add to 112, so the other two add to 62. A range of 21 with 19 as the smallest makes the largest 40, and 62 − 40 = 22. (If 37 were the largest the smallest would be 16 and the other 46, which is bigger than 37.)

html:
Seven positive numbers have

a mean of 12

a median of 13

a mode of 14

Four of the numbers are

8     10     14     19

Work out the range of the seven numbers.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 13 — the median of seven numbers is the 4th, so 13 is one of them; the mode 14 needs a second 14. 7 × 12 = 84 and 8 + 10 + 14 + 19 + 13 + 14 = 78, so the last is 6. The numbers are 6, 8, 10, 13, 14, 14, 19 and 19 − 6 = 13.

html:
Rachel recorded the temperature in her town on each day for 1 week.

The mean temperature for the 5 days from Monday to Friday was 11°C

The mean temperature for all 7 days was 13°C

On Saturday, the temperature was 21°C

Work out the temperature for Sunday.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 15°C — 7 × 13 = 91 for the week and 5 × 11 = 55 for Monday to Friday; 91 − 55 − 21 = 15.

html:
15 students complete a maths test.

The mean score of all 15 students is 71%

One of the students is found to have cheated in the test.

The score of the student who cheated is removed and the mean score of the remaining students is 69%

Work out the test score of the student who cheated in the test.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths

html:
The mean mass of Mercury, Earth and Mars is 2.3 × 1024 kg

The mean mass of Mercury, Earth, Mars and Venus is 2.95 × 1024 kg

Work out the mass of Venus.

Give your answer in standard form.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 4.9 × 1024 kg — the four planets weigh 4 × 2.95 = 11.8 × 1024 kg and the three weigh 3 × 2.3 = 6.9 × 1024 kg; 11.8 − 6.9 = 4.9.

html:
From Monday to Thursday the mean amount of time it took Ryan to travel to work was 35 minutes.

On Friday there are roadworks on Ryan’s route to work.

The mean amount of time it took Ryan to get to work from Monday to Friday was 44 minutes.

On Friday Ryan left his house at 7:45 am. He must arrive to work by 9:00 am.

Show clearly that Ryan was late to work.

You must show all your working.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: Friday’s journey took 80 minutes, so he arrived at 9:05 am — 4 × 35 = 140 minutes for Monday to Thursday and 5 × 44 = 220 for the week, so Friday took 80 minutes; 7:45 am + 80 minutes = 9:05 am, which is after 9:00 am.

html:
In a class there are 15 males and 12 females

The mean height of the males is 172 cm

The mean height of the females is 163 cm

Work out the mean height for all of the students in the class.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths

html:
A theme park wants to ensure that the mean amount of time spent queuing for rides is less than 1 hour.

On Friday, Saturday and Sunday some visitors were asked how long they queued for a ride.

DayFridaySaturdaySunday
Number of visitors asked155200187
Mean time spent queuing (minutes)546658

Show clearly that the mean amount of time spent queuing for all visitors asked on Friday, Saturday and Sunday was less than 1 hour.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: the mean is 59.8 minutes, which is less than 60 — 155 × 54 = 8370, 200 × 66 = 13 200 and 187 × 58 = 10 846 make 32 416 minutes for 542 visitors; 32 416 ÷ 542 = 59.8 minutes.

html:
A film trilogy contains 3 films.

The mean length of films in the trilogy is 1 hour 47 minutes

The first film is 1 hours 54 minutes long

The second film is 1 hour 22 minutes long

Work out the length of the third film.

Give your answer in hours and minutes.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 2 hours 5 minutes — in minutes: 3 × 107 = 321 altogether; 114 + 82 = 196, and 321 − 196 = 125 minutes = 2 hours 5 minutes.
accept: 2 hours 5 minutes | 2 hours and 5 minutes | 2 h 5 min | 2h 5min | 2hr 5min | 2 hours 5 mins

html:
In a garden there are 50 rose plants and 45 tulip plants.

The mean height of the rose plants is 40 cm

The mean height of the tulip plants is 21 cm

Work out the mean height of all plants in the garden
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths

html:
A vet is caring for 6 cats and 5 dogs.

The mean mass of the 5 dogs is 13.3 kg

The mean mass of all the cats and dogs is 7.9 kg

Work out the mean mass of the 6 cats.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 3.4 kg — all 11 animals: 11 × 7.9 = 86.9 kg; the dogs: 5 × 13.3 = 66.5 kg; the cats weigh 20.4 kg and 20.4 ÷ 6 = 3.4.

html:
In a class there are 18 males and 12 females

The students all complete a test with a maximum score of 40 marks.

The mean mark for the male students is 27

The mean mark for the female students is 34

The teacher will reward the students if the mean mark for all students is greater than 75% of the maximum score.

Show clearly that the teacher will not reward the students.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: the mean is 29.8, which is not more than 30 (75% of 40) — 18 × 27 = 486 and 12 × 34 = 408 make 894 for 30 students; 894 ÷ 30 = 29.8, and 75% of 40 is 30.

html:
An officer recorded the mean speed of 30 cars and 20 lorries on a motorway.

The mean speed of the cars was 68 mph

The mean speed of all of the vehicles was 62 mph

Work out the mean speed of the lorries.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 53 mph — 50 × 62 = 3100 for all the vehicles and 30 × 68 = 2040 for the cars; 1060 ÷ 20 = 53.

html:
A teacher asked 20 Year 9 students, 30 Year 10 students and 25 Year 11 students how long they spent on their homework.

The mean amount of time spent on homework by Year 9 students was 26 minutes

The mean amount of time spent on homework by Year 10 students was 31 minutes

The mean amount of time spent on homework by all students was 32 minutes

Work out the mean amount of time spent on homework by Year 11 students.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 38 minutes — 75 × 32 = 2400 altogether; Year 9 is 20 × 26 = 520 and Year 10 is 30 × 31 = 930, leaving 950 for 25 students: 950 ÷ 25 = 38.

html:
6 athletes compete in a 100 metre race with a mean race time of 12.1 seconds.

The race times for 5 of the athletes are shown below.

AthleteJasonZachBillyTriniKimberley
Time (seconds)11.612.113.112.211.9

Tommy also competed in the race and claims that he was the winner.

Show clearly that Tommy is incorrect.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: Tommy’s time was 11.7 seconds, slower than Jason’s 11.6 — 6 × 12.1 = 72.6 seconds altogether and the five add to 60.9, so Tommy took 11.7 seconds.

html:
A basketball team plays 18 games in a season.

In September the team plays 8 games

In October the team plays 4 games.

In November the team plays 6 games.

The mean number of points scored by the team in September is 71.

The mean number of points scored by the team in September and October is 74.

The mean number of points scored by the team in November is the same as the mean number of points scored in October.

Work out the total number of points the team scores during the entire season.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 1368 — September: 8 × 71 = 568; September and October: 12 × 74 = 888, so October is 320 in 4 games, a mean of 80; November: 6 × 80 = 480; 888 + 480 = 1368.

html:
A bag contains

55   2p coins

16   5p coins

9   10p coins

Jordan adds more 5p coins to the bag until the mean value of the coins in the bag is 4p

Work out how many 5p coins Jordan adds to the bag.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 40 — the bag holds 80 coins worth 110 + 80 + 90 = 280p. Adding n 5p coins: (280 + 5n) ÷ (80 + n) = 4, so 280 + 5n = 320 + 4n and n = 40.

html:
Bag A, bag B and bag C each contain only blue and red counters.

Bag A contains 5 red counters and 3 blue counters.

Bag B contains 10 red counters and 4 blue counters.

The mean number of red counters in all three bags is 6.

The mean number of blue counters in all three bags is 5.

Work out the probability that a counter randomly selected from bag C is red.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄11 — 3 × 6 = 18 red altogether, so bag C has 18 − 5 − 10 = 3 red; 3 × 5 = 15 blue, so bag C has 15 − 3 − 4 = 8 blue. 3 red out of 11.

html:
Adam tracked how many minutes he spent on social media each day from Monday to Friday.

DayMondayTuesdayWednesdayThursdayFriday
Time spent on social media (minutes)4018510570

The mean amount of time he spent on social media from Monday to Friday was 30% greater than the mean amount of time he spent on social media for Monday and Tuesday.

Work out how many minutes Adam spent on social media on Monday.
name: Reverse Mean
subject: Maths
answer: 120 minutes — call Monday m: (m + 400) ÷ 5 = 1.3 × (m + 40) ÷ 2, so 2m + 800 = 6.5m + 260 and m = 120. Check: 520 ÷ 5 = 104 and 160 ÷ 2 = 80, and 80 × 1.3 = 104.

html:
A company’s profit this year is £246,400.

This is a 12% increase from last year.

Work out the profit last year.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: £220,000 — this year is 112% of last year, so last year = 246,400 ÷ 1.12 = 220,000. Check: 220,000 × 1.12 = 246,400.

html:
A laptop is on sale for £816 after a 15% discount has been applied.

Work out the original price of the laptop.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: £960 — £816 is 100% − 15% = 85% of the original, so 816 ÷ 0.85 = 960. Check: 960 × 0.85 = 816.

html:
The value of a car is now £12,240.

This is a 32% reduction from its original value.

Work out the original value of the car.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: £18,000 — £12,240 is 68% of the original, so 12,240 ÷ 0.68 = 18,000. Check: 18,000 × 0.68 = 12,240.

html:
The number of subscribers to a channel is 540,000.

This is 25% more than the number of subscribers last year.

Work out how many subscribers the channel had last year.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths

html:
Emma has 396 followers on social media.

This is 10% fewer than Josh.

Work out how many followers Josh has on social media.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 440 — 396 is 90% of Josh’s number, so 396 ÷ 0.9 = 440. Check: 10% of 440 is 44, and 440 − 44 = 396.

html:
On Wednesday, a factory produced 1,054 toys.

This is 15% less than on Tuesday.

Work out how many toys the factory produced on Tuesday.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 1,240 — 1,054 is 85% of Tuesday’s number, so 1,054 ÷ 0.85 = 1,240. Check: 1,240 × 0.85 = 1,054.

html:
35% of a number is 42

Work out the number.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths

html:
11% of a number is 27.5

Work out the number.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths

html:
30% of a number is 55.5

Work out 140% of the number.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 259 — 10% is 55.5 ÷ 3 = 18.5, so 140% is 18.5 × 14 = 259. (The number itself is 185, and 185 × 1.4 = 259.)

html:
Mia ran 56.7 km this week.

This is 35% more than last week.

Work out how far Mia ran last week.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 42 km — 56.7 is 135% of last week, so 56.7 ÷ 1.35 = 42. Check: 42 × 1.35 = 56.7.

html:
On Friday, a store sold 48 video games.

This is 20% fewer than Thursday.

Work out how many video games were sold on Thursday.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 60 — 48 is 80% of Thursday’s sales, so 48 ÷ 0.8 = 60. Check: 20% of 60 is 12, and 60 − 12 = 48.

html:
A mobile game had 69850 downloads this week.

This is 27% more than the previous week.

Work out how many downloads the game had the previous week.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 55,000 — 69,850 is 127% of the previous week, so 69,850 ÷ 1.27 = 55,000. Check: 55,000 × 1.27 = 69,850.

html:
Emma buys a new book with 550 pages.

She reads the book on Saturday and Sunday.

On Sunday she read 286 pages.

This is 30% more pages than she read on Saturday.

Work out how many pages of the book Emma will still have left to read.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 44 pages — Sunday is 130% of Saturday, so Saturday = 286 ÷ 1.3 = 220 pages. She has read 220 + 286 = 506, leaving 550 − 506 = 44.

html:
Oberon and Europa are moons of Uranus and Jupiter.

The mass of Europa is 60% more than Oberon.

The mass of Europa is 4.8 × 1022 kg

Work out the mass of Oberon giving your answer in standard form.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 3 × 1022 kg — Europa is 160% of Oberon, so Oberon = 4.8 × 1022 ÷ 1.6 = 3 × 1022. Check: 3 × 1.6 = 4.8.

html:
Rich adds £36 to his savings account.

This increases the amount of money Rich’s savings by 12%

Work out how much money was in Rich’s savings account originally.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: £300 — the £36 added is 12% of the original amount, so 1% is 36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 100% is £300. Check: 12% of 300 = 36.

html:
A jar contains some sweets.

Poppy eats 39 of the sweets in the jar.

This reduces the number of sweets in the jar by 25%

Work out how many sweets are now in the jar.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 117 — the 39 eaten are 25% of the jar, so there were 39 × 4 = 156 sweets, and now there are 156 − 39 = 117 (75% of 156).

html:

This increases the number of books in the library by 8%.

Work out how many books were in the library originally.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 3,000 — the 240 new books are 8% of the original, so 1% is 240 ÷ 8 = 30 and 100% is 3,000. Check: 8% of 3,000 = 240.

html:
The pass mark for an exam decreases by 8 marks between 2024 and 2025.

These 8 marks represent a 5% decrease in the pass mark.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths

html: Work out the pass mark for the exam in 2024.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 160 — 8 marks are 5% of the 2024 pass mark, so 1% is 1.6 and 100% is 160.

html: Work out the pass mark for the exam in 2025.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 152 — 160 − 8 = 152 (which is 95% of 160).

html:
A bag contains counters that are either red, blue or green.

48 of the counters are red.

40% of the counters are red.

There are the same number of blue counters as green counters.

Work out the number of blue counters in the bag.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 36 — 48 is 40%, so 10% is 12 and the bag holds 120 counters. 120 − 48 = 72 are blue or green, split equally: 72 ÷ 2 = 36.

html:
George has 3 attempts at the long jump.

His second jump is 10% further than his first jump.

His third jump is 20% further than his second jump.

His best jump was 7.26 m

Work out the mean of his three jumps.
name: Reverse Percentages
subject: Maths
answer: 6.27 m — each jump is longer than the one before, so the best is the third, 7.26 m. Second = 7.26 ÷ 1.2 = 6.05 m, first = 6.05 ÷ 1.1 = 5.5 m. Mean = (5.5 + 6.05 + 7.26) ÷ 3 = 18.81 ÷ 3 = 6.27 m.

answer: 48π cm² — for sector A, 27π = θ⁄360 × 81π gives θ = 120°, so its arc is 1⁄3 × 18π = 6π. Sector B’s arc is 12π and it is 3⁄4 of a circle: 3⁄4 × 2πR = 12π, so R = 8, and its area is 3⁄4 × π × 64 = 48π.

html:
A shop sells pencils and rulers.

The cost of 5 pencils and 2 rulers is £0.99

The cost of 1 pencil and 10 rulers is £1.35
name: Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths

html: Work out the cost of 1 pencil.
name: Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: 15p — in pence, 5p + 2r = 99 and p + 10r = 135; substituting p = 135 − 10r gives 675 − 48r = 99, so r = 12 and p = 135 − 120 = 15.

html: Work out the cost of 1 ruler.
name: Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: 12p — 48r = 576 gives r = 12. Check: 5 × 15 + 2 × 12 = 99 and 15 + 10 × 12 = 135.
examiner_note: The worksheet gives 3 marks for the whole question, not one per price, so all 3 sit on this last part: both prices (pencil 15p, ruler 12p) right, with working, for full marks.

html:
A machine makes hats and gloves but only makes one item at a time.

The time taken to make a hat is 2 minutes longer than the time taken to make a glove.

The machine makes 4 hats and 6 gloves in 13 minutes.

Work out how long the machine would take to make 1 hat and 1 glove.
name: Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: 3 minutes — with a glove taking g minutes, 4(g + 2) + 6g = 13 gives 10g = 5, so a glove takes 0.5 minutes and a hat 2.5 minutes; 0.5 + 2.5 = 3.

html:
A cinema has adult tickets and child tickets.

The price of each ticket type is fixed.

Tom buys 3 adult tickets and 4 child tickets costing a total of £35.50

Lily buys 2 adult tickets and 3 child tickets costing a total of £25.00

Carolyn buys 1 adult tickets and 2 child tickets.

Work out how much Carolyn paid for the tickets.
name: Simultaneous Equations
subject: Maths
answer: £14.50 — 3a + 4c = 35.5 and 2a + 3c = 25; doubling the first and tripling the second gives c = 4, then a = 6.50, so 6.50 + 2×4 = 14.50.

Choose two words.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: increasing and positive — from 0 to 10 seconds the line climbs from 0 to 20 m/s, so the speed is going up, and it is above 0, so it is positive.

html: Between 0 and 10 seconds the acceleration is ………
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: positive — the line slopes upwards, so its gradient, the acceleration, is above 0: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s2.

html: Between 10 and 20 seconds the acceleration is ………
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: zero — the line is flat at 20 m/s, so the speed is not changing.

html: Between 20 and 30 seconds the acceleration is ………
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: negative — the line slopes down from 20 to 10 m/s, so the gradient is −10 ÷ 10 = −1 m/s2.

html:
Between 20 and 30 seconds the speed is ……… and ………

Choose two words.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: decreasing and positive — the speed drops from 20 to 10 m/s, so it is decreasing, but it stays above 0, so it is positive.

html: The acceleration is greatest between 15 and 20 seconds.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: False — between 15 and 20 seconds the line is flat, so the acceleration is 0; the greatest is between 0 and 5 seconds (40 ÷ 5 = 8 m/s2).

html: The acceleration between 15 and 20 seconds is the same as the acceleration between 30 and 35 seconds.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: True — both stretches of the graph are flat, so both accelerations are 0.

html: The acceleration between 25 and 30 seconds is the same as the acceleration between 35 and 40 seconds.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: False — from 25 to 30 seconds the speed rises 20 m/s in 5 seconds (+4 m/s2), but from 35 to 40 seconds it falls 20 m/s in 5 seconds (−4 m/s2).

html: The distance travelled in the first 5 seconds is the same as the distance travelled in the last 10 seconds.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: True — first 5 seconds: ½ × 5 × 40 = 100 m; last 10 seconds: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

subject: Maths

The car is travelling on a road with a speed limit of 90 km/h

Work out percentage of the 40 second journey that the car was above the speed limit.

subject: Maths
answer: about 35% — 90 km/h = 90,000 ÷ 3,600 = 25 m/s. The curve is above 25 from about 10 to about 24 seconds, which is 14 seconds: 14 ÷ 40 × 100 = 35% (about 33% to 38%).

html: At what time is Tommy halfway between his house and the docks?
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 22.5 seconds — call the top speed 4 squares; in squares the areas are 2 (0–5 s), 20 (5–30 s), 6 (30–40 s) and 4 (40–60 s), 32 in all. Halfway is 16: 2 by 5 seconds, then 0.8 a second, so 14 more takes 17.5 seconds: 5 + 17.5 = 22.5.

html:
The total distance between Tommy’s house and the docks is 320 metres.

Work out the maximum speed that Tommy reaches on his way to the docks.
name: Speed Time Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 8 m/s — the area under the graph is 32 squares = 320 m, so a square is 10 m; a square is 5 seconds by one row, so one row is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s, and the top speed, 4 rows, is 8 m/s.

name: Straight Line Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: x ≈ 1.3 — the lines cross a little past x = 1.2; solving exactly, 7⁄3x = 3 gives x = 9⁄7 = 1.29, so a reading from 1.2 to 1.4 is right.

The rule for continuing the sequence is

multiply the previous term by 2 then add 3
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths

html: Work out the second term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 5 — 1 × 2 + 3 = 5.

name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 13 — the second term is 5, and 5 × 2 + 3 = 13.

subject: Maths
answer: 29 — the third term is 13, and 13 × 2 + 3 = 29.

html:
The first term of a sequence is 24

24            

The rule for continuing the sequence is

subtract 4 from the previous term and then divide by 2

Work out the third term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — (24 − 4) ÷ 2 = 10, then (10 − 4) ÷ 2 = 3.

html:
The second term of a different sequence is 46

    46        

The rule for continuing the sequence is

multiply the previous term by 5 then add 1

Work out the first term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 9 — work backwards with the inverse operations: subtract 1, then divide by 5: (46 − 1) ÷ 5 = 9. Check: 9 × 5 + 1 = 46.

    9        

The rule for continuing the sequence is

subtract 1 from the previous term and then divide by 2

Work out the first term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 19 — undo it: multiply by 2, then add 1: 9 × 2 + 1 = 19. Check: (19 − 1) ÷ 2 = 9.

The third term of a different sequence is 750

        750    

The rule for continuing the sequence is

add 5 to the previous term then multiply by 10

Work out the first term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — undo it twice (divide by 10, then subtract 5): 750 ÷ 10 − 5 = 70, then 70 ÷ 10 − 5 = 2. Check: (2 + 5) × 10 = 70, (70 + 5) × 10 = 750.

multiply the previous term by 5 then subtract 4

html: Work out the first term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — undo it: (11 + 4) ÷ 5 = 3.

name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 51 — 11 × 5 − 4 = 51.

answer: 251 — 51 × 5 − 4 = 251.

add k to the previous term

subject: Maths

answer: −1 — 6 × 2 − 7 = 5, 5 × 2 − 7 = 3, 3 × 2 − 7 = −1.

−9

multiply the previous term by 3 then add 20

Work out the value of the first positive term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: 17 — −9 × 3 + 20 = −7, −7 × 3 + 20 = −1, −1 × 3 + 20 = 17.

html:
The third term of a sequence is 4

        4    

The rule for continuing the sequence is

add 4 to the previous term then multiply by 2

Work out the first term of the sequence.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: −5 — undo the rule (divide by 2, then subtract 4) twice: 4 ÷ 2 − 4 = −2, then −2 ÷ 2 − 4 = −5. Check: (−5 + 4) × 2 = −2, (−2 + 4) × 2 = 4.

html:
The first term of sequence A and sequence B is 6

Sequence A6        
Sequence B6        

The rules for continuing the sequences are

Sequence A    add 3 to the previous term then multiply by 2

Sequence B    multiply the previous term by 3 then subtract 3

Show that the third terms in both sequences are equal.
name: Term to term rule
subject: Maths
answer: both third terms are 42 — A: (6 + 3) × 2 = 18, then (18 + 3) × 2 = 42. B: 6 × 3 − 3 = 15, then 15 × 3 − 3 = 42.

html: Draw the graph of   y = f(x) + 1   onto the first grid.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: the same curve moved up 1 — + 1 outside the bracket adds 1 to every y: lowest point (0, −1), ends at (−3, 4) and (3, 4)

html: Draw the graph of   y = g(x) − 2   onto the second grid.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: the same graph moved down 2 — − 2 outside takes 2 from every y: (−2, −1), (−1, 0), (0, −3), (1, −1), (2, −1).

answer: the curve moved 1 right and 3 up — from (0, 5) up to a maximum at (2, 7) and down to (4, 2)

html:
Point A(3, −1) is on the graph y = f(x)

When the graph of y = f(x) is transformed to the graph with equation y = −f(−x) the point A is mapped to point B.

Write down the coordinates of point B.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: B(−3, 1) — −f(−x) changes the sign of both coordinates, so (3, −1) goes to (−3, 1).

graph A has been translated to give graph C.

The equation of graph A is y = f(x)

html: On the grid sketch the graph of   y = sin x° − 2   for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: moved down 2 — from (0, −2) up to (90, −1), down to (270, −3), back to (360, −2)

html: On the grid sketch the graph of   y = sin (x + 90°)   for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: moved 90° left — starts at 1 when x = 0, 0 at 90°, −1 at 180°, 0 at 270°, 1 at 360°

html: On the grid sketch the graph of   y = −sin x°   for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: reflected in the x-axis — 0, −1 at 90°, 0 at 180°, 1 at 270°, 0 at 360°.

html:
The graph of   y = 3x2 + 2x − 5   is reflected in the x-axis.

The reflected graph has equation y = f(x)

Work out f(x).

Give your answer in the form   ax2 + bx + c   where a, b and c are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: −3x2 − 2x + 5 — reflecting in the x-axis is y = −f(x), so every term changes sign.

html:
The graph of   y = x2 + 5   is translated 3 units to the left.

The translated graph has equation y = f(x)

Work out f(x).

Give your answer in the form   x2 + ax + b   where a and b are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: x2 + 6x + 14 — 3 to the left replaces x with x + 3: (x + 3)2 + 5 = x2 + 6x + 9 + 5.

html:
The graph of   y = 2x2 − 5x + 3   is reflected in the y-axis.

The reflected graph has equation y = f(x)

Work out f(x).

Give your answer in the form   ax2 + bx + c   where a, b and c are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 2x2 + 5x + 3 — reflecting in the y-axis replaces x with −x: 2(−x)2 − 5(−x) + 3.

html:
The graph of   y = x3 − 5   is translated 2 units to the right.

The translated graph has equation y = f(x)

Work out f(x).

Give your answer in the form   x3 + ax2 + bx + c   where a, b and c are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: x3 − 6x2 + 12x − 13 — 2 to the right replaces x with x − 2: (x − 2)3 = x3 − 6x2 + 12x − 8, then − 5.

html:
Here are sketches of two graphs.

Graph A has equation y = x2 + 4x

Graph A is translated to give graph B so that the turning point (−2, −4) on graph A is mapped to the point (5, −1) on graph B.

Work out an equation for graph B.

Give your answer in the form   x2 + ax + b   where a and b are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: y = x2 − 10x + 24 — the turning point of B is (5, −1), so y = (x − 5)2 − 1 = x2 − 10x + 25 − 1. (It is A moved 7 right and 3 up.)

html:
The graph of   y = 10 − 2x2   is translated 3 units to the right and 1 unit up.

The translated graph has equation y = f(x)

Work out f(x).

Give your answer in the form   ax2 + bx + c   where a, b and c are integers.
name: Transformations of Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: −2x2 + 12x − 7 — y = 10 − 2(x − 3)2 + 1 = 11 − 2(x2 − 6x + 9) = −2x2 + 12x − 7.

html: Work out the maximum possible total amount of money.
name: Bounds
subject: Maths
answer: £10.13 — Eric has at most £8.49 and Nicky at most £1.64 (money goes in whole pence), so 8.49 + 1.64 = 10.13. Using the bounds £8.50 and £1.65 gives £10.15, which is also accepted.

answer: £6.24 — Eric has at most £8.49 and the case costs at least £2.25, so 8.49 − 2.25 = 6.24 (or £6.25 using the bound £8.50).

subject: Maths
answer: 8040 ml — a can is 325 ≤ c < 335, so the upper bound is 335 × 24 = 8040.

html: Work out the lower bound for the capacity of the multipack of cans.

answer: 7800 ml — a can is at least 325 ml, so the lower bound is 325 × 24 = 7800.

Work out the lower bound for the amount of drink that could be left in the can.

subject: Maths
answer: 252.5 ml — the least left is the smallest can minus the most drunk: 325 − 72.5 = 252.5.

html: The height of the new cuboid is 3 times the height of the original cuboid.
name: Volume and Surface Area Cuboids
subject: Maths
answer: True — the three copies are stacked one on top of another, so the new cuboid is three heights tall.

html: The volume of the new cuboid is 3 times the volume of the original cuboid.
name: Volume and Surface Area Cuboids
subject: Maths
answer: True — the new cuboid is made of exactly three of the original, so it holds three times the space.

html: The surface area of the new cuboid is 3 times the surface area of the original cuboid.
name: Volume and Surface Area Cuboids
subject: Maths
answer: False — where the copies touch, four faces are hidden inside the stack, so the surface area is less than 3 times the original.

html:
A cuboid is placed onto a flat surface so that the bottom face is no longer visible.

The five visible faces of the cuboid are to be painted.

Each tin of paint can cover an area of 1 m² and costs £3.50

Work out how much it would cost to buy enough tins of paint to paint the five visible faces of the cuboid.
name: Volume and Surface Area Cuboids
subject: Maths
answer: £17.50 — Visible area = 2 × (1 × 0.8) + 2 × (1 × 1.2) + 1.2 × 0.8 = 1.6 + 2.4 + 0.96 = 4.96 m², so 5 tins are needed: 5 × 3.50 = 17.50.

Work out the volume of the cuboid.
name: Volume and Surface Area Cuboids
subject: Maths
answer: 30 cm³ — Call the depth x. Front and back: 2 × 5 × 2.5 = 25; the other four faces: 2 × 5x + 2 × 2.5x = 15x. So 15x = 61 − 25 = 36, x = 2.4, and the volume is 5 × 2.5 × 2.4 = 30.

html:
Two friends share £30 in the ratio 5 : 1

Work out the value of the larger share.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £25 — 6 parts = £30, so 1 part = £5 and the larger share is 5 × 5 = £25.

html:
A bag contains 40 counters that are either red or blue.

number of red counters : number of blue counters = 2 : 3

Work out the number of blue counters in the bag.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 24 — 5 parts = 40, so 1 part = 8; blue = 3 × 8 = 24.

html:
There are 200 students in Year 11.

number of students who study history : number of students who do not study history = 3 : 7

Work out the number of students who do not study history.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 140 — 10 parts = 200, so 1 part = 20; 7 × 20 = 140.

html:
Adam and Bella share £63 in the ratio 2 : 5

Work out how much money Bella receives.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £45 — 7 parts = £63, so 1 part = £9; Bella gets 5 × 9 = £45.

html:
A bag contains 32 counters that are either green or blue.

green counters : blue counters = 5 : 3

Work out the number of blue counters in the bag.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 12 — 8 parts = 32, so 1 part = 4; blue = 3 × 4 = 12.

html:
Alice and Ben share £42 in the ratio 2 : 1

Work out how much money Alice receives.

subject: Maths
answer: £28 — 3 parts = £42, so 1 part = £14; Alice gets 2 × 14 = £28.

html:

red counters : blue counters = 5 : 3

Work out the number of blue counters.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths

html:

Charlie receives £28

subject: Maths

html:

Length of shorter piece : length of longer piece = 4 : 5

The longer piece is 90 cm long.

Work out the length of the shorter piece.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 72 cm — 5 parts = 90 cm, so 1 part = 18 cm; 4 × 18 = 72.

html: Ethan, Freya and Grace share £65 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths

html: Work out how much money Ethan receives.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £13 — 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts = £65, so 1 part = £6.50 and Ethan gets 2 × 6.50 = £13.

html: Work out how much money Freya receives.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £19.50 — 1 part = 65 ÷ 10 = £6.50, and Freya gets 3 × 6.50 = £19.50.

html: Work out how much money Grace receives.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £32.50 — 1 part = 65 ÷ 10 = £6.50, and Grace gets 5 × 6.50 = £32.50.

html:
Isla takes part in a triathlon where she must swim, ride a bike and then run.

The ratio of the time she spends swimming, riding and running is:

swimming : riding : running = 5 : 14 : 8

Isla spent 20 minutes running.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths

html: Work out how long she spent swimming.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 12.5 minutes — running is 8 parts = 20 minutes, so 1 part = 2.5 minutes and swimming is 5 × 2.5 = 12.5.
accept: 12.5 | 12.5 minutes | 12.5 mins | 12.5 min | 12 minutes 30 seconds | 12 min 30 s

html: Work out how long she spent riding.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 35 minutes — 1 part = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 minutes, and riding is 14 × 2.5 = 35.
examiner_note: The worksheet gives 3 marks for the question as a whole (1 part = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 minutes, then both times), so all 3 sit on this last part: both times right for full marks.

html:
Kai buys one tea, one coffee and one cake from a shop.

price of a tea : price of a coffee : price of a cake = 3 : 5 : 8

Kai pays a total of £6.72

Work out the price of a tea from the shop.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £1.26 — 16 parts = £6.72, so 1 part = £0.42; tea = 3 × 0.42 = £1.26.

html:
A country kept track of the gold, silver and bronze medals they win at a sporting competition.

gold medals : silver medals : bronze medals = 1 : 4 : 7

The country won 24 silver medals.

Work out how many medals the country won in total.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 72 — 4 parts = 24, so 1 part = 6; the total is 12 parts = 72.

html:

Millie receives £35 more than Leo.

Work out how much money Leo receives.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: £10 — The difference is 9 − 2 = 7 parts = £35, so 1 part = £5; Leo gets 2 × 5 = £10.

html:

There are 85 more black counters than white counters.

Work out how many counters are in the bag in total.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 153 — 5 parts = 85, so 1 part = 17; the total is 9 parts = 153.

html:
Hannah uploads the same video to YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

YouTube views : TikTok views : Instagram views = 7 : 9 : 3

The video receives 14 400 more views on TikTok than YouTube.

Work out how many views the video received on Instagram.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 21 600 — 9 − 7 = 2 parts = 14400, so 1 part = 7200; Instagram = 3 × 7200 = 21600.

subject: Maths

html:

Ruby’s distance thrown : Paige’s distance thrown = 5 : 9

Paige threw the shotput 3.6 m further than Ruby.

Work out how far Paige threw the shot put.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 8.1 m — 9 − 5 = 4 parts = 3.6 m, so 1 part = 0.9 m; Paige = 9 × 0.9 = 8.1.

html:

Sebastian’s Paper 1 mark was greater than 50 but less than 60.

Work out how many marks he scored in total for all three papers.

subject: Maths

html:
The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7

Show that the triangle has exactly two acute angles.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: The angles are 30°, 45° and 105° — 12 parts = 180°, so 1 part = 15°: 2 × 15 = 30° and 3 × 15 = 45° are acute, and 7 × 15 = 105° is obtuse — so exactly two are acute.

html:
Sky Blue paint is made by mixing blue and white paint as shown below.

Sky Blue Paint

blue : white = 5 : 3

Laura wants to make Sky Blue paint.

She mixes 720 ml of blue paint with 400 ml of white paint.

Work out how much more white paint she should add to make Sky Blue paint.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 32 ml — 720 ml is 5 parts, so 1 part = 144 ml and she needs 3 × 144 = 432 ml of white; 432 − 400 = 32.

html:
A drink is made using juice and water in the ratio shown below.

juice : water = 2 : 11

Umar has 500 ml of juice and 3000 ml of water.

Work out the maximum amount of drink Umar can make.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 3250 ml — Juice allows 1 part = 500 ÷ 2 = 250 ml; water allows 3000 ÷ 11 ≈ 273 ml. Juice runs out first, so 1 part = 250 ml and the drink is 13 × 250 = 3250 ml (500 juice + 2750 water).

html:
A paint mixture is made by mixing yellow and white paint in the ratio shown.

yellow : white = 10 : 3

Zaria has 1.8 litres of yellow paint and 600 ml of white paint.

Work out the greatest amount of paint mixture that Zaria can make.

Give your answer in millilitres.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 2340 ml — Yellow allows 1 part = 1800 ÷ 10 = 180 ml; white allows 600 ÷ 3 = 200 ml. Yellow runs out first: 13 × 180 = 2340 ml.

html:
A cake recipe uses butter, sugar and flour in the ratio shown below.

butter : sugar : flour = 2 : 3 : 5

Nadia has

400 g of butter

500 g of sugar

750 g of flour

Nadia makes the largest cake possible using the recipe.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths

html: Work out how much butter Nadia will use.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 300 g — one part can be at most 400 ÷ 2 = 200 (butter), 500 ÷ 3 ≈ 167 (sugar) or 750 ÷ 5 = 150 (flour); flour limits it, so 1 part = 150 g and butter is 2 × 150 = 300 g.

html: Work out how much sugar Nadia will use.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 450 g — the flour limits the cake to 1 part = 150 g, so sugar is 3 × 150 = 450 g.

html: Work out how much flour Nadia will use.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 750 g — 1 part = 150 g, so flour is 5 × 150 = 750 g: all of her flour.
examiner_note: The worksheet gives 4 marks for the question as a whole (finding which ingredient limits the cake, 1 part = 150 g, then all three amounts), so all 4 sit on this last part: all three amounts right for full marks.

html:
A shop sells red balloons and blue balloons.

Red balloons are sold in packs of 10

Blue balloons are sold in packs of 12

Tom buys twice as many packs of red balloons as he does blue balloons.

In total Tom buys 128 balloons.

Work out how many packs of red balloons Tom buys.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 8 packs — For every 1 blue pack (12) there are 2 red packs (20): 32 balloons per set. 128 ÷ 32 = 4 sets, so 4 blue packs and 8 red packs.

html:
A shop sells AA and AAA batteries.

AA batteries are sold in packs of 8

AAA batteries are sold in packs of 6.

One day the shop sells a total of 960 batteries.

AA battery packs sold : AAA battery packs sold = 5 : 4

Work out the number of AA battery packs that were sold.
name: Working with Ratio
subject: Maths
answer: 75 — Each set of 5 AA packs and 4 AAA packs holds 5 × 8 + 4 × 6 = 64 batteries. 960 ÷ 64 = 15 sets, so 5 × 15 = 75 AA packs.

html:

l : w = 3 : 2

subject: Maths

lead: Source: an extract from the middle of a novel, describing a spotted hyena. Lines 1 to 6.
html:
Read again the first part of the source, from lines 1 to 6.

List four things about hyenas from this part of the source.
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — June 2023
subject: English Language
answer:
Any four true points about hyenas, taken only from lines 1 to 6

—

identify and interpret explicit information (4 marks)

One mark for each acceptable point, to a maximum of four. Points must come from lines 1 to 6 only; a correct fact from elsewhere in the source earns nothing. A quotation counts if it carries the point.

Points the mark scheme credits (one mark each): hyenas worry Pi; they attack in packs; they go for any animal they can run down; they attack zebras, gnus and water buffalo; they attack full-grown animals, not only the old or the weak; they are hardy and get straight back up after being kicked or butted; they never give up; they are clever. A point that joins two of these still earns one mark each, up to four.

lead: Lines 10 to 19 of the source, describing the hyena's appearance.
html:
Look in detail at the extract from lines 10 to 19 of the source.

How does the writer use language here to describe the hyena’s appearance?

You could include the writer’s choice of: words and phrases; language features and techniques; sentence forms.
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — June 2023
subject: English Language
answer:
Analysis of the words, language features and sentence forms in lines 10–19 that show the hyena’s appearance —

AO2 — language (8 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed (7–8 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant (5–6 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some understanding and comment (3–4 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–2 marks)

The question names words and phrases, language features and sentence forms. A response that identifies a device without saying what it does stays in Level 2.

What to look for in lines 10–19: the blunt short sentence calling the hyena ugly “beyond redemption” — a judgement, and a hint of something bad inside it; the comparison with a leopard’s “classy” spots, which makes the hyena’s look like a skin disease; the bear comparison with a “receding hairline” and the “ridiculously mouse-like” ears, which mock it as well as describe it; the run of short flat statements about mouth, nostrils and tail that pile up the faults; and the ending — doglike, but no dog anyone would want as a pet — ugly, unloved and not to be trusted.

lead: The whole of the source.
html:
You now need to think about the whole of the source. This text is from the middle of a novel.

How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?

You could write about: what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning of the source; how and why the writer changes this focus as the source develops; any other structural features that interest you.
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — June 2023
subject: English Language
answer:
Perceptive analysis of structure across the whole source: where it begins, where the focus shifts, how it ends —

AO2 — structure (8 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed (7–8 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant (5–6 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some understanding and comment (3–4 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–2 marks)

Structure means the whole source: where it begins, where the focus shifts, how it ends. Analysing one paragraph’s language here is the commonest way to lose the marks.

The shape of the source: it opens on Pi’s worry and his father’s warning, so the hyena arrives as a threat before we see it; it narrows to a close-up of the hyena’s appearance; it shifts to the hyena’s wild behaviour in the boat, where the tension rises; and it ends in an anticlimax — the hyena stops and does not move for the rest of the day, so the danger is held off rather than over.

lead: The second part of the source, from line 20 to the end.
html:
Focus this part of your answer on the second part of the source, from line 20 to the end.

A student said, “This part of the story, where the hyena behaves wildly, is funny rather than frightening. The writer suggests that the hyena is actually no serious threat to Pi.”

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could: consider your impressions of how the hyena behaves; evaluate how the writer presents the threat of the hyena to Pi; support your response with references to the text.
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — June 2023
subject: English Language
answer:
A perceptive, detailed evaluation of how far the hyena is funny rather than a threat, with references from line 20 on —

AO4 — evaluate critically (20 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed evaluation (16–20 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant evaluation (11–15 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some evaluation (6–10 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited evaluation (1–5 marks)

The student’s statement is the thing being evaluated. Agreement is not required; a response that only describes what happens, without judging how well it is done, stays in Level 2.

Both sides are there to weigh. Funny: the hyena’s frantic, pointless circling, the absurd detail, and Pi’s wry, mocking voice. Frightening: what Pi already knows about hyenas from his father, how close and unpredictable it is in a small boat, and the sense that it has stopped for now rather than for good. The strongest answers decide how far they agree and keep testing the statement against particular moments from line 20 on.

name: Physics Paper 1 — June 2023

subject: Combined Science

html:
The hot coffee increases the temperature of the air in the chamber.

Explain how the pressure in the chamber changes.
name: Physics Paper 1 — June 2023
subject: Combined Science
answer: The pressure increases — the air particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls of the chamber more often and with more force, giving a greater force per unit area.
examiner_note: Not checked against the paper or its mark scheme: neither is in the owner's Drive. Worked from the question as typed here.

html:
For the device to work, the air in the chamber must increase in temperature quickly.

Explain why the bottom of the air chamber is made of metal rather than plastic.
name: Physics Paper 1 — June 2023
subject: Combined Science
answer: Metal is a better thermal conductor than plastic — so energy is transferred from the hot coffee to the air in the chamber at a higher rate.

html: 3⁄8  −  1⁄4
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄8 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 8 is the smallest number both 8 and 4 divide into, so it becomes 3⁄8 − 2⁄8 = 1⁄8.

html: 7⁄20  +  2⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄4 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 20 is the smallest number both 20 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 7⁄20 + 8⁄20 = 15⁄20. 15⁄20 cancels down to 3⁄4.

html: 11⁄18  +  1⁄6
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 7⁄9 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 18 is the smallest number both 18 and 6 divide into, so it becomes 11⁄18 + 3⁄18 = 14⁄18. 14⁄18 cancels down to 7⁄9.

html: 7⁄15  −  1⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths

html: 39⁄100  −  7⁄20
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄25 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 100 is the smallest number both 100 and 20 divide into, so it becomes 39⁄100 − 35⁄100 = 4⁄100. 4⁄100 cancels down to 1⁄25.

html: 1⁄2  +  2⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths

html: 3⁄4  −  2⁄5

What fraction of the cars in car park are red or blue?

This week Harry spent 2⁄3 of his pocket money on a ticket for a match

What fraction of his pocket money has Harry spent?

subject: Maths
answer: 7⁄9 — ninths are already thirds cut smaller, so only the first fraction moves: 2⁄3 is 6⁄9, and 6 + 1 = 7 ninths.

subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄10 — there are only three colours, so they make one whole between them. Green and white are 1⁄10 + 6⁄10 = 7⁄10, and 10⁄10 − 7⁄10 = 3⁄10.

subject: Maths

She pours out some orange juice and now has 1⁄4 litre left.

How much orange juice did Yasmin pour out?

subject: Maths
answer: 9⁄20 litre — what was poured out is what has gone: 7⁄10 − 1⁄4. Twentieths take both, so 14⁄20 − 5⁄20 = 9⁄20.

name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 19⁄30 — three at once is no different from two: find one bottom they all divide into, which is 30, and add the tops. 10⁄30 + 6⁄30 + 3⁄30 = 19⁄30, and 19 is prime, so nothing cancels.

html: 3⁄4  +  11⁄12
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths

name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths

html: 21⁄4  +  5⁄8
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 27⁄8 — turn the mixed number into 9⁄4 first, then the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 8 is the smallest number both 4 and 8 divide into, so it becomes 18⁄8 + 5⁄8 = 23⁄8. That is more than one whole, so it is written 27⁄8.

Kayleigh is walking from Antrim to Randalstown

Work out the distance from Antrim to Randalstown

subject: Maths

subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄9 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are subtracted: 7 − 5 = 2, over 9.

html: 6⁄11  +  2⁄11
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 8⁄11 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 6 + 2 = 8, over 11.

html: 16⁄25  −  4⁄25
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 12⁄25 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are subtracted: 16 − 4 = 12, over 25.

html: 2⁄3  +  2⁄3
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 11⁄3 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 2 + 2 = 4, over 3. That is more than one whole, so it is written 11⁄3.

html: 3⁄8  +  7⁄8
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths

html:
1⁄12 of the cupcakes in a box are lemon

4⁄12 of the cupcakes in the box are strawberry

What fraction of the cupcakes in the box are lemon or strawberry?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄12 — “or” means put the two groups together, so add them: 1 + 4 = 5 twelfths. It does not cancel, because 5 and 12 share no factor.

html:
1⁄3 of the students in a class are left handed.

What fraction of the class are right handed?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄3 — everybody is one or the other, so the whole class is 1, which is 3⁄3. Take away the left handers: 3 − 1 = 2 thirds.

html:
On Monday, Kenneth ate 2⁄8 of a cake.

On Tuesday he ate 3⁄8 of the same cake.

In total, how much of the cake has Kenneth eaten?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄8 — “in total” is an add: 2 + 3 = 5 eighths. It is the same cake both days, which is what lets the eighths be added at all.

html:
In one season, a netball team won 4⁄9 of their matches.

They drew 2⁄9 of their matches.

What fraction of the matches did they lose?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄3 — a match is won, drawn or lost and nothing else, so the three make one whole. Won and drawn together are 4 + 2 = 6 ninths, and 9⁄9 − 6⁄9 = 3⁄9, which cancels to 1⁄3.

html:
In a school, the children study French, German or Spanish.

1⁄7 of the children study Spanish.

Half of the remaining children study French.

What fraction of the children study French?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄7 — the trap is “half”, which is half of what is LEFT and not half of the school. Spanish takes 1⁄7, leaving 6⁄7, and half of six sevenths is three sevenths.

html: Write down Angle 2 and Angle 3 for the scalene triangle.
name: Angles in a Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Two different angles that add to 160°, e.g. 60° and 100° — the angles make 180°, so the other two make 180 − 20 = 160°; a scalene triangle has no two angles equal, so not 80° and 80° nor 20° and 140°, and 70° and 90° would be the right-angled triangle again.
examiner_note: Many answers are right: any two different angles adding to 160°, neither of them 20°, and not 70° with 90°. So it is left for a person to mark.

html: Write down Angle 2 and Angle 3 for the right-angled triangle.
name: Angles in a Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: 90° and 20° — one angle is the right angle, 90°, and the third is 180 − 90 − 70 = 20°.

html: Write down Angle 2 and Angle 3 for the first isosceles triangle.
name: Angles in a Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: 50° and 80°, or 65° and 65° — either the 50° is repeated, leaving 180 − 50 − 50 = 80°, or the 50° is the odd angle and the equal pair share 130°, 65° each.

html: Write down Angle 2 and Angle 3 for the second isosceles triangle. It must be different from the first.
name: Angles in a Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Whichever of 50° and 80° or 65° and 65° was not used for the first — the triangles are all different, so the two isosceles triangles take one way each: 50°, 50°, 80° and 50°, 65°, 65°.
examiner_note: Right only if it is the other isosceles pair from part (c), so it is left for a person to mark.

html:
The area of a football pitch is 6,040m².

A hockey pitch is 91 metres long and 37 metres wide.

How much larger is the area of the football pitch than the area of the hockey pitch?
name: Area of a Square / Area of a Rectangle
subject: Maths
answer: 2,673 m² — the hockey pitch is 91 × 37 = 3,367 m², and 6,040 − 3,367 = 2,673.

html:
Mrs Jenkins is a chicken farmer

Her rectangular chicken pen is 18 metres long and 8 metres wide.

Each chicken needs at least 3m² of space.

How many chickens can Mrs Jenkins keep?
name: Area of a Square / Area of a Rectangle
subject: Maths
answer: 48 chickens — the pen is 18 × 8 = 144 m², and 144 ÷ 3 = 48.

html:
A square measures 30cm by 30cm

A rectangle is 7cm longer and 2cm narrower than the square.

What is the difference in area between the two shapes?
name: Area of a Square / Area of a Rectangle
subject: Maths
answer: 136 cm² — the square is 30 × 30 = 900; the rectangle is 37 by 28, which is 1,036; and 1,036 − 900 = 136.

html:
Rosie says

“If two rectangles have the same area, they must have the same perimeter.”

Is Rosie right? Circle Yes or No

Yes / No

Explain your answer
name: Area of a Square / Area of a Rectangle
subject: Maths
answer: No — a 1cm by 12cm rectangle and a 3cm by 4cm rectangle both have an area of 12cm², but their perimeters are 26cm and 14cm.

html: Altogether, how many children play a musical instrument
name: Bar Charts
subject: Maths
answer: 150 — the “play” bars are 100 in Year 4 and 50 in Year 6, and 100 + 50 = 150.

html: How many more children are there in Year 4 than Year 6?
name: Bar Charts
subject: Maths
answer: 10 — Year 4 has 100 + 70 = 170 children and Year 6 has 50 + 110 = 160, and 170 − 160 = 10.
