html: List the factors of 10
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 2, 5, 10 — a factor divides the number exactly. Work in PAIRS from the outside in and you cannot miss one: 1 × 10, 2 × 5, and 3 and 4 do not go, so you are done.

html: List the factors of 18
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 — in pairs: 1 × 18, 2 × 9, 3 × 6. The next try is 4 (no) then 5 (no), and by then the pairs have met in the middle, which is how you know to stop.

html: List the factors of 25
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 5, 25 — only three, because 25 is a square number: 1 × 25 and 5 × 5. A square always has an odd number of factors, since one pair is a number with itself.

html: List the factors of 40
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 40 — in pairs: 1 × 40, 2 × 20, 4 × 10, 5 × 8. Eight of them, and 3, 6, 7 and 9 all fail.

34567913
name: Factors
subject: Maths

html: From the list, write down a factor of 14
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — 14 = 2 × 7, and 7 is the only number on the list that goes into 14.

html: From the list, write down a factor of 26
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 13 — 26 = 2 × 13, and 13 is the only number on the list that goes into 26.

html:
Here is a list of numbers.

Circle any number in the list that is a factor of 24
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 4, 6, 8, 12 — 24 = 4 × 6 = 8 × 3 = 12 × 2. From the list, 5, 7, 10, 13 and 14 all leave a remainder. 14 is the tempting one: 24 is even and 14 is even, but even does not mean it divides.

html: Write three factors of 40 which are also factors of 30
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Any three of 1, 2, 5, 10 — these are the four numbers that divide BOTH 40 and 30, and a quick way to find them all at once is that they are exactly the factors of 10, the highest common factor. Any three of the four earns the mark.

html: Write all the factors of 36 which are also factors of 27
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 3, 9 — all of them this time, not a choice. They are the factors of 9, which is the highest common factor of 36 and 27. Note what changed from the question before: "write all" means the complete list, so leaving out the 1 loses it.

html: Write four factors of 48 that are not factors of 30
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Any four of 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 — 48 has factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 and 30 has 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30, so knock out the ones they share (1, 2, 3, 6) and six are left. Any four of those six.

html:
Jemima has 32 sweets and is able to share them equally between her friends.

Jemima has more than 5 friends but less than 20 friends.

Write down how many friends Jemima might have.
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 8 or 16 — sharing 32 equally means the number of friends is a factor of 32: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. More than 5 and fewer than 20 leaves 8 and 16. Both are right, so either earns it — the question says "might have".

html:
Shannon writes down three different factors of 36

She adds her three numbers together.

The answer is greater than 30 but less than 35.

What three numbers could Shannon have written down?
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Several work, and 4, 12, 18 is the neatest — the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, and you want three DIFFERENT ones adding to between 31 and 34. Start from the big ones: 18 has to be in it, because without it the three largest left are 12 + 9 + 6 = 27, short of 31. Then 12 + 18 = 30 needs 1, 2, 3 or 4 alongside, and 9 + 18 = 27 needs 4 or 6. The full set is 1+12+18, 2+12+18, 3+12+18, 4+12+18, 4+9+18 and 6+9+18.

html: Write all the numbers between 12 and 50 that are factors of 90
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 15, 18, 30, 45 — the factors of 90 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 15, 18, 30, 45, 90, and "between 12 and 50" keeps four of them. Watch both ends: 10 is below 12 and 90 is above 50, and neither counts.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: In a school, 2⁄5 of the children wear glasses.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: What fraction of the children do not wear glasses?
answer: 3⁄5 — the whole school is 5⁄5, so 5⁄5 − 2⁄5 = 3⁄5.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: What percentage of the children do not wear glasses?
answer: 60% — 3⁄5 is 60⁄100, which is 60%.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html:
There are 30 sweets in a bag.

20 sweets are red.

What fraction of the sweets are red?
answer: 2⁄3 — 20 out of 30 is 20⁄30, and 20 and 30 both divide by 10.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: CORBETTMATHS

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: What fraction of the letters are the letter T?
answer: 1⁄4 — three of the 12 letters are T, and 3⁄12 cancels to 1⁄4.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: What fraction of the letters are the letter A?
answer: 1⁄12 — one of the 12 letters is A, and 1⁄12 does not cancel.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html:
In a town in Cornwall, it rained for 13 days during April.

What fraction of the days in the month did it rain?
answer: 13⁄30 — April has 30 days, and 13 and 30 share no factor so it does not cancel. The 30 is not printed in the question: knowing it is the part of this one that is not arithmetic.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html:
During a day, Madeleine slept for 6 hours.

What percentage of the day is Madeleine awake?
answer: 75% — a day is 24 hours, so she is awake for 24 − 6 = 18 of them; 18⁄24 cancels to 3⁄4, which is 75%.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html:
Danny scored 9 out of 10 in a quiz.

What percentage of the questions did Danny answer correctly?
answer: 90% — 9⁄10 is 90⁄100, and a percentage is hundredths.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: Write 17% as a fraction.
answer: 17⁄100 — a percentage is hundredths, and 17 and 100 share no factor so it does not cancel.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: Write 7⁄20 as a percentage.
answer: 35% — 20 × 5 = 100, so multiply the top by 5 as well: 7⁄20 is 35⁄100.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: Write 14⁄25 as a percentage.
answer: 56% — 25 × 4 = 100, so multiply the top by 4 as well: 14⁄25 is 56⁄100.

name: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
subject: Maths
html: Write 1⁄8 as a decimal.
answer: 0.125 — 1 ÷ 8. Halving three times gets there too: 1⁄2 is 0.5, 1⁄4 is 0.25, 1⁄8 is 0.125.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 1⁄4 of 24
answer: 6 — 1⁄4 of 24 is 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 1⁄3 of 18
answer: 6 — 1⁄3 of 18 is 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 1⁄5 of 60
answer: 12 — 1⁄5 of 60 is 60 ÷ 5 = 12.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 2⁄3 of 15
answer: 10 — one third is 15 ÷ 3 = 5, and there are 2 of them: 5 × 2 = 10.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 3⁄4 of 36
answer: 27 — one quarter is 36 ÷ 4 = 9, and there are 3 of them: 9 × 3 = 27.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 2⁄5 of 40
answer: 16 — one fifth is 40 ÷ 5 = 8, and there are 2 of them: 8 × 2 = 16.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html: Work out 6⁄7 of 56
answer: 48 — one seventh is 56 ÷ 7 = 8, and there are 6 of them: 8 × 6 = 48.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html:
James has 20 sweets.

3⁄4 of the sweets are red.

How many sweets are red?
answer: 15 — one quarter is 20 ÷ 4 = 5, and there are 3 of them: 5 × 3 = 15.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html:
In a class, there are 27 children.

2⁄9 of the children wear glasses.

How many children do not wear glasses?
answer: 21 — one ninth is 27 ÷ 9 = 3, and there are 2 of them: 3 × 2 = 6. So 6 wear glasses, and 27 − 6 = 21 do not. The question asks for the ones who do NOT, so the fraction answer is an intermediate step and not the answer.

name: Fraction of Amounts
subject: Maths
html:
Raphael has a book with 120 pages.

He has read 3⁄5 of the pages in his book.

How many pages has Raphael read?
answer: 72 — one fifth is 120 ÷ 5 = 24, and there are 3 of them: 24 × 3 = 72.

html: 3⁄7 ÷ 3
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄7 — 3 divides by 3, so only the top changes: 3 ÷ 3 = 1, which leaves 1⁄7.

html: 2⁄3 ÷ 2
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄3 — 2 divides by 2, so only the top changes: 2 ÷ 2 = 1, which leaves 1⁄3.

html: 5⁄9 ÷ 5
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄9 — 5 divides by 5, so only the top changes: 5 ÷ 5 = 1, which leaves 1⁄9.

html: 9⁄10 ÷ 3
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄10 — 9 divides by 3, so only the top changes: 9 ÷ 3 = 3, which leaves 3⁄10.

html: 4⁄11 ÷ 2
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄11 — 4 divides by 2, so only the top changes: 4 ÷ 2 = 2, which leaves 2⁄11.

html: 6⁄7 ÷ 3
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄7 — 6 divides by 3, so only the top changes: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, which leaves 2⁄7.

html: 1⁄3 ÷ 2
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄6 — 1 does not divide by 2, so cut each part into 2 instead: the bottom becomes 3 × 2 = 6 and the top stays 1, which gives 1⁄6.

html: 1⁄4 ÷ 3
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄12 — 1 does not divide by 3, so cut each part into 3 instead: the bottom becomes 4 × 3 = 12 and the top stays 1, which gives 1⁄12.

html: 1⁄2 ÷ 10
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄20 — 1 does not divide by 10, so cut each part into 10 instead: the bottom becomes 2 × 10 = 20 and the top stays 1, which gives 1⁄20.

html: 5⁄8 ÷ 2
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄16 — 5 does not divide by 2, so cut each part into 2 instead: the bottom becomes 8 × 2 = 16 and the top stays 5, which gives 5⁄16.

html: 3⁄10 ÷ 2
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄20 — 3 does not divide by 2, so cut each part into 2 instead: the bottom becomes 10 × 2 = 20 and the top stays 3, which gives 3⁄20.

html: 4⁄5 ÷ 3
name: Fractions: Division
subject: Maths
answer: 4⁄15 — 4 does not divide by 3, so cut each part into 3 instead: the bottom becomes 5 × 3 = 15 and the top stays 4, which gives 4⁄15.

html: How many degrees warmer was it at 2pm than 11am?
name: Line Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 7°C — at 11am it was −2°C and at 2pm 5°C: from −2 up to 0 is 2 degrees and on to 5 is 5 more, 7 in all.

html:
At 4pm the temperature was 3 degrees lower than at 3pm

What was the temperature at 4pm?
name: Line Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: −1°C — at 3pm it was 2°C, and 3 degrees lower is 2 − 3 = −1.

html: Change 5 miles into kilometres
name: Line Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 8 km — go up from 5 miles to the line and across: 8 km.

html: Change 10 miles into kilometres
name: Line Graphs
subject: Maths
answer: 16 km — 10 miles is past the end of the line, so double: 10 miles is 2 × 5 miles, so it is 2 × 8 = 16 km.

html:
Here is an arrow.

Draw any lines of symmetry on the arrow
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: One line, straight down the middle of the arrow from its tip to the middle of its bottom edge — folded along it, the two halves of the head and of the stem land exactly on each other. A line across the arrow does not work, because the head and the stem are different shapes.

html: On the rectangle, draw all the lines of symmetry
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: Two lines: one straight down the middle and one straight across the middle — each joins the middles of two opposite sides. The diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry: fold a rectangle along a diagonal and the corners do not meet.

html:
Here is a rhombus

Draw any lines of symmetry on the rhombus
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: Two lines: the two diagonals, top corner to bottom corner and left corner to right corner — a rhombus folds onto itself along each diagonal. Lines through the middles of its sides do not work, because its corners are not right angles.

html:
The diagram below shows a regular hexagon.

How many lines of symmetry does the hexagon have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — a regular hexagon has as many lines of symmetry as sides: 3 joining opposite corners and 3 joining the middles of opposite sides.

html: How many lines of symmetry does sign (a), the warning triangle with a road hump, have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — it folds only down its middle, from the top corner to the middle of the bottom edge.

html: How many lines of symmetry does sign (b), the round no-waiting sign with one diagonal bar, have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — it folds along its bar and straight across the bar.

html: How many lines of symmetry does sign (c), the round keep-left sign with its arrow, have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — it folds only along the arrow; any other fold turns the arrowhead the wrong way.

html: How many lines of symmetry does sign (d), the roundabout triangle with three curved arrows, have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 0 — the three arrows all chase the same way round, so any fold would turn them backwards. It has rotation, not a line of symmetry.

html: How many lines of symmetry does sign (e), the round national speed limit sign with one diagonal band, have?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — it folds along its band and straight across the band.

html: Which two shapes have a line of symmetry?
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: C and D — D is a trapezium that folds down its middle; C folds along the diagonal through its bottom right corner and its inside corner. A and B only match themselves when turned half a turn, which is rotation, not a line of symmetry.
accept: C and D | D and C | C, D | C & D | CD

html: Draw a triangle that does not have a line of symmetry
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: Any triangle with all three sides different lengths — a scalene triangle has no line of symmetry. If two sides are the same length the triangle folds down its middle, so avoid isosceles and equilateral triangles.

name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: Shade the square nearest the top left corner, or the middle square of the bottom row — the first gives a line of symmetry straight across the middle; the second gives one along the diagonal from the top left corner to the bottom right corner. Either works and each gives exactly one line; every other square leaves a shaded square with no partner.

html:
The diagram below shows a regular pentagon.

Draw all the lines of symmetry
name: Line Symmetry
subject: Maths
answer: Five lines, each from a corner to the middle of the opposite side — a regular pentagon has as many lines of symmetry as sides. With an odd number of sides every line runs corner to side, never corner to corner.

html:
Molly visits a restaurant with her friends.
This is a menu.

StartersMains
SoupChicken
Prawn CocktailBeef
MelonPizza

Molly chooses one starter and one main.

List all the possible combinations.
name: Listing Outcomes
subject: Maths
answer: 9 combinations: each of Soup, Prawn Cocktail and Melon with each of Chicken, Beef and Pizza — Soup and Chicken, Soup and Beef, Soup and Pizza, Prawn Cocktail and Chicken, Prawn Cocktail and Beef, Prawn Cocktail and Pizza, Melon and Chicken, Melon and Beef, Melon and Pizza. 3 starters, each with any of 3 mains, is 3 × 3 = 9; listing one starter at a time is what makes sure none is missed.

html:
Orla has four types of vegetable.

Peas
Carrots
Turnip
Spinach

Orla is going to choose 2 different types of vegetable.

List all the possible combinations of vegetable she can choose
name: Listing Outcomes
subject: Maths
answer: Peas and Carrots, Peas and Turnip, Peas and Spinach, Carrots and Turnip, Carrots and Spinach, Turnip and Spinach — six pairs. Carrots and Peas is the same choice as Peas and Carrots, so each pair is written once, and Peas and Peas is not allowed because the two must be different.

html:
A rugby team plays two matches.

They can win, draw or lose each match.

Write the seven missing combinations.

The rugby team could:

Win and Win

Win and Draw
name: Listing Outcomes
subject: Maths
answer: Win and Lose, Draw and Win, Draw and Draw, Draw and Lose, Lose and Win, Lose and Draw, Lose and Lose — 3 results in the first match and 3 in the second make 3 × 3 = 9, and two are given. Draw and Win is NOT the same as Win and Draw: it is a different match that was won.

html:
Magnus flips a fair coin once and rolls an ordinary dice once.

One possible result that Magnus could get is a Tail and a 1

Write down all the other possible results
name: Listing Outcomes
subject: Maths
answer: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6 (H for a Head, T for a Tail) — Head and 1, Head and 2, Head and 3, Head and 4, Head and 5, Head and 6, Tail and 2, Tail and 3, Tail and 4, Tail and 5, Tail and 6. 2 sides of the coin with 6 numbers on the dice is 2 × 6 = 12 results, and Tail and 1 is already given, leaving 11.

html:
William is going to attend a two day summer camp.

He can take part in one activity on Monday and one activity on Tuesday.

MondayTuesday
GolfIce-skating
FootballSwimming
RugbyDodgeball
HockeyBasketball

List all the possible combinations of activity he can take part in.
name: Listing Outcomes
subject: Maths
answer: 16 combinations: each of Golf, Football, Rugby and Hockey with each of Ice-skating, Swimming, Dodgeball and Basketball — Golf and Ice-skating, Golf and Swimming, Golf and Dodgeball, Golf and Basketball, Football and Ice-skating, Football and Swimming, Football and Dodgeball, Football and Basketball, Rugby and Ice-skating, Rugby and Swimming, Rugby and Dodgeball, Rugby and Basketball, Hockey and Ice-skating, Hockey and Swimming, Hockey and Dodgeball, Hockey and Basketball. 4 Monday activities, each with any of 4 on Tuesday, is 4 × 4 = 16.

html: Write down the size of the angle being measured
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: 30° — the base arm points left, to the 0 of the outer scale, so read the outer scale: the other arm crosses it at 30. The inner scale says 150 at the same place, but the angle is small and acute, so 150 cannot be it.

html: Write down the size of the angle being measured
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: 75° — the base arm points left, to the 0 of the outer scale, and the other arm crosses that scale halfway between 70 and 80. The angle is acute, so it is not the 105 on the inner scale.

html: Write down the size of the angle being measured
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: 20° — this time the base arm points RIGHT, to the 0 of the inner scale, so read the inner scale: 20. The outer scale gives 160 at the same spot, which is far too big for an angle this small.

html: Write down the size of the angle being measured
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: 130° — the marked angle is the obtuse one, opening from the left-hand arm over the top. That arm sits on the outer scale's 0, and the outer scale reads 130 where the other arm crosses; 50 is the angle on the other side of the arm.

html: Draw a 40° angle
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: An angle of 40° — draw one straight line, put the protractor's centre on one end with the base line along it, count up from the 0 on that line to 40, mark it and join the mark to the end. It should look a little less than half a right angle.

html: Draw an 80° angle
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: An angle of 80° — draw one straight line, put the protractor's centre on one end with the base line along it, count up from the 0 on that line to 80, mark it and join the mark to the end. It should look a little less than a right angle.

html: Draw a 110° angle
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: An angle of 110° — draw one straight line, put the protractor's centre on one end with the base line along it, count up from the 0 on that line to 110, mark it and join the mark to the end. It should look obtuse, 20° more than a right angle.

html: Draw a 160° angle
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: An angle of 160° — draw one straight line, put the protractor's centre on one end with the base line along it, count up from the 0 on that line to 160, mark it and join the mark to the end. It should look obtuse, only 20° short of a straight line.

name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing

answer: 109° — measured on the paper's own drawing. It is obtuse, so if the protractor says 71, that is the other scale. Anything from 107° to 111° is a fair measurement.

name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths

answer: 78° — measured on the paper's own drawing. It is just under a right angle, so if the protractor says 102, that is the other scale. Anything from 76° to 80° is a fair measurement.

html:
Lauren has been asked to measure this angle.

Her answer is 65°

Explain her mistake
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
answer: She read the wrong scale: the angle is obtuse, so it is 115°, not 65° — the base arm points right, to the 0 of the INNER scale, so that is the scale to count on, and it reads 115. 65 is on the outer scale, which counts from the 0 at the other end. An angle wider than a right angle cannot be 65°.

Measure the size of the largest angle
name: Angles: Measuring & Drawing
subject: Maths
diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 340 166" role="img" aria-label="A long thin triangle. Its bottom side is horizontal; from its right-hand end a short side goes steeply up to the right to the top corner, and the longest side slopes back down from the top corner to the bottom-left corner. answer: 134° — the largest angle is the obtuse one at the right-hand end of the bottom side. On the paper's drawing it measures 134° (the other two are about 25° and 22°, and the three make 180°). Anything from 132° to 136° is a fair measurement.

html: A can of beans has a mass of 450 grams
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths

html: Draw an arrow on the scale to show 450g
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: An arrow pointing at 450 g, halfway between the 400 and 500 marks — each small mark is 20 g, so 450 is between the second and third small marks after 400.

html:
Olivia has two cans of beans.

What is the mass of two cans of beans?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 900 g — 450 × 2 = 900 g, which is 0.9 kg.

html:
Two apples have the same mass.

Together they have a mass of 320g

What is the mass of one apple?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 160 g — 320 ÷ 2. The word doing the work is "same": two apples of equal mass, so one is half the pair.

html: Draw a 5 centimetre line.
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: A line 5 cm long — measure from the 0 on the ruler, not from the ruler's end, which is the commonest way to be 3 mm out on a question that is otherwise free.

html:
Chloe weighs 58 kilograms.

David weighs 26 kilograms less than Chloe.

Draw an arrow on the scale to show how much David weighs.
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: An arrow pointing at 32 kg, one small mark past 30 — 58 − 26 = 32. “26 kilograms LESS than Chloe” is a subtraction from her mass. Each small mark on the scale is 2 kg.

html: Change 4 metres into centimetres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 400 cm — 4 × 100, and the check is which way it should move: a centimetre is smaller than a metre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 300 centimetres into metres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 3 m — 300 ÷ 100, and the check is which way it should move: a metre is bigger than a centimetre, so the number gets smaller.

html: Change 80 millimetres into centimetres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 8 cm — 80 ÷ 10, and the check is which way it should move: a centimetre is bigger than a millimetre, so the number gets smaller.

html: Change 9 kilometres into metres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 9000 m — 9 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a metre is smaller than a kilometre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 6 litres into millilitres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 6000 ml — 6 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a millilitre is smaller than a litre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 20 kilograms into grams
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 20000 g — 20 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a gram is smaller than a kilogram, so the number gets bigger.

html:
Frank places some oranges on a scale.

He takes away one orange.

The mass goes down by 130 grams.

Draw the pointer in its new position.
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: The pointer at 650 g, halfway between the 640 and 660 marks — the pointer starts at 780 g, one small mark below 800, and each small mark is 20 g. 780 − 130 = 650.

html:
5 identical pink blocks have a mass of 1 kilogram.

Find the mass of one pink block
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 200 g — 1 kg is 1000 g, and 1000 ÷ 5 = 200. Converting FIRST is what makes it easy: 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 kg is the same answer and harder to trust.

html:
Ruth runs 800 metres on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.

How far has she run in total?
Give your answer in kilometres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 4 km — 800 × 5 = 4000 m, and 4000 ÷ 1000 = 4 km. Five days, so five lots of 800 — Monday to Friday is the list, and counting it as four is the slip.

html: Change 2.8 metres into centimetres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 280 cm — 2.8 × 100, and the check is which way it should move: a centimetre is smaller than a metre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 55 centimetres into metres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 0.55 m — 55 ÷ 100, and the check is which way it should move: a metre is bigger than a centimetre, so the number gets smaller.

html: Change 780 metres into kilometres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 0.78 km — 780 ÷ 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a kilometre is bigger than a metre, so the number gets smaller.

html: Change 0.04 kilometres into metres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 40 m — 0.04 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a metre is smaller than a kilometre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 750 millilitres into litres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 0.75 L — 750 ÷ 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a litre is bigger than a millilitre, so the number gets smaller.

html: Change 5.2 kilograms into grams
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 5200 g — 5.2 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a gram is smaller than a kilogram, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 13.5 litres into millilitres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 13500 ml — 13.5 × 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a millilitre is smaller than a litre, so the number gets bigger.

html: Change 16 grams into kilograms
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 0.016 kg — 16 ÷ 1000, and the check is which way it should move: a kilogram is bigger than a gram, so the number gets smaller.

html:
Matthew is 1.74 metres tall.

Write this height in centimetres
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 174 cm — 1.74 × 100. A metre is 100 cm, so the decimal point moves two places, which is the same rule as question 5 dressed as a height.

html:
James and Jack buy 3 litres of orange juice.

Each boy drinks 650 millilitres of orange juice.

How much orange juice is left?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 1700 ml, which is 1.7 litres — 3 litres is 3000 ml, two boys drink 2 × 650 = 1300 ml, and 3000 − 1300 = 1700. EACH boy drinks 650, so it is doubled before it is taken away.

html:
Rebecca has two dogs, Lucky and Pepe

Lucky has a mass of 7.2 kilograms

Pepe is 900 grams lighter than Lucky

How heavy is Pepe?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 6.3 kg — 7.2 kg is 7200 g, minus 900 g is 6300 g, which is 6.3 kg. The two masses are in different units and subtracting 900 from 7.2 is what this question is set to catch.

html:
Michael and Rosie each have a bottle of water.

Michael’s bottle contains 13⁄4 litres

Rosie’s bottle contains 2.2 litres.

How many more millilitres of water does Rosie have than Michael?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 450 ml — 1¾ litres is 1000 + 750 = 1750 ml and 2.2 litres is 2200 ml, so Rosie has 2200 − 1750 = 450 ml more.

html:
Four friends are in a race.

Alice is 4 metres ahead of Barry.

Ciara is 9 metres behind Dylan

Barry is 5 metres behind Dylan

Write the names of the runners in order, starting with the friend who is furthest ahead.
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: Dylan, Alice, Barry, Ciara — put everybody against Dylan. Barry is 5 m behind Dylan; Alice is 4 m ahead of Barry, so she is 1 m behind Dylan; Ciara is 9 m behind Dylan. Fixing on ONE runner is what turns four separate sentences into one line.
examiner_note: THE ORDER IS THE ANSWER: the same items in any other order are wrong. No accept, deliberately: the marker compares a typed list as a set, sorted, so an accept here passed every order, the question's own list copied out unchanged included.

html:
A bottle of cola holds 3 litres.

How many 150 millilitre glasses can be poured from the bottle?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 20 glasses — 3 litres is 3000 ml, and 3000 ÷ 150 = 20. Both numbers have to be in millilitres before you divide; 3 ÷ 150 answers a different question.

html:
Grapes cost £4.80 per kilogram
Blueberries cost £8 per kilogram

Work out the total cost of 250g of grapes and 100g of blueberries
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: £2.00 — 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, so the grapes are 4.80 ÷ 4 = £1.20; 100 g is a tenth of a kilogram, so the blueberries are 8 ÷ 10 = £0.80; and 1.20 + 0.80 = £2.00. Both prices are PER KILOGRAM and both weights are in grams, which is the only hard part.

html:
There are 14 children at a birthday party.

There are 8 litres of lemonade at the beginning of the party.

Each child drank 280 millilitres of lemonade.

How much lemonade is left?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 4080 ml, which is 4.08 litres — 8 litres is 8000 ml, the children drink 14 × 280 = 3920 ml, and 8000 − 3920 = 4080.

html:
A gram of saffron costs £6.18 per gram.

What is the cost of half a kilogram of saffron
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: £3090 — half a kilogram is 500 g, and 500 × 6.18 = 3090. The price is per GRAM and the amount is given in kilograms, so the conversion has to happen before the multiplication — and the answer being enormous is right: saffron is.

html:
A box contains 3kg of rice.

Mario uses 75 grams of rice for each meal.

How many meals did Mario make?
name: Metric Units
subject: Maths
answer: 40 meals — 3 kg is 3000 g, and 3000 ÷ 75 = 40.

html:
Natalie has these coins.

How much money does Natalie have?

subject: Maths

html:
Tilly has £61

Georgina has £14 less than Tilly

How much money do they have in total?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £108 — Georgina has 61 − 14 = £47, and 61 + 47 = £108. The £14 is a difference, not an amount she has.

html:
Lauren puts nine 20p pieces into her piggy bank.

Her mum puts seven 50p pieces into the piggy bank.
Her dad puts six 5p pieces into the piggy bank.

How much money is in the piggy bank?
name: Money
subject: Maths

How much was the sandwich?

html:
Daniel chooses his coins first.
Ben takes the rest of the coins.

Which coins could Daniel choose?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: Any coins making £3.21, for example £2, £1, 20p and 1p — the fifteen coins total £6.42, so each boy must have half of it, £3.21.

html: Which coins would be left for Ben?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: All the other coins, which also make £3.21 — with Daniel’s £2, £1, 20p and 1p, Ben has £1, £1, 50p, 50p, 10p, 5p, 2p, 1p, 1p, 1p and 1p. Whatever Daniel chooses, Ben’s coins must also add up to £3.21.

html:
Henry has £4

He buys 3 packets of crisps costing 70p each.

How much money does he have left?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £1.90 — three packets at 70p are 210p, and 400 − 210 = 190p.

html:
Sam has a bag of 10p coins.
Tyler has a bag of 50p coins.

Both bags have the same amount of money inside.

There are forty 10p coins in Sam’s bag.

How many 50p coins are there in Tyler’s bag?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — forty 10p coins are 400p = £4. The same amount in 50p coins is 400 ÷ 50 = 8 coins.

html:
Sophie saved 50p every day in September

How much money did she save in total?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £15 — September has 30 days, and 30 × 50 = 1500p. The 30 is not printed in the question: knowing it is the part of this one that is not arithmetic.

html:
Jaymin buys three ice creams.

He pays with a £5 note and here is his change

Work out the cost of one ice cream
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £1.35 — the change is 50p + 20p + 20p + 5p = 95p, so three ice creams cost £5.00 − £0.95 = £4.05, and one costs 4.05 ÷ 3 = £1.35.

html:
Hannah has 10p
Erin has 64p

How much money should Erin give Hannah so that they have the same amount of money?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: 27p — together they have 74p, so each should end with 37p. Erin has 64p and needs to get down to 37, so she hands over 64 − 37 = 27p — which is HALF the difference between them, not the whole difference.

html:
Nicole buys a tie and 2 pairs of socks.

She pays with a £20 note.

How much change does she get?
name: Money
subject: Maths
diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 350.6 74" role="img" aria-label="Three price cards: a tie, 1 for £7.50; socks, 2 pairs for £4.99; trainers, 1 pair for £13."><rect x="8" y="6" width="87.3" height="62" rx="7" class="tag"/><text x="51.7" y="32" class="cap">Tie</text><text x="51.7" y="54" class="num">1 for £7.50</text><rect x="103.3" y="6" width="125.1" height="62" rx="7" class="tag"/><text x="165.9" y="32" class="cap">Socks</text><text x="165.9" y="54" class="num">2 pairs for £4.99</text><rect x="236.4" y="6" width="106.2" height="62" rx="7" class="tag"/><text x="289.5" y="32" class="cap">Trainers</text><text x="289.5" y="54" class="num">1 pair for £13</text></svg>
answer: £7.51 — a tie is £7.50 and 2 pairs of socks are £4.99, so she spends £12.49, and £20.00 − £12.49 = £7.51. The trainers are not part of it.

html:
Emma and Tom each buy a toy.

Emma’s toy cost £14

Tom pays with a £10 note and gets £4.25 change.

How much more does Emma’s toy cost than Tom’s toy?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £8.25 — Tom paid £10 and got £4.25 back, so his toy cost 10 − 4.25 = £5.75. Emma’s cost £14, and 14 − 5.75 = £8.25.

html:
Sarah has the same number of 2p coins as 5p coins.

Sarah has £2.10 in 2p coins.

How much money does Sarah have in total?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £7.35 — £2.10 in 2p coins is 210 ÷ 2 = 105 coins, so she has 105 5p coins as well, worth 105 × 5 = 525p. Altogether 210 + 525 = 735p.

html:
Raheem is putting 50p coins into bags.

Each bag holds 20 coins

He has 645 coins

How many bags can Raheem fill?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: 32 — 645 ÷ 20 = 32 remainder 5. The 33rd bag would only have 5 coins in it, and the question asks how many he can FILL.

html:
Magnus has five coins

Three of the coins add up to £1.40
Three of the coins add up to £2.40

All five coins add up to £3.60

What coins does Magnus have?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: Three 20p coins, a £1 and a £2 — the two groups of three overlap by exactly one coin, because 3 + 3 = 6 and there are only 5 coins. 1.40 + 2.40 = £3.80, which is 20p more than the £3.60 total, so the shared coin is 20p. That leaves two coins making £1.20 (a £1 and a 20p) and two making £2.20 (a £2 and a 20p). Checked against every five-coin combination there is, and it is the only one that works.

html:
Sophie has £2.12
Orla has 84p

How much money should Sophie give Orla so that they have the same amount of money?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: 64p — together they have 212 + 84 = 296p, so each should end with 148p. Sophie has 212p and hands over 212 − 148 = 64p — half the difference between them.

html:
Cafe Red sells 3 sandwiches for £5.25

Sandwich World sells 4 sandwiches for £7.08

Which shop is better value for money?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: Cafe Red — work out what ONE sandwich costs at each: 525 ÷ 3 = 175p at Cafe Red and 708 ÷ 4 = 177p at Sandwich World. 175p is less, so Cafe Red is the better value by 2p a sandwich.

html:
Jack buys three pens.

He pays with a £20 note.

His change is £13.49

How much would two pens cost?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £4.34 — the three pens cost 2000 − 1349 = 651p, so one pen is 651 ÷ 3 = 217p and two are 2 × 217 = 434p. The question asks for TWO, not three and not one.

Miles and Megan buy 24 cans of lemonade

How much more money does Miles pay than Megan?

answer: £1.67 — Miles pays 24 × 62p = 1488p = £14.88 for single cans, Megan pays £13.21 for the pack of 24, and 14.88 − 13.21 = £1.67.

html:
A 2p coin has a mass of 7 grams.

Find the total mass of £8 of 2p coins.
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: 2,800 g, which is 2.8 kg — £8 in 2p coins is 800 ÷ 2 = 400 coins, and 400 × 7 = 2800 g.

html:
Tomas bought a new car that cost £18,000
He paid a deposit of £2,000.

Tomas paid the rest of the money over 50 equal monthly payments.

How much was each monthly payment?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £320 — after the deposit there is 18,000 − 2,000 = £16,000 left, and 16,000 ÷ 50 = £320 a month.

html:
Adam organised a charity concert at school.

The hall holds 35 rows of 42 seats.
There were 50 empty seats.

Each person paid £12.

How much money did Adam raise for charity?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £17,040 — the hall holds 35 × 42 = 1,470 seats, 50 were empty so 1,420 people came, and 1,420 × 12 = £17,040.

html:
For every seven 50p coins, Cain has six 20p coins.

Cain has £18 in 20p coins.

How much money does Cain have altogether?
name: Money
subject: Maths
answer: £70.50 — £18 in 20p coins is 1800 ÷ 20 = 90 coins. They come six to a group, so there are 15 groups, each with seven 50p coins: 105 of them, worth 105 × 50 = 5250p = £52.50. Altogether 52.50 + 18 = £70.50.

html: Write down the first five multiples of 3
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — the multiples of 3 are just the 3 times table, so count up in 3s — and 3 itself is the first one, not 6.

html: Write down the first five multiples of 8
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 — the multiples of 8 are just the 8 times table, so count up in 8s — and 8 itself is the first one, not 16.

html: Write down the first five multiples of 13
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 13, 26, 39, 52, 65 — the multiples of 13 are just the 13 times table, so count up in 13s — and 13 itself is the first one, not 26.

html: Write down two multiples of 4
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 4 and 8 — any two from the four times table: 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on.

html: Write down two multiples of 9
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 9 and 18 — any two from the nine times table: 9, 18, 27, 36 and so on.

html: Write down a number that is a multiple of both 4 and 9
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 36 — a number in BOTH has to be a multiple of 4 × 9 = 36, so 36, 72, 108 and so on.

subject: Maths
answer: For example 4 — any even number that is not in the 7 times table: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16 … (14 and 28 are out: they are multiples of 7).

html: Write a number for box (b): a multiple of 7 that is not a multiple of 2.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: For example 21 — any odd number in the 7 times table: 7, 21, 35, 49 … (14 and 28 are out: they are even).

html: Write a number for box (c): not a multiple of 2 and not a multiple of 7.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: For example 9 — any odd number that is not in the 7 times table: 1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13, 15 … (7 and 21 are out).

answer: 21 — 7 × 3 = 21 is the only multiple of 7 in the list.

html: Write a multiple of 20 from 50 to 99.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 60 (or 80) — the multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 …, and 60 and 80 are the two from 50 to 99. Either is right.

html: Write a multiple of 30 from 100 to 149.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 120 — the multiples of 30 go 90, 120, 150, so 120 is the only one from 100 to 149.

html: Write a multiple of 40 from 150 to 199.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 160 — the multiples of 40 go 120, 160, 200, so 160 is the only one from 150 to 199.

html:
Write one number which fits all three of these statements

It is odd

It is a multiple of 9

It is between 30 and 50
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 45 — the multiples of 9 between 30 and 50 are 36 and 45, and only 45 is odd.

html:
Here are six number cards.

33   32   30   28   27   26

Use each card once to make every statement below correct.

(a) □ is a multiple of 2
(b) □ is a multiple of 5
(c) □ is a multiple of 9
(d) □ is a multiple of 4
(e) □ is a multiple of 11
(f) □ is a multiple of 7
name: Multiples
subject: Maths

html: □  is a multiple of 2
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 26 — four cards are even, but 30 is needed for 5, 28 for 7 and 32 for 4, so 26 is the one left for 2.

html: □  is a multiple of 5
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 30 — 30 is the only card in the 5 times table: it is the only one ending in 0 or 5.

html: □  is a multiple of 9
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 27 — 27 = 3 × 9, and it is the only card in the 9 times table.

html: □  is a multiple of 4
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 32 — 32 = 8 × 4. 28 is a multiple of 4 too, but it is the only multiple of 7, so it goes there and 32 comes here.

html: □  is a multiple of 11
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 33 — 33 = 3 × 11, and it is the only card in the 11 times table.

html: □  is a multiple of 7
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 28 — 28 = 4 × 7, and it is the only card in the 7 times table.

html: Write all the common multiples of 4 and 6 less than 50
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 12, 24, 36 and 48 — a number in both times tables is a multiple of 12, because 12 is the smallest number 4 and 6 both divide into. 60 is the next one and it is over 50.

name: Multiples

name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 15 (any multiple of 5 that is not a multiple of 10: 5, 15, 25, 35…) — B is “multiple of 5” and “not a multiple of 10”, so the number must end in 5.

html:
Section C can never have any numbers in it.

Explain why
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: Every multiple of 10 is also a multiple of 5 — 10 = 2 × 5, so anything in the 10 times table is in the 5 times table too; no number can be a multiple of 10 without being a multiple of 5.

html: Find the multiple of 18 that is closest to 100
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 108 — the multiples either side of 100 are 18 × 5 = 90 and 18 × 6 = 108. 100 − 90 = 10 and 108 − 100 = 8, so 108 is the closer.

html:
Olivia uses these digit cards

6   7   3

She makes a 1-digit number and a 2-digit number.

She multiplies them together.

Her answer is a multiple of 4

What could Olivia’s multiplication be?

□ × □□
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 7 × 36 = 252 (or 3 × 76 = 228) — of the six ways to use the cards only these two give a multiple of 4: 252 = 4 × 63 and 228 = 4 × 57. 6 × 73 = 438, 6 × 37 = 222, 7 × 63 = 441 and 3 × 67 = 201 are not.

html:
171 is a multiple of 3.

220 is a multiple of 11.

Find a number between 171 and 220 that is both a multiple of 3 and a multiple of 11.
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 198 — a number in both is a multiple of 3 × 11 = 33. The multiples of 33 are 165, 198, 231 … and 198 is the only one between 171 and 220.

html:
A light flashes every 8 seconds.

How many times will it flash in 3 minutes?
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: 22 times — 3 minutes is 180 seconds, and 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5. The 22nd flash is at 176 seconds and the 23rd would be at 184, which is past the 3 minutes — so it is 22, not 22 and a half.

html:
m and n stand for two numbers

m is a multiple of 5
n is a multiple of 8

m⁄n = 3⁄4

Find numbers that m and n stand for
name: Multiples
subject: Maths
answer: m = 30, n = 40 — m and n are in the ratio 3 : 4, so m = 3k and n = 4k; 3k is a multiple of 5 only when k is, and 4k a multiple of 8 only when k is even, so k = 10 gives 30 and 40 (60 and 80, 90 and 120 … also work).

subject: Maths
answer: 84 days — 12 × 7 = 84.

html:
A teacher wants to give each child in her class 4 sweets each.

In the class there are 30 children.

How many sweets does the teacher need?
name: Multiplication
subject: Maths
answer: 120 sweets — 30 × 4 = 120.

html:
Six identical boxes are placed in a line.

The length of each box is 18cm

What is the total length of all six boxes?
name: Multiplication
subject: Maths
answer: 108 cm — 6 × 18.

html:
There are 8 cupcakes in a box.

Neil buys 27 boxes of cupcakes

How many cupcakes did Neil buy?
name: Multiplication
subject: Maths
answer: 216 cupcakes — 8 × 27.

html: Work out the product of 179 and 5
name: Multiplication
subject: Maths
answer: 895 — 179 × 5.

html:
At a wedding there are 24 tables.

19 tables seat 8 guests

5 tables seat 6 guests

Work out the total number of chairs needed
name: Multiplication
subject: Maths
answer: 182 chairs — 19 × 8 = 152 and 5 × 6 = 30, so 152 + 30 = 182. The 24 is there to be checked, not used: 19 + 5 = 24 accounts for every table, which is how you know no group has been missed.

Six different numbers in three pairs that multiply to 100 come from 100 = 1 × 100 = 2 × 50 = 4 × 25 = 5 × 20 (not 10 × 10, which repeats a number).

html:
Here are four statements.

For each statement, choose whether it is possible or impossible.
name: Parallel Lines Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths

html: A triangle can have 2 parallel sides
name: Parallel Lines Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Impossible — two parallel sides never meet, so the third side could not close them up into a triangle.

html: A triangle can have 2 perpendicular sides
name: Parallel Lines Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Possible — a right-angled triangle has two sides meeting at a right angle.

html: A quadrilateral can have 2 parallel sides
name: Parallel Lines Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Possible — a trapezium has a pair of parallel sides, and so do a rectangle and a parallelogram.

html: A quadrilateral can have 2 perpendicular sides
name: Parallel Lines Perpendicular Lines
subject: Maths
answer: Possible — every corner of a square or a rectangle is a right angle.

html:
The following quadrilaterals all have a perimeter of 32cm.

Here is a table to show the length of each side.

Side Lengths
Rectangle10cm6cm10cm6cm
Rhombus8cm
Parallelogram11cm
Kite9cm

Complete the table
name: Perimeter
subject: Maths

html: The rhombus has a side of 8cm. What is the length of each of its other three sides?
name: Perimeter
subject: Maths
answer: 8 cm — a rhombus has four equal sides: 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so its row is 8, 8, 8, 8.

html: The parallelogram has a side of 11cm. What is the length of each of its two shorter sides?
name: Perimeter
subject: Maths
answer: 5 cm — opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so two sides are 11cm: 32 − 22 = 10, and 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Its row is 11, 5, 11, 5.

html: The kite has a side of 9cm. What is the length of each of its two shorter sides?
name: Perimeter
subject: Maths
answer: 7 cm — a kite has two pairs of equal sides next to each other, so two sides are 9cm: 32 − 18 = 14, and 14 ÷ 2 = 7. Its row is 9, 9, 7, 7.

subject: Maths
answer: £30 — Jack is paid £24 for 4 hours, so the rate is 24 ÷ 4 = £6 an hour. Harry works 5 hours, so 5 × 6 = £30.

subject: Maths

serves 5
500g cod
400g haddock
600ml milk
120g butter
40g flour
1kg potatoes

Oscar wants to make enough fish pie for 2 people.

How much haddock should Oscar use?
name: Proportion
subject: Maths
answer: 160g — 400g for 5 people is 400 ÷ 5 = 80g each, so 2 people need 2 × 80 = 160g.

html:
A boat is 12 metres long and 8 metres tall.

Victoria makes a scale model of the boat.

Her model is 20 centimetres tall

How long is her model?
name: Proportion
subject: Maths
answer: 30 cm — the real boat is 8 m tall and the model is 20 cm, so every metre of boat is 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 cm of model. The boat is 12 m long, so the model is 12 × 2.5 = 30 cm.

html:
Freya is making shortbread biscuits.

makes 8
Butter150g
Caster Sugar60g
Plain Flour200g
Cornflour50g

Freya has only 100g of butter.

How much caster sugar should Freya use?
name: Proportion
subject: Maths
answer: 40g — 100g of butter is two thirds of the 150g in the recipe, so she needs two thirds of the 60g of sugar: 60 ÷ 3 × 2 = 40g.

html:
For every seven 50p coins, Alan has six 20p coins.

Alan has £18 in 20p coins.

How much money does Alan have altogether?
name: Proportion
subject: Maths
answer: £70.50 — £18 in 20p coins is 1800 ÷ 20 = 90 coins. They come six to a group, so there are 90 ÷ 6 = 15 groups, and each group also holds seven 50p coins: 15 × 7 = 105 of them, worth 105 × 50 = 5250p = £52.50. Altogether 52.50 + 18 = £70.50.

answer: Any two such as a rectangle that is not a square and a parallelogram that is not a rhombus — their diagonals cross but not at 90°; squares, rhombuses and kites are the ones to avoid.

kite    rectangle    rhombus    square    parallelogram

For each of the following descriptions, choose the correct name from the list.
name: Quadrilaterals
subject: Maths

html:
All four sides are the same length.
All four angles are equal.
name: Quadrilaterals
subject: Maths
answer: square — equal sides and equal angles make a square.

html:
Two pairs parallel sides.
Opposite angles are equal.
No lines of symmetry.
name: Quadrilaterals
subject: Maths
answer: parallelogram — a rectangle and a rhombus both have lines of symmetry, which leaves the parallelogram.

html:
All four sides are the same length.
There are no right angles.
name: Quadrilaterals
subject: Maths
answer: rhombus — equal sides with no right angles is a rhombus.

html:

He works out one-quarter of the number.

The result is 20.

What was the number that Harry started with?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 80 — a quarter of the number is 20, so the whole number is 4 × 20 = 80.

html:

7 children in the class have brown hair.

How many children are in the class?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 21 — a third of the class is 7, so the class is 3 × 7 = 21.

How old is Sam?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 60 — Jackson is a fifth of Sam, so Sam is 5 × 12 = 60.

name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 64 — three quarters are right handed, so the 16 left-handers are the other QUARTER, and the year group is 4 × 16 = 64. The three quarters is there to be gone past.

html:
Kyle had some money.

He spent £12.50 on a ticket to a football match.

He spent £6 on a scarf.

He has two-thirds of his money left.

How much money did Kyle have to start with?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: £55.50 — he spent 12.50 + 6 = £18.50, and with two thirds left that spending is the other THIRD, so he started with 3 × 18.50 = £55.50.

html:
Rebecca is 1⁄3 of Barry’s age.

Barry is 1⁄6 of Neville’s age.

Rebecca is 4 years old.

How old is Neville?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 72 — Rebecca is a third of Barry, so Barry is 3 × 4 = 12. Barry is a sixth of Neville, so Neville is 6 × 12 = 72. Two steps, and the second one uses the answer to the first.

html:
A new snack bar contains 9g of sugar.

3⁄10 of the snack bar is sugar.

Work out the mass of the snack bar.
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 30 g — three tenths of the bar is 9 g, so one tenth is 9 ÷ 3 = 3 g, and the whole bar is 10 × 3 = 30 g.

html:
On Monday, Beth read 7⁄10 of her book.

On Tuesday she read the other 42 pages to finish her book.

How many pages are there in Beth’s book?
name: Fractions: Finding the Original Amount
subject: Maths
answer: 140 — she read seven tenths on Monday, so the 42 pages are the other THREE tenths. One tenth is 42 ÷ 3 = 14, so the book is 10 × 14 = 140 pages.

html:
Here is a list of numbers

2,  6,  11,  14,  16,  18,  24,  25

From the list, write down the square numbers

□ and □
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 16 and 25 — 16 is 4 × 4 and 25 is 5 × 5. Nothing else in the list is a whole number times itself.

html: Write down the value of 3²
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 9 — 3 squared means 3 × 3.

html: Write down the value of 7²
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 49 — 7 squared means 7 × 7.

html: Write down the value of 10²
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 100 — 10 squared means 10 × 10.

html: Write down the value of eight squared
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 64 — 8 × 8 = 64.

html: Write down the value of 12²
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 144 — 12 squared means 12 × 12.

html: Circle all the square numbers
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 100, 36, 4 and 81 — 10 × 10, 6 × 6, 2 × 2 and 9 × 9.

html: Write down all the square numbers between 40 and 110
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 49, 64, 81 and 100 — 7², 8², 9² and 10². 36 is below 40 and 121 is above 110.

html:
100 can be found by adding together two different square numbers

□ + □ = 100

(square number + square number)

Fill in the missing square numbers
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 36 + 64 — 6² = 36 and 8² = 64, and it is the only pair of DIFFERENT square numbers that makes 100.

name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 106 — square first: 9² = 81 and 5² = 25, then add: 81 + 25 = 106.

name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 225 — 15 squared means 15 × 15.

name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 441 — 21 squared means 21 × 21.

name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 3,600 — 60 squared means 60 × 60.

html:
Gareth chooses a square number.

He rounds it to the nearest hundred.

His answer is 100.

Write all the possible square numbers that Gareth could have chosen
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144 — to round to 100 a number has to be from 50 up to 149. The square numbers in that range are 8², 9², 10², 11² and 12². 49 rounds to 0 and 169 rounds to 200.

html:
A square number and a multiple of 3 have a total of 90.

□ + □ = 90

(square number + multiple of 3)

Write two possible numbers in the boxes
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 81 and 9 — 81 is 9² and 9 is 3 × 3, so it is a multiple of 3, and 81 + 9 = 90. 36 and 54 work too, and so do 9 and 81 the other way round.

html:
Megan says

“When you square a number, the answer is always bigger.”

Explain why Megan is wrong
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 1 and 0 are the counter-examples — 1 × 1 = 1 and 0 × 0 = 0, so squaring those leaves them exactly where they were. One number that breaks a rule is enough to show the rule is wrong.

html:
A square number and a prime number have a total of 17

What are the two numbers?

□ + □ = 17

(square number + prime number)
name: Square Numbers
subject: Maths
answer: 4 and 13 — 4 is 2² and 13 is prime, and 4 + 13 = 17. The other squares below 17 do not work: 17 − 1 = 16 and 17 − 9 = 8, and neither is prime.

html:
w = 4

What is 3w − 2?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 10 — w = 4, so 3w − 2 = 3 × 4 − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

html:
x = 25

What is 5x − 31?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 94 — x = 25, so 5x − 31 = 5 × 25 − 31 = 125 − 31 = 94.

html:
The cost of hiring a car is found using the rule

Hire cost = £50 plus an extra £30 for each day
name: Substitution
subject: Maths

html: How much will it cost to hire a car for 4 days?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths

html: How much will it cost to hire a car for one week?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: £260 — a week is 7 days, so 50 + 30 × 7 = 50 + 210 = £260. The £50 is paid once, however many days.

html:
The time it takes to cook a turkey is given by this rule

Time = 20 minutes for each kilogram plus an extra 70 minutes
name: Substitution
subject: Maths

html: How many minutes will it take to cook a 2kg turkey?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 110 minutes — 20 × 2 + 70 = 40 + 70 = 110 minutes.

html: What is the mass of a turkey that takes 170 minutes to cook?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 5 kg — 170 − 70 = 100 minutes of cooking at 20 minutes a kilogram, and 100 ÷ 20 = 5 kg.

html:
Mrs Jones is preparing the food for a party.

She uses this rule to work out how many sausage rolls to prepare

3 sausage rolls per guest plus an extra 20
name: Substitution
subject: Maths

html: How many sausage rolls should she prepare if there are 42 guests?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 146 — 3 × 42 + 20 = 126 + 20 = 146 sausage rolls.

html:
For the last party, Mrs Jones made 86 sausage rolls

How many guests were there at the last party?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: 22 — 86 − 20 = 66 rolls for the guests, and 66 ÷ 3 = 22 guests.

subject: Maths

html: How much will a book with 70 pages cost?
name: Substitution
subject: Maths
answer: £3.95 — 70 × 5 = 350p, plus 45p for the cover is 395p = £3.95.

subject: Maths
answer: 112 — £6.05 is 605p; take off the 45p cover and 560p is left, and 560 ÷ 5 = 112 pages.

subject: Maths

How many years younger is Emma than her grandmother?

subject: Maths

subject: Maths

name: Subtraction
subject: Maths
answer: 3,750 — 4,500 − 750. "Difference" means subtract, and it is always the smaller taken from the larger.

subject: Maths
answer: £216 — Riley has 95 − 26 = £69, Alice has 69 − 17 = £52, and 95 + 69 + 52 = £216. Alice is measured against RILEY, not against Aiden — taking 17 off 95 is the slip this question is built around.

html:
Erin thinks of a number

She multiplies it by 3.
Then she adds 4.

Her answer is 22

What was the number Erin started with?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — undo it backwards: 22 − 4 = 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Check: 6 × 3 = 18, 18 + 4 = 22.

html:
Danny thinks of a number

He subtracts 8 and then multiplies by 6.

His answer is 30

What was the number Danny first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 13 — undo it backwards: 30 ÷ 6 = 5, and 5 + 8 = 13. Check: 13 − 8 = 5, 5 × 6 = 30.

html:
Eva thinks of a number

She divides the number by 4.
Then she adds 7.

Her answer is 13.

What was the number Eva first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 24 — undo it backwards: 13 − 7 = 6, and 6 × 4 = 24. Check: 24 ÷ 4 = 6, 6 + 7 = 13.

html:
John thinks of a number

He add 19.
Then he doubles the answer.

His final answer is 100.

What was the number John first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 31 — undo it backwards: 100 ÷ 2 = 50, and 50 − 19 = 31. Check: 31 + 19 = 50, doubled is 100.

html:
Sam thinks of a number.

He halved his number and then added 75.

The answer is 101.

What was the number Sam first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 52 — undo it backwards: 101 − 75 = 26, and 26 × 2 = 52. Check: half of 52 is 26, 26 + 75 = 101.

html:
Harry thinks of a number.

He multiplies his number by 3.
Harry then adds 8.
He then multiplies his result by 4.

His final answer is 80

What was the number Harry first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 4 — undo all three backwards: 80 ÷ 4 = 20, 20 − 8 = 12, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Check: 4 × 3 = 12, 12 + 8 = 20, 20 × 4 = 80.

html:
Isabelle thinks of a whole number

She multiplies it by 3

She rounds her answer to the nearest 10.

The result is 40.

Write all the possible numbers that Isabelle could have started with
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 12, 13 and 14 — tripling has to land somewhere that rounds to 40, which means from 35 up to but not including 45. The multiples of 3 in that range are 36, 39 and 42, so the starting numbers are 36 ÷ 3 = 12, 39 ÷ 3 = 13 and 42 ÷ 3 = 14. 11 gives 33, which rounds to 30, and 15 gives 45, which rounds to 50.

html:
Jonathan thinks of a number.

He adds 9
He multiplies his result by 12
Then he takes away 16.
His final answer is 80.

What number did Jonathan start with?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: −1 — undo it backwards: 80 + 16 = 96, 96 ÷ 12 = 8, and 8 − 9 = −1. Check: −1 + 9 = 8, 8 × 12 = 96, 96 − 16 = 80. The starting number really is negative.

html:
Shannon thinks of a number

She multiplies the number by 6 and then subtracts 70 from the result

Her answer equals the number she started with.

What was the number Shannon started with?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 14 — the answer comes back to the starting number, so 6n − 70 = n. Six of the number minus one of it is five of it, so 5n = 70 and n = 14. Check: 14 × 6 = 84, and 84 − 70 = 14.

html:
Pip thinks of a number

He multiplies the number by 4 and then subtracts 72 from the result

His answer equals the number he started with.

What was the number Pip started with?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 24 — the answer comes back to the starting number, so 4n − 72 = n, which leaves 3n = 72 and n = 24. Check: 24 × 4 = 96, and 96 − 72 = 24.

html:
Molly thinks of a number

She adds half of the number to a third of the number.

Her answer is 75.

What was the number Molly first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 90 — a half and a third together are five sixths, so five sixths of the number is 75. One sixth is 75 ÷ 5 = 15, so the number is 15 × 6 = 90. Check: 45 + 30 = 75.

html:
Luke thinks of a number

He adds half of the number to a third of the number.

His answer is 100.

What was the number Luke first thought of?
name: Think of a Number
subject: Maths
answer: 120 — a half and a third together are five sixths, so five sixths of the number is 100. One sixth is 100 ÷ 5 = 20, so the number is 20 × 6 = 120. Check: 60 + 40 = 100.

html: What number goes in the first box — how many minutes past?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 5 — the long minute hand points at I, the 1, which is 5 minutes past.

html: What number goes in the second box — past which hour?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 4 — the short hour hand has just passed IIII, which is 4, so the time is 5 minutes past 4.

html:
A television programme begins at 7:30pm

The television programme ends at 8:15pm

How long did the television programme last?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 45 minutes — 7:30pm to 8:00pm is 30, then 15 more to 8:15pm.

html: How many seconds are in one minute?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 60 — there are 60 seconds in a minute.

html: How many minutes are in one hour?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 60 — there are 60 minutes in an hour.

html: How many hours are there in one day?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 24 — there are 24 hours in a day.

html: How many days are there in one week?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — Monday to Sunday is 7 days.

html: How many days are there in August?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 31 — August is one of the months with 31 days.

html: How many months are in one year?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 12 — January to December is 12 months.

html: How many days are there in a year? (not a leap year)
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 365 — an ordinary year has 365 days.

html: How many days are there in a leap year?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 366 — a leap year adds 29 February, so 366 days.

html: How many years are in a decade?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 10 — a decade is 10 years.

html: How many years are in a century?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 100 — a century is 100 years.

name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: C — the long hand is on 1 (5 minutes past) and the short hand has just left 12. (B is twenty-five past twelve and D is one o’clock.)

html: Which clock shows five o’clock?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: A — the long hand is on 12 and the short hand on 5.

A clock shows this time

How long is it until 2pm?

html:
Chloe is late arriving at school.

She is meant to arrive at school at 8:45am

The clock shows the time she arrived.

How many minutes late is she?
name: Time
subject: Maths

answer: 29 minutes — 8:45am to 9:00am is 15 minutes, then 14 more to 9:14am: 15 + 14 = 29.

html:
Carlos does his French and English homework.

It takes him a total of two hours.

He spends 80 minutes doing his English homework.

How many minutes does he spend doing his French homework?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 40 minutes — two hours is 120 minutes, and 120 − 80 = 40.

html: How many seconds are there in five minutes?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 300 seconds — 5 × 60.

html:
A train leaves Bath at 5:55pm

It takes 23 minutes to reach Bradford-on-Avon

What time does the train arrive in Bradford-on-Avon?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 6:18pm — 5:55pm plus 5 minutes is 6:00pm, then 18 more.

subject: Maths
answer: Thursday — the 14th is a Monday, so the 17th is three days on, in the second T column.

html:
In 1999, the 28th September was a Tuesday.

What day was the 3rd October?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: Sunday — 28 September is a Tuesday, so the 3rd of October is 5 days later: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

html: What is 235 minutes in hours and minutes?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 3 hours 55 minutes — 3 × 60 = 180, and 235 − 180 = 55.
accept: 3 hours 55 minutes | 3 hours and 55 minutes | 3h 55m | 3 h 55 min

html:
Write these times in order, starting with the shortest

35 days,  3 weeks,  1 month,  240 hours
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 240 hours, 3 weeks, 1 month, 35 days — in days they are 10, 21, 28 to 31 and 35; a month is at most 31 days, so it is shorter than 35 days whichever month it is.

html: How many minutes are there in a day?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 1,440 minutes — 24 × 60.

html:
Dexter finished a puzzle in 44 minutes 19 seconds

Theresa finished 9 minutes 50 seconds after Dexter.
name: Time
subject: Maths

html: How long did Theresa take?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 54 minutes 9 seconds — 44:19 + 9:50 = 53 minutes 69 seconds = 54 minutes 9 seconds.

html:
Selina finished 6 minutes 27 seconds before Dexter.

How long did Selina take?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 37 minutes 52 seconds — 44:19 − 6:27 — take a minute across: 79 seconds − 27 = 52, and 43 − 6 = 37 minutes.

html:
Connor’s watch is 17 minutes slow

Joseph’s watch is 5 minutes fast

The time on Joseph’s watch is 19:01

What time is shown on Connor’s watch?
name: Time
subject: Maths
answer: 18:39 — Joseph is 5 minutes fast, so the real time is 18:56, and Connor is 17 minutes slow, so 18:56 − 17 minutes is 18:39.

html: How long does the PE lesson last?
name: Timetables
subject: Maths
answer: 1 hour 15 minutes — PE runs from 1:05 to 2:20: 1:05 to 2:05 is an hour, and 15 minutes more.

html:

What time did Jenson leave the English lesson?
name: Timetables
subject: Maths
answer: 11:35am — English ends at 12:10pm, and 35 minutes before that is 11:35am.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Write 7⁄3 as a mixed number
answer: 21⁄3 — 7 ÷ 3 goes 2 times with 1 left over, so it is 2 whole and 1⁄3 more.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Write 13⁄10 as a mixed number
answer: 13⁄10 — 13 ÷ 10 goes 1 time with 3 left over, so it is 1 whole and 3⁄10 more.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Write 13⁄4 as an improper (top-heavy) fraction
answer: 7⁄4 — one whole is 4⁄4, so 1 whole is 1 × 4 = 4 of them, and the 3 already there makes 7.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Write 23⁄10 as an improper fraction
answer: 23⁄10 — one whole is 10⁄10, so 2 wholes are 2 × 10 = 20 of them, and the 3 already there makes 23.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html:
Match up the equivalent mixed numbers and the improper fractions

21⁄4,  21⁄3,  13⁄4,  32⁄3

7⁄4,  11⁄3,  7⁄3,  9⁄4

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Which improper fraction is equal to 21⁄4?
answer: 9⁄4 — 2 wholes are 2 × 4 = 8 quarters, and the 1 quarter more makes 9.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Which improper fraction is equal to 21⁄3?
answer: 7⁄3 — 2 wholes are 2 × 3 = 6 thirds, and the 1 third more makes 7.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Which improper fraction is equal to 13⁄4?
answer: 7⁄4 — 1 whole is 4 quarters, and the 3 quarters more make 7.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html: Which improper fraction is equal to 32⁄3?
answer: 11⁄3 — 3 wholes are 3 × 3 = 9 thirds, and the 2 thirds more make 11.

name: Top Heavy Fractions Mixed Numbers
subject: Maths
html:
Gregory the cat eats 2⁄5 of a can of cat food each day.

Work out how much cat food is eaten in one week. Give your answer as a mixed number.
answer: 24⁄5 cans — a week is 7 days, so it is 2⁄5 × 7 = 14⁄5, and 14 ÷ 5 goes 2 times with 4 left over.

html: How many squares to the left has the parallelogram moved?
name: Translations
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — the top left corner of A is (2, −3) and of B is (−4, 1): from 2 back to −4 is 6 squares.

html: How many squares up has the parallelogram moved?
name: Translations
subject: Maths
answer: 4 — from −3 up to 1 is 4 squares.

html: What type of angle is the first angle, at the top?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Right — it has the small square that marks a square corner, exactly 90°.

html: What type of angle is the second angle?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Obtuse — it opens wider than a square corner but not as far as a straight line.

html: What type of angle is the third angle?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Acute — it is narrower than a square corner, less than 90°.

html: What type of angle is the fourth angle, at the bottom?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Reflex — the arc is drawn round the outside, the long way round, which is more than a straight line (180°).

subject: Maths

name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: A — a straight line on one side and an arm going up at 45° leaves 135°, between 90° and 180°.

name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: C — each arm goes one square across for one square up, which makes a square corner.

html: What time is shown on the clock?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: 4 o’clock — the minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand to 4.

html: What type of angle marked between the hour and minute hand?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Obtuse — each hour gap is 30°, so the angle is 4 × 30 = 120°: bigger than a right angle, smaller than a straight line.

html:
Ava measures 5 angles: 180°, 79°, 90°, 198° and 94°.

Match each measurement to the correct type of angle
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths

html: Which type of angle is 180°?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Straight line — exactly 180° is a straight line.
choices: Reflex angle | Acute angle | Straight line | Right angle | Obtuse angle

html: Which type of angle is 79°?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Acute angle — less than 90° is acute, and 79° is only just under.
choices: Reflex angle | Acute angle | Straight line | Right angle | Obtuse angle

html: Which type of angle is 90°?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Right angle — exactly 90° is a right angle.
choices: Reflex angle | Acute angle | Straight line | Right angle | Obtuse angle

html: Which type of angle is 198°?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Reflex angle — more than 180° is reflex.
choices: Reflex angle | Acute angle | Straight line | Right angle | Obtuse angle

html: Which type of angle is 94°?
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Obtuse angle — between 90° and 180° is obtuse, and 94° is only just over.
choices: Reflex angle | Acute angle | Straight line | Right angle | Obtuse angle

html:
Eddie says

“I can draw a triangle with 3 acute angles”

Draw a triangle to show Eddie is right
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Any triangle with every angle less than 90°, e.g. an equilateral triangle — its angles are all 60°.

html:
Hannah says

“I can draw a triangle with 2 acute angles”

Draw a triangle to show Hannah is right
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: Any triangle with one right or obtuse angle, e.g. a right-angled triangle — the other two angles share 90° and are both acute.

html:
Matthew says

“I can draw a triangle with 2 obtuse angles”

Is Matthew right?   Yes □   No □
name: Types of Angle
subject: Maths
answer: No — the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°, and two obtuse angles alone would already be more than 180°.

html: What is the name of the top triangle?
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Right angled — its upright side and its flat side meet square-on.

html: What is the name of the second triangle?
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Scalene — its three sides are all different lengths and none is marked equal.

html: What is the name of the third triangle?
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Equilateral — all three of its sides carry a tick, so all three are equal.

html: What is the name of the bottom triangle?
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Isosceles — its two long sides carry a tick each, so two sides are equal.

html: Draw a right-angled triangle
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Any triangle with one angle of exactly 90° — for example draw one side straight across, a second straight up from one end of it, and join the two free ends.

html: Draw a scalene triangle
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Any triangle with all three sides different lengths — then its three angles are all different too. No two sides may be the same length.

html: Join 3 points to make a right angled triangle
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Two opposite points and any third point — two opposite points, such as 12 o’clock and 6 o’clock, make a side straight through the centre, and a side through the centre always makes a right angle at the third corner.

Here is a different circle with 12 equally spaced points

Join 3 points to make an equilateral triangle
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: Every fourth point, e.g. the 12, 4 and 8 o’clock points — points four apart split the 12 into three equal parts, so all three sides are the same length.

html:
Liam says

“I have drawn a triangle with one acute angle, one right angle and one obtuse angle.”

Explain why Liam must be wrong
name: Types of Triangle
subject: Maths
answer: A right angle and an obtuse angle already add up to more than 180° — the three angles of a triangle add up to exactly 180°, and 90° plus anything over 90° is past 180° before the acute angle is even counted.
