name: Accumulation
subject: English Language
description: Piling up words or points one after another for force. “He was rude, loud, careless, cruel.”

name: Adynaton
subject: English Language
description: Hyperbole so extreme it says something is impossible. “When pigs fly.”

name: Allegory
subject: English Language
description: A story whose characters and events stand for something else — usually a moral or political idea.

name: Alliteration
subject: English Language
description: The same sound starting words close together. “The slow, sad song.”

name: Allusion
subject: English Language
description: A passing reference to something outside the text — a book, a myth, an event — without explaining it.

name: Amblysia
subject: English Language
description: Softening bad news before delivering it.

name: Amphiboly
subject: English Language
description: A sentence that can be read two ways because of how it is built, not because of a word’s meaning.

name: Anachronism
subject: English Language
description: Something in the wrong time period — a clock in a Roman play.

name: Anacoluthon
subject: English Language
description: A sentence that starts one way and finishes another, as speech often does.

name: Anadiplosis
subject: English Language
description: Ending a clause and starting the next with the same word. “Fear leads to anger, anger leads to hate.”

name: Analogue
subject: English Language
description: A thing that corresponds to another — a parallel drawn between two situations.

name: Anaphora
subject: English Language
description: The same words at the start of each line or clause. “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight…”

name: Anastrophe
subject: English Language
description: Words put in an unusual order for effect. “Powerful you have become.”

name: Anecdote
subject: English Language
description: A short personal story used to make a point.

name: Anesis
subject: English Language
description: Ending with a detail that undercuts everything said before it.

name: Antagonist
subject: English Language
description: The character working against the protagonist.

name: Antanaclasis
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a word with a different meaning each time. “Put out the light, then put out the light.”

name: Anthropomorphism
subject: English Language
description: Giving an animal or object a human body or human behaviour — not just human feelings.

name: Anthimeria
subject: English Language
description: Using one part of speech as another. “I’ll text you” — a noun made a verb.

name: Antipophora
subject: English Language
description: Asking a question and immediately answering it yourself.

name: Antimetabole
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a phrase with the order reversed. “Ask not what your country can do for you…”

name: Antiphrasis
subject: English Language
description: Using a word to mean its opposite, usually sarcastically. Calling a giant “Tiny”.

name: Antithesis
subject: English Language
description: Two opposite ideas set against each other in a balanced way. “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.”

name: Antonomasia
subject: English Language
description: Replacing a name with a description, or a description with a name. “The Bard” for Shakespeare.

name: Aphorism
subject: English Language
description: A short statement of a general truth. “Less is more.”

name: Aposiopesis
subject: English Language
description: Breaking off mid-sentence, leaving it unfinished. “If you don’t stop —”

name: Apostrophe
subject: English Language
description: Speaking directly to somebody absent, dead, or to an idea. “O Death, where is thy sting?”

name: Archaism
subject: English Language
description: An old-fashioned word or form used on purpose. “Thou”, “hither”.

name: Assonance
subject: English Language
description: The same vowel sound repeated in nearby words. “The rain in Spain.”

name: Asyndeton
subject: English Language
description: Leaving out the conjunctions to speed a list up. “I came, I saw, I conquered.”

name: Aside
subject: English Language
description: A remark to the audience the other characters cannot hear.

name: Bathos
subject: English Language
description: A sudden drop from the lofty to the ridiculous, usually by accident.

name: Black comedy
subject: English Language
description: Finding humour in things normally too grim to laugh at.

name: Blank verse
subject: English Language
description: Unrhymed lines in iambic pentameter — the usual line of Shakespeare’s plays.

name: Blazon
subject: English Language
description: Listing a person’s features one by one in praise, common in love poetry.

name: Bombast
subject: English Language
description: Language far grander than the subject deserves.

name: Burlesque
subject: English Language
description: Mocking something by treating a serious subject lightly, or a trivial one seriously.

name: Cacophony
subject: English Language
description: Harsh, clashing sounds put together on purpose.

name: Caesura
subject: English Language
description: A deliberate pause in the middle of a line of verse.

name: Catachresis
subject: English Language
description: A word used wrongly or a strained metaphor. “To take arms against a sea of troubles.”

name: Catalexis
subject: English Language
description: Dropping a syllable from the end of a line of verse.

name: Catharsis
subject: English Language
description: The release of emotion an audience feels at the end of a tragedy.

name: Chiasmus
subject: English Language
description: Ideas mirrored in an ABBA order. “Fair is foul, and foul is fair.”

name: Circumlocution
subject: English Language
description: Taking many words to say what could be said in few.

name: Cliché
subject: English Language
description: A phrase worn out by overuse. “At the end of the day.”

name: Conceit
subject: English Language
description: An extended, surprising comparison held across a whole poem.

name: Connotation
subject: English Language
description: What a word suggests beyond its plain meaning — “home” against “house”.

name: Consonance
subject: English Language
description: The same consonant sounds repeated, usually at the ends of words. “pitter patter”.

name: Couplet
subject: English Language
description: Two lines together, usually rhyming.

name: Cyclical ending
subject: English Language
description: An ending that returns to where the piece began.

name: Call to Action
subject: English Language
description: A direct instruction to the reader to do something. Common at the end of persuasive writing.

name: Defamiliarisation
subject: English Language
description: Describing an ordinary thing strangely so it is noticed again.

name: Denotation
subject: English Language
description: A word’s plain dictionary meaning, with nothing suggested on top.

name: Depitation
subject: English Language
description: Cutting a word short by removing its ending.

name: Dissonance
subject: English Language
description: Deliberately awkward, unmusical sound.

name: Double entendre
subject: English Language
description: A phrase with two meanings, one of them usually rude.

name: Dramatic irony
subject: English Language
description: The audience knows something a character does not.

name: Dysphemism
subject: English Language
description: A harsher word used where a neutral one would do — the opposite of a euphemism.

name: Direct Mode of address
subject: English Language
description: Speaking straight to the reader as “you”.

name: Ecphonema
subject: English Language
description: An exclamation — a sudden cry of emotion.

name: Ekphrasis
subject: English Language
description: A vivid description of a work of art inside a piece of writing.

name: Elegy
subject: English Language
description: A poem of mourning for somebody who has died.

name: Elision
subject: English Language
description: Leaving a sound out, usually to fit a rhythm. “o’er” for “over”.

name: Ellipsis
subject: English Language
description: Leaving words out, or the three dots that show it.

name: Emotive language
subject: English Language
description: Word choices picked to stir feeling rather than to inform.

name: Enjambment
subject: English Language
description: A sentence running over the end of a line of verse without a pause.

name: Epanados
subject: English Language
description: Repeating an idea in reverse order to expand on it.

name: Epanalepsis
subject: English Language
description: Beginning and ending a clause with the same word. “The king is dead, long live the king.”

name: Epexegesis
subject: English Language
description: Adding words to make an earlier phrase clearer.

name: Epideictic oratory
subject: English Language
description: Speech of praise or blame — a eulogy, a tribute.

name: Epistrophe
subject: English Language
description: The same word ending each clause — the opposite of anaphora.

name: Epitasis
subject: English Language
description: The part of a play where the action builds toward its climax.

name: Epizeuxis
subject: English Language
description: The same word repeated immediately, with nothing between. “Never, never, never.”

name: Euphemism
subject: English Language
description: A gentler phrase for something harsh. “Passed away.”

name: Euphony
subject: English Language
description: Sounds chosen because they are pleasant together.

name: Farce
subject: English Language
description: Comedy built on absurd situations and improbable coincidence.

name: Feminine rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme on two syllables, the last unstressed. “motion / ocean”.

name: Flyting
subject: English Language
description: A contest of insults, traded in verse.

name: Foil
subject: English Language
description: A character whose opposite qualities highlight another’s.

name: Frame Narrative
subject: English Language
description: A story told inside another story.

name: Flashback
subject: English Language
description: A scene that jumps back to an earlier time.

name: Foreshadowing
subject: English Language
description: A hint early on of what is to come.

name: Free verse
subject: English Language
description: Poetry with no fixed metre or rhyme scheme.

name: Hamartia
subject: English Language
description: The flaw or mistake that brings a tragic hero down.

name: Hemistich
subject: English Language
description: Half a line of verse, usually split by a pause.

name: Hendiadys
subject: English Language
description: One idea expressed as two nouns joined by “and”. “Sound and fury” for furious sound.

name: Homonym
subject: English Language
description: Words spelt and said the same with different meanings. “bat”.

name: Homophone
subject: English Language
description: Words that sound the same but are spelt differently. “there / their”.

name: Hubris
subject: English Language
description: Excessive pride, usually the thing that causes the fall.

name: Hypallage
subject: English Language
description: Swapping which word an adjective belongs to. “A sleepless night.”

name: Hyperbaton
subject: English Language
description: Words separated from the ones they belong with, for emphasis.

name: Hyperbole
subject: English Language
description: Deliberate exaggeration, not meant literally. “I’ve told you a thousand times.”

name: Hypocorism
subject: English Language
description: A pet name or affectionate diminutive.

name: Hypostatisation
subject: English Language
description: Treating an idea as though it were a real thing that can act.

name: Hypotyposis
subject: English Language
description: Description so vivid the scene seems to be in front of you.

name: Hypozeuxis
subject: English Language
description: Giving every clause its own subject and verb, for weight.

name: Idiom
subject: English Language
description: A phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words. “Kick the bucket.”

name: Imagery
subject: English Language
description: Language that appeals to the senses to build a picture.

name: Invective
subject: English Language
description: Abusive, attacking language.

name: Inversion
subject: English Language
description: Reversing the normal word order. “Into the valley rode the six hundred.”

name: Invocation
subject: English Language
description: Calling on a muse or a god for help, usually at the start of an epic.

name: In media res
subject: English Language
description: Beginning in the middle of the action rather than at the start.

name: Irony
subject: English Language
description: Saying one thing and meaning another, or an outcome that is the opposite of what was expected.

name: Isocolon
subject: English Language
description: Clauses of matching length and structure. “Veni, vidi, vici.”

name: Juxtaposition
subject: English Language
description: Two things placed side by side so the contrast shows.

name: Jargon
subject: English Language
description: Specialist vocabulary belonging to a trade or group.

name: Kenning
subject: English Language
description: A compound phrase standing in for a noun. “Whale-road” for the sea.

name: Light rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme where one syllable is stressed and the other is not.

name: Litotes
subject: English Language
description: Understatement made by denying the opposite. “Not bad” for good.

name: Malapropism
subject: English Language
description: The wrong word used for one that sounds like it, comically. “Dance a flamingo.”

name: Masculine rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme on a single stressed syllable. “hand / stand”.

name: Meiosis
subject: English Language
description: Belittling something by describing it as far less than it is.

name: Melodrama
subject: English Language
description: Exaggerated emotion and sensational plot, characters drawn broadly.

name: Metalepsis
subject: English Language
description: A reference so indirect it needs a second leap to follow.

name: Metaphor
subject: English Language
description: Saying one thing IS another. “Time is a thief.”

name: Meter
subject: English Language
description: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line.

name: Metonymy
subject: English Language
description: Naming something by a thing closely linked to it. “The Crown” for the monarchy.

name: Monologue
subject: English Language
description: One character speaking at length, alone or to others.

name: Motif
subject: English Language
description: An image or idea that recurs through a work and builds meaning.

name: Mythopoeia
subject: English Language
description: Making a myth — inventing a legend rather than retelling one.

name: Neologism
subject: English Language
description: A newly invented word.

name: Nonce-word
subject: English Language
description: A word coined for one occasion and not used again.

name: Onomatopoeia
subject: English Language
description: A word that sounds like the thing it names. “Buzz”, “crash”.

name: Oxymoron
subject: English Language
description: Two contradictory words together. “Bittersweet”, “deafening silence”.

name: Palilogy
subject: English Language
description: Immediate repetition of a word for emphasis.

name: Paradox
subject: English Language
description: A statement that contradicts itself and is still true. “Less is more.”

name: Paralipsis
subject: English Language
description: Drawing attention to something by saying you will not mention it.

name: Parallelism
subject: English Language
description: Matching grammatical structure across phrases or clauses.

name: Parataxis
subject: English Language
description: Short clauses set side by side without conjunctions.

name: Parenthesis
subject: English Language
description: An aside inserted into a sentence, in brackets or dashes.

name: Paronomasia
subject: English Language
description: A pun — wordplay on words that sound alike.

name: Pathetic fallacy
subject: English Language
description: Weather or landscape reflecting a character’s mood.

name: Periphrasis
subject: English Language
description: Using more words than needed — a roundabout way of naming something.

name: Personification
subject: English Language
description: Giving human qualities to something that is not human. “The wind whispered.”

name: Platitude
subject: English Language
description: A flat, obvious remark offered as though it were wisdom.

name: Polyptoton
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a word in different forms. “With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder.”

name: Polysyndeton
subject: English Language
description: Repeating conjunctions to slow a list down. “and… and… and…”

name: Prolepsis
subject: English Language
description: Treating a future event as though it had already happened.

name: Prodiorthosis
subject: English Language
description: Warning the audience that what comes next may shock them.

name: Protagonist
subject: English Language
description: The main character, whose choices drive the story.

name: Repartee
subject: English Language
description: Quick, witty reply — conversation as a duel.

name: Rhetorical question
subject: English Language
description: A question asked for effect, not for an answer.

name: Rhyme
subject: English Language
description: Matching sounds at the ends of words or lines.

name: Rhythm
subject: English Language
description: The beat of the language — how stresses fall as it is read.

name: Satire
subject: English Language
description: Using humour and exaggeration to criticise people or institutions.

name: Sentence structure
subject: English Language
description: How a sentence is built — short and blunt, or long and layered — and what that does.

name: Setting
subject: English Language
description: Where and when a piece takes place, and the mood that creates.

name: Simile
subject: English Language
description: Comparing with “like” or “as”. “As cold as stone.”

name: Statistics
subject: English Language
description: Numbers used as evidence to make an argument harder to argue with.

name: Stichomythia
subject: English Language
description: Rapid dialogue in single alternating lines, used in argument.

name: Stream of consciousness
subject: English Language
description: Writing that follows thought as it actually runs, unordered.

name: Symbolism
subject: English Language
description: An object standing for an idea beyond itself.

name: Synaesthesia
subject: English Language
description: Describing one sense in terms of another. “A loud shirt.”

name: Syncope
subject: English Language
description: Dropping a sound from the middle of a word. “ne’er”.

name: Synecdoche
subject: English Language
description: A part standing for the whole. “All hands on deck.”

name: Tapinosis
subject: English Language
description: Language that belittles its subject.

name: Tmesis
subject: English Language
description: Splitting a word and putting something inside it. “Abso-bloody-lutely.”

name: Theme
subject: English Language
description: The underlying idea a work keeps returning to.

name: Tone
subject: English Language
description: The attitude the writing takes toward its subject.

name: Topothesia
subject: English Language
description: A description of an imaginary place.

name: Triple (Rule of Three)
subject: English Language
description: Three items together, which is the number that sounds complete. “Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.”

name: Unreliable Narrator
subject: English Language
description: A narrator whose account cannot be trusted.

name: Verisimilitude
subject: English Language
description: The appearance of being true to life.

name: Voice
subject: English Language
description: The distinct personality that comes through in the writing.

name: Zeugma
subject: English Language
description: One word governing two others, often oddly. “She took her coat and her leave.”

html:
There are 48 counters in a bag. There are only red counters and blue counters in the bag.

number of red counters : number of blue counters = 1 : 2

Helen has to work out how many red counters are in the bag. She says,

“There are 24 red counters in the bag because 1 is half of 2 and 24 is half of 48”

Is Helen correct? You must give a reason for your answer.
answer: No — the ratio 1 : 2 makes 3 equal parts, so red = 48 ÷ 3 = 16, not 24.

He says that the probability that the sweet will be red is 7⁄10

Show why the probability cannot be 7⁄10
answer: n ÷ (n + 8) = 7⁄10 gives n = 56⁄3, not a whole number — 10n = 7n + 56, so 3n = 56; there must be a whole number of sweets.

answer: 28 (n(n − 1) ⁄ ((n + 8)(n + 7)) = 3⁄5 gives n2 − 25n − 84 = 0, so n = 28)

You must show all your working.

html: Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate of the actual distance the car travelled in the first 30 seconds? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: An underestimate — the curve lies above the straight edges of the trapezia, so they leave out some of the area under it.

html:
Julian used the graph to answer this question.

Work out an estimate for the acceleration of the car at time 60 seconds.

Here is Julian’s working.

acceleration = speed ÷ time
= 13 ÷ 60
= 0.216̇ m/s2

Julian’s method does not give a good estimate of the acceleration at time 60 seconds.

Explain why.
answer: He found the average acceleration over 60 s; at 60 s it is the gradient of the tangent — speed ÷ time is the gradient of the chord from the origin, and the graph is a curve.

ABCDEF is a regular hexagon with sides of length x.

This hexagon is enlarged, centre F, by scale factor p to give hexagon FGHIJK.

Show that the area of the shaded region in the diagram is given by  3√32(p2 − 1)x2
answer: Shaded area = 3√32p2x2 − 3√32x2 = 3√32(p2 − 1)x2 — a regular hexagon of side x is six equilateral triangles: 6 × ½x2 sin 60° = 3√32x2; the big one has side px.

6x2 = 7xy + 20y2 where x > 0 and y > 0

Find the ratio x : y
answer: 5 : 2 — 6x2 − 7xy − 20y2 = (3x + 4y)(2x − 5y) = 0, and since x and y are positive the first bracket cannot be zero, so 2x = 5y

There are only blue cubes, red cubes and yellow cubes in a box.

The table shows the probability of taking at random a blue cube from the box.

Colourblueredyellow
Probability0.2  

The number of red cubes in the box is the same as the number of yellow cubes in the box.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths

html:
Complete the table.

What is the probability of taking a red cube?
answer: 0.4 — the three probabilities add up to 1, so red and yellow share 1 − 0.2 = 0.8; there are as many red cubes as yellow, so red is 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths

html: What is the probability of taking a yellow cube?
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 0.4 — there are as many yellow cubes as red, so yellow has the same share of the 0.8 left after blue: 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4.
examiner_note: The paper prints 2 marks for part (a) and does not divide them between the red box and the yellow box, so both are counted on this last sub-part.

Work out the total number of cubes in the box.

html:
Deon needs 50 g of sugar to make 15 biscuits.

She also needs

  • three times as much flour as sugar
  • two times as much butter as sugar

Deon is going to make 60 biscuits.

html: Work out the amount of flour she needs.
answer: 600 g (60 biscuits need 200 g of sugar, and flour is three times that)

html:
Deon has to buy all the butter she needs to make 60 biscuits.

She buys the butter in 250 g packs.

How many packs of butter does Deon need to buy?
answer: 2 packs — she needs 2 × 200 = 400 g, and one 250 g pack is not enough.

html:
There are only r red counters and g green counters in a bag.

A counter is taken at random from the bag. The probability that the counter is green is 3⁄7. The counter is put back in the bag.

2 more red counters and 3 more green counters are put in the bag. A counter is taken at random from the bag.

The probability that the counter is green is 6⁄13
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths

html: Find the number of red counters that were in the bag originally.
answer: 12 — 3⁄7 green gives 7g = 3(r + g), so 4g = 3r and 6r = 8g; afterwards 13(g + 3) = 6(r + g + 5) gives 7g + 9 = 6r = 8g, so g = 9 and r = 12.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths

html: Find the number of green counters that were in the bag originally.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 9 — 7g + 9 = 8g from the two probabilities, so g = 9. Check: 9⁄21 = 3⁄7, and with 14 red and 12 green, 12⁄26 = 6⁄13.
examiner_note: The paper prints 5 marks for the whole question and does not divide them between the red counters and the green counters, so all 5 are counted on this last part.

html: Show that  6 + [(x + 5) ÷ x2 + 3x − 10x − 1]  simplifies to  ax − bcx − d  where a, b, c and d are integers.
answer: 7x − 13x − 2 — x2 + 3x − 10 = (x + 5)(x − 2), so the bracket is x − 1x − 2; 6 + that = 6x − 12 + x − 1x − 2

html:
Sean has drawn a time series graph to show the numbers, in thousands, of visitors to a fun park.

Write down two things that are wrong or could be misleading with this graph.
answer: The vertical scale is not uniform; the points are joined with curves — 9 to 10 takes the same space as each 0.5 step, and a time series joins its points with straight lines. Also, there is no data for quarter 1.

The diagram shows a hexagon.

The hexagon has one line of symmetry.

FA = BC
EF = CD
Angle ABC = 117°

Angle BCD = 2 × angle CDE

Work out the size of angle AFE.

You must show all your working.
answer: 162° — by symmetry FAB = 117°, AFE = BCD, FED = CDE; 2 × 117 + 2(BCD + CDE) = 720, so BCD + CDE = 243 and CDE = 81°, BCD = 162°

The histogram gives information about the distribution of the weights of some onions grown by a farmer.

Onions less than 60 grams in weight are used for pickling.
Onions greater than 120 grams in weight are sold at the market.
The rest of the onions are sent to a food processing factory.

A pie chart is drawn using the information opposite to show what the farmer does with the onions he grows.

The sectors are: used for pickling, sold at the market, and sent to the food processing factory.

The angle of the sector for the onions sent to the food processing factory is x°.

Work out the value of x.
answer: x = 210 — the bars give frequencies 120, 150, 270, 90 and 90, a total of 720 onions. 120 are for pickling and 180 for the market, leaving 420 for the factory, and 420⁄720 × 360 = 210.

The nth term of a sequence is 2n2 − 1

The nth term of a different sequence is 40 − n2

Show that there is only one number that is in both of these sequences.
answer: Only 31 is in both — the second sequence is 39, 36, 31, 24, ... and never exceeds 39; the first is 1, 7, 17, 31, 49, ...; of 1, 7, 17, 31 only 31 = 40 − 32 is in the second.

The histogram gives information about the heights, in metres, of the trees in a park.

The histogram is incomplete.

20% of the trees in the park have a height between 10 metres and 12.5 metres.

None of the trees in the park have a height greater than 25 metres.

Complete the histogram.
answer: A bar from 10 to 12.5 with frequency density 3.2 — the drawn bars hold 3 + 5 + 14 + 10 = 32 trees, which is 80%, so there are 40 trees and the missing class holds 8; 8 ÷ 2.5 = 3.2

The point C is the midpoint of the arc AB.

The diagram also shows a hollow cone with vertex O.

The cone is formed by joining OA and OB.

Curved surface area of cone = πrl

Calculate the size of angle AOB of sector OACB.

answer: 264° — 1⁄3πr2 × 3.6 = 56.8 gives r = 3.8816; l = √(r2 + 3.62) = 5.2940; the arc becomes the base circle, so the angle is 360 × r ÷ l = 263.95...°

OX⃗ = a
OY⃗ = b

A and B are points on a circle, centre O.

BC is a tangent to the circle.
AOC is a straight line.
Angle ABO = x°.

Find the size of angle ACB, in terms of x.
Give your answer in its simplest form.
Give reasons for each stage of your working.
answer: (90 − 2x)° — OA = OB are radii, so angle OAB = x° (base angles of an isosceles triangle) and angle AOB = (180 − 2x)°. AOC is straight, so angle BOC = 2x°. The tangent meets the radius at 90°, so in triangle OBC angle BCO = 180 − 90 − 2x.

html: Prove that the square of an odd number is always 1 more than a multiple of 4
answer: An odd number is 2n + 1, and (2n + 1)2 = 4n2 + 4n + 1 = 4(n2 + n) + 1, which is 1 more than a multiple of 4.

A force of 70 newtons acts on an area of 20 cm2

pressure = force⁄area

The force is increased by 10 newtons.

The area is increased by 10 cm2

Helen says,

“The pressure decreases by less than 20%”

Is Helen correct?

answer: No: the pressure falls from 3.5 to 2.67 N/cm<sup>2</sup>, a decrease of 23.8%, which is more than 20% — The pressure starts at 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5 N/cm<sup>2</sup> and becomes 80 ÷ 30 = 2.666… N/cm<sup>2</sup>, a fall of 0.8333…, which is 23.8% of 3.5 — more than 20%, not less.

60 people were asked if they prefer to go on holiday in Britain or in Spain or in Italy.

38 of the people were male.

11 of the 32 people who said Britain were female.

8 males said Italy.

12 people said Spain.

One of the females is chosen at random.

What is the probability that this female said Spain?

html:
Show that  y − x = 90

You must give a reason for each stage of your working.
answer: OBD = x (isosceles), BCD = 90 − x (angle at centre), y + 90 − x = 180 (cyclic quadrilateral), so y − x = 90 — OB = OD because both are radii, so triangle OBD is isosceles and angle OBD = x° (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal). The angles of triangle OBD add to 180°, so angle BOD = (180 − 2x)°. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so angle BCD = (90 − x)°. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles add to 180°: y + 90 − x = 180, giving y − x = 90

html:
Martin did this question.

Rationalise the denominator of 14⁄2 + √3

Here is how he answered the question.

14⁄2 + √3 = 14 × (2 − √3)⁄(2 + √3)(2 − √3)

= 28 − 14√3⁄4 + 2√3 − 2√3 + 3

= 28 − 14√3⁄7

= 4 − 2√3

Martin’s answer is wrong.

Find Martin’s mistake.
answer: The last term of the denominator: −√3 × √3 = −3, not +3, so the denominator is 4 − 3 = 1, not 7 — Expanding (2 + √3)(2 − √3) ends in −√3 × √3 = −3, not +3, so the denominator is 4 − 3 = 1 and the answer is 28 − 14√3

html:
Jackson is trying to find the density, in g/cm3, of a block of wood.

The block of wood is in the shape of a cuboid.

He measures

the length as 13.2 cm, correct to the nearest mm

the width as 16.0 cm, correct to the nearest mm

the height as 21.7 cm, correct to the nearest mm

He measures the mass as 1970 g, correct to the nearest 5 g.

By considering bounds, work out the density of the wood.

Give your answer to a suitable degree of accuracy.

You must show all your working and give a reason for your final answer.
answer: 0.43 g/cm<sup>3</sup> — the mass lies between 1967.5 g and 1972.5 g and each length is within 0.05 cm, so the volume lies between 13.15 × 15.95 × 21.65 = 4540.6… and 13.25 × 16.05 × 21.75 = 4625.4… cm<sup>3</sup>. Dividing the smallest mass by the largest volume gives 0.42536… and the largest mass by the smallest volume gives 0.43438…. Both round to 0.43, so the density is 0.43 g/cm<sup>3</sup> to 2 decimal places — the bounds agree that far and no further.

Show that  area of shaded region⁄area of square = π⁄8
answer: Shown: the shaded region is 50π and the square 400, and 50π⁄400 = π⁄8 — The arc from A to C has centre B and radius BA = BC = 20, and the angle at B is the square’s right angle, so it cuts off a quarter circle of area ¼ × π × 202 = 100π. The semicircle on AB has radius 10 and area ½ × π × 102 = 50π. The shaded region is the difference, 50π, and the square is 400, so the ratio is 50π⁄400 = π⁄8

html:
Jack and Sadia work for a company that sells boxes of breakfast cereal.

The company wants to have a special offer.

Here is Jack’s idea for the special offer.

Put 25% more cereal into each box and do not change the price.

Here is Sadia’s idea.

Reduce the price and do not change the amount of cereal in each box.

Sadia wants her idea to give the same value for money as Jack’s idea.

By what percentage does she need to reduce the price?
answer: 20% — take a box costing £1 holding 100 g. Jack sells 125 g for £1, which is 0.8p per gram. For Sadia to match that on 100 g she must charge 80p

html:
A, B and C are points on the circumference of a circle, centre O.

DAE is the tangent to the circle at A.

Angle BAE = 56°

Angle CBO = 35°

Work out the size of angle CAO.

You must show all your working.
answer: 21° — by the alternate segment theorem the tangent-chord angle BAE equals the angle in the alternate segment, so angle ACB = 56°. OB = OC are radii, so triangle OBC is isosceles and angle OCB = 35°, which leaves angle ACO = 56 − 35 = 21°. OA = OC are radii too, so triangle OAC is isosceles and angle CAO = angle ACO

There are only green pens and blue pens in a box.

There are three more blue pens than green pens in the box.

There are more than 12 pens in the box.

Simon is going to take at random two pens from the box.

The probability that Simon will take two pens of the same colour is 27⁄55

Work out the number of green pens in the box.
answer: 21 — with g green and g + 3 blue in a box of 2g + 3, the chance of a matching pair is [g(g − 1) + (g + 3)(g + 2)] ÷ [(2g + 3)(2g + 2)] = 27⁄55. That has exactly two whole-number solutions, g = 4 (a box of 11) and g = 21 (a box of 45) — which is what the “more than 12 pens” condition is there to settle.

html:
Triangle P is reflected in the line y = −x to give triangle Q.

Triangle Q is reflected in the line x = −1 to give triangle R.

Describe fully the single transformation that maps triangle R to triangle P.
answer: A rotation of 90° anticlockwise about (−1, 1) — Following P through: the first reflection sends (−1, 3), (3, 3), (3, 5) to (−3, 1), (−3, −3), (−5, −3), and the second sends those to (1, 1), (1, −3), (3, −3), which is R. All three of those rotate back onto P about (−1, 1), the point where the two mirror lines cross — two reflections in lines meeting at 45° always make a 90° turn about that point.

Robert makes 50 litres of green paint by mixing litres of yellow paint and litres of blue paint in the ratio 2 : 3

Yellow paint is sold in 5 litre tins.

Each tin of yellow paint costs £26

Blue paint is sold in 10 litre tins.

Each tin of blue paint costs £48

Robert sells all the green paint he makes in 10 litre tins.

He sells each tin of green paint for £66.96

Work out Robert’s percentage profit on each tin of green paint he sells.
answer: 35% — the mix is 20 litres of yellow (four 5 litre tins, £104) and 30 litres of blue (three 10 litre tins, £144), so 50 litres costs £248. He sells five 10 litre tins for £334.80, a profit of £86.80, and 86.80 ÷ 248 = 0.35 exactly

html:
In a restaurant there are

9 starter dishes
15 main dishes
8 dessert dishes

Janet is going to choose one of the following combinations for her meal.

a starter dish and a main dish
or  a main dish and a dessert dish
or  a starter dish, a main dish and a dessert dish

Show that there are 1335 different ways to choose the meal.
answer: Shown: 9 × 15 + 15 × 8 + 9 × 15 × 8 = 135 + 120 + 1080 = 1335 — A main and a dessert is 15 × 8 = 120. All three courses is 9 × 15 × 8 = 1080. The three choices cannot happen together, so they add: 135 + 120 + 1080 = 1335

html: Write  4x2 − 9⁄6x + 9 × 2x⁄x2 − 3x  in the form  ax + b⁄cx + d  where a, b, c and d are integers.
answer: (4x − 6)⁄(3x − 9) — factorise everything: 4x2 − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3), 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) and x2 − 3x = x(x − 3). The (2x + 3) and the x cancel, leaving 2(2x − 3) over 3(x − 3)

html: Express  3⁄x + 1 + 1⁄x − 2 − 4⁄x  as a single fraction in its simplest form.
answer: (8 − x)⁄x(x + 1)(x − 2) — over the common denominator x(x + 1)(x − 2) the tops are 3x(x − 2), x(x + 1) and −4(x + 1)(x − 2). Those come to 3x2 − 6x + x2 + x − 4x2 + 4x + 8, and the x2 terms cancel

There are 78 red counters in the bag.

How many blue counters are there in the bag?
answer: 42 — the 78 red counters are 0.65 of the bag, so there are 78 ÷ 0.65 = 120 counters in all (a whole number, as it must be), leaving 120 − 78 blue

html:
p and q are two numbers such that p > q

When you subtract 5 from p and subtract 5 from q the answers are in the ratio 5 : 1

When you add 20 to p and add 20 to q the answers are in the ratio 5 : 2

Find the ratio p : q

Give your answer in its simplest form.
answer: 4 : 1 — the first ratio gives p − 5 = 5(q − 5), so p = 5q − 20. The second gives 2(p + 20) = 5(q + 20), so 2p = 5q + 60. Substituting, 10q − 40 = 5q + 60, so q = 20 and p = 80. Both conditions check: 75 : 15 is 5 : 1 and 100 : 40 is 5 : 2

html:
The straight line L1 passes through the points with coordinates (4, 6) and (12, 2)

The straight line L2 passes through the origin and has gradient −3

The lines L1 and L2 intersect at point P.

Find the coordinates of P.
answer: (−3.2, 9.6) — L1 has gradient (2 − 6) ÷ (12 − 4) = −0.5, so it is y = −0.5x + 8, and L2 is y = −3x. Setting them equal gives −2.5x = 8. Both equations give y = 9.6 at that x

Solve  22 < m2 + 7⁄4 < 32

Show all your working.
answer: −11 < m < −9 or 9 < m < 11 — multiplying through by 4 gives 88 < m2 + 7 < 128, and taking 7 off gives 81 < m2 < 121. Squaring loses the sign, so m can be negative as well as positive: both intervals count.

html:
Here is a frustum of a cone.

The diagram shows that the frustum is made by removing a cone with height 3.2 cm from a solid cone with height 6.4 cm and base diameter 7.2 cm.

The frustum is joined to a solid hemisphere of diameter 7.2 cm to form the solid S shown below.

The density of the frustum is 2.4 g/cm3

The density of the hemisphere is 4.8 g/cm3

Calculate the average density of solid S.

Volume of sphere = 4⁄3πr3

Volume of cone = 1⁄3πr2h
answer: 3.75 g/cm<sup>3</sup> — the removed cone is half the height, so its radius is half too: 1.8 cm. The frustum is <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>π × 3.6<sup>2</sup> × 6.4 − <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>π × 1.8<sup>2</sup> × 3.2 = 76.00… cm<sup>3</sup> and the hemisphere is <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>π × 3.6<sup>3</sup> = 97.72… cm<sup>3</sup>. The masses are 182.40 g and 469.04 g, so the average density is 651.44 ÷ 173.72, which comes out at exactly 3.75. Note it is total mass ÷ total volume, not the average of 2.4 and 4.8

html:
A, B, R and P are four points on a circle with centre O.

A, O, R and C are four points on a different circle.

The two circles intersect at the points A and R.

CPA, CRB and AOB are straight lines.

Prove that angle CAB = angle ABC.
answer: ARB = 90° (semicircle), so ARC = 90°, AC is a diameter, AOC = 90°; CO bisects AB at 90°, so CA = CB and CAB = ABC — AOB is a straight line through the centre O, so AB is a diameter of the first circle and angle ARB = 90° (the angle in a semicircle). CRB is a straight line, so angle ARC = 180 − 90 = 90° (angles on a straight line). Now A, O, R and C lie on the second circle and angle ARC is 90°, so AC must be a diameter of that circle (the converse of the angle in a semicircle). O is on that circle too, so angle AOC = 90° for the same reason. That makes CO perpendicular to AB, and O is the midpoint of AB because it is the centre of the first circle — so CO is the perpendicular bisector of AB and CA = CB. Triangle CAB is therefore isosceles, and angle CAB = angle ABC (base angles of an isosceles triangle).

html: Show that (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3) can be written in the form ax3 + bx2 + cx + d where a, b, c and d are positive integers.
answer: (x2 + 3x + 2)(x + 3) = x3 + 6x2 + 11x + 6, so a = 1, b = 6, c = 11, d = 6 — The first two brackets give x2 + 3x + 2. Multiplying that by (x + 3) gives x3 + 3x2 + 2x + 3x2 + 9x + 6 = x3 + 6x2 + 11x + 6. So a = 1, b = 6, c = 11, d = 6, all positive integers as required

html:
White shapes and black shapes are used in a game.
Some of the shapes are circles.
All the other shapes are squares.

The ratio of the number of white shapes to the number of black shapes is 3 : 7

The ratio of the number of white circles to the number of white squares is 4 : 5

The ratio of the number of black circles to the number of black squares is 2 : 5

Work out what fraction of all the shapes are circles.
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> — the white shapes split into 9 parts and the black into 7, so scale the 3 : 7 up to 27 : 63 to make both splits whole. Then the white circles are <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> of 27 = 12 and the black circles <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>7</sub> of 63 = 18, giving 30 circles out of 90 shapes

n is an integer greater than 1

Prove algebraically that  n2 − 2 − (n − 2)2  is always an even number.
answer: It simplifies to 4n − 6 = 2(2n − 3), which is even — Expand the bracket: (n − 2)2 = n2 − 4n + 4. So the expression is n2 − 2 − n2 + 4n − 4 = 4n − 6. That is 2(2n − 3), which is 2 times a whole number and therefore even for every integer n.

html:
There are 9 counters in a bag.

7 of the counters are green.

2 of the counters are blue.

Ria takes at random two counters from the bag.

Work out the probability that Ria takes one counter of each colour.

You must show your working.
answer: <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>18</sub> — the counters are not replaced, so the second denominator is 8. Green then blue is <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> and blue then green is <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> × <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> — the same product, so double it: <sup>28</sup>⁄<sub>72</sub>

answer: y = −2x + 21 — the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles, so the gradient of AC is the negative reciprocal of ½, which is −2. Then AC passes through A(5, 11): 11 = −2 × 5 + c gives c = 21

Solve algebraically the simultaneous equations

x2 + y2 = 25
y − 3x = 13
answer: x = −3, y = 4 and x = −4.8, y = −1.4 — the linear equation gives y = 3x + 13. Substituting, 10x2 + 78x + 144 = 0, which divides by 2 to 5x2 + 39x + 72 = 0. Its discriminant is 81, a perfect square, so it factorises. Both pairs check in the circle: 9 + 16 = 25 and 23.04 + 1.96 = 25

html:
ABCD is a quadrilateral.

AB = CD.
Angle ABC = angle BCD.

Prove that AC = BD.
answer: Triangles ABC and DCB are congruent (SAS: AB = DC, angle ABC = angle DCB, BC shared), so AC = BD — Compare triangles ABC and DCB. AB = DC, which is given. Angle ABC = angle DCB, which is given — it is the same pair of angles read the other way round. And BC = CB, the side both triangles share. Two sides and the angle between them match, so the triangles are congruent (SAS). Congruent triangles have equal corresponding sides, and AC and DB are the two that correspond.

html:
The diagram shows a hexagon ABCDEF.

ABEF and CBED are congruent parallelograms where AB = BC = x cm.
P is the point on AF and Q is the point on CD such that BP = BQ = 10 cm.

Given that angle ABC = 30°,

prove that cos PBQ = 1 − (2 − √3)200x2
answer:
Proved: PQ = AC, and the cosine rule in triangles ABC and PBQ gives it — First, PQ = AC. AF and CD are both parallel to BE because each is a side of one of the parallelograms, so AP is parallel to CQ; and the parallelograms are congruent with BP = BQ, so AP = CQ. A quadrilateral with one pair of sides equal and parallel is a parallelogram, so APQC is one and PQ = AC.
Now the cosine rule twice. In triangle ABC, with AB = BC = x and the angle between them 30°: AC2 = x2 + x2 − 2x2cos 30° = 2x2 − √3x2 = (2 − √3)x2, since cos 30° = √3⁄2.
In triangle PBQ, with BP = BQ = 10: PQ2 = 100 + 100 − 200 cos PBQ. Setting the two equal, because PQ = AC: (2 − √3)x2 = 200 − 200 cos PBQ. Rearranging gives cos PBQ = 1 − ((2 − √3)⁄200)x2

html:
On Saturday, some adults and some children were in a theatre.
The ratio of the number of adults to the number of children was 5 : 2

Each person had a seat in the Circle or had a seat in the Stalls.

3⁄4 of the children had seats in the Stalls.
117 children had seats in the Circle.

There are exactly 2600 seats in the theatre.

On this Saturday, were there people on more than 60% of the seats?
You must show how you get your answer.
answer: Yes: 468 children and 1170 adults make 1638 people, which is 63% of the 2600 seats — The 117 children in the Circle are the quarter not in the Stalls, so there were 468 children, and the 5 : 2 ratio makes that 1170 adults. That is 1638 people in 2600 seats, which is exactly 63% — above 60%.

On the centimetre grid below, draw the front elevation and the side elevation of the prism.
Use a scale of 2 cm to 1 m.
answer: Front: the trapezium. Side: a 2 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a line 1 cm up — Front elevation (looking along the arrow marked front): the trapezium itself, 4 cm along the bottom, 4 cm up the left-hand side and 1 cm up the right-hand side, with the sloping line joining their tops. Side elevation (looking along the arrow marked side): a rectangle 2 cm wide and 4 cm tall, with a horizontal line across it 1 cm above the bottom — the edge where the 0.5 m upright face meets the sloping face behind it. At 2 cm to the metre every length doubles; the depth of the prism is the 1 m, and the 2.5 m is the slope, which does not appear at its true length in either view.

html:
The diagram shows triangle A drawn on a grid.

Kyle reflects triangle A in the x-axis to get triangle B.
He then reflects triangle B in the line y = x to get triangle C.

Amy reflects triangle A in the line y = x to get triangle D.
She is then going to reflect triangle D in the x-axis to get triangle E.

Amy says that triangle E should be in the same position as triangle C.

Is Amy correct?
You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No: C is at (−3, 3), (−3, 4), (−1, 4) but E is at (3, −3), (3, −4), (1, −4) — Draw the four triangles. B is (3, −3), (4, −3), (4, −1), and reflecting that in y = x swaps each pair, so C is (−3, 3), (−3, 4), (−1, 4). D is (3, 3), (3, 4), (1, 4), and reflecting that in the x-axis gives E at (3, −3), (3, −4), (1, −4). C is top left and E is bottom right — a half turn apart — so the order of the two reflections matters. In general Kyle sends (x, y) to (−y, x) and Amy to (y, −x).

Owen and Wasim play for the school football team.

The probability that Owen will score a goal in the next match is 0.4
The probability that Wasim will score a goal in the next match is 0.25

Mr Slater says,
“The probability that both boys will score a goal in the next match is 0.4 + 0.25”

Is Mr Slater right?
Give a reason for your answer.
answer: No: for both to happen you multiply, 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.1 — For both events to happen you MULTIPLY: 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.1. Adding is for one event OR another, and his 0.65 is larger than either probability on its own, which cannot be right for “both”.

20% of the members of the sports club who are over 50 years of age are female.

Work out an estimate for the number of female members who are over 50 years of age.
answer: 7 — frequency is frequency density × class width, so read each bar’s height and multiply: 1.1 × 10 = 11, 2.8 × 10 = 28, 2.3 × 20 = 46, 1.4 × 20 = 28 and 0.7 × 30 = 21. Those add to 134, the membership the question states, so the bars have been read correctly. Over 50 is half of the 40–60 bar (1.4 × 10 = 14) plus all of the 60–90 bar (21), which is 35, and 20% of 35 = 7.

Prove that triangle ABE and triangle DCE are similar.

html: Using algebra, prove that 0.13̇6̇ × 0.2̇ is equal in value to 1⁄33
answer: Proved: 3⁄22 × 2⁄9 = 1⁄33 — Take the first: let x = 0.1363636…, so 100x = 13.6363636…. The recurring tails match, so subtracting gives 99x = 13.5 and x = 13.5⁄99 = 27⁄198 = 3⁄22. Take the second: let y = 0.222…, so 10y = 2.222… and 9y = 2, giving y = 2⁄9. Multiplying, 3⁄22 × 2⁄9 = 6⁄198 = 1⁄33

Find an equation of the tangent to L at the point P.
answer: 3x + √7y = 8, that is y = (8 − 3x)⁄√7 — the tangent is perpendicular to the radius OP, whose gradient is (√7⁄2) ÷ (3⁄2) = √7⁄3. The negative reciprocal is −3⁄√7, and putting P into y = mx + c finishes it. Two checks: P really is on the circle, since 9⁄4 + 7⁄4 = 4, and P satisfies the tangent, since 4.5 + 3.5 = 8

Show that polygon P is a hexagon.
You must show your working.
answer: Shown: P’s interior angle is 360 − 90 − 150 = 120°, so it has 6 sides — The three interior angles at B make a full turn, 360°. The square gives 90° and the regular 12-gon gives (12 − 2) × 180 ÷ 12 = 150°, so polygon P’s interior angle is 360 − 90 − 150 = 120°. Its exterior angle is therefore 60°, and 360 ÷ 60 = 6 sides — a hexagon

The density of apple juice is 1.05 grams per cm3.

The density of fruit syrup is 1.4 grams per cm3.

The density of carbonated water is 0.99 grams per cm3.

25 cm3 of apple juice are mixed with 15 cm3 of fruit syrup and 280 cm3 of carbonated water to make a drink with a volume of 320 cm3.

Work out the density of the drink.
Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
answer: 1.01 g/cm<sup>3</sup> — densities cannot be averaged, but masses can be added. 25 × 1.05 = 26.25 g, 15 × 1.4 = 21 g and 280 × 0.99 = 277.2 g, giving 324.45 g in 320 cm<sup>3</sup>. 324.45 ÷ 320 = 1.01390…

html:
A square, with sides of length x cm, is inside a circle.
Each vertex of the square is on the circumference of the circle.

The area of the circle is 49 cm2.

Work out the value of x.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 5.59 — 49 is the area in cm2, not 49π, so πr2 = 49 gives r = √(49 ÷ π) = 3.9493… and the diameter is 7.8986… cm. The square’s diagonal IS that diameter, so by Pythagoras x2 + x2 = 7.8986…2 and x = 7.8986… ÷ √2 = 5.5851…, which is 5.59 to 3 significant figures — the next digit is a 5 with more after it, so it rounds up. 5.58 comes from rounding r too early

html:
Chris says,

“The box plots show that the female students spent more money than the male students.”

Is Chris correct?

Give a reason for your answer.
answer: Either, with a reason: Yes, the female median £300 is above the male £250; or No, box plots do not show total spending — Yes: the female median is £300 against the male £250, so a typical female student spent more (and her lower quartile, £180, is higher too). No: the biggest spender was male — £750 against £650 — and box plots show how each group’s spending is spread, not how many students are in it, so they cannot show which group spent more money in total. An opinion with no figure from the plots behind it is not a reason

html:
Naoby invests £6000 for 5 years.
The investment gets compound interest of x% per annum.

At the end of 5 years the investment is worth £8029.35

Work out the value of x.
answer: 6 — five years of compound interest multiply by the same factor five times, so 6000 × k5 = 8029.35 and k5 = 1.338225. Taking the fifth root gives k = 1.06, which is a 6% rise each year. Checking forwards: 6000 × 1.065 = 8029.35

html:
Jeff is choosing a shrub and a rose tree for his garden.
At the garden centre there are 17 different types of shrubs and some rose trees.

Jeff says,

“There are 215 different ways to choose one shrub and one rose tree.”

Could Jeff be correct?
You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No: the total must be a multiple of 17, and 215 ÷ 17 = 12.6… is not a whole number — a multiple of 17. 215 ÷ 17 = 12.6…, which is not a whole number, so no number of rose trees gives 215. (17 × 12 = 204 and 17 × 13 = 221 straddle it.)

html:
The points A, B, C and D lie in order on a straight line.

AB : BD = 1 : 5
AC : CD = 7 : 11

Work out AB : BC : CD
answer: 3 : 4 : 11 — both ratios split the same whole AD, into 6 parts and into 18 parts, so scale the first up to eighteenths: AB : BD = 3 : 15. Now AB = 3 and AC = 7 measured from A, so BC = 7 − 3 = 4, and CD = 11. Check: 3 + 4 + 11 = 18

html: Write down the three inequalities that define the shaded region.
answer: y ≥ −2, y ≤ ½x + 1 and y ≥ x — Find each line first: the shallow one cuts the y-axis at 1 and rises 1 for every 2 across, so y = ½x + 1; the steep one passes through the origin and (2, 2), so y = x; the flat one is y = −2. Then test one point inside, say (−3, −1): it is below the first line, above the second and above −2. All three lines are solid, so all three are ≤ or ≥ rather than strict

html: Simplify  x2 − 162x2 − 5x − 12
answer: (x + 4) ⁄ (2x + 3) — the top is a difference of two squares, (x − 4)(x + 4). The bottom factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 4), since 2 × −12 = −24 splits as +3 and −8. The (x − 4) cancels

html: Make v the subject of the formula  w = 15(t − 2v)v
answer: v = 15t ⁄ (w + 30) — v appears twice, so gather it. Multiply through by v: wv = 15t − 30v. Move every v term to one side: wv + 30v = 15t, then factorise, v(w + 30) = 15t

answer: 2.63 — the two given sides enclose the given angle, so area = ½ab sin C: ½(x + 3)(2x − 1) sin 45° = 6√2. Since sin 45° = √2⁄2, the √2 cancels off both sides and leaves (x + 3)(2x − 1) = 24, so 2x2 + 5x − 27 = 0. html: Explain the relationship between the values of x1, x2 and x3 and the equation x3 + 2x2 + 4 = 0
answer: They are converging on a solution of that equation — The iteration IS the equation rearranged: x3 + 2x2 + 4 = 0 gives x2(x + 2) = −4, so x + 2 = −4 ⁄ x2 and x = −2 − 4 ⁄ x2. The values oscillate either side of the root and close in on about −2.59

html:
A train travelled along a track in 110 minutes, correct to the nearest 5 minutes.

Jake finds out that the track is 270 km long.
He assumes that the track has been measured correct to the nearest 10 km.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Could the average speed of the train have been greater than 160 km/h?
You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No: the fastest possible is 275 km in 107.5 minutes, which is 153.5 km/h, under 160 km/h — Speed is greatest when the distance is at its largest and the time at its smallest, so take 275 km (the upper bound of 270 to the nearest 10) and 107.5 minutes (the lower bound of 110 to the nearest 5). 107.5 minutes is 107.5 ÷ 60 = 1.79166… hours, and 275 ÷ 1.79166… = 153.48… km/h. Even the fastest the figures allow is under 160
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Jake’s assumption was wrong.

The track was measured correct to the nearest 5 km.

Explain how this could affect your decision in part (a).
answer: No effect: the upper bound falls to 272.5 km, so the fastest possible speed is about 152 km/h, still under 160 — The nearest 5 km puts the upper bound at 272.5 km instead of 275, which is a SMALLER distance, so the fastest possible speed drops to 272.5 ÷ 1.79166… = 152.09… km/h — still under 160. A tighter measurement can only narrow the bounds, never widen them

html:
A, B and C are points on a circle of radius 5 cm, centre O.
DA and DC are tangents to the circle.
DO = 9 cm

Work out the length of arc ABC.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 21.6 cm — a tangent meets the radius at 90°, so OAD is right-angled with hypotenuse OD = 9 and OA = 5. cos(angle AOD) = 5 ÷ 9 gives 56.25…°, and by symmetry angle AOC = 112.50…°. Arc ABC goes the long way round through B, so its angle is 360 − 112.50… = 247.49…°, and the arc is 247.49… ÷ 360 × 2π × 5 = 21.598…. Taking the minor arc instead gives 9.82, and that is the trap

answer: x < −2 or x > ½ — factorise to (2x − 1)(x + 2) > 0, with roots ½ and −2. The curve opens upwards, so it is ABOVE the axis outside the roots, not between them. The answer is two separate pieces, and writing it as a single chain like −2 < x < ½ is the region where it is negative

answer: 2<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup>, that is 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 — keep halving and then dividing by 3: 36 = 2 × 18 = 2 × 2 × 9 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. A product means it must be written as a multiplication, not as a list

html:
Kiaria is 7 years older than Jay.

Martha is twice as old as Kiaria.

The sum of their three ages is 77

Find the ratio of Jay’s age to Kiaria’s age to Martha’s age.
answer: 14 : 21 : 42, or 2 : 3 : 6 — the mark scheme prints the first and accepts any equivalent, so a simplified answer is right too. Call Jay’s age j. Kiaria is j + 7 and Martha is 2(j + 7) = 2j + 14, so 4j + 21 = 77 and j = 14. The ages are 14, 21 and 42, and every one divides by 7

html:
ABCD is a parallelogram.
EDC is a straight line.
F is the point on AD so that BFE is a straight line.

Angle EFD = 35°
Angle DCB = 75°

Show that angle ABF = 70°
Give a reason for each stage of your working.
answer: AFB = 35° (vertically opposite), BAF = 75° (opposite angles of a parallelogram), so ABF = 70° (angles in a triangle) — Angle AFB = 35°, vertically opposite angle EFD (AD and BE are both straight lines crossing at F) — Angle BAF = angle BAD = 75°, because opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so it matches angle DCB. Then angle ABF = 180 − 35 − 75 = 70°, because angles in a triangle add to 180°. The marks are for the REASONS as much as the numbers

html:
James and Peter cycled along the same 50 km route.

James took 2½ hours to cycle the 50 km.

Peter started to cycle 5 minutes after James started to cycle.

Peter caught up with James when they had both cycled 15 km.

James and Peter both cycled at constant speeds.

Work out Peter’s speed.
answer: 22.5 km/h — James rode 50 km in 2.5 hours, so 20 km/h, and 15 km took him 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75 hours = 45 minutes. Peter started 5 minutes later and arrived at the same moment, so he covered the same 15 km in 40 minutes = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> hour. 15 ÷ <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> = 22.5

html: Find the value of 1252⁄3
answer: 25 — the bottom of the fraction is the root and the top is the power, so take the cube root first and square it: ∛125 = 5, then 5<sup>2</sup> = 25. Doing it the other way round works too but means cube-rooting 15 625

3 teas and 2 coffees have a total cost of £7.80

5 teas and 4 coffees have a total cost of £14.20

Work out the cost of one tea and the cost of one coffee.
answer: Tea £1.40, coffee £1.80 — with t and c, 3t + 2c = 7.80 and 5t + 4c = 14.20. Doubling the first gives 6t + 4c = 15.60, and subtracting the second leaves t = 1.40. Then 4.20 + 2c = 7.80. Check both: 3(1.40) + 2(1.80) = 7.80 and 5(1.40) + 4(1.80) = 14.20

The box plot below shows information about the heights, in cm, of a group of Year 7 girls.

Compare the distribution of heights of the Year 7 girls with the distribution of heights of the Year 11 girls.
answer: Year 11 girls are taller on average (median 165 cm against 157.5 cm) and less spread out (IQR 7 cm against 10.5 cm) — Two comparisons are wanted, one about average and one about spread, and at least one of them has to be in context — The Year 11 median (165 cm) is higher than the Year 7 median (157.5 cm), so the Year 11 girls are taller on average. The Year 11 interquartile range (7 cm) is smaller than the Year 7 one (165 − 154.5 = 10.5 cm), so the Year 11 heights are less spread out. Ranges do the second job too: 20 cm against 170.5 − 146 = 24.5 cm

On Monday Milo calculated that he needed exactly 4 chicken pies in his sample.

Work out the total number of chicken pies that were made on Monday.
answer: 120 — the sample is <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>15</sub> chicken, so the day’s pies are too: <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>15</sub> × 450. Or scale up: 15 goes into 450 thirty times, so 4 × 30
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
On Tuesday, the number of steak pies Milo needs in his sample is 6 correct to the nearest whole number.

Milo takes at random a pie from the 450 pies made on Tuesday.

Work out the lower bound of the probability that the pie is a steak pie.
answer: <sup>11</sup>⁄<sub>30</sub>, about 0.367 — “6 to the nearest whole number” means anything from 5.5 up to 6.5, so the smallest the sample count could be is 5.5. The probability is that share of the sample, 5.5 ÷ 15 = <sup>11</sup>⁄<sub>30</sub>. The 450 never enters it — the proportion is the same in the sample and in the day’s pies

html:
The ratio (y + x) : (y − x) is equivalent to k : 1

Show that y = x(k + 1)k − 1
answer: Shown: y + x = k(y − x) rearranges to x(k + 1) = y(k − 1) — A ratio equal to k : 1 means the first part divided by the second is k, so (y + x) ⁄ (y − x) = k and y + x = k(y − x) = ky − kx. Collect the y terms on one side and the x terms on the other: x + kx = ky − y, so x(k + 1) = y(k − 1)
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
x = 0.43•6•

Prove algebraically that x can be written as 2455
answer: Proved: 990x = 432, so x = 432⁄990 = 24⁄55 — Multiply by two powers of ten whose decimal parts match, then subtract. 10x = 4.363636… and 1000x = 436.363636…, so 990x = 432 exactly. Then x = 432⁄990, and dividing top and bottom by 18 gives 24⁄55. Picking 10x and 1000x rather than x and 100x is what lines the recurring parts up, because the 4 does not repeat
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
y is directly proportional to ∛x

y = 116 when x = 8

Find the value of y when x = 64
answer: 21⁄3, that is 7⁄3 — the variable is the CUBE ROOT of x, not x cubed. So y = k∛x, and 7⁄6 = k × 2 gives k = 7⁄12. At x = 64 the cube root is 4, so y = 7⁄12 × 4. Or note that x going 8 → 64 doubles the cube root, so it doubles y
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
n is an integer.

Prove algebraically that the sum of 12n(n + 1) and 12(n + 1)(n + 2) is always a square number.
answer: The sum factorises to (n + 1)2, a square number — Both terms share ½(n + 1), so factorise rather than expand: ½(n + 1)[n + (n + 2)] = ½(n + 1)(2n + 2) = ½(n + 1) × 2(n + 1) = (n + 1)2. Since n is an integer so is n + 1, and a square of an integer is a square number
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2017

Enlarge shape P by scale factor −12 with centre of enlargement (0, 0).
Label your image Q.
answer: The triangle with vertices (−1, −3½), (−1, −1½) and (−2, −1½) — With the centre at the origin, just multiply every coordinate by −½. The minus sign puts the image on the opposite side of the centre, turned through 180°, and the ½ halves every length

ABCD is a rectangle.

A, E and B are points on the straight line L with equation x + 2y = 12
A and D are points on the straight line M.

AE = EB

Find an equation for M.
answer: y = 2x + 36 — L cuts the axes at E(0, 6) and B(12, 0), and AE = EB makes E the midpoint of AB, so A = 2E − B = (−12, 12). AD is a side of a rectangle meeting AB, so M is perpendicular to L: L has gradient −½, so M has gradient 2. Then 12 = 2(−12) + c. The diagram is not to scale, which is why A looks nearer the origin than it is

The table shows some values of x and y that satisfy the equation y = a cos x° + b.

x0306090120150180
y31 + √32101 − √3−1

Find the value of y when x = 45
answer: 1 + √2 — find a and b from the two easy columns. cos 90° = 0, so the x = 90 entry gives b = 1 straight away; cos 0° = 1, so a + b = 3 and a = 2. Then y = 2 cos 45° + 1, and cos 45° = √2⁄2, so the 2 cancels. Check against x = 60: 2 × ½ + 1 = 2, as the table says

html: Show that 6 − √8√2 − 1 can be written in the form a + b√2 where a and b are integers.
answer: 2 + 4√2 — Simplify √8 = 2√2 first, then rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by √2 + 1. The bottom becomes (√2)<sup>2</sup> − 1 = 1, which is why the answer comes out with integers. The top is (6 − 2√2)(√2 + 1) = 6√2 + 6 − 4 − 2√2 = 2 + 4√2. Check on a calculator: both sides are 7.657

The two triangles in the diagram are similar.

There are two possible values of x.

State any assumptions you make in your working.
answer: x = 2 or x = 14.5 — Both triangles share the angle at A, and AC = 8 + x while AD = 15. Which pairs of sides correspond depends on an assumption. Assuming BE is parallel to CD, so angle ABE = angle ACD: 8 ⁄ (8 + x) = 12 ⁄ 15, giving x = 2. Assuming instead that angle ABE = angle ADC: 8 ⁄ 15 = 12 ⁄ (8 + x), giving 8 + x = 22.5 and x = 14.5. Here is a rectangle and a right-angled triangle.

All measurements are in centimetres.
The area of the rectangle is greater than the area of the triangle.

Find the set of possible values of x.
answer: x > 2 — The rectangle is (3x − 2)(x − 1) = 3x2 − 5x + 2 and the triangle is ½ × x × 2x = x2, so 2x2 − 5x + 2 > 0, which factorises to (2x − 1)(x − 2) > 0 with roots ½ and 2. That inequality alone allows x < ½ as well — but the rectangle’s side is x − 1, which must be positive, so x > 1 and that branch is impossible. Throwing it away is the last mark

answer: x = 1.5, or 3⁄2 — expand the bracket first: 5x − 6 = 3x − 3. Then 2x = 3. Check by substituting: both sides come to 1.5

Emily buys a pack of 12 bottles of water.

The pack costs £5.64

Emily sells all 12 bottles for 50p each.

Work out Emily’s percentage profit.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
answer: 6.4% — she takes 12 × 50p = £6.00, so the profit is £6.00 − £5.64 = £0.36. Percentage profit is measured against what she PAID: 0.36 ÷ 5.64 × 100 = 6.382…. Dividing by 6.00 instead gives 6.0%, and that is the common slip

There are only blue cubes, yellow cubes and green cubes in a bag.

There are

twice as many blue cubes as yellow cubes
and
four times as many green cubes as blue cubes.

Hannah takes at random a cube from the bag.

Work out the probability that Hannah takes a yellow cube.
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>11</sub> — build the ratio from the smallest group. Call yellow 1 part; blue is twice that, 2 parts; green is four times BLUE, so 8 parts, not 4. That is 1 : 2 : 8, eleven parts in all. Reading “four times as many green as blue” as four times yellow is the trap

A triangle has vertices P, Q and R.

M is the midpoint of PQ.

N is the midpoint of QR.

Prove that MN is parallel to PR.

answer: Shown: MN and PR both have gradient ½ — Parallel means EQUAL GRADIENTS, so find both. The midpoints come from averaging the coordinates: M = ((−3 + 1)⁄2, (−6 + 4)⁄2) = (−1, −1) and N = ((1 + 5)⁄2, (4 − 2)⁄2) = (3, 1). Gradient of MN = (1 − −1) ⁄ (3 − −1) = 2⁄4 = ½. Gradient of PR = (−2 − −6) ⁄ (5 − −3) = 4⁄8 = ½. Same gradient, so parallel — and the sentence saying so is a mark

html: Work out the probability of taking 3 red counters.
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> — equal numbers of three colours out of 12 means 4 of each. The counters are not replaced, so the bag shrinks each time: <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> × <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>11</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> = <sup>24</sup>⁄<sub>1320</sub>

html:
The 3 counters are put back into the bag.

Some more counters are now put into the bag.

There is still an equal number of red counters, blue counters and yellow counters in the bag.

There are no counters of any other colour in the bag.

3 counters are taken at random from the bag.

Is it now less likely or equally likely or more likely that the 3 counters will be red?

You must show how you get your answer.
answer: More likely: with 5 of each, P(3 red) = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>91</sub> = 0.0220, more than the <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> = 0.0182 before — say 15 counters, 5 of each: <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>15</sub> × <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>14</sub> × <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>13</sub> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>91</sub> = 0.0220, against <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> = 0.0182. The reason is that taking counters out matters less in a big bag: each draw stays nearer <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, and the probability climbs towards <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>27</sub>

answer: a = 7, b = −1 — Each condition gives one equation. g(3) = 20 means 3a + b = 20. For the other, f−1(33) asks what input f sends to 33: 5x + 3 = 33 gives 6, so g(1) = 6 and a + b = 6. Subtracting leaves 2a = 14. Check: g(3) = 21 − 1 = 20

Given that (√x − 1), 1 and (√x + 1) are the first three terms of S, find the value of x.

answer: x = 2 — in a geometric sequence each term divided by the one before gives the same ratio, so 1 ⁄ (√x − 1) = (√x + 1) ⁄ 1. Cross multiplying gives (√x − 1)(√x + 1) = 1, and that is a difference of two squares: x − 1 = 1

html: Show that the 5th term of S is 7 + 5√2
answer: With x = 2 the terms start √2 − 1, 1, √2 + 1, so the common ratio is √2 + 1 — The 4th term is (√2 + 1)2 = 2 + 2√2 + 1 = 3 + 2√2, and the 5th is (3 + 2√2)(√2 + 1) = 3√2 + 3 + 4 + 2√2 = 7 + 5√2. Note 2√2 × √2 = 4, not 2√2

html:
In London, 1 litre of petrol costs 108.9p

In New York, 1 US gallon of petrol costs $2.83

1 US gallon = 3.785 litres

£1 = $1.46

In which city is petrol better value for money, London or New York?

You must show your working.
answer: New York: $2.83 ÷ 3.785 ÷ 1.46 = £0.512 a litre, 51.2p against London’s 108.9p — Bring both to the same unit and the same currency: $2.83 for 3.785 litres is $0.7477 a litre, and dividing by 1.46 gives £0.5121, which is 51.2p against London’s 108.9p. Multiplying by 1.46 instead of dividing turns dollars into nothing useful — the rate is dollars PER pound, so dollars divide

A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg.

The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm3

Work out the volume of the gold bar.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 648 cm<sup>3</sup> — the density is in grams, so convert the mass first: 12.5 kg = 12 500 g. Volume = mass ÷ density = 12 500 ÷ 19.3 = 647.66…. Forgetting the kilogram-to-gram step gives 0.648 and is the whole of the difficulty

html:
There are only blue pens, green pens and red pens in a box.

The ratio of the number of blue pens to the number of green pens is 2 : 5

The ratio of the number of green pens to the number of red pens is 4 : 1

There are less than 100 pens in the box.

What is the greatest possible number of red pens in the box?
answer: 15 — link the two ratios through green, which is 5 in one and 4 in the other, so scale both to 20: blue : green = 8 : 20 and green : red = 20 : 5. That makes blue : green : red = 8 : 20 : 5, which is 33 pens per set. Under 100 allows 3 sets (99 pens), so red is 3 × 5

html:
Here is a rectangle.

The length of the rectangle is 7 cm longer than the width of the rectangle.

4 of these rectangles are used to make this 8-sided shape.

The perimeter of the 8-sided shape is 70 cm.

Work out the area of the 8-sided shape.
answer: 147 cm2 — Call the width w, so the length is w + 7. Walking the outline gives eight sides that pair up: two of (w + length), two of w, two of (length − w) and two of the length — which simplifies to 2w + 6 × length. So 2w + 6(w + 7) = 70, giving 8w = 28 and w = 3.5, length = 10.5. The area is just the four rectangles: 4 × 3.5 × 10.5. Nothing overlaps and there is no hole, which is why the area needs no subtraction

When a drawing pin is dropped it can land point down or point up.

Lucy, Mel and Tom each dropped the drawing pin a number of times.

LucyMelTom
point down315316
point up14279

Rachael is going to drop the drawing pin once.

Whose results will give the best estimate for the probability that the drawing pin will land point up?

Give a reason for your answer.
answer: Mel’s: she dropped the pin the most times (80) — she dropped the pin 80 times, more than Lucy’s 45 or Tom’s 25, and a relative frequency from more trials is the more reliable estimate. Nothing about the proportions themselves matters here

html:
Stuart is going to drop the drawing pin twice.

Use all the results in the table to work out an estimate for the probability that the drawing pin will land point up the first time and point down the second time.
answer: <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> — pool every trial: 14 + 27 + 9 = 50 point up out of 45 + 80 + 25 = 150 drops, so P(up) = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> and P(down) = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. The drops are independent, so multiply: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. “All the results” is an instruction — using Mel’s alone is a different answer

Jack bought a new boat for £12 500

The value, £V, of Jack’s boat at the end of n years is given by the formula

V = 12 500 × (0.85)n

At the end of how many years was the value of Jack’s boat first less than 50% of the value of the boat when it was new?
answer: 5 years — the 12 500 cancels, so the question is when 0.85n first drops below 0.5. The powers run 0.85, 0.7225, 0.6141, 0.5220, 0.4437: still above a half after 4 years, below it after 5. Trying values is the expected method here

html:
A savings account pays interest at a rate of R% per year.

Jack invests £5500 in the account for one year.

At the end of the year, Jack pays tax on the interest at a rate of 40%.

After paying tax, he gets £79.20

Work out the value of R.
answer: 2.4 — work backwards. The £79.20 is what is LEFT after 40% tax, so it is 60% of the interest: interest = 79.20 ÷ 0.6 = £132. Then R = 132 ÷ 5500 × 100. Taking 40% off the 79.20 instead of dividing by 0.6 is the trap

Jamil says,

“80 − 40 = 40 so the range of the weights is 40 g.”

Is Jamil correct?

answer: No. The curve starts at 40 g with a cumulative frequency of 2, which says two potatoes weigh 40 g or LESS — it does not say how much less. The graph never shows the lightest or the heaviest potato, so 40 is at best an estimate of the range and could be an underestimate

He does this a number of times.

The number of times both spinners land on red is 24

Work out an estimate for the number of times both spinners land on white.
answer: 48 — find how many goes there were first. P(both red) = 0.25 × 0.6 = 0.15, and 0.15 of the goes came to 24, so there were 24 ÷ 0.15 = 160 goes. P(both white) = 0.75 × 0.4 = 0.3, so 0.3 × 160. The 160 is the step that is easy to skip

html:
Cone A and cone B are mathematically similar.

The ratio of the volume of cone A to the volume of cone B is 27 : 8

The surface area of cone A is 297 cm2

Show that the surface area of cone B is 132 cm2
answer: Shown: lengths 3 : 2, so areas 9 : 4, and 297 × <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> = 132 — Volumes scale as the cube of the length ratio, so take cube roots: ∛27 : ∛8 = 3 : 2. Areas scale as the SQUARE of that, 9 : 4. So area B = 297 × <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> = 132. Going straight from 27 : 8 to areas gives 88 and is the mistake this question exists to catch

html: Show that the equation x3 + 7x − 5 = 0 has a solution between x = 0 and x = 1
answer: At x = 0 it is −5 and at x = 1 it is 3; the sign changes, so there is a solution between 0 and 1 — It changes from negative to positive, and the graph of a cubic is continuous, so it must cross zero somewhere between. Saying “there is a sign change” is what earns the second mark
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Show that the equation  x3 + 7x − 5 = 0  can be arranged to give  x = 5⁄x2 + 7
answer: Move the 5 across: x3 + 7x = 5. Both terms on the left have an x, so factorise: x(x2 + 7) = 5, and divide by the bracket
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017

html: Starting with x0 = 1, use the iteration formula  xn + 1 = 5⁄xn2 + 7  three times to find an estimate for the solution of  x3 + 7x − 5 = 0
answer: 0.6704 (to 4 decimal places) — Feed each answer back in: x1 = 5 ÷ (1 + 7) = 0.625; x2 = 5 ÷ (0.6252 + 7) = 0.676533…; x3 = 5 ÷ (0.6765332 + 7) = 0.670448…. Keep every figure on the calculator between steps; rounding as you go drifts the answer
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: By substituting your answer to part (c) into x3 + 7x − 5, comment on the accuracy of your estimate for the solution to x3 + 7x − 5 = 0
answer: Putting 0.670448 in gives 0.3013 + 4.6931 − 5 = −0.0055, which is very close to 0 — so the estimate is a good one, and being slightly negative says the true root is a little ABOVE 0.6704. The comment has to name the number; “it is accurate” on its own earns nothing

html:
The petrol consumption of a car, in litres per 100 kilometres, is given by the formula

Petrol consumption = 100 × Number of litres of petrol used⁄Number of kilometres travelled

Nathan’s car travelled 148 kilometres, correct to 3 significant figures.

The car used 11.8 litres of petrol, correct to 3 significant figures.

Nathan says,

“My car used less than 8 litres of petrol per 100 kilometres.”

Could Nathan be wrong?

You must show how you get your answer.
answer: Yes: at the bounds, 100 × 11.85 ÷ 147.5 = 8.03, which is more than 8 — Yes, he could be. His own figures give 100 × 11.8 ÷ 148 = 7.97, just under 8 — but both are rounded. Consumption is largest when the petrol is at its upper bound and the distance at its lower: 100 × 11.85 ÷ 147.5 = 8.03, which is more than 8. So the true figure could be either side of 8 and his claim is not safe. Pairing 11.85 with 148.5 instead pushes it the wrong way and proves nothing
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
ABC and ADC are triangles.

The area of triangle ADC is 56 m2

Work out the length of AB.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
answer: 14.4 m — Three steps, and AC is the bridge between the two triangles. First the area formula on ADC: ½ × 11 × DC × sin 105° = 56 gives DC = 10.54… m. Then the cosine rule for the side between them: AC2 = 112 + 10.542 − 2 × 11 × 10.54 × cos 105° = 292.1, so AC = 17.09… m. Finally the sine rule in ABC: AB ⁄ sin 48° = AC ⁄ sin 118°, giving 14.385…. Carry full accuracy through all three or the last figure moves

html: Prove algebraically that the straight line with equation x − 2y = 10 is a tangent to the circle with equation x2 + y2 = 20
answer: Proved: substituting gives (y + 4)2 = 0, one repeated root, so one meeting point — Substitute and show the quadratic has a REPEATED root. From the line, x = 10 + 2y, so (10 + 2y)2 + y2 = 20 gives 5y2 + 40y + 80 = 0, that is y2 + 8y + 16 = 0, which is (y + 4)2 = 0. One repeated solution y = −4 means the line meets the circle at exactly one point, (2, −4) — which is what a tangent is. Quoting the discriminant, 82 − 4 × 1 × 16 = 0, does the same job

Sophia says that the result in part (a) shows that the difference of the squares of any two odd numbers must be a multiple of 4

answer: £186.15 — Take the garden in four pieces, and get the missing lengths from the rectangles first: OA = BC = 7, OC = AB = 11, OF = ED = 7 and OD = FE = 9. Is Oscar correct?

answer: Yes: 6y = 3x + 7 is y = ½x + 7⁄6, so both lines have gradient ½ — Parallel means equal GRADIENTS, so put the second into the same form: dividing 6y = 3x + 7 by 6 gives y = ½x + 7⁄6. Both have gradient ½, and the different intercepts are exactly what makes them two distinct parallel lines. Comparing 6y = 3x + 7 with the first equation as they stand compares nothing

answer: £17 500 — this runs backwards. Losing 23% leaves 77% and losing 19% leaves 81%, so the value was multiplied by 0.77 × 0.81 = 0.6237. Divide rather than multiply: 10 914.75 ÷ 0.6237. Check forwards: 17 500 × 0.77 = 13 475, and × 0.81 gives the £10 914.75 back

answer: 6 years — The population is multiplied by 1.13 every year, so after n years it is 1.13n times what it started at, and the starting number never matters. html: Using algebra, prove that 1.062̇ can be written as 114⁄225
answer: 900x = 1062.2… − 106.2… = 956, so x = 956⁄900 = 114⁄225 — Only the 2 recurs, so multiply by the two powers of ten whose decimal parts match: 100x = 106.2222… and 1000x = 1062.2222…. Subtracting kills the recurring tail exactly: 900x = 956, so x = 956⁄900 = 239⁄225 = 114⁄225. Using x and 10x instead leaves the 06 misaligned and the tail does not cancel

html:
Faiza is studying the population of rabbits in a park.

She wants to estimate the number of rabbits in the park.

On Monday she catches a random sample of 20 rabbits in the park, marks each rabbit with a tag and releases them back into the park.

On Tuesday she catches a random sample of 42 rabbits in the park.

12 of the rabbits are marked with a tag.

Find an estimate for the number of rabbits in the park.
answer: 70 — the proportion tagged in Tuesday’s sample should match the proportion tagged in the park: 12⁄42 = 20⁄N, so N = 20 × 42 ÷ 12. It assumes the tagged rabbits mixed back in and that nothing was born, died or moved between the two days

answer: 56° — Three steps, each in a different flat face. FD is the diagonal of the front face, so Pythagoras gives the height AF = √(132 − 92) = √88 = 9.38. f(x) = x3

g(x) = 2x + 3

h(x) = fg(x)

Find  h−1(x)
answer: h−1(x) = (∛x − 3) ⁄ 2. First build the composite: fg means do g FIRST and put the answer into f, so h(x) = (2x + 3)3 — not 2x3 + 3. Then invert by undoing the steps in reverse: cube root, subtract 3, halve
