html:
A race is measured to have a distance of 10.6 km, correct to the nearest 0.1 km.

Sam runs the race in a time of 31 minutes 48 seconds, correct to the nearest second.

Sam’s average speed in this race is V km/hour.

By considering bounds, calculate the value of V to a suitable degree of accuracy.

You must show all your working and give a reason for your answer.
answer: V = 20 km/h, to 2 significant figures — The distance lies between 10.55 and 10.65 km; the time is 1908 seconds between 1907.5 and 1908.5, which in hours is 0.52986 to 0.53014. Speed is largest with the most distance and the least time, 10.65 ÷ 0.52986 = 20.0996, and smallest the other way round, 10.55 ÷ 0.53014 = 19.9004. The two bounds agree to 2 significant figures and disagree at the third, so 20 is as far as the data can be trusted — and saying WHY is the last mark

html:
A circle has equation  x2 + y2 = 12.25

The point P lies on the circle.

The coordinates of P are (2.1, 2.8)

The line L is the tangent to the circle at point P.

Find an equation of L.

Give your answer in the form ax + by = c, where a, b and c are integers.
answer: 6x + 8y = 35 — The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, and the radius OP has gradient 2.8 ÷ 2.1 = 4⁄3, so the tangent’s gradient is the negative reciprocal, −3⁄4. Through (2.1, 2.8) that is y − 2.8 = −3⁄4(x − 2.1), which tidies to 3x + 4y = 17.5 — and 17.5 is not an integer, so double everything. Check P really is on the circle: 4.41 + 7.84 = 12.25

html:
Insert — Source A

20th century prose fiction · The Midwich Cuckoos by John Wyndham · an extract from near the beginning of a novel written in 1957

This extract is taken from near the beginning of a novel by John Wyndham. The story begins on the night of 26th September in the quiet village of Midwich.

From 10.17 that night, information about Midwich became episodic. Its telephones remained dead. The bus that should have passed through it failed to reach its destination, and a truck that went to look for the bus did not return. Someone in Oppley reported a house on fire in Midwich, with, apparently, nothing being done about it. The Trayne fire engine turned out – and thereafter failed to make any reports. The Trayne police station despatched a car to find out what had happened to the fire engine, and that, too, vanished into silence. Constable Gobby was sent off on his bicycle to Midwich; and no more was heard of him, either…

The early morning of the 27th was an affair of slatternly* rags soaking in a dishwater sky, with a grey light weakly filtering through. Nevertheless, in Oppley cocks crowed and other birds welcomed the dawn more melodiously. In Midwich, however, no birds sang. In Oppley, as in other places, hands were soon reaching out to silence alarm clocks, but in Midwich the clocks rattled on until they ran down. For Midwich lay entranced.

While the rest of the world began to fill the morning with clamour, Midwich slept on. Its men and women, its horses, cows and sheep; its pigs, its poultry, its larks, moles and mice all lay still. There was a pocket of silence in Midwich, broken only by the rustling of the leaves, the chiming of the church clock, and the gurgle of the River Opple as it slid over the weir beside the mill.

And while the dawn was still a poor, weak thing, an olive-green van, with the words ‘Post Office Telephones’ just discernible on it, set out from Trayne with the object of putting the rest of the world in touch with Midwich again.

In Stouch it paused at the village phone box to enquire whether Midwich had yet shown any signs of life. Midwich had not; it was still as deeply incommunicado as it had been since 10.17 the previous night. The van restarted and rattled on through the uncertainly gathering daylight.

A little out of Stouch the van swung sharply to the right and bounced along the byroad to Midwich for half a mile or so. Then it rounded a corner to encounter a situation which called for all of the driver’s presence of mind.

He had a sudden view of a fire engine, half keeled over, with its nearside wheels in the ditch, and a black saloon car which had climbed halfway up the bank on the other side a few yards further on, with a man and a bicycle lying half in the ditch behind it. He pulled hard over, attempting an S-turn which would avoid both vehicles. But before he could complete it his own van ran on to the narrow verge, bumped along for a few more yards, then ploughed to a stop, with its side in the hedge.

Half an hour later, the first bus of the day rattled round the same corner to jam itself neatly into the gap between the fire engine and the van and block the road completely.

The mail van was the first vehicle to stop without becoming involved. One of its occupants got out and walked forward to investigate the disorder. He was just approaching the rear of the stationary bus when, without any warning, he quietly folded up and dropped to the ground. The driver’s jaw fell open and he stared. Then, looking beyond his fallen companion, he saw the heads of some of the bus passengers, all quite motionless. He reversed hastily, turned and made for Oppley and the nearest telephone.

* slatternly — adjective meaning dirty or untidy

html:
Fahima buys

  • 2 packets of bread rolls costing £1.50 for each packet
  • 1 bottle of ketchup costing £1.60
  • 3 packets of sausages

Fahima pays with a £10 note.
She gets 30p change.

Fahima works out that one packet of sausages costs £2.30

Is Fahima right?
You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No: £10 − 30p − £3 − £1.60 = £5.10, so one packet costs £5.10 ÷ 3 = £1.70 — one packet of sausages costs £1.70. She spent £10 − 30p = £9.70. The bread rolls are 2 × £1.50 = £3 and the ketchup £1.60, so £4.60 together, which leaves £9.70 − £4.60 = £5.10 for the three packets of sausages: £5.10 ÷ 3 = £1.70. Or check her answer forwards: 3 × £2.30 = £6.90, and £6.90 + £4.60 = £11.50, more than the £10 she paid with. Her £2.30 is what comes out of £10 − £1.50 − £1.60 = £6.90, ÷ 3 — forgetting both the 30p change and the second packet of bread rolls. The decision on its own earns nothing: the working has to be there.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
Insert — Source A

20th Century prose fiction · The Grass is Singing by Doris Lessing · an extract from the middle of a novel published in 1950

This extract is taken from the middle of a novel, set in Southern Africa in the 1940s. Mary has recently moved from town to a farm after marrying Dick, a poor farmer.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html: And then, suddenly, the heat became intolerable. Outside in the bush the cicadas shrilled incessantly, and Mary’s head ached; her limbs were heavy and tense. She would get up and go into the bedroom, to examine her clothes, to see if there was anything she could do: any bit of embroidery, or an alteration. With nothing to do, she would wander on to the verandah* until at last her head began to swim, and she had to go back to the house to get a glass of water.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html: As time passed, the heat became an obsession. Outside, there was a rough heap of giant boulders, and she would watch the heat-waves beat up out of the hot stone, where the heat lizards, vivid red and blue and emerald, darted over the rocks like flames. Inside, she could not bear the sapping, undermining waves that beat down from the iron roof. Even the usually active dogs used to lie all day on the verandah. Mary could hear them panting softly, or whining with exasperation because of the flies. She would lock them out of the house, and in the middle of the morning she would tell a worker to carry a petrol tin full of lukewarm water into the bedroom, and, having made sure he was out of the house, she stood in a basin on the brick floor, pouring it over her. The scattering drops fell on the porous brick, which hissed with dryness.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
‘When is it going to rain?’ she asked Dick.

‘Oh, not for another month yet,’ he answered easily, but looking surprised at her question. Surely she knew when the rains were likely to fall? She had been in the country longer than he had. But it seemed to her that in the town there had been no seasons, really, not as there were here. She had been out of the rhythm of cold and heat and rain. It had been hot, it had rained, the cold weather had come – yes, certainly; but it was something happening independently of her. Here, body and mind were subservient to the slow movement of the seasons; she had never in her life watched the implacable sky for signs of rain, as she did now, standing on the verandah, and screwing up her eyes at the great massed white cloud, like blocks of glittering crystal quartz sailing through the blue.

‘The water is going very quickly,’ said Dick, one day, frowning.

It was fetched twice a week from the bottom of the hill where the well was. Mary would hear shouting and yelling, as if someone were in agonised pain, and going out in front of the house, she watched the water-cart come through the trees, drawn by two slow-moving beautiful oxen, straining their hindquarters up the slope.

‘What are you using it for?’ asked Dick. She told him. His face darkened, and he looked at her in incredulous horror, as if she had committed a crime.

‘What, wasting it like that?’

‘I am not wasting it,’ she said coldly. ‘I am so hot I can’t stand it. I want to cool myself.’

Dick swallowed, trying to keep calm. ‘Listen to me,’ he said angrily, in a voice he had never before used to her. ‘Listen to me! Every time I order the water-cart to fetch water for the house, it means a driver, and two workers, and two oxen off other work for a whole morning. It costs money to fetch water. And then you go and throw it away! Why don’t you fill the bath with water and get into it, instead of wasting it and throwing it away each time?’

She was furious. This seemed the last straw. Here she was, living here uncomplainingly, suffering these hardships; and then she could not use a couple of gallons of water! She opened her mouth to shout at him, but before she could, he had become suddenly sorry because of the way he had spoken to her; and there was another of those little scenes which comforted and soothed her: he apologising, blaming himself, and she forgiving him.

* verandah — an open, roofed area along the outside of a house.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
Read again the first part of the source, from lines 1 to 6.

List four things about Mary from this part of the source.
answer:
Any four true things about Mary, from lines 1 to 6 only —

AO1 — identify and interpret explicit and implicit information (4 marks)

One mark for each acceptable point, to a maximum of four, taken only from lines 1 to 6. A quotation counts if it carries the point.

Points the mark scheme credits (one mark each): Mary doesn’t like the heat; her head ached; her limbs were heavy; her limbs were tense; she went to the bedroom; she examined her clothes; she was looking for things to do; she had no embroidery or alterations to do; she had nothing to do; she wandered on to the verandah; her head began to swim; she went back to the house to get a glass of water; she could hear the cicadas; she was bored / thirsty / hot / unwell. Reject: ‘it was hot’, ‘she was tired’, ‘she drank a glass of water’, ‘she was dehydrated’, ‘she liked embroidery’, anything about the setting that is not about Mary.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
Look in detail at this extract, from lines 7 to 17 of the source.

How does the writer use language here to describe the effects of the heat?

You could include the writer’s choice of:

  • words and phrases
  • language features and techniques
  • sentence forms.
answer:
Analysis of the words, language features and sentence forms in lines 7–17 that describe the effects of the heat —

AO2 — language (8 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed (7–8 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant (5–6 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some understanding and comment (3–4 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–2 marks)

Identifying a device without saying what it does stays in Level 1 or 2. Material from outside the named lines earns nothing.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
You now need to think about the whole of the source.

This text is taken from the middle of a novel.

How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?

You could write about:

  • what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning of the source
  • how and why the writer changes this focus as the source develops
  • any other structural features that interest you.
answer:
Top band: perceptive, detailed analysis —

Analysis of how the whole source is structured: what the opening focuses on, how and why the focus shifts, and how it ends.

AO2 — structure (8 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed (7–8 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant (5–6 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some understanding and comment (3–4 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–2 marks)

Structure means the whole text. Analysing one paragraph’s language here is the commonest way to lose the marks.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
Focus this part of your answer on the second part of the source, from line 18 to the end.

A student said, “Dick’s anger towards Mary is really unfair. The writer makes it clear that Mary is totally powerless in this relationship.”

To what extent do you agree?

In your response you could:

  • consider whether Dick’s anger is unfair
  • evaluate how the writer presents Mary and Dick’s relationship
  • support your response with references to the text.
answer:
Top band: a perceptive, detailed evaluation —

A perceptive, detailed evaluation of how far Dick’s anger is unfair and how far Mary is powerless in the relationship (line 18 to the end), with well-chosen references.

AO4 — evaluate critically (20 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed evaluation (16–20 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant evaluation (11–15 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some evaluation (6–10 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited evaluation (1–5 marks)

The student’s statement is what is evaluated. Agreement is not required; a response that only retells the extract, without judging how far the statement holds, stays in Level 1 or 2.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
A magazine has asked for contributions for their creative writing section.

Either

Write a description of a very hot place as suggested by this picture:

or

Write a story about a disagreement.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)

The picture above is drawn here. AQA prints a photograph of the same scene and it is third-party copyright, so what is on this card is an impression of it — the hot sky, the sun, the hazy ranges and the bare ground — rather than the photograph itself.
answer:
Top band: compelling, convincing writing —

A compelling description of a very hot place, or story about a disagreement, consistently accurate, with ambitious vocabulary.

AO5 — content and organisation (24 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Compelling, convincing (19–24 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Consistent, clear (13–18 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some successful communication (7–12 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–6 marks)

AO6 — technical accuracy (16 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Consistently accurate, ambitious vocabulary (13–16 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Generally accurate, varied sentences (9–12 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some accuracy (5–8 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Occasional accuracy (1–4 marks)

Describe a method the student could have used to collect the data needed to plot the graph.
answer: Vary the length between the clips, measure current and p.d., and use V = IR — Level-marked out of 6. answer: The potential difference is very low, so there is no risk of electric shock

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 4 shows a static electricity generator: a rubber belt inside a column carries charge up to a metal dome on top.

The rubber belt is turned by a motor.

As the rubber belt moves, charge is transferred from the rubber belt to the metal dome.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 5 shows a student touching the metal dome of the static electricity generator; her hair is standing on end.

The dome is negatively charged.

Explain why the student’s hair stands up on end.
answer: Electrons are transferred to the student, so her hair is negatively charged, and like charges repel
examiner_note: Figures 4 and 5 are photographs in the PDF and are not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The charged metal dome creates an electric field. What is an electric field?
answer: The region around a charged object where another charged object experiences a force

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: How does the electric field strength vary as the distance from the charged metal dome increases?
answer: It decreases

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 6 shows the negatively charged metal dome and an earthed conductor. When the earthed conductor is moved towards the metal dome, there is a spark between the dome and the earthed conductor.

The spark transfers 0.60 J of energy, and 2.0 µC of charge is transferred from the dome to the earthed conductor. Calculate the potential difference between the metal dome and the earthed conductor.
examiner_note: Figure 6 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which of the following changes would increase the distance a spark can jump between the dome and the earthed conductor? Tick one box.
answer: Decreased electrical resistance of air
choices: Decreased charge on the metal dome | Decreased electric field strength | Decreased electrical resistance of air | Decreased potential difference

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Figure 7 shows a student putting a coin into a vending machine that sells food.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The vending machine is connected to the mains electricity supply.

What is the frequency of the mains electricity supply in the UK?
answer: 50 Hz — the UK mains supply is alternating, at 50 hertz.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the potential difference of the mains electricity supply in the UK?
answer: 230 V — the UK mains supply is about 230 volts.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The vending machine identifies the value of a coin by measuring the resistance of the coin. The power dissipated by the coin is 340 mW when the current in the coin is 0.75 A. Calculate the resistance of the coin.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Coins that are dirty are not recognised by the vending machine. Suggest one reason why.
answer: The dirt changes the measured resistance of the coin, so it does not match the resistance expected for that coin

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In a ride at a theme park, a person is strapped into a pod that is attached to two stretched bungee cords.

The bungee cords behave like springs.

Figure 10 shows a person using the ride: the pod is held at ground level with a stretched cord running up to a tower on each side.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which energy store increases as the bungee cords are stretched?
answer: Elastic potential energy store
examiner_note: Figure 10 is a photograph in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
When the pod is released, the pod accelerates upwards. Before the pod is released the extension of each of the two bungee cords is 8.0 m. The spring constant of each bungee cord is 735 N/m. The mass of the pod is 240 kg.

gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

Calculate the maximum height reached by the pod.
answer: 20 m. One cord stores 0.5 × 735 × 8.0² = 23 520 J, so the two store 47 040 J; 47 040 = 240 × 9.8 × h

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The actual maximum height reached by the pod will be lower than the correct answer to Question 06.2 Explain why.
answer: Air resistance: not all the elastic energy reaches the gravitational store — Air resistance opposes the pod's motion upwards, so not all of the elastic potential energy is transferred to the gravitational potential store

Which type of error would have been caused if the student’s eye was not in line with the level of the water?

Tick one box.
answer: Random error
choices: Random error | Systematic error | Zero error

html: The student tied a piece of thick string to the metal ring and lowered the ring into the water. Suggest one reason why the student should have used thin string instead of thick string.
answer: Thin string would affect the volume measurement less — it displaces less water

The true volume of the ring was 0.44 cm³. Even without using the string, the measuring cylinder could not give an accurate value for the volume of the ring. Give one reason why.
answer: The measuring cylinder cannot be read to two decimal places — its resolution is 0.2 cm³

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The student used a balance to measure the mass of the ring. After the ring was removed from the balance, the reading on the balance was 0.02 g. How could the student use the readings from the balance to determine the correct mass of the ring?
answer: Subtract 0.02 g from the measured value

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated how the pressure in a fixed mass of air varies with the volume of the air.

Figure 12 shows the equipment used: a syringe with a plunger, its nozzle connected to a pressure gauge.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
When the plunger was pushed slowly into the syringe, the pressure in the syringe increased.

The temperature of the air remained constant.

Explain why the pressure increased.
answer: The particles collide with the walls more often, on a smaller area — The air particles are closer together, so the frequency of collisions between the particles and the syringe walls increases, giving a larger total force on a smaller surface area
examiner_note: Figure 12 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A fire piston is a special type of syringe that can be used to start fires. The plunger is pushed quickly downwards and compresses the air. When the air is compressed quickly, the temperature of the air increases.

How does an increase in temperature affect the air particles inside the piston? Tick one box.
answer: The mean kinetic energy of the particles increases
examiner_note: Figure 13 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.
choices: The mean kinetic energy of the particles increases. | The mean potential energy of the particles increases. | The mean separation of the particles increases.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
When the air is hot enough, a small piece of cotton wool in the piston catches fire. The energy transferred to the air in the piston is 0.0130 J. The mass of air in the piston is 2.60 × 10⁻⁸ kg.

specific heat capacity of air = 1.01 kJ/kg °C

Calculate the temperature change of the air.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A teacher investigated the radiation emitted by two different radioactive sources, A and B.

Figure 14 shows a radiation detector positioned near one of the radioactive sources: the detector, connected to a counter, is clamped on one stand and the source on another, a measured distance away.

The teacher measured the count rate at different distances for each radioactive source.

Figure 15 shows the results.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain how Figure 15 shows that Source A only emits alpha radiation.
answer: Source A emits alpha: its count falls to background after about 3 cm of air — Radiation from Source A travels about 3 cm in air, after which the count rate falls to the background level, because alpha radiation has a short range in air

specific latent heat of fuse wire = 60 kJ/kg

Calculate the mass of the fuse wire.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The calculation in Question 10.4 assumes there is no energy transferred to the surroundings.

How would the time taken for the wire to melt be affected if some energy was transferred to the surroundings?

Tick one box.
answer: Time taken would increase — some of the energy goes to the surroundings instead of into the wire, so it takes longer for the wire to get the energy it needs to melt.
choices: Time taken would decrease | Time taken would stay the same | Time taken would increase

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give a reason for your answer about the time taken for the wire to melt.
answer: More energy has to be transferred in total — the energy that goes to the surroundings does not heat or melt the wire, so more energy (and so more time) is needed before the wire has received enough to melt.

Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction with a protractor. Repeat over a range of angles of incidence — 10° to 60° in 10° steps. Methods using mirrors and reflection score zero.

answer: The line curves — it is not straight

Figure 4 shows a ray of light incident on the reflective surface.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Figure 5 shows a young child using a baby walker.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The child is standing still.

What is the resultant vertical force on the child?

Give a reason for your answer.
answer: 0 N, because the child is not accelerating vertically — the upward forces equal the downward forces, so the forces are balanced
examiner_note: Figure 5 is a photograph in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Write down the equation which links distance (s), force (F) and work done (W).
answer: work done = force × distance, or W = F × s

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The child pushed the baby walker 2.8 m across a horizontal floor. The work done by the child was 35 J.

Calculate the horizontal force the child applied to the baby walker.
answer: 12.5 N (13 N is also accepted)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The child pushed the baby walker from a carpet onto a hard floor. The child applied the same horizontal force to the baby walker.

Explain why the speed of the baby walker increased.
answer: The resistive force (friction between the wheels and the floor) has decreased, so the resultant force increases — the friction between the wheels and the floor — has decreased, so the resultant force increases

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Write down the equation which links distance (d), force (F) and moment of a force (M).
answer: moment = force × distance, or M = F × d

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
There are some toy gears on the front of the baby walker; Figure 6 shows two of them, gear A and gear B, meshed together. The child applies a force to gear A, which causes a moment about the pivot, so gear A rotates.

The child applies a force of 2.0 N on gear A. The perpendicular distance between the force and the pivot is 7.5 cm.

Calculate the moment of the force about the pivot.

examiner_note: Figure 6 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics

answer: Gear B turns the opposite way to gear A: A exerts a force on B, causing a moment about B’s pivot — or clockwise, or faster than gear A — because gear A exerts a force on gear B, causing a moment about gear B's pivot
examiner_note: Figure 6 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: The Universe contains many stars.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system.

Give three other types of object that form our solar system.
answer: Any three of: planets; dwarf planets; moons (natural satellites); asteroids; meteors, meteoroids or meteorites; comets

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Some main sequence stars will eventually form black holes. Table 3 gives the mass of four stars.

StarMass in kg
Arcturus2.2 × 1030
Betelgeuse2.2 × 1031

The Sun2.0 × 1030

Which star in Table 3 is most likely to form a black hole?
answer: Betelgeuse

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The distance from Cygni A to the Earth is 1.1 × 108 gigametres.

Which distance is the same as 1.1 × 108 gigametres? Tick one box.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024

The light spectrum from every galaxy includes dark lines. The lines have the same pattern. Figure 7 shows the position of dark lines in the visible spectra of light from the Sun and from two distant galaxies.

Explain what these light spectra tell us about the velocities of galaxy A and galaxy B.
answer: Both are moving away from us (red-shift), and A faster than B, as A's red-shift is greater — Both show red-shift — the wavelength of the absorption lines has increased — so both galaxies are moving away from us. A shows a greater red-shift than B, so A is travelling faster than B.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The distance between Arcturus and the Earth is 3.6 × 1014 km.

speed of light = 3.0 × 108 m/s

Calculate the time taken for light from Arcturus to reach the Earth. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.
answer: 1.2 × 10^9 s (1 200 000 000 s) — convert the distance to 3.6 × 10^17 m first

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
When stars are formed, they contain mostly hydrogen.

Describe how stars produce all other naturally occurring elements.
answer: By fusion: hydrogen to helium, then up to iron; heavier elements in supernovae — Level-marked out of 4. Fusion occurs at high temperatures and produces new elements. Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei. When hydrogen in the core begins to run out, helium nuclei fuse to make heavier elements, up to iron. Some massive stars become supernovae, creating the elements heavier than iron.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The Mariana Trench is the deepest part of the Pacific Ocean.

Figure 8 shows a submarine going to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The depth of the submarine increases.

Explain what happens to the pressure on the submarine.
answer: The column of water above it gets taller, so the pressure increases — The height of the column of water above the submarine increases, which increases the weight of water acting on it, so the pressure increases. (Or: p = ρgh, and ρ and g stay the same, so pressure increases.)
examiner_note: Figure 8 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The submarine moved from the surface of the water to the bottom of the Mariana Trench. The change in pressure was 110 000 kPa.

mean density of sea water = 1026 kg/m3
gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

Calculate the depth of the Mariana Trench. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.
answer: 10 940 m (11 000 m is accepted with working) — convert 110 000 kPa to 110 000 000 Pa first

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Earthquakes often occur at the Mariana Trench. P-waves and S-waves are produced by earthquakes.

Which statement describes P-waves and S-waves? Tick one box.
answer: P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse
choices: Both P-waves and S-waves are longitudinal. | Both P-waves and S-waves are transverse. | P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse. | P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 9 shows the layers inside the Earth. An earthquake occurs at the position shown.

Which letter shows the position where only P-waves will be detected? Give a reason for your answer. Tick one box: A, B, C or D.
answer: D: only P-waves can travel through the liquid outer core — because only P-waves can travel through liquids, so only they get through the liquid outer core. (S-waves cannot travel through the outer core.)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
An S-wave has a frequency of 3.6 Hz. The S-wave has a speed of 4.5 km/s.

Calculate the wavelength of this S-wave. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.
answer: 1250 m (1300 m accepted) — convert 4.5 km/s to 4500 m/s first

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A seismometer is a device that detects earthquakes. P-waves travel at a known speed between an earthquake and a seismometer. S-waves travel at a slower speed than P-waves. A P-wave and an S-wave from the earthquake arrive at the seismometer at different times.

Describe the relationship between the distance from the earthquake to the seismometer and the time between the P-wave and the S-wave arriving.
answer: The distance is directly proportional to the time between the two waves arriving — (A greater distance means a greater time, or a positive correlation, scores 1 of the 2.)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated how the acceleration of a trolley varies with the resultant force on the trolley.

Figure 10 shows some of the equipment used: a trolley on a horizontal runway, with a string running from it over a pulley at the end of the bench to a hanging mass.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 10 shows the force F which acts through the string.

What name is given to force F?
answer: Tension
examiner_note: Figure 10 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give one variable that should have been a control variable in this investigation.
answer: The combined mass of the trolley and the mass hanger (the mass or weight of the trolley, or of the hanger, is accepted)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The student held the trolley stationary and then released it. The trolley moved along the runway with a constant acceleration. The student recorded the time taken for the trolley to travel a measured distance along the runway.

Describe how the acceleration of the trolley can be calculated using the time taken and distance travelled by the trolley.
answer: Mean velocity = distance ÷ time; double it for the final velocity; acceleration = that velocity ÷ time — Double the mean velocity to give the maximum velocity. Divide the change in velocity by the time taken to give the acceleration. (Using v² = u² + 2as, or s = ut + ½at², is also accepted.)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
For one set of results, the force acting through the string was 2.0 N. The student released the trolley three times and determined the following values for acceleration:

1.36 m/s2   1.39 m/s2   1.33 m/s2

Calculate the uncertainty in the values of acceleration.
answer: ± 0.03 m/s² — the range is 0.06 m/s² (the mean is 1.36 m/s²), and the uncertainty is half the range

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The runway was then raised at one end. The force acting through the string remained the same. Figure 11 shows this.

Explain how the acceleration was affected by raising the end of the runway.
answer: It increases: part of the weight now acts down the slope, so the resultant force is larger — A component of the weight of the trolley now acts parallel to the runway, so the resultant force increases and the acceleration increases. (Also accepted: work is done raising the trolley so it gains gravitational potential energy, which is transferred to kinetic energy, increasing the final velocity and the acceleration.)
examiner_note: Figure 11 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Radio waves and gamma rays both transfer energy.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give three other similarities between radio waves and gamma rays.
answer: Same speed in a vacuum; travel through a vacuum; transverse; electromagnetic — Any three of: they travel at the same speed in a vacuum (the speed of light); they can travel through a vacuum (they need no medium); they are transverse waves; they are electromagnetic waves. Being reflected, refracted, absorbed, transmitted or diffracted is ignored.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Both radio waves and gamma rays are used in medicine.

Give one medical use of gamma rays.
answer: Medical imaging — a PET scan, a tracer or a gamma camera — or a medical treatment such as radiotherapy or a gamma knife. Sterilising medical equipment is also accepted. Ultrasound, CT, X-rays, MRI and chemotherapy are not.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain why exposure to gamma rays can be harmful but exposure to radio waves is not harmful.
answer: Gamma rays are ionising and radio waves are not, so gamma rays can cause mutations in genes or DNA — increasing the risk of cancer, or damaging and killing cells

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Some medical scanners produce radio waves at a specific frequency.

Explain how radio waves are produced at a specific frequency.
answer: An alternating current (oscillating electrons) in a circuit produces radio waves of the same frequency — an alternating current, or oscillating electrons in an aerial — and the radio waves have the same frequency as those oscillations

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Figure 12 shows a velocity–time graph for a train travelling between two stations.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Determine the distance travelled by the train in the first 600 s of the journey.
answer: 27 440 m — the triangle is ½ × 56 × 220 = 6160 m and the rectangle is 56 × 380 = 21 280 m

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain what happens to the braking force as the train decelerates. Use information from Figure 12.
answer: It decreases: the gradient, and so the deceleration, is smaller after 720 s — The gradient is less after 720 s (after the velocity has fallen to 20 m/s), so the deceleration is smaller, so the braking force is smaller

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Determine the maximum deceleration of the train.
answer: 0.3 m/s² — the steepest section is from 600 s to 720 s, where the gradient is −36 ÷ 120

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Another train travels at a speed of 60 m/s. A constant braking force of 270 000 N causes the train to decelerate and stop.

mass of train = 240 000 kg

Calculate the distance travelled while the braking force is applied. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.
answer: 1600 m — By forces: a = −270 000 ÷ 240 000 = −1.125 m/s², then 0 = 60² + 2(−1.125)s, so s = 3600 ÷ 2.25. By energy: Ek = ½ × 240 000 × 60² = 432 000 000 J, which equals the work done, so s = 432 000 000 ÷ 270 000. By momentum: p = 14 400 000 kg m/s, t = 53.3 s, mean speed 30 m/s, s = 30 × 53.3.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
It is illegal for train drivers to drink alcohol before driving a train.

Explain how drinking alcohol would affect the stopping distance of a train.
answer: It increases: alcohol increases reaction time, so the thinking distance and the stopping distance increase — Stopping distance is braking distance plus thinking distance — Alcohol increases the driver's reaction time, which increases the thinking distance, so the stopping distance increases.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 13 shows some apparatus used by a teacher in a demonstration: a wire, held between the poles of two magnets, connected in a loop to a centre-zero ammeter reading from −1.0 to 1.0.

The teacher moved the wire upwards between the magnets.

The needle on the ammeter deflected to a value of +0.4 mA and then returned to zero.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: What effect did this demonstrate?
answer: The generator effect (electromagnetic induction)
examiner_note: Figure 13 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain why a current was detected when the wire in Figure 13 was moved upwards.
answer: The wire cuts the magnetic field, inducing a p.d. in a complete circuit — The wire cuts through the magnetic field between the magnets, so a potential difference is induced across the wire, and as the wire is part of a complete circuit there is a current in the circuit
examiner_note: Figure 13 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The teacher reversed the direction of the magnetic field.

The teacher replaced the wire in its original position.

The teacher moved the wire upwards in the same way as before.

What was the deflection of the needle on the ammeter?

Tick one box.
answer: The needle will deflect to −0.4 mA
choices: The needle will deflect to −0.4 mA. | The needle will not move. | The needle will deflect to +0.4 mA.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 14 shows a sound wave incident on the diaphragm of a moving-coil microphone. The inside of the microphone includes a small coil of wire and a magnet.

Explain why the sound waves have an effect on the electric circuit.
answer: Sound vibrates the diaphragm and coil in the magnet’s field, inducing an alternating current — The pressure variations in the sound waves cause the diaphragm to vibrate; the diaphragm causes the coil to vibrate; and as the coil repeatedly changes direction it induces an alternating current in the circuit.
examiner_note: Figure 14 is artwork in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student produced a salt by reacting copper carbonate with sulfuric acid.

This is the method used.

  1. Measure 50 cm3 of sulfuric acid into a beaker.
  2. Add copper carbonate powder.
  3. Stir the mixture.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until copper carbonate is in excess.
  5. Filter the mixture.
  6. Warm the filtrate gently until crystals start to appear.
  7. Leave the solution to cool and crystallise.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Complete the word equation for the reaction.

copper carbonate + sulfuric acid → ............... + ............... + carbon dioxide
answer: copper sulfate + water (CuSO₄ and H₂O are accepted)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one observation the student could make during Step 4 which shows that the copper carbonate is in excess.
answer: Solid remains in the mixture — or there is no more effervescence, bubbling or fizzing

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one reason for filtering the mixture in Step 5.
answer: To remove the excess copper carbonate

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Name the equipment that can be used to warm the filtrate gently in Step 6.
answer: An electric heater, or a water bath. (A Bunsen burner is ignored.)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The maximum theoretical mass of the salt that could be produced using 50 cm3 of the sulfuric acid is 12.5 g. The percentage yield of the salt is 92.8%.

Calculate the mass of salt actually produced. Use the equation:

% yield = (mass of salt actually produced ÷ maximum theoretical mass of salt that could be produced) × 100

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Some salts can be produced by reacting sulfuric acid with a metal. Neither copper nor sodium is used to produce a salt with sulfuric acid.

Give one reason why each metal is not used.
answer: Copper does not react with the acid; sodium reacts dangerously (it could explode) — Copper: it does not react with the acid — it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it will not displace hydrogen. Sodium: the reaction is dangerous — it could explode, or get too hot.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
This question is about the periodic table.

Sodium and potassium are in Group 1 of the periodic table.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one similarity and one difference between the electronic structures of sodium and potassium.
answer: Similarity: both have one electron in their outer shell. Difference: sodium has 3 shells and potassium has 4.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Group 1 elements react with water.

Give two observations made when potassium reacts with water.
answer: Any two: fizzing, floats, moves around, gets smaller, melts into a ball, a flame — Any two of: effervescence, bubbling or fizzing; the potassium floats; it moves around; it gets smaller; it melts or forms a ball; a flame; an explosion

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Potassium hydroxide solution is produced when potassium reacts with water.

What is the colour of universal indicator when added to potassium hydroxide solution? Give one reason for your answer.
answer: Blue, violet or purple, because the solution is alkaline (it contains hydroxide ions) — because the solution is alkaline (it contains hydroxide, OH⁻, ions)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Table 1 shows the densities of some of the elements in Group 0 of the periodic table.

ElementAtomic numberDensity in mg/cm3
Helium20.2
Neon100.8
Argon181.6
Krypton36X
Xenon545.4
Radon869.1

html: Name model A of the atom shown in Figure 2.
answer: The plum pudding model — a ball of positive charge with the negative electrons embedded in it (Thomson’s model).
accept: plum pudding | plum pudding model | the plum pudding model | plum-pudding | plum-pudding model | Thomson | Thomson model | Thomson's model

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Name model B of the atom shown in Figure 2.
answer: The Bohr model — a small positive nucleus with the electrons in fixed shells (energy levels) around it. Nuclear, planetary and Rutherford-Bohr model are also accepted.
accept: Bohr | Bohr model | the Bohr model | Bohr's model | nuclear | nuclear model | the nuclear model | planetary | planetary model | Rutherford-Bohr | Rutherford-Bohr model | Rutherford Bohr | Rutherford Bohr model

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Compare model A with the model of the atom used today.

Use Figure 2.
answer: Model A has no nucleus and no empty space; today: nucleus, shells, mostly empty space — Level-marked out of 4. Similarities: both contain electrons; both are neutral overall. Differences: model A has no nucleus, no protons and no neutrons, where today's model has all three. In model A the positive charge and the mass are spread throughout the atom; today the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in the centre. In model A the electrons are distributed randomly; today they are in shells or energy levels. Model A has no empty space; today's atom is mostly empty space.

subject: Chemistry

Chadwick's experiments showed the existence of neutrons in an atom. This led to an understanding of isotopes.

Define the term 'isotopes'. Refer to subatomic particles in your answer.
answer: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated the energy change of the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate solution.

This is the method used.

  1. Measure 25 cm3 of copper sulfate solution into a polystyrene cup.
  2. Measure the temperature of the copper sulfate solution.
  3. Add 0.20 g of zinc powder to the copper sulfate solution.
  4. Stir the reaction mixture.
  5. Record the highest temperature reached.
  6. Repeat steps 1 to 5 with different masses of zinc powder.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 3 shows the results.

Draw two lines of best fit on Figure 3. The lines should cross.
answer: One line of best fit through the first five points (the rising part), and a second through the last four (the flat part) — Maximum 1 mark if the lines do not intersect.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain the results shown in Figure 3. Do not refer to anomalous points. Use data from Figure 3.
answer: Exothermic, so it heats up until 0.8 g of zinc is added (47 °C); then the copper sulfate is used up, zinc in excess — energy is transferred to the surroundings — until 0.8 g of zinc is added (where the temperature reaches 47 °C). After that there is no additional reaction, because the zinc is in excess and the copper sulfate has been used up.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain why using a polystyrene cup gives more accurate results than using a glass beaker.
answer: Polystyrene is a better thermal insulator, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings

Calcium chloride is an ionic compound.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Calcium and chlorine react to produce calcium chloride.

Describe what happens to calcium atoms and chlorine atoms when the ionic compound calcium chloride is formed.
answer: Each Ca atom gives two electrons, one to each of two Cl atoms: Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ — Each calcium atom loses two electrons and each chlorine atom gains one electron, so one calcium atom reacts with two chlorine atoms, forming Ca²⁺ ions and Cl⁻ ions — all with full outer shells. Just 'calcium atoms lose electrons and chlorine atoms gain electrons' scores 1 of the 4.

Write the symbols of the five metals in Table 3 in order of reactivity, most reactive first.

subject: Chemistry

html:
The voltage produced by a chemical cell depends on the concentration of the electrolyte solution.

Plan an experiment to investigate how the voltage produced by a chemical cell varies with the concentration of the electrolyte solution. The following substances are available:

  • the metal electrodes in Table 3
  • 1.0 mol/dm3 sodium chloride solution
  • pure water.
answer: Measure the cell’s voltage at different NaCl concentrations, same metals and volume — Level-marked out of 6. subject: Chemistry

html: Describe how a hydrogen fuel cell produces a potential difference.
answer: Hydrogen is oxidised electrochemically: it loses electrons, producing water — it loses electrons — to produce water

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Iron is a metal.

Describe how iron conducts thermal energy.
answer: Thermal energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Pure iron is too soft for many uses.

Explain why mixing iron with other metals makes alloys which are harder than pure iron.
answer: Different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide easily — The alloy contains atoms of different sizes, so the layers are distorted, so the layers cannot easily slide over each other

subject: Chemistry

html:
Fe2O3 reacts with carbon to produce carbon dioxide. The equation for the reaction is:

2 Fe2O3(s) + 3 C(s) → 4 Fe(s) + 3 CO2(g)

Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide gas at room temperature and pressure that is produced from 40.0 kg of Fe2O3 using excess carbon.

Relative formula mass (Mr): Fe2O3 = 160
The volume of 1 mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure is 24 dm3.
answer: 9000 dm³ — 40.0 kg is 40 000 g, which is 40 000 ÷ 160 = 250 mol of Fe₂O₃; that gives 250 × <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> = 375 mol of CO₂; and 375 × 24 = 9000 dm³

html: Explain why propane has a low boiling point.

Not the covalent bonds — those are not broken when propane boils.

name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 9 shows the displayed formula equation for the reaction between propane and oxygen:

C3H8 + 5 O=O → 3 O=C=O + 4 H—O—H

The overall energy change of this exothermic reaction is 2219 kJ/mol. Table 4 shows the bond energies of the bonds in the reaction.

BondC — CC — HO = OC = OO — H
Energy in kJ/mol347X498805464

Calculate the bond energy of the C — H bond (X).
answer: 392 kJ/mol — Bonds broken = 2(347) + 8X + 5(498) = 3184 + 8X. Bonds made = 6(805) + 8(464) = 8542. Energy released = bonds made − bonds broken, so 2219 = 8542 − (3184 + 8X), giving 8X = 3139 and X = 392.375.

answer: An acid which is only partially ionised (partially dissociated) in aqueous solution

answer: The pH increases, because the concentration of hydrogen ions decreases

NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O

Calculate the volume of hydrochloric acid in cm3 needed in the titration.
answer: 30 cm³ — 0.0045 ÷ 0.15 = 0.030 dm³, which is 30 cm³

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A calcium atom is larger than a magnesium atom.

Explain why calcium reacts more vigorously than magnesium with hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
answer: Its outer electrons are further from the nucleus, so they are lost more easily — Calcium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus (it has more shells, so they are more shielded), so they are less strongly attracted to the nucleus, so positive ions are formed more easily — the electrons are more easily lost

Describe a test to identify sodium ions.

Give the result of the test.
answer: Test: a flame test. Result: a yellow flame. (Or: flame emission spectroscopy, and the lines match the sodium spectrum.)

subject: Chemistry

answer: Add acidified silver nitrate: a white precipitate — Test: add acidified silver nitrate solution. Result: a white precipitate. The result mark depends on getting the test right.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The student determined the concentration of sodium chloride in the salt solution. This is the method used.

  1. Weigh an empty evaporating dish.
  2. Add 25.0 cm3 of the salt solution into the evaporating dish.
  3. Heat the evaporating dish and contents.
  4. Weigh the evaporating dish and contents.

answer: Mass of evaporating dish and dry contents − mass of empty evaporating dish

35.234.636.433.8

Water collected from rivers is used in the home for drinking and flushing toilets.

Water used in the home must be potable.

Potable water is safe to drink.

Waste water produced after use in the home is called sewage.

Figure 3 shows how water is collected from rivers and returned to rivers after use.

Explain what happens to water in Process A and in Process B in Figure 3.

Do not refer to use of water in the home.
answer: A: filter, sterilise (chlorine, ozone, UV). B: screen, sediment, digest sludge anaerobically, treat effluent aerobically — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs both halves. Process A — making water potable: pass the water through filter beds to remove solids, then sterilise it with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light to destroy microbes. Process B — treating waste water: screening through a metal grid to remove solids and grit, then sedimentation to separate sewage sludge from effluent, then anaerobic digestion of the sludge and aerobic biological treatment of the effluent.

The student calculated that the Rf value of the orange dye in the experiment shown in Figure 5 was 0.48.

Calculate the distance moved by the solvent front when the orange dye had moved 5.4 cm.
answer: 11.25 cm — 0.48 = 5.4 ÷ distance moved by solvent, so the distance is 5.4 ÷ 0.48 = 11.25 cm

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Why is the Rf value of a dye not affected by how far the solvent front is allowed to travel?
answer: Because the Rᶠ value is a ratio — the distance moved by the spot is directly proportional to the distance moved by the solvent, so the proportion stays the same

Another type of chromatography is called gas chromatography. Gas chromatography is an instrumental method of chemical analysis. Scientists tested the orange dyes using gas chromatography.

Suggest two advantages of using the instrumental method of gas chromatography rather than paper chromatography.
answer: Any two: more sensitive, more accurate, faster, a smaller sample, better resolution — Any two of: it is more sensitive; it is more accurate; it is faster; it needs a smaller sample; it gives greater resolution

Explain one positive impact on the environment of burning hydrogen rather than natural gas as a fuel.

Use Table 2.
answer: Less climate change (less global warming), because burning hydrogen produces no carbon dioxide — 0.00 g against 1.83 g

answer: More oxides of nitrogen (6.6 × 10⁻⁴ g against 4.9 × 10⁻⁴ g), so more acid rain — 6.6 × 10⁻⁴ g against 4.9 × 10⁻⁴ g — so more acid rain, or more respiratory problems

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Air is 20% oxygen.

Calculate the volume of air needed to provide enough oxygen to react with 3.50 dm3 of hydrogen gas. The equation for the reaction is

2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O
answer: 8.75 dm³ — the equation needs half as much oxygen as hydrogen, so 3.50 × ½ = 1.75 dm³ of oxygen, and 1.75 × 100 ÷ 20 = 8.75 dm³ of air

html:

Explain how kerosene is produced from these hydrocarbon vapours.
answer: The column is cooler going up, and kerosene condenses at the level matching its boiling point range — There is a temperature gradient in the fractionating column — it gets cooler going up — so the kerosene condenses at the level in the column that matches kerosene's boiling point range. Both of the last two marks need kerosene named.

name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Table 3 shows information about two materials used to make bicycle frames.

Material
Aluminium alloyBamboo
Raw materialaluminium orebamboo plant
Cost of frame in £2501500
Strength in arbitrary units290193
Mass in kilograms1.62.4
Lifespan in years6–1010–15
One method of disposal at end of liferecycled to make new productsburned to produce heat energy

Evaluate the use of aluminium alloy and of bamboo for making bicycle frames.

Use Table 3.
answer: A reasoned judgement weighing bamboo (renewable, lasts longer) against aluminium (cheaper, stronger, lighter) — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs a reasoned judgement. For bamboo: it is renewable, it can be burned to give renewable heat and is carbon neutral, and the frame lasts longer (10–15 years against 6–10) — but it costs six times as much, is weaker (193 against 290), is heavier (2.4 kg against 1.6 kg) and growing it uses agricultural land. For aluminium alloy: it is cheaper, stronger, lighter — so the bicycle is faster and easier to carry — and it is recyclable, so the ore is conserved; but aluminium is a finite resource and mining the ore is polluting. Neither material need reach landfill.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain why aluminium alloy bicycle frames do not need protection from corrosion.
answer: Aluminium alloy has an oxide coating, which stops water and oxygen reaching the aluminium underneath — (Not sacrificial protection.)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Bicycle chains are made from an alloy of iron. Bicycle chains rust without protection. Paint is not used to protect bicycle chains from rusting.

Suggest how bicycle chains can be protected from rusting.
answer: Coat them with grease or oil (galvanising, or using stainless steel, is also accepted)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Bicycle frames can also be made from a composite of carbon fibres embedded in a polymer resin.

What description is given in this composite to:

  • the carbon fibre component
  • the polymer resin component?
answer: Carbon fibre: the reinforcement. Polymer resin: the matrix (or binder).

Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions.

Describe the test for the presence of sulfate ions in sulfuric acid.

Give the result of the test.
answer: Add barium chloride solution: a white precipitate — Test: add barium chloride solution (barium nitrate is accepted). Result: a white precipitate. The result mark depends on getting the test right.

subject: Chemistry

html:
One stage in the industrial production of sulfuric acid is the reaction of sulfur dioxide with oxygen to produce sulfur trioxide.

This reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium.

Which statement about the forward reaction is correct?

Use Figure 7.

Tick (✓) one box.
answer: The yield is smaller at higher temperatures because the reaction is exothermic
choices: The yield is greater at higher temperatures because the reaction is exothermic. | The yield is greater at higher temperatures because the reaction is endothermic. | The yield is smaller at higher temperatures because the reaction is exothermic. | The yield is smaller at higher temperatures because the reaction is endothermic.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The equation for the reaction is:

2 SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2 SO3(g)

Explain why the percentage yield of sulfur trioxide in this reaction is greater if the pressure is higher.
answer: Fewer moles of gas on the right (2 against 3), so high pressure shifts equilibrium right — There are more moles of gas on the left-hand side (3 against 2), so raising the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium to the right

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
In industry, the reaction is done at 450 °C and atmospheric pressure. Under these conditions the yield of sulfur trioxide is 86%.

Suggest two reasons why a higher pressure is not used.
answer: Any two: the yield is already high, more energy, explosion risk, the extra cost outweighs the gain — Any two of: the yield is already high; more energy would be needed; the risk of explosion increases; the extra income from a higher yield is outweighed by the extra cost; stronger vessels and more safety precautions cost more

answer: Vanadium (V) — it is the only transition metal in the list

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A different student investigated how the concentration of sulfuric acid affected the rate of the reaction.

The student did a different experiment using sulfuric acid of concentration 0.40 mol/dm3.

The student calculated the number of moles of hydrogen collected after every 20 seconds.

Figure 12 shows the results.

Determine the rate of reaction at 45 seconds.

You should draw a tangent on Figure 12.

Give your answer in standard form.
answer: about 1.1 × 10−4 mol/s — The tangent at 45 s runs from about (0 s, 0.0084 mol) to (80 s, 0.0174 mol), so rate = y step ÷ x step ≈ 0.0090 ÷ 80 = 1.1 × 10−4 mol/s. Any value from a correctly drawn tangent (about 0.9 to 1.3 × 10−4) is credited; the scheme marks the tangent, the two readings, the division, the calculation and the standard form.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 13 shows the results for 0.40 mol/dm3 sulfuric acid.

The student repeated the experiment using 0.20 mol/dm3 sulfuric acid instead. Excess zinc was used in each experiment.

Sketch a line on Figure 13 to show the results you would expect.
answer: A line starting at the origin, less steep than the one already drawn, levelling off at 0.0084 mol — half the final value, because there is half as much acid and the zinc is in excess in both.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain how increasing the temperature would affect the rate of reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid.
answer: It increases the rate, because the particles have more energy and move faster, so the frequency of collisions increases — and a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react

Which term describes a group of tissues working together?

Tick (✓) one box.

subject: Biology

html:
Figure 1 shows the tissues in a leaf.

Match each leaf tissue to an important feature of the tissue.

Which feature goes with the palisade mesophyll?
answer: Contains the most chloroplasts — the palisade cells sit just under the upper epidermis, where the light is strongest, packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

html: Which feature goes with the spongy mesophyll?
answer: Contains many air spaces — the spaces let carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour diffuse between the cells and the stomata.

Figure 1 is repeated below.

The upper epidermis is transparent.

Explain why the upper epidermis needs to be transparent.

Use Figure 1.
answer: So that light can reach the palisade and spongy mesophyll below, whose chloroplasts use it for photosynthesis — the layers with the chloroplasts — for photosynthesis

subject: Biology

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The stomach contains acid to kill pathogens.

A scientist investigated the effect of acid on the survival of bacteria.

This is the method used.

  1. Prepare four test tubes each with 10 cm3 of culture solution.
  2. Use acid to adjust the pH of the solutions to be pH1, pH2, pH3 and pH5.
  3. Add 1 cm3 of bacteria mixture to each test tube.
  4. Take a 0.1 cm3 sample from each test tube and record the number of live bacteria.
  5. Keep the test tubes at 37 °C for 24 hours.
  6. Repeat step 4.

Table 1 shows some of the results.

Time in hoursNumber of live bacteria
pH1pH2pH3pH5
0210210210216
2423X63185

What fraction of the bacteria present at 0 hours for pH3 survived for 24 hours?

Give your answer in its simplest form.
answer: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> — 63 out of 210, which cancels to <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> (0.3 is accepted; 30% is ignored). Getting to <sup>63</sup>⁄<sub>210</sub> alone scores 1.

answer: 187 — 210 live bacteria at 0 hours and 23 at 24 hours, so 210 − 23 = 187 were killed.

subject: Biology

answer: 31 — 216 live bacteria at 0 hours and 185 at 24 hours, so 216 − 185 = 31 were killed.

answer: 156 — 187 killed at pH1 and 31 at pH5, so 187 − 31 = 156 more.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Measles is caused by a virus.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The measles vaccine is given to children to prevent them becoming ill with measles.

Match each blood component to its function when someone is vaccinated against measles.

What is the function of the platelets?
answer: Help clot the blood where the vaccine was injected — platelets clump together to seal the small wound the needle makes.
choices: Help clot the blood where the vaccine was injected | Produce antibodies to the measles virus | Produce the measles skin rash | Transport oxygen to the measles virus

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the function of the white blood cells?
answer: Produce antibodies to the measles virus — the vaccine carries the virus’s antigens, and white blood cells make antibodies against them.
choices: Help clot the blood where the vaccine was injected | Produce antibodies to the measles virus | Produce the measles skin rash | Transport oxygen to the measles virus

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 3 shows information about trends in the UK for:

  • percentage of children vaccinated
  • the number of people with measles.

What year was the measles vaccine first used?

Use Figure 3.
answer: 1968 (1969 is accepted)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Describe the trend in the number of people with measles from 1945 to 1975.

Use Figure 3.
answer: It increases, then levels off (reaching a maximum between about 1956 and 1968), then decreases — An overall decrease alone scores 1 of the 3.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In 1998, a scientific paper was published suggesting a link between condition X and one type of measles vaccine.

What happened to the percentage of children vaccinated against measles after the scientific paper was published in 1998?

Use Figure 3.
answer: It decreased, from about 92% to about 80%, and then increased again

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Why might the claims made in the scientific paper have affected the percentage of children vaccinated? Tick one box.
answer: Parents were worried their children would get condition X
choices: The measles pathogen did not exist in the UK anymore. | Parents were worried their children would get condition X. | The health service in the UK did not have any vaccines.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In 2010, the scientific paper linking condition X and the measles vaccine was shown to be based on false claims.

What should scientists do with scientific research to help detect false claims? Tick one box.
answer: Have the research peer reviewed
choices: Have the research peer reviewed. | Publish the research on the internet. | Send a research questionnaire to the public.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The person who wrote the scientific paper was paid to research the link between condition X and the measles vaccine.

Why are the claims in the scientific paper likely to be considered not valid?
answer: Any one: the author was biased, not peer reviewed, too little evidence, a small sample — Any one of: the author was biased; the author was influenced by money; the research was not peer reviewed; there was not enough evidence; the sample size was small. (Simply 'the author was paid' is ignored.)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Starch and sugar are two types of carbohydrate.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Describe the chemical tests that a student could use to show if bread contains:

  • starch
  • sugar.

You should include the results of a positive test and a negative test for each type of carbohydrate.
answer: Starch: iodine turns blue-black (else stays orange). Sugar: heat with Benedict’s, turns brick red (else stays blue) — it turns blue-black if starch is present, and stays yellow, orange or brown if it is not. Sugar: add Benedict's solution and heat to at least 60 °C — it turns green, yellow, orange or brick red if sugar is present, and stays blue if it is not.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated the effect of different concentrations of salt solution on the mass of uncooked pieces of potato.

This is the method used.

  1. Cut four pieces of a potato to the same size.
  2. Record the mass of each piece of potato.
  3. Put one of the pieces of potato into a beaker containing 100 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 salt solution.
  4. Repeat step 3 using the other pieces of potato, each in a different concentration of salt solution.
  5. After 20 minutes, remove the pieces of potato from the solutions.
  6. Record the mass of each piece of potato.

subject: Biology

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The pancreas produces several digestive enzymes.

CF reduces the amount of each enzyme that reaches the small intestine.

Explain why a person with CF has:

  • difficulty digesting food
  • difficulty gaining body mass.
answer: Fewer enzymes, so less food digested into small molecules, so less absorbed to build body mass — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs both halves. Digesting food: less lipase, so less fat broken down into fatty acids and glycerol; less amylase, so less starch broken down into glucose; less protease, so less protein broken down into amino acids. Gaining body mass: less absorption of those small soluble molecules, so fewer amino acids for building protein, muscle and tissue, less fat stored, less respiration and so less energy for building new cells and tissues.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli in the lungs.

Describe three features of the alveoli that help maximise gas exchange.
answer: A large surface area (or surface area to volume ratio); a large capillary network; thin walls, one cell thick — a good blood supply; walls that are thin, one cell thick. ('Thin alveoli' and 'moist' are ignored.)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
CF reduces the amount of oxygen that can enter the blood from the alveoli.

Explain how a reduced amount of oxygen entering the blood will affect the human body.
answer: There is less aerobic respiration, so less energy is released, which means less muscle contraction — or a reduced metabolism, or an increased breathing rate or heart rate. Alternatively: more anaerobic respiration, so lactic acid is produced, causing muscle fatigue.

Complete the order of structures to link a stimulus to a response.

Choose answers from the box.

coordinator   effector   receptor

stimulus → (i) ............... → (ii) ............... → (iii) ............... → response

Which structure goes in box (i)?
answer: receptor — the receptor detects the stimulus, so it comes straight after it.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
stimulus → (i) ............... → (ii) ............... → (iii) ............... → response

Which structure goes in box (ii)?
answer: coordinator — the coordinator (the brain or spinal cord) takes the impulse from the receptor and sends one on to the effector.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
stimulus → (i) ............... → (ii) ............... → (iii) ............... → response

Which structure goes in box (iii)?
answer: effector — the effector (a muscle or a gland) carries out the response, so it comes just before it.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for the whole order, receptor → coordinator → effector: 2 marks for all three boxes right, 1 mark if only one adjacent pair is right (receptor then coordinator, or coordinator then effector).

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Scientists think the grey wolf and the domestic dog had a common ancestor.

The common ancestor:

  • lived about 32 thousand years ago
  • is now extinct.

Give two possible causes of extinction.
answer: Any two: drought, an ice age, new predators or disease, competition, loss of habitat — Any two of: drought; an ice age; global warming; volcanic activity; an asteroid collision; new predators or hunters; new disease; competition for food; competition for mates; loss or change of habitat. 'Climate change' alone scores 1.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
32 thousand years ago, humans hunted other animals for food. Wolves also hunted other animals for food.

Suggest one reason why wolves began to follow groups of humans.
answer: Any one of: wolves ate the humans; wolves got the left-over food from humans; humans gave food to the wolves

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Some wolves are more aggressive than other wolves.

Describe how selective breeding of wolves could produce a domestic animal that is less aggressive than the wolf.
answer: Breed the least aggressive wolves, then the least aggressive of their offspring, and repeat over many generations — and keep repeating that over many generations

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A long time ago, vaccines were made in a different way. The virus was heated to stop it reproducing. The vaccine contained whole viruses.

Why might the vaccine containing heat-treated viruses be dangerous? Tick one box.
answer: The viruses may cause an infection
choices: The viruses may be inactive. | The viruses may cause an infection. | The viruses will not mutate.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Genetic engineering can also be used in agriculture. Weeds are a problem for farmers because the weeds compete with crop plants.

Give three factors that the weeds and crop plants compete for.
answer: Any three: light, water, mineral ions, oxygen in the soil, space — Any three of: light; water; mineral ions or salts; oxygen in the soil; space. ('Nutrients' and 'carbon dioxide' are ignored.)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Glyphosate is a weed killer used in agriculture. Genetically modified (GM) maize is a food crop that is resistant to glyphosate weed killer. Farmers can spray glyphosate on a field to kill the weeds where the GM maize is growing.

Suggest one advantage of using glyphosate on fields where GM maize is growing.
answer: The crop plants grow better — a higher yield

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Suggest one problem of using glyphosate on fields where GM maize is growing. Do not refer to cost in your answer.
answer: Any one: it may kill other plants, pollute water or soil, harm animals, or cut biodiversity — Any one of: it may kill or harm other plants; it may pollute streams, rivers or soil; it may harm humans or animals; it may reduce biodiversity

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: The human eye can make clear images of objects.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Figure 4 shows how the human eye focuses light rays from a distant object onto the retina.

Label structures A and B on Figure 4.

Choose answers from the box.

cornea   lens   optic nerve   sclera

What is structure A?

subject: Biology

People with Type 2 diabetes:

  • often have a high concentration of glucose in their blood.

Why do people with Type 2 diabetes often have a high concentration of glucose in their blood?

Tick (✓) one box.
answer: The body cells take in a low amount of glucose from the blood

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Drug X is used for treating people who have Type 2 diabetes. Scientists investigated the effect of drug X on the concentration of glucose in the blood of mice. This is the method used.

  1. Give two groups of mice the same diet for 8 weeks.
  2. Give each mouse in group A 2 cm3 of water to drink.
  3. Give each mouse in group B 2 cm3 of drug X to drink.
  4. After 30 minutes, give each mouse 1 cm3 of glucose solution to drink.
  5. Measure the concentration of glucose in the blood of each mouse at intervals for 3 hours.

Give two control variables used in the investigation.
answer: Any two: same diet, same 8 weeks, same 30 minutes, same 2 cm³ drink, same 1 cm³ glucose — Any two of: the same diet; the same 8-week duration; the same 30 minutes before the glucose; the same 2 cm³ volume of drink; the same 1 cm³ of glucose solution

name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Plan an investigation to show the effect of light from one direction on the growth of plant seedlings.

You should include:

  • a control
  • the measurements you would record
  • any other observations you would make.

You may use the equipment shown in Figure 7 and any other laboratory apparatus.
answer: Seedlings lit from one side, in the dark and in full light; compare mean growth; control variables — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs a comparison with plants in full light or darkness plus a control variable. Put one pot of seedlings in the box with the slit, one in the dark and one in full light. Measure the heights of the shoots at the start and again at the end — straightening bent shoots or following them with thread — record how the seedlings look, calculate the mean increase in height for each group, and compare them. Control the temperature, the volume of water, the soil, the age of the seedlings, the species and the time left.

html:
A gardener investigated the growth of roots on cuttings from a geranium plant.

This is the method used.

  1. Take 6 cuttings from the stems of the same plant.
  2. Prepare 6 test tubes, each containing a different concentration of a solution of chemical Q.
  3. Place 1 cutting in each test tube with the cut end of each stem in the solution.
  4. Leave the test tubes at room temperature for 10 days.

Figure 8 shows the results.

Tube 1 contains no chemical Q.

Tube 1 is a control.

Why did the gardener include tube 1 in the investigation?
answer: To compare with the other tubes — to show what difference chemical Q makes
