subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The gardener has four types of geranium plant: A, B, C and D.

Plant A produces larger, more brightly-coloured flowers than any of the other plants.

The gardener wants to grow more plants of type A.

Explain why the gardener chooses to take cuttings from plant A instead of growing seeds from plant A.
answer: Cuttings are quicker and asexual (mitosis, no mixing of alleles), so the new plants are clones of A with its flowers — no waiting for flowers, fruit and seed. They are asexual reproduction, so there is no fusing of gametes and no mixing of alleles from two parents: it is mitosis, which copies the genetic material exactly, rather than meiosis. So every offspring is a clone of plant A and has the same large, brightly-coloured flowers, where seeds would vary through pollination from other geraniums. That also means consistent quality and a quicker turnover for the gardener.

In 1866, a monk called Gregor Mendel published the results of his investigations into inheritance in pea plants.

Pea plants produce seeds in a pod.

Figure 9 shows a pea pod.

Pea seeds can be round or wrinkled in shape.

Mendel crossed pea plants that produced round seeds with pea plants that produced wrinkled seeds.

Figure 10 shows the results.

In questions 08.1 to 08.3 use the following symbols to represent the alleles:

R = dominant allele for round seeds
r = recessive allele for wrinkled seeds.

subject: Biology

Mendel published his work in 1866.

Suggest two reasons why the importance of Mendel's work was not recognised until the early 1900s.
answer: Any two: few knew of it, blending inheritance was accepted, he was a monk, his maths was new — Any two of: other scientists were not aware of his work, or it was published in an obscure journal and lost for years; other theories such as blending inheritance were accepted at the time; he was not considered a scientist — he was only a monk; his mathematical approach was a novel idea nobody understood; peas gave unusual results compared with other species, and his results were not corroborated; later discoveries were what made his work relevant.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: What is a mutation?
answer: A change in the DNA — in a base, in the base sequence, in a gene or allele, or in part of or the number of chromosomes

subject: Biology
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Describe the process of natural selection.
answer: Variation; the best adapted survive and reproduce, passing on favourable alleles — Any three of: there is variation between members of a species; the better adapted individuals survive; those survivors reproduce; and they pass on the favourable alleles to their offspring

name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Explain why most of the dead remains of plants in layer B do not decay.
answer: There is not enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so less energy is released, in the decomposers — the microorganisms, bacteria and fungi. Alternatively: the low pH denatures their enzymes, so there are fewer reactions and less energy released in the decomposers.

Humans have destroyed large areas of peat bog to collect peat.

The peat comes from layer B in Figure 13.

Layer B:

  • contains the dead remains of plants
  • has a low pH
  • contains very little oxygen
  • contains carbon dioxide and methane.

Figure 14 shows the removal of peat from a peat bog.

[Figure 14: a photograph of peat being removed from a bog, not reproduced here.]

Explain how the destruction of peat bogs and the use of peat affects the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere.
answer: It increases: carbon dioxide is released from the bog and by burning and decay of the peat, and methane from the bog — global warming. Carbon dioxide is released from the peat bog; carbon dioxide is produced by burning the peat and by its decay once it is exposed; and methane is released from the bog as well. There are also fewer plants left to take carbon dioxide in by photosynthesis.

Frogs are animals that lay their eggs in water. The eggs hatch as tadpoles.

  2. Count the number of tadpoles collected.
  3. Put the tadpoles back into the pond.
  4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 another three times in different parts of the pond.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Name the pieces of equipment labelled A, B and C in Figure 4. Choose answers from the box.

What is equipment A?
answer: Pipette — it measures out an exact volume of the alkali into the flask.
choices: beaker | burette | conical flask | measuring cylinder | pipette | test tube

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is equipment B in Figure 4?
answer: Conical flask — it holds the alkali and indicator and can be swirled without spilling.
choices: beaker | burette | conical flask | measuring cylinder | pipette | test tube

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is equipment C in Figure 4?
answer: Burette — it adds the acid a little at a time, and the volume added is read from its scale.
choices: beaker | burette | conical flask | measuring cylinder | pipette | test tube

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In Step 2 in Figure 4 the acid is added to the alkali until the solution is neutralised.

The volume of acid added is then read from equipment C.

Name a suitable indicator for use in Step 2 of the titration.
answer: Methyl orange or phenolphthalein (litmus is accepted). Universal indicator is not.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one observation that shows the alkali is neutralised.
answer: A colour change

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give two ways to make sure that the volume of acid added is accurate.
answer: Any two: swirl, add drop by drop near the end, read at eye level, no bubbles, white tile — Any two of: swirl the flask; add the acid drop by drop near the end point; read the burette at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus; make sure there are no bubbles in the burette; stand the flask on a white tile; repeat and take a mean

Figure 5 shows the reading on equipment C at the end of Step 2.

answer: 16.6 cm³ — a burette is numbered downwards from the top, and the meniscus is read at its bottom

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A salt is produced when an acid neutralises an alkali. Barium chloride is a salt containing the ions Ba2+ and Cl−.

What is the formula of barium chloride? Tick one box.
answer: BaCl₂ — two 1− ions balance one 2+ ion

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
This question is about energy changes of reactions.

Zinc reacts with copper sulfate solution.

The word equation for the reaction is:

zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
What type of reaction is the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate solution?

Tick (✓) one box.
answer: Displacement

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Calculate the percentage (%) by mass of copper in copper sulfate (CuSO4). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

Relative atomic mass (Ar): Cu = 63.5
Relative formula mass (Mr): CuSO4 = 159.5
answer: 39.8% — 63.5 ÷ 159.5 × 100 = 39.81191…, which to 3 significant figures is 39.8

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated the energy change in the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate solution. This is the method used.

  1. Measure 25 cm3 of copper sulfate solution into a polystyrene cup.
  2. Weigh 0.20 g of zinc powder.
  3. Add the zinc powder to the copper sulfate solution.
  4. Measure the highest temperature reached by the mixture.
  5. Repeat steps 1 to 4 using different masses of zinc powder.

Control variables are used to make an investigation a fair test.

Which is a control variable in the investigation? Tick one box.
answer: Volume of copper sulfate solution
choices: Highest temperature reached by the mixture | Mass of zinc powder | Volume of copper sulfate solution

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 6 shows the results.

What is the minimum mass of zinc powder needed to react with all the copper sulfate solution?

Use Figure 6.
answer: 0.80 g — the mass at which the temperature stops rising, so all the copper sulfate has reacted

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the maximum temperature change in the reaction between zinc powder and 25 cm3 of copper sulfate solution? Use Figure 6.
answer: 25 °C — 47 °C minus the starting 22 °C

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
25 cm3 of copper sulfate solution contained 6.75 g of copper sulfate.

Calculate the concentration of the solution in g/dm3.

You should:

  • calculate the volume of the solution in dm3 (1000 cm3 = 1 dm3)
  • use the equation:

concentration of solution in g/dm3 = mass of copper sulfate in grams⁄volume of solution in dm3

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Another student investigated the energy change of the reaction between sodium hydrogencarbonate and hydrochloric acid.

This is the method used.

  1. Measure 25 cm3 of hydrochloric acid.
  2. Weigh 1.0 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate.
  3. Add the sample of sodium hydrogencarbonate to the hydrochloric acid.
  4. Measure the lowest temperature reached by the mixture.
  5. Repeat steps 1 to 4 using different masses of sodium hydrogencarbonate.

Figure 7 shows the results.

Draw two straight lines of best fit on Figure 7.

The lines should cross.
answer: Two straight lines, one through the first five (falling) points and one through the last four (level), crossing — the falling part — and a second through the last four, the level part. Maximum 1 mark if the lines do not intersect.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which statement describes the energy change in the reaction shown in Figure 7? Tick one box.
answer: Energy is taken in from the surroundings so the reaction is endothermic — the temperature falls
choices: Energy is transferred to the surroundings so the reaction is endothermic. | Energy is transferred to the surroundings so the reaction is exothermic. | Energy is taken in from the surroundings so the reaction is endothermic. | Energy is taken in from the surroundings so the reaction is exothermic.

subject: Chemistry

Nanoparticles are used in sun creams and in wound dressings.

A wound dressing is placed next to the skin to prevent infection.

Figure 8 shows a wound dressing.

[Figure 8: a photograph of a wound dressing, not reproduced here.]

SubstanceProperty
CarbonStrong
Silicon dioxideHard
SilverKills bacteria

Match each use to the best substance for that use.

choices: Carbon | Silicon dioxide | Silver | Titanium dioxide

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Table 3 shows the products of the electrolysis of some molten compounds. Complete Table 3.

Molten compoundProduct at negative electrodeProduct at positive electrode
Lead chloride(i)Chlorine
Potassium iodidePotassium(ii)
(iii)ZincBromine

What is the product at the negative electrode when molten lead chloride is electrolysed?
answer: Lead — the metal ions (Pb2+) are attracted to the negative electrode and gain electrons there.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the product at the positive electrode when molten potassium iodide is electrolysed?
answer: Iodine — the iodide ions (I−) are attracted to the positive electrode and lose electrons there.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which molten compound gives zinc at the negative electrode and bromine at the positive electrode?
answer: Zinc bromide — the metal comes from the positive ion and the non-metal from the negative ion.

subject: Chemistry

Aluminium is extracted by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide.

Balance the equation for the reaction. Choose numbers from the box.

2 Al2O3 → □ Al + ___ O2

Which number goes in front of Al?
answer: 4 — 2 Al2O3 holds 2 × 2 = 4 aluminium atoms.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
2 Al2O3 → ___ Al + □ O2

Which number goes in front of O2?
answer: 3 — 2 Al2O3 holds 2 × 3 = 6 oxygen atoms, which is 3 O2 molecules.

html:
Figure 13 shows part of the reactivity series of metals.

The non-metal carbon has been included.

Metals can be extracted from their compounds by:

  • electrolysis
  • reduction with carbon.

Electrolysis is more expensive than reduction with carbon.

Use Figure 13 to predict one metal that would be extracted by electrolysis.
answer: Potassium (or lithium) — a metal above carbon in the reactivity series, which carbon cannot reduce, so it has to be extracted by electrolysis.

name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student made the hypothesis: 'The voltage produced by a cell depends on the difference in the reactivity of metal A and metal B.'

Plan an investigation to test this hypothesis. Your plan should produce valid results. Use Figure 14.
answer: Measure the voltage for different pairs of metals, one metal kept the same, same electrolyte — Level-marked out of 6. subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student produced a salt by reacting copper carbonate with sulfuric acid.

This is the method used.

  1. Measure 50 cm3 of sulfuric acid into a beaker.
  2. Add copper carbonate powder.
  3. Stir the mixture.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until copper carbonate is in excess.
  5. Filter the mixture.
  6. Warm the filtrate gently until crystals start to appear.
  7. Leave the solution to cool and crystallise.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Complete the word equation for the reaction.

copper carbonate + sulfuric acid → ............... + ............... + carbon dioxide
answer: copper sulfate + water (CuSO₄ and H₂O are accepted)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one observation the student could make during Step 4 which shows that the copper carbonate is in excess.
answer: Solid remains in the mixture — or there is no more effervescence, bubbling or fizzing

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give one reason for filtering the mixture in Step 5.
answer: To remove the excess copper carbonate

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Name the equipment that can be used to warm the filtrate gently in Step 6.
answer: An electric heater, or a water bath. (A Bunsen burner is ignored.)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The maximum theoretical mass of the salt that could be produced using 50 cm3 of the sulfuric acid is 12.5 g. The percentage yield of the salt is 92.8%.

Calculate the mass of salt actually produced. Use the equation:

% yield = (mass of salt actually produced ÷ maximum theoretical mass of salt that could be produced) × 100

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Some salts can be produced by reacting sulfuric acid with a metal. Neither copper nor sodium is used to produce a salt with sulfuric acid.

Give one reason why each metal is not used.
answer: Copper does not react with the acid; sodium reacts dangerously, it could explode or get too hot — it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it will not displace hydrogen. Sodium: the reaction is dangerous — it could explode, or get too hot.

answer: Similarity: both have one electron in their outer shell. Difference: sodium has 3 shells and potassium has 4.

Group 1 elements react with water.

answer: Any two: fizzing, floats, moves around, gets smaller, melts into a ball, a flame — Any two of: effervescence, bubbling or fizzing; the potassium floats; it moves around; it gets smaller; it melts or forms a ball; a flame; an explosion

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024

Potassium hydroxide solution is produced when potassium reacts with water.

What is the colour of universal indicator when added to potassium hydroxide solution? Give one reason for your answer.
answer: Blue, violet or purple: the solution is alkaline (it contains OH⁻ ions) — because the solution is alkaline (it contains hydroxide, OH⁻, ions)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Compare model A with the model of the atom used today.

Use Figure 16.
answer: Model A has no nucleus and no empty space; today: nucleus, shells, mostly empty space — Level-marked out of 4. Similarities: both contain electrons; both are neutral overall. Differences: model A has no nucleus, no protons and no neutrons, where today's model has all three. In model A the positive charge and the mass are spread throughout the atom; today they are concentrated in the centre. In model A the electrons are distributed randomly; today they are in shells. Model A has no empty space; today's atom is mostly empty space.

name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: This question is about paper chromatography.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated substance Y using paper chromatography.

This is the method used.

  1. Draw a start line in ink on a piece of chromatography paper.
  2. Put spots of four different dyes, A, B, C and D, and a spot of substance Y, on the start line.
  3. Dip the paper into water so that the water level is below the start line.
  4. Wait until the water has risen to near the top of the paper.

The student’s method contains a mistake in Step 1.

What is the mistake in Step 1?
answer: The start line is drawn in ink — it should be drawn in pencil.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give one reason why it is a mistake.
answer: The ink would dissolve in the water and separate too — ink runs or smudges in the solvent, so its colours would move up the paper with the dyes; pencil does not dissolve.

html:

Use Figure 4.
answer: 2 — substance Y separated into two spots

html:
A student investigated the rate of the reaction of sodium thiosulfate solution with hydrochloric acid.

When sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with hydrochloric acid, the mixture becomes cloudy.

Figure 6 shows the apparatus.

This is the method used.

  1. Put 75 cm3 of sodium thiosulfate solution in a conical flask.
  2. Draw a pencil cross on paper.
  3. Put the conical flask on the pencil cross.
  4. Add 15 cm3 of hydrochloric acid to the contents of the conical flask.
  5. Swirl the conical flask to mix the contents and immediately start a timer.
  6. Stop the timer when the pencil cross is no longer visible through the reaction mixture.
  7. Repeat steps 1 to 6 using different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate solution.

A student investigated an aqueous solution of a salt.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Describe a test to identify sodium ions.
answer: A flame test — put a little of the solution into a blue Bunsen flame on a clean wire loop. (Flame emission spectroscopy is also accepted.)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give the result of the test if sodium ions are present.
answer: A yellow flame — sodium ions colour a flame yellow. (With flame emission spectroscopy: the lines match the sodium spectrum.)

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024

answer: Add acidified silver nitrate solution — dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate; the silver ions react with chloride ions.

subject: Chemistry
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give the result of the test if chloride ions are present.
answer: A white precipitate — of silver chloride. The result mark depends on getting the test right.

The student determined the concentration of sodium chloride in the salt solution. This is the method used.

  2. Add 25.0 cm3 of the salt solution into the evaporating dish.
  3. Heat the evaporating dish and contents.
  4. Weigh the evaporating dish and contents.
  5. Repeat steps 3 to 4 until there is no further change in mass.

answer: To make sure all the water had evaporated

Do not refer to use of water in the home.
answer: A: filter, sterilise (chlorine, ozone, UV). B: screen, sediment, digest sludge anaerobically, treat effluent aerobically — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs both halves. Process A — making water potable: pass the water through filter beds to remove solids, then sterilise it with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light to destroy microbes. The potential difference between the metal dome and earth is 300 000 V. When the spark jumps there is a charge flow of 0.000 002 C.

Calculate the energy transferred by the spark. Use the equation:

energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference

html:

Calculate the resistance of the coin. Use the equation:

resistance = potential difference ÷ current

name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give a reason for your answer: why does the thermistor have that potential difference across it?
answer: The thermistor has the same resistance as the resistor — in series, the potential difference is shared in the ratio of the resistances, so equal resistances get half of the 3.0 V each.

answer: 400 Ω — the resistance at 15 °C is 200 Ω, and 600 − 200 = 400

html:
In a ride at a theme park, a person is strapped into a pod that is attached to two stretched bungee cords.

The bungee cords behave like springs.

Figure 7 shows a person using the ride: the pod is held at ground level with a stretched cord running up to a tower on each side.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
How is the extension of each bungee cord calculated?

Tick one box.
answer: stretched length − original length
examiner_note: Figure 7 is a photograph in the PDF and is not transcribed.
choices: stretched length + original length | stretched length − original length | stretched length × original length | stretched length ÷ original length

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Before the pod is released, the extension of each bungee cord is 7.5 m.

spring constant of the bungee cord = 800 N/m

Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in each stretched bungee cord. Use the equation:

elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)2

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The maximum speed of the pod is 15 m/s. The mass of the pod is 240 kg.

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the pod. Use the equation:

kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)2

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which equation links gravitational field strength (g), gravitational potential energy (Ep), height (h) and mass (m)? Tick one box.
answer: E_p = m × g × h
choices: E<sub>p</sub> = m × g ÷ h | E<sub>p</sub> = m ÷ (g × h) | E<sub>p</sub> = m × g × h

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The pod has 24 000 J of gravitational potential energy when at its maximum height. The mass of the pod is 240 kg.

gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

Calculate the maximum height reached by the pod.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Why is the maximum gravitational potential energy of the pod less than the initial elastic potential energy of the bungee cords? Tick two boxes.
answer: Energy is transferred to the surroundings; work is done against air resistance
choices: Energy is created. | Energy is destroyed. | Energy is transferred to the surroundings. | Work is done against air resistance. | Work is done by the force of gravity. | Work is done by the person in the pod.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Figure 8 shows a measuring cylinder containing some water. Its scale runs from 0.0 to 10.0 cm3, with a line every 0.2 cm3.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
What range of volumes can be measured using the measuring cylinder?

Tick one box.
answer: 0.0 to 10.0 cm³ — the range is the whole scale; 0.2 cm³ is the resolution
examiner_note: Figure 8 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: 0.0 to 0.2 cm<sup>3</sup> | 0.0 to 2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> | 0.0 to 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup>

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student used the measuring cylinder to measure the volume of a metal ring. The student tied the metal ring to some very thin string and lowered the ring into the measuring cylinder. The student could have used thick string instead of thin string.

How would using thick string have affected the measured volume of the metal ring? Tick one box.
answer: The measured volume would be larger — the string itself displaces water too
choices: The measured volume would be smaller. | The measured volume would not be affected. | The measured volume would be larger.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Table 1 shows the results.

Volume of water in cm3Volume of water and ring in cm3Volume of ring in cm3
5.05.4X

Calculate value X in Table 1.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The student measured the volume of the ring three times. The results were all the same.

Which of the following describes the student's results? Tick one box.
answer: The results are repeatable
choices: The results are anomalies. | The results are repeatable. | The results contain random errors.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The student used a balance to measure the mass of the ring. Figure 9 is a photograph of the balance. The student noticed that the balance had a reading of 0.02 g when there was no object on it.

How should the student correct this error after the mass of the ring had been measured? Tick one box.
answer: Subtract 0.02 from the measurement — it is a zero error and every reading is 0.02 g too big
examiner_note: Figure 9 is a photograph in the PDF and is not transcribed.
choices: Add 0.02 to the measurement | Divide the measurement by 0.02 | Multiply the measurement by 0.02 | Subtract 0.02 from the measurement

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Write down the equation which links density (ρ), mass (m) and volume (V).
answer: density = mass ÷ volume, or ρ = m ÷ V

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A different metal ring has a volume of 0.3 cm3. The density of this ring is 22 g/cm3.

Calculate the mass of this ring. Give your answer in grams.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated how the pressure in a fixed mass of air varies with the volume of the air.

Figure 10 shows the equipment used: a syringe with a plunger, its nozzle connected to a pressure gauge.

When the plunger was pushed slowly into the syringe, the temperature of the air stayed the same.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
How did pushing the plunger in affect the volume of air in the syringe?

Tick one box.
answer: The volume decreased
examiner_note: Figure 10 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: The volume decreased. | The volume stayed the same. | The volume increased.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: How did pushing the plunger in affect the distance between the air particles in the syringe? Tick one box.
answer: The distance decreased
choices: The distance decreased. | The distance stayed the same. | The distance increased.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: How did pushing the plunger in affect the frequency of collisions between the air particles and the syringe walls? Tick one box.
answer: The frequency of collisions increased
choices: The frequency of collisions decreased. | The frequency of collisions stayed the same. | The frequency of collisions increased.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: How did pushing the plunger in affect the air pressure in the syringe? Tick one box.
answer: The air pressure increased
choices: The air pressure decreased. | The air pressure stayed the same. | The air pressure increased.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A fire piston is a special type of syringe that can be used to start fires. Figure 11 shows one: a narrow cylinder with a plunger, and a small piece of cotton wool in the bottom. The plunger is pushed quickly downwards and compresses the air. When the air is compressed quickly, the temperature of the air increases.

How does an increase in temperature affect the mean speed of the air particles inside the syringe? Tick one box.
answer: The mean speed of the particles increases
examiner_note: Figure 11 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: The mean speed of the particles decreases. | The mean speed of the particles does not change. | The mean speed of the particles increases.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
When the air is hot enough, a small piece of cotton wool in the piston catches fire. The energy transferred to the air in the piston is 0.0130 J. The mass of air in the piston is 2.60 × 10−8 kg.

specific heat capacity of air = 1010 J/kg °C

Calculate the temperature change of the air. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: A teacher measured the background radiation in a laboratory.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Which sources of background radiation are natural and which are man-made?

Are cosmic rays a natural or a man-made source?
answer: Natural — cosmic rays come from space.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Are medical X-rays a natural or a man-made source of background radiation?
answer: Man-made — X-rays are made by machines in hospitals.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Are nuclear accidents a natural or a man-made source of background radiation?
answer: Man-made — radioactive material released from nuclear power stations, such as at Chernobyl.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Is radon gas a natural or a man-made source of background radiation?
answer: Natural — radon seeps out of rocks in the ground.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for the four rows together, not one per row, so both sit on this last row: all four right for 2 marks, and two or three right for 1.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The teacher measured the radiation emitted by four different types of radioactive rock. Figure 12 shows the equipment: a detector clamped above a bench, with a rock placed below it and a space for a sheet of material in between. Each rock was placed below the detector one at a time and the radiation recorded as counts in 1 minute, with different materials between rock and detector.

Table 2 shows the results.

Number of counts in 1 minuteNo materialOne sheet of paperThick aluminium sheet
No rock212022
Rock A45044818
Rock B385387356
Rock C8702120
Rock D620473214

Which radioactive rock emitted only alpha radiation?

Tick one box.
answer: Rock C — one sheet of paper cut its count from 870 to 21, the background level.
examiner_note: Figure 12 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: Rock A | Rock B | Rock C | Rock D

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give a reason for your answer: what in Table 2 shows which rock emitted only alpha radiation?
answer: A sheet of paper brought its count down to background — for Rock C, paper cut the count from 870 to 21 (background is about 21), and alpha radiation is stopped by paper.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Which radioactive rock emitted only beta radiation?

Tick one box.
answer: Rock A — paper made almost no difference to its count, but thick aluminium cut it to background.
choices: Rock A | Rock B | Rock C | Rock D

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give a reason for your answer: what in Table 2 shows which rock emitted only beta radiation?
answer: Paper barely changed the count but aluminium brought it down to background — for Rock A, 450 with no material and 448 through paper, but 18 through thick aluminium: beta passes through paper and is stopped by aluminium.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The teacher took safety precautions during the experiment.

Which precaution would prevent the teacher from becoming contaminated by the radioactive rocks? Tick one box.
answer: Wearing protective gloves — contamination is getting the radioactive material itself on you
choices: Displaying the radiation hazard symbol | Handling the rocks with clean hands | Wearing protective gloves

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the activity of each rock after one half-life? Tick one box.
answer: The activity is half the original activity
choices: The activity is a quarter of the original activity. | The activity is half the original activity. | The activity is double the original activity. | The activity is zero.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: How does the activity of a radioactive source affect the risk of harm from the source? Tick one box.
answer: The greater the activity, the greater the risk of harm
choices: The smaller the activity, the greater the risk of harm. | The activity does not affect the risk of harm. | The greater the activity, the greater the risk of harm.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
An electrical appliance is connected to the mains electricity supply using a three-core cable.

Figure 13 shows a three-core cable, cut back to show the three insulated wires inside the outer sheath.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
What colour is the insulation covering the live wire inside the cable?

Tick one box.
answer: Brown
examiner_note: Figure 13 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: Blue | Brown | Green and yellow | Orange

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What colour is the insulation covering the neutral wire inside the cable? Tick one box.
answer: Blue
choices: Blue | Brown | Green and yellow | Orange

name: Paper 1 — June 2024

The plug connected to the cable contains a fuse.

Tick one box.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The wire in the fuse melts when there is a charge flow of 2.0 C in a time of 0.40 s.

Calculate the current in the wire when it melts. Use the equation:

current = charge flow ÷ time

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The mass of the wire is 0.016 g.

specific latent heat of fusion of the wire = 60 000 J/kg

Calculate the change in thermal energy needed to melt the wire. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.
answer: 0.96 J — convert 0.016 g to 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ kg first, then E = 0.000016 × 60 000

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The fuse transfers some energy to the surroundings as it melts.

How does transferring energy to the surroundings affect the total energy needed to melt the fuse? Tick one box.
answer: The total energy will be greater
choices: The total energy will be smaller. | The total energy will be the same. | The total energy will be greater.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 16 shows a wind turbine.

Wind turbines may generate electricity when the electricity is not needed.

Two methods that can be used to store the energy from the turbine are:

Method A: Heating water to a high temperature.
Method B: Pumping water uphill into a reservoir.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which energy store increases when water is heated?
answer: The thermal (internal) energy store — or the kinetic store of the water particles
examiner_note: Figure 16 is a photograph in the PDF and is not transcribed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which energy store increases when water is pumped uphill into a reservoir?
answer: The gravitational potential energy store

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Table 4 shows information about the two methods of storing energy.

MethodEnergy stored per 100 kg of water in kJPercentage of stored energy wastedInstallation
A: Increasing water temperature by 80 °C33 60040%Anywhere
B: Pumping water uphill to a height of 500 m49025%High mountains

Compare the advantages and disadvantages of the two methods of storing energy. Include calculations in your answer.
answer: A is 60% efficient and stores far more; B is 75% efficient but needs a mountain site — Level-marked out of 4, and Level 2 needs a calculation that compares the two. Method A: useful energy per 100 kg = 20 160 kJ, wasted = 13 440 kJ, efficiency 60%; it stores far more energy per 100 kg and can be installed anywhere, but the hot water needs insulating. Method B: useful = 367.5 kJ, wasted = 122.5 kJ, efficiency 75%; more efficient, but it needs a high mountain site.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Decreasing the amount of carbon dioxide released by different activities will help slow down climate change. Transport and generating electricity are the two activities that released the largest amounts of carbon dioxide in the UK in 2018.

Explain one change that would reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released by each activity.
answer: Electric or hydrogen vehicles, cycling, walking or public transport; renewables or nuclear — Transport: stop burning petrol or diesel, and use electric or hydrogen cars, a bicycle, public transport or walking instead. Generating electricity: stop using coal, oil or gas, and use renewables or nuclear instead — or use fewer appliances, to cut the demand for electricity generated from fossil fuels. Two marks for each activity.

The process of nuclear fission is used in nuclear power stations.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Complete the sentences.

In nuclear power stations, energy is released from uranium ............... .
answer: nuclei — fission splits the nucleus of a uranium atom, and the energy comes from the nucleus.
examiner_note: Figure 17 is artwork in the PDF; what it shows is stated in the question.
choices: electrons | gamma rays | neutrons | nuclei | protons

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The uranium in Figure 17 splits into two parts and releases three ............... .
answer: neutrons — one neutron goes in and the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, giving out three neutrons (which can go on to cause more fissions).
choices: electrons | gamma rays | neutrons | nuclei | protons

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: The process of nuclear fission releases electromagnetic radiation in the form of ............... .
answer: gamma rays — the only electromagnetic radiation in the box; electrons, neutrons, nuclei and protons are all particles.
choices: electrons | gamma rays | neutrons | nuclei | protons

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Write down the equation which links energy (E), power (P) and time (t).
answer: energy = power × time, or E = P × t

subject: Physics

subject: Physics

Radioactive waste produced by nuclear power stations has a long half-life.

Suggest one precaution taken to reduce the hazard caused by radioactive waste from power stations.
answer: Bury it, or store it in metal containers or concrete — Any one of: bury it; put it in cooling ponds; transport it in secure vessels; store it in metal containers; cover it in concrete

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024

Nuclear power stations do not generate electricity every day of the year. One nuclear power station generated electricity for 92% of a year.

one year = 365 days

Calculate the number of days during the year that the nuclear power station generated electricity.
answer: 335.8 days — 92 ÷ 100 × 365. 335 and 336 are accepted.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The student plotted a graph of resistance against the length of wire.

Describe a method the student could have used to collect the data needed to plot the graph.
answer: Vary the length between the clips, measure current and p.d., and use V = IR — Level-marked out of 6. Measure the length of wire between the crocodile clips with the ruler; vary the length by moving the clips; measure the current with the ammeter and the potential difference with the voltmeter; record both for each length; use V = IR to calculate the resistance for each length. Also: repeat and take means, remove anomalies, keep the current low so the wire does not heat up, and disconnect the circuit between readings.

name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
When the total mass of the trolley was 1.5 kg, the acceleration of the trolley was 0.62 m/s2.

Calculate the resultant force acting on the trolley. Use the equation:

resultant force = mass × acceleration

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Figure 7 represents a transverse wave.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Which arrow represents the amplitude of the wave?

Tick one box.
answer: C — the amplitude is measured from the undisturbed middle line to a crest or trough, not from crest to trough

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Which arrow represents the wavelength of the wave?

Tick one box.
answer: B — one whole cycle, from a point on the wave to the same point on the next

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A wave has a frequency of 5000 Hz.

Calculate the period of the wave. Use the equation:

period = 1 ÷ frequency

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give one example of a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum.
answer: Any named electromagnetic wave — light, radio waves, X-rays, and so on

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A sound wave has a frequency of 750 Hz.

speed of sound in air = 330 m/s

Calculate the wavelength of the sound wave. Use the equation:

wavelength = wave speed ÷ frequency

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Describe a method that could be used to determine the speed of sound in air.
answer: Time a sharp sound over a measured distance (source to listener or microphone), then speed = distance ÷ time — cymbals, wooden blocks, a starting pistol. Measure the distance between the source and the detector with a tape measure, trundle wheel or metre rule — the distance to a wall, along a track, or between two microphones. Start timing when the sound is made and stop when it is heard, using a stopwatch, oscilloscope or data logger. For an echo method, double the distance or halve the time. Then use speed = distance ÷ time.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
When a sound wave moves from air into water, the speed of the wave increases. The frequency of the sound wave does not change.

Complete the sentence.

When a sound wave moves from air into water its wavelength ............... .
answer: increases — wavelength is speed ÷ frequency, and the speed has gone up while the frequency has not

html:

Tick one box: A, B or C.
answer: B — section B is the least steep part of the distance–time graph.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give a reason for your choice of section.
answer: It has the smallest gradient — on a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed, so the shallowest section is the slowest.

When sunlight shines on a red flower, the red light is ............... .
answer: reflected — the flower looks red because the red light bounces off it into our eyes.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2024
html: All other colours of light shining on the red flower are ............... .
answer: absorbed — only the red is reflected, so every other colour is taken in by the flower.

html: 23⁄1000  ☐  0.23
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: < — 23⁄1000 is 0.023, which is smaller than 0.23. Both pairs use the same digits, which is the trap.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for both symbols correct.

Draw the full-size triangle accurately. Use an angle measurer (protractor) and a ruler.

On the paper one line, 8 cm long, has been drawn for you — rule your own 8 cm line first.

Complete the table.

Round 39,476
to the nearest 10,000(a)
to the nearest 1,000(b)
to the nearest 100(c)
Round 39,476 to the nearest 10,000.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 40,000 — the digit after the ten thousands is 9, so 39,476 rounds up.

html: Round 39,476 to the nearest 1,000.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 39,000 — the digit after the thousands is 4, so it rounds down. The whole number is the answer: 9,000 is refused.

html: Round 39,476 to the nearest 100.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 39,500 — the digit after the hundreds is 7, so 39,400 rounds up to 39,500. 500 on its own is refused.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for all three correct, or 1 mark for any two rounded correctly. 9,000 or 500 are not accepted for the second and third.

html:
Amina asked 60 children to choose their favourite flavour of jelly. These were her results.

FlavourNumber of children
Raspberry12
Lemon8
Orange15
Blackcurrant25
Total60

What percentage of the 60 children chose orange?
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 25% — 15 out of 60 is a quarter, and a quarter is 25%. The other three flavours are there to be ignored.

html:
Write the missing number.

6 + 2 × 2 − ☐ = 6
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 4 — the multiplication goes first, so it is 6 + 4 − ☐ = 6, which makes the box 4. Working left to right instead gives 8 × 2 and the wrong answer.

html:
These two shapes have the same perimeter.

The length of each side of the hexagon is 8 centimetres.

Calculate the area of the square.

Show your method
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 144 cm² — the hexagon has six sides of 8 cm, so its perimeter is 48 cm; the square has the same perimeter, so each side is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm; and 12 × 12 = 144. Three steps, and the side of the square is the one worth writing down.

html: 95   89   87
Circle the prime number.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 89 — nothing but 1 and 89 divides it: it is odd, its digits add to 17 so 3 does not go, it does not end in 0 or 5, and 7 × 13 = 91 is past it.

html: Explain how you know the other numbers are not prime.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 87 = 3 × 29 and 95 = 5 × 19 — 87 divides by 3 (its digits add to 15, which is in the three times table) and 95 divides by 5 (it ends in 5), so each has a factor besides 1 and itself. The explanation has to cover BOTH numbers.
examiner_note: The paper’s 1 mark is for a correct explanation of why 95 AND 87 are not prime; no mark is awarded for circling 89 alone.

html:
A machine pours 250 millilitres of juice every 4 seconds. How many litres of juice does the machine pour every minute?

Show your method
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 3.75 litres — a minute is 60 seconds, which is 60 ÷ 4 = 15 lots of four seconds, so 15 × 250 = 3,750 ml, and 3,750 ÷ 1000 = 3.75 litres. The conversion at the end is the half people drop: the question asks for litres and every number in it is in millilitres and seconds.

html: Tick the fractions that are equal to 20%.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄5 and 3⁄15 — 20% is 20⁄100, which cancels to 1⁄5; and 3⁄15 cancels to 1⁄5 as well (divide top and bottom by 3). The other three are not 20%: 1⁄20 is 5%, 20⁄40 is a half, which is 50%, and 2⁄100 is 2%. Two marks for both right boxes and nothing else ticked; one mark for one right box with nothing wrong, or both right with one wrong.

html:
Adam has this rectangular piece of card. It is marked with grid lines.

Adam makes two straight cuts along the grid lines. The two cuts divide the rectangle into 3 shapes:

  • 2 squares of different size, and
  • 1 rectangle.

Using the grid lines, draw two lines that show where Adam could have made his cuts. Use a ruler.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: Cut off a 5 by 5 square, then a 2 by 2 square — The card is 7 squares across and 5 down, so the biggest square it holds is 5 by 5: one cut from top to bottom, 5 squares in from either end. That leaves a strip 2 squares wide and 5 tall; one cut across it, 2 squares from its top or its bottom, makes a 2 by 2 square and leaves a 2 by 3 rectangle. The scheme shows all four versions (big square at either end, small square at the top or bottom of the strip) and any one earns the mark. No other pair of cuts works.

html: This graph shows the maximum temperature for five days.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
examiner_note: Every value is the paper’s own, printed beside its cross on the graph.

html: For what fraction of the five days was the maximum temperature below 10 °C?
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄5 — two of the five days, Monday (8.1 °C) and Tuesday (9.3 °C), were below 10 °C. The scheme also accepts 4⁄10 or 0.4.

html:
What was the mean maximum temperature, to one decimal place?

Show your method
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 10.7 °C — 8.1 + 9.3 + 11.9 + 11.8 + 12.4 = 53.5, and 53.5 ÷ 5 = 10.7. It lands on one decimal place exactly, so nothing has to be rounded.

html: The original price of a car is £8,999. There is £1,100 off in the sale. What is the sale price of the car?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: £7,899 — 8,999 − 1,100. Only the thousands and hundreds change.

html: Which digit is in the ten thousands place?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — count the columns from the right: 9 ones, 1 ten, 2 hundreds, 6 thousands, 7 ten thousands. The scheme refuses 70,000: the question asks for the DIGIT, not its value.

html: Round 3,576,219 to the nearest million.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 4,000,000 — the digit below the millions is 5, so it rounds up. Writing 4 on its own is refused: the answer is the whole rounded number.

html: Dev says, "I had £10. I gave some money away." a is the amount of money, in pounds, that Dev gave away. Which expression shows how much money Dev has left? Tick one.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 10 − a — he started with 10 and gave a away, so a comes off the 10. a − 10 is the same two numbers the wrong way round and would be negative whenever he gave away less than he had.

name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
html:
Write these masses in order, starting with the lightest.

1.25 kg   0.99 kg   1.025 kg   0.009 kg
Which mass goes first, as the lightest?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 0.009 kg — written to three places the four are 1.250, 0.990, 1.025 and 0.009, and 0.009 is the smallest.

html: Which mass goes second?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 0.99 kg — 0.990 is under 1 kg, so it comes before both masses over a kilogram.

html: Which mass goes third?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1.025 kg — 1.025 looks longer than 1.25 and is smaller: 0 tenths against 2.

html: Which mass goes last, as the heaviest?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1.25 kg — 1.250 is the largest of the four.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for all four masses in the correct order.

name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
html:
Write the missing digits to make this addition correct.

(a) 2 (b) + (c) 2 = 200
What digit goes in box (a)?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — it is 128 + 72 = 200. The tens column carries 1 into the hundreds, and (a) + 1 = 2.

html: What digit goes in box (b)?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — the ones must make the 0 of 200: 8 + 2 = 10, carrying 1.

html: What digit goes in box (c)?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — the tens must make 0 as well: 2 + 7 + the carried 1 = 10, carrying 1 again.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for all three digits correct: 128 + 72 = 200.

html:
John buys one toy car at £1.49 and one pack of stickers at £1.64. He pays with a £10 note. How much change does John get?

Show your method
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths

html:
This picture shows the masses of eight kittens.

305 g375 g
310 g255 g
275 g410 g
360 g345 g
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths

html: What is the difference in mass between the heaviest kitten and the lightest kitten?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 155 g — the heaviest is 410 g and the lightest 255 g, and 410 − 255 = 155. Finding the two ends of a list of eight is the work; the subtraction is easy.

html:
The masses of the kittens are to be put in four groups. Write the missing numbers in the table. One has been done for you.

Mass in gNumber of kittens
250–299(i)
300–349(ii)
350–399(iii)
400–4491

How many kittens go in the 250–299 g group?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — 255 g and 275 g.

html: How many kittens go in the 300–349 g group?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — 305 g, 310 g and 345 g.

html: How many kittens go in the 350–399 g group?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — 360 g and 375 g. With the 410 g kitten already in the table, 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 8, every kitten.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for all three numbers correct; tally marks on their own are not accepted.

html:
Ken is playing a game. He has 4,289 points. Then he scores another 355 points. Ken's target is 6,000 points. How many more points does Ken need to reach his target?

Show your method
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1,356 — 4,289 + 355 = 4,644, and 6,000 − 4,644 = 1,356. Two steps, and stopping at 4,644 answers a question nobody asked.

html:
This pictogram shows the number of satellites above the Earth in 2016.

How many satellites were above the Earth in 2016?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2,250 — two whole circles are 2 × 1,000 = 2,000, and the last symbol is a quarter of a circle, so it stands for a quarter of 1,000, which is 250. The scheme refuses 2,000¼, 2¼ and 2.25: the question asks how many satellites, not how many symbols.

html: On the grid there are three points joined by two lines.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The three points are the paper’s: (−2, 3), (−1, −2) and (1, 2).

html:
Lara plots another point on the grid at (−1, 2). She joins the points to make a quadrilateral.

Complete Lara’s quadrilateral on the grid. Use a ruler.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: Plot (−1, 2) and rule lines from it to (−2, 3) and to (1, 2) — one square left of the y-axis and two up — and rule a line from it to (−2, 3) and another to (1, 2), the two loose ends of the lines already drawn. The quadrilateral’s corners are (−2, 3), (−1, −2), (1, 2) and (−1, 2).

html: Then Lara translates the quadrilateral 4 squares to the right. Draw the quadrilateral in its new position on the grid.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: Corners at (2, 3), (3, −2), (5, 2) and (3, 2), joined in the same order — Move every corner 4 squares right and keep its y-coordinate: (−2, 3) goes to (2, 3), (−1, −2) to (3, −2), (1, 2) to (5, 2) and (−1, 2) to (3, 2). Join them in the same order. A translation only moves a shape — same size, same way up. The scheme also gives the mark for a correct translation of a wrong quadrilateral from part (a).

name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
html:
Here are five numbers.

2   3   4   5   6

Write each number on the correct cards. The number 2 has been written on the correct cards for you: Prime numbers and Factors of 12.

Cards: Prime numbers   Factors of 12   Factors of 15
Which numbers go on the Prime numbers card?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2, 3 and 5 — each has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 4 and 6 do not.

html: Which numbers go on the Factors of 12 card?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 2, 3, 4 and 6 — each divides 12 exactly; 5 does not.

html: Which numbers go on the Factors of 15 card?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 3 and 5 — 15 = 3 × 5. 3 goes on all three cards; 2, 4 and 6 do not divide 15.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for all four given numbers placed completely correctly, or 1 mark for three of them placed completely correctly. The numbers may be in any order on a card.

name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
html: Amina’s bed is 190 cm in length and 91 cm in width. She is making a one-tenth scale model of the bed.
What is the length of Amina’s model?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 19 cm — one tenth of 190: the digits move one place to the right.

html: What is the width of Amina’s model?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 9.1 cm — one tenth of 91, so the 1 becomes a tenth.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for both answers correct: length 19 cm and width 9.1 cm.

html: Kirsty says, "When you double the size of an acute angle, you always get an obtuse angle." Explain why Kirsty is not correct.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: Give a COUNTER-EXAMPLE: an acute angle of 27° doubles to 54°, which is still acute, not obtuse — Any acute angle under 45° does it, and 45° itself doubles to a right angle, which is not obtuse either. "Sometimes it will be acute" earns nothing — the scheme wants a number or the reason, not the observation.

html: How many days are there in September, October and November altogether?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 91 days — September 30, October 31, November 30. Thirty days hath September, April, June and November; October is one of the long ones between them.

html: The International Space Station orbits the Earth at a height of 250 miles. What is the height of the International Space Station in kilometres? Use 8 kilometres equals 5 miles.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 400 km — 250 ÷ 5 = 50 lots of five miles, and each is 8 km, so 50 × 8 = 400. A kilometre is shorter than a mile, so the number has to get BIGGER, which is the check on which way round to divide.

html:
Potatoes cost £1.50 per kg and carrots cost £1.80 per kg. Jack buys 11⁄2 kg of potatoes and 1⁄2 kg of carrots. How much change does he get from £5?

Show your method
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: £1.85 — the potatoes are 1.50 + 0.75 = £2.25, the carrots are half of 1.80 = 90p, together £3.15, and 5.00 − 3.15 = £1.85. Both prices are PER KILOGRAM and neither amount is a whole kilogram.

html: x + 2y = 20. x and y are whole numbers less than 10. What could x and y be?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: x = 8 and y = 6 is one answer; the others are (6, 7), (4, 8) and (2, 9) — Any of the four earns the mark. x has to be even, because 20 and 2y both are, which cuts the search in half straight away.

html: Tick the fractions less than 5⁄8.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄2, 2⁄8 and 7⁄16 — 5⁄8 is 0.625, so compare each against that: 1⁄2 is 0.5, 2⁄8 is 0.25 and 7⁄16 is 0.4375, all smaller; 3⁄4 and 24⁄32 both cancel to 3⁄4, which is 0.75 and bigger. The two that are wrong are the two that look different and are the same.

html:
Layla makes jewellery to sell at a school fair. Each bracelet has 53 beads and she makes 68 bracelets. Each necklace has 105 beads and she makes 34 necklaces. How many beads does Layla use altogether?

Show your method
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 7,174 beads — 53 × 68 = 3,604 and 105 × 34 = 3,570, and 3,604 + 3,570 = 7,174. Three marks, and the scheme gives one for either long multiplication on its own, so writing both out is worth doing even if the addition goes wrong.

html:
Adam is making booklets. Each booklet must have 34 sheets of paper. He has 2 packets of paper. There are 500 sheets of paper in each packet. How many complete booklets can Adam make from 2 packets of paper?

Show your method
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 29 booklets — 2 × 500 = 1,000 sheets, and 1,000 ÷ 34 = 29 remainder 14. The word is COMPLETE, so the remainder is thrown away and 30 is wrong — there is not enough paper for a thirtieth. Dividing 500 first and doubling loses the remainder and can give 28.

ABDE is a rectangle on coordinate axes. The sides of the rectangle are parallel to the axes.

Point C is the centre of the rectangle.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
examiner_note: Drawn not to scale, as the paper’s is: the coordinates are to be worked out, not measured.

html: What are the coordinates of B?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: (55, 30) — C is halfway along the rectangle, so it is 40 − 25 = 15 to the right of A, and B is another 15 beyond C, at 55. B is on the same top edge as A, so its y-coordinate is still 30. Write it with x first: (30, 55) is a different point.

html: What are the coordinates of D?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: (55, 14) — D is the corner diagonally opposite A, so C is halfway between them in BOTH directions: across, 55 as in part (a); down, 22 is 8 below 30, so D is 8 below that again, at 14. The scheme gives one mark for the right y-coordinates even if B and D share the same wrong x.

html:
Six identical right-angled triangles are arranged to make a rectangle.

Calculate the length of the rectangle.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: 10.5 cm — the six triangles are identical, so match their sides. On the right, two triangles sit either side of a diagonal and each runs the full 7 cm height. On the left, four triangles are stacked two high, so each has a side of half of 7, which is 3.5 cm — and since every triangle is the same, a triangle’s two short sides are 3.5 cm and 7 cm. The left part is therefore 7 cm wide and the right part 3.5 cm wide: 7 + 3.5 = 10.5 cm. The scheme also accepts 10½.

html: The distance from point P to point R is 800 metres. The distance from point P to point Q is 4 times the distance from point Q to point R. Olivia says, "It is 600 metres from point P to point Q." Explain why Olivia is not correct.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2019
subject: Maths
answer: If PQ were 600 m then QR would be 800 − 600 = 200 m, and 600 is only THREE times 200, not four — The real split is five equal parts: 800 ÷ 5 = 160 m for QR and 4 × 160 = 640 m for PQ. Either sentence earns the mark; "Olivia is wrong" on its own does not.

answer: cuboid — a box whose faces are rectangles, not all squares.

name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: 6 — six square faces.

html: How many edges does a cube have?
name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: 12 — an edge is a LINE where two squares meet; counting the corners instead is the commonest slip.

html: How many vertices does a cube have?
name: 3D Shapes

html: Here is a triangular prism.

name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: 5 — two triangles at the ends and three rectangles round the middle.

name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: 9 — three edges on each triangle and three joining them.

html: How many vertices does a triangular prism have?
name: 3D Shapes

answer: 6 — three corners at each end.

How many faces does a pentagonal prism have?
name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: 7 faces — two pentagons at the ends and one rectangle for each of the pentagon's five sides, so 2 + 5. Every prism works that way: two ends plus one face per side.

html:
Here are some 3-D shapes

Tick each shape that has more vertices than faces
name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: Triangular prism (6 vertices, 5 faces) and cuboid (8 vertices, 6 faces) — the two that are NOT ticked are both pyramids, and a pyramid always has the same number of each: a square-based pyramid has 5 and 5, a pentagonal pyramid 6 and 6, because every face round the side meets one corner of the base.
choices: Square-based pyramid | Triangular prism | Cuboid | Pentagonal pyramid

html:
Chloe has drawn a 3-D shape.

Her shape has 5 vertices.

It has 8 edges.

It has 5 faces.

What 3-D shape has Chloe drawn?
name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: A square-based pyramid — the square base has 4 corners and the apex is the fifth; four edges round the base and four up to the point make 8; and the base plus four triangles make 5 faces. The check is Euler's: 5 − 8 + 5 = 2, which every solid of this kind satisfies.
accept: square-based pyramid | square based pyramid | square pyramid | a square-based pyramid

html:
Edward has drawn a 3-D shape.

His shape has 6 vertices.

It has 9 edges.

It has 5 faces.

What 3-D shape has Edward drawn?
name: 3D Shapes
subject: Maths
answer: A triangular prism — the same 5 faces as Chloe's shape but one more vertex and one more edge, which is exactly question 3 read backwards. 6 − 9 + 5 = 2 again.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Which blood vessels are affected by coronary heart disease?

Tick one box.
answer: Arteries

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A person’s heart stops beating.

The person stops breathing.

A first-aider pushes down on the person’s chest.

Pushing down on the person’s chest puts pressure on the heart.

Explain why putting pressure on the heart helps the person.
answer: It pushes or moves blood, which gets oxygen around the body — A description of getting oxygen around the body, or to a named organ, is accepted; 'to the lungs' is not, and references to restarting the heart or to the pacemaker are ignored.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The first-aider also forces air into the person’s lungs by blowing into their mouth.

Describe how forcing air into the person’s lungs helps the person.
answer: It provides oxygen for respiration. (The idea of carbon dioxide triggering breathing to restart is also allowed.)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The person’s heart starts to beat again and the person starts breathing. The person has a high level of cholesterol in their blood.

Name one type of drug that would decrease the level of cholesterol in the person’s blood.
answer: Statins (a named statin is accepted)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A doctor decides that the person needs to have a stent fitted.

Explain how a stent works to treat coronary heart disease.
answer: It opens or widens the blocked blood vessel, or keeps it open, so more blood, glucose and oxygen reach the heart muscle — The stent opens or widens the blocked blood vessel — or keeps it open — so that more blood can flow, or more glucose and oxygen reach the heart muscle. The type of blood vessel is ignored, and so is 'unblocks'.

Give two conclusions that can be made from the data in Table 1.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The pancreas produces several digestive enzymes. CF reduces the amount of each enzyme that reaches the small intestine.

Explain why a person with CF has:

  • difficulty digesting food
  • difficulty gaining body mass.
answer: Fewer enzymes, so less food digested into small molecules, so less absorbed to build body mass — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs both halves. Digesting food: less or no lipase, so less fat broken down into fatty acids and glycerol; less or no carbohydrase or amylase, so less starch broken down into glucose; less or no protease, so less protein broken down into amino acids. Gaining body mass: less absorption of those small soluble molecules, so fewer amino acids available for building protein, muscle, cells and tissues; less fat stored; less respiration, so less energy for building new molecules and cells.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli in the lungs.

Describe three features of the alveoli that help maximise gas exchange.
answer: A large surface area (or surface area to volume ratio); a large capillary network; thin walls, one cell thick — a good, efficient blood supply; walls that are thin, one cell thick. References to the alveoli being moist, and to a steep concentration gradient, are ignored, and 'thin cell walls' is not accepted.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
CF reduces the amount of oxygen that can enter the blood from the alveoli.

Explain how a reduced amount of oxygen entering the blood will affect the human body.
answer: There is less aerobic respiration, so less energy is released, which results in less muscle contraction — or a reduced metabolism, or an increased breathing rate or depth, or an increased heart rate. The alternative route also scores three: more anaerobic respiration, so lactic acid is produced, causing muscle fatigue or any of the same consequences. 'Less energy produced or made' is not accepted.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Cake and bread each contain the same two types of carbohydrate.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Describe the chemical tests that could be used to show the presence of the two types of carbohydrate in cake.

Include a risk assessment in your answer.
answer: Iodine turns blue-black (starch); Benedict’s, heated in a water bath, turns brick red (sugar); wear eye protection — Level-marked out of 6, and Level 3 needs both reagents with their correct positive results and a risk assessment. Iodine solution tests for starch and changes from yellow-orange-brown to blue-black. Benedict's reagent tests for sugar: heat the cake with it to at least 60 °C, and it changes from blue to green, yellow, orange, brown or brick red. Risks: burns from the flame, hot glass or boiling water — use a water bath and let equipment cool; Benedict's spitting into the face — wear eye protection and point the tube away; Benedict's and iodine as irritants — clean spills at once, wear gloves or eye protection, use a dropper bottle.

A student investigated three types of bread.

For each type of bread, the student:

  • put a square piece of bread into their mouth
  • did not chew the bread
  • recorded the time taken for the bread to taste sweet.

Table 2 shows the results.

Type of breadTime taken for bread to taste sweet in seconds

What was the dependent variable in the investigation?
answer: The time taken for the bread to taste or become sweet ('time' on its own is ignored)

Type of breadTime taken for bread to taste sweet in seconds
Brown43

Give one control variable the student should have used in the investigation.

Xylem tissue transports water through a plant. The walls of xylem cells contain cellulose.

Name one other substance that strengthens xylem tissue.

Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars around a plant.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024

The phloem tissue transports sugars to other parts of the plant. The concentration of dissolved sugars in the phloem cell in Figure 3 is higher than in cell X.

Explain how sub-cellular structures help to move dissolved sugars from cell X into the phloem cell.
answer: Mitochondria respire to release energy for active transport against the gradient — Cell X contains mitochondria; they carry out aerobic respiration; which releases energy; the energy is needed to move the dissolved sugars against the concentration gradient — from a low concentration to a high one; by active transport. Anaerobic respiration is not accepted, nor is energy being 'produced' or 'made'.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024

New phloem cells form when unspecialised plant cells differentiate and become specialised.

answer: Any one: loses its nucleus, cytoplasm or organelles, or its end walls become sieve plates — Any one of: loss of cytoplasm; loss of the nucleus; loss of mitochondria; loss of ribosomes; loss of sub-cellular structures; the end walls become perforated (sieve plates form). A larger vacuole forming is also allowed; a change in size or shape is ignored.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Plan a method that could be used to obtain the results in Figure 4.
answer: Weigh pieces, soak in three or more salt concentrations, blot, reweigh, repeat, find mean change — Level-marked out of 6. Measure and record the mass of the potato pieces; place them into at least three different concentrations of salt solution; leave them; remove and blot them dry; measure the mass again and calculate the change; repeat each concentration twice more and calculate a mean change in mass. Control variables: the same size or mass of piece, the same potato or type of potato, the same blotting technique, no skin on the pieces, the same time (at least 10 minutes) and the same temperature. For Level 3 the method must be able to produce the graph in Figure 4.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain the result for the potato pieces in the 0.6 mol/dm3 salt concentration.
answer: Water left the cells by osmosis, because the solution inside them is more dilute than the salt solution outside — more dilute — than the solution outside; and the water left by osmosis. Correct references to water concentration or water potential are allowed; 'water moves from a high solute concentration to a low one' is not.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain why the result for the potato pieces at 1.0 mol/dm3 was different from the result at 0.6 mol/dm3.
answer: They lost more mass: more water left by osmosis, as the concentration gradient is steeper at 1.0 mol/dm³ — The pieces at 1.0 mol/dm³ lost more mass because more water left them — more osmosis occurred out of the potato; because the concentration gradient between the inside and the outside of the cells is steeper at 1.0 mol/dm³.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
This question is about pathogens.

A scientist investigated antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Name one antibiotic.
answer: Penicillin, or any other named antibiotic — ('penicillium' is ignored — that is the mould)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The scientist grew one type of bacterium on agar in a Petri dish.

The scientist placed paper discs each containing a different antibiotic on the agar.

Figure 5 shows the appearance of the Petri dish after 2 days.

A student said:

‘The bacterium is resistant to antibiotic C.’

Explain how the results in Figure 5 show that the student is not correct.
answer: A zone of inhibition surrounds disc C, so C kills the bacterium; resistant bacteria would grow right up to the disc — there is a zone of inhibition around it; if the bacterium were resistant the bacteria would grow right up to the edge of the disc, and there would be no zone of inhibition.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Suggest why doctors are concerned about antibiotic resistance.
answer: Some bacteria can no longer be killed, so diseases become hard or impossible to treat — Any two of: the antibiotics currently available do not kill (have no effect on) certain bacteria; diseases become more common, or there will be diseases that cannot be cured or treated, or become harder to treat; new antibiotics have to be developed, which takes time and money.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Diseases caused by viruses cannot be treated using antibiotics.

Suggest why viruses cannot be grown on agar.
answer: Viruses only exist and reproduce inside living cells — and agar is not made of cells.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Why is it difficult for scientists to develop drugs to destroy viruses?
answer: The drugs damage the body's own cells and tissues, or it is hard to get the drugs inside living cells — That viruses mutate frequently, giving resistance, is also allowed.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which disease is caused by a virus that damages white blood cells? Tick one box.
answer: AIDS

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: A student investigated the effect of different factors on photosynthesis.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The student used three leaves growing on the same plant.

Each leaf was treated in a different way.

After 48 hours the student tested each leaf for starch.

Table 3 shows the results.

Leaf testedTreatmentResult after 48 hours
1Upper and lower surfaces covered with black paperNo starch present
2Upper and lower surfaces covered and sealed with transparent plasticNo starch present
3Not coveredStarch present

Explain the results for the three leaves.
answer: Leaves 1 (no light) and 2 (no CO<sub>2</sub>) cannot photosynthesise, so make no glucose for starch; leaf 3 can — Leaf 1, covered with black paper: no light, so no photosynthesis. Leaf 2, sealed in transparent plastic: no carbon dioxide, so no photosynthesis. Leaf 3, not covered: light and carbon dioxide are both present, so the leaf can photosynthesise. For leaves 1 and 2: glucose is not made, and so glucose cannot be converted to starch. (If neither of those last two is earned, 'the starch already present has been broken down' scores one.)

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In another investigation the student used a different type of plant, left uncovered in the light for 48 hours. Figure 6 shows the leaf before it was tested for starch: it is variegated, with green areas and white areas.

Complete Table 4 to show the results you would expect for the starch test on the leaf in Figure 6.

What is the result for the green part of the leaf?
answer: Starch present — the iodine turns blue-black: the green part has chlorophyll, so it photosynthesised and stored the glucose as starch.
examiner_note: Figure 6 is artwork in the PDF; that the leaf is variegated is stated in the question, and the pattern of the green and white areas is not otherwise described.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: What is the result for the white part of the leaf?
answer: No starch present — the iodine stays orange-brown: the white part has no chlorophyll, so it could not photosynthesise.
examiner_note: The paper gives 1 mark for the two rows together, so it sits on this last row: both rows right for the mark.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain the results you gave in Question 07.2.
answer: Only the green part has chlorophyll, so only it photosynthesises and makes starch — The green part contains chlorophyll and the white part does not; so light is absorbed by the green part but not by the white, photosynthesis occurs there, and starch can be formed.
examiner_note: Figure 6 is artwork in the PDF; see 07.2.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In some leaves, the green parts become yellow because of an ion deficiency.

Which ion is deficient in a plant with yellow leaves?
answer: Magnesium (Mg or Mg²⁺). Nitrate and iron are also allowed.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Give the scientific term that describes the yellow colour of the leaves.
answer: Chlorosis

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The rate of photosynthesis is affected by different factors.

How could the oxygen produced during photosynthesis be used to measure the rate of photosynthesis?
answer: Measure the volume of oxygen, or count the bubbles, released in a given time — Measure the volume of oxygen released in a given time, or count the number of bubbles released in a given time. 'Measure the amount released in a given time' is ignored — it does not say how.

subject: Biology
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Light, carbon dioxide and temperature are limiting factors of photosynthesis.

Figure 7 shows how the rate of photosynthesis is affected by light, carbon dioxide and temperature.

At point A on Figure 7, light is a limiting factor.

What is meant by a ‘limiting factor’?
answer: A factor that, if increased, would increase the rate of the reaction — or a factor that prevents the rate increasing, or prevents the maximum rate being reached.
