subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The Earth’s natural resources are used to manufacture useful products.

One useful product is potable water.

Potable water can be produced from sea water by distillation.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Give one disadvantage of using distillation to produce potable water.
answer: Large amounts of energy are required. References to time and to cost are ignored.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html: Describe one other method to produce potable water from sea water.
answer: Reverse osmosis; using membranes. 'Desalination' on its own is ignored.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
A student investigated the mass of dissolved solids in a 100 cm3 sample of sea water. This is the method used.

  1. Weigh an evaporating basin.
  2. Measure 100 cm3 of sea water.
  3. Pour the sea water into the evaporating basin.
  4. Heat the evaporating basin.
  5. Weigh the evaporating basin and contents.
  6. Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in the sea water.

Explain how repeating steps 4 and 5 would improve this method.
answer: Heat until the mass is constant; to ensure that all the water has evaporated.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
The total mass of dissolved solids in a 100 cm3 sample of sea water is 3.50 g.

The percentage of sodium chloride in the dissolved solids is 77.8%.

Calculate the mass of sodium chloride dissolved in the 100 cm3 sample of sea water.
answer: 2.72 g — mass = (77.8 ÷ 100) × 3.50 = 2.723 g, and 2.723 g is also accepted.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Biological methods are used to extract metal compounds from metal ores.

One method of producing copper from low-grade copper ores is by using bacteria. The bacteria produce leachate solutions that contain copper compounds.

Give two methods that can be used to extract copper from these leachate solutions.
answer: Displacement using scrap iron; and electrolysis.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds from low-grade ores.

Describe how the metal compounds are obtained from the plants.
answer: Three marks, one each: the plants are harvested; and burned; to produce ash that contains the metal compounds.

subject: Combined Science
name: Chemistry Paper 2 — June 2024
html:
Nickel is produced by phytomining.

One hectare of plants produces 215 kg of nickel.

Determine the area required to produce 750 kg of nickel.

Give your answer in m2.

One hectare = 10 000 m2
answer: 34 900 m2 (3.49 × 104 m2 is accepted). Area = 750 ÷ 215 = 3.49 hectares — 3.488372093 correctly rounded to at least 2 significant figures is allowed — then 3.49 × 10 000 = 34 900 m². The scheme's alternative route scores the same: 215 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0215 kg/m², then 750 ÷ 0.0215 = 34 900 m².

subject: Maths

subject: Maths
answer: 7 — 7 appears four times, more than any other number.

subject: Maths
answer: 11 — 12 − 1.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 June
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — in order 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 12, the 6th of the 11 is 7.

html:
Figure: a triangle standing on a line that is extended past its bottom-right corner. The bottom-left angle is 75° and the top angle is 45°. The angle x is the exterior angle at the bottom right, between the extended line and the triangle's right side.

Find x
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 June
subject: Maths
answer: x = 120° — the third angle is 180 − 75 − 45 = 60°, and x = 180 − 60 (an exterior angle is the sum of the two opposite interior angles, 75 + 45).

html:
Figure: the side of a house, a pentagon: a rectangle 15m wide with a triangular roof on top. The whole height from the ground to the top of the roof is 10m, and the roof is 4m high.

William is painting the side of his house.
He has 8 litres of paint and each litre of paint covers 16m²
Does William have enough paint?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 June
subject: Maths
answer: Yes: the side is 90 + 30 = 120 m² and 8 litres cover 8 × 16 = 128 m² — the wall is 15 × 6 = 90 m² and the roof triangle is ½ × 15 × 4 = 30 m², 120 m² in all; 8 × 16 = 128 m² of paint is enough.

Write down an expression, in terms of s and t, for the number of seats on the airplane.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 2 July
subject: Maths
answer: 24s + 9t — 24 economy rows of s seats and 9 first-class rows of t seats.

A lorry travels 100 miles at an average speed of 25 mph.

Work out how long the journey lasts.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 July
subject: Maths
answer: 4 hours — time = distance ÷ speed = 100 ÷ 25.

html:
Olivia is measuring an obtuse angle in her maths exam.

What angle should Olivia have put on her exam?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 July
subject: Maths
answer: 148° — the two scales on a protractor add to 180°, and the angle is obtuse, so 180 − 32.

A jar contains 240g of sugar.
How many grams of strawberries are in the jar?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 July
subject: Maths
answer: 400g — 3 parts = 240g so one part is 80g, and strawberries are 5 × 80.

subject: Maths

answer: 640g — the jam is all 8 parts, 8 × 80 (or 240 + 400).

subject: Maths
answer: 20 cm² — ½(a + b)h = ½ × (3 + 7) × 4.

subject: Maths
answer: Multiply the previous number by 2 — 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24.

html:
A design is made from some identical rectangles and identical squares.
Each rectangle is twice as long as each square.
The perimeter of each square is 28cm.

Figure: five shapes joined edge to edge in one row: square, rectangle, square, rectangle, square. The rectangles lie along the row, so the whole design is one row of the same height.

Calculate the perimeter of the design.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 6 July
subject: Maths
answer: 112 cm — a square is 7cm a side, so a rectangle is 14cm by 7cm; the design is 3×7 + 2×14 = 49cm long and 7cm tall, and 2 × (49 + 7) = 112.

answer: 19:52 — the real time is 2 minutes earlier than Connor's, 20:01, and Grace's is 9 minutes behind that.

html: Find the probability of a score of 12
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 8 July
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄9 — 12 appears 4 times in the 36 cells (2×6, 3×4, 4×3, 6×2), and 4⁄36 = 1⁄9.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 8 July
subject: Maths
html: Find the probability of a score of 10 or more
answer: 19⁄36 — 19 of the 36 cells are 10 or more (2 in row 2, 3 in row 3, 4 in row 4, 5 in row 5, 5 in row 6).

html:
Figure: an arrowhead (a concave quadrilateral). Its top angle is 77°, its bottom right angle is 40°, the reflex angle at the dent in the bottom edge is 212°, and the bottom left angle is x.

Find the size of angle x
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 9 July
subject: Maths
answer: 31° — the four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°: 360 − 77 − 40 − 212.

html:
Reggie drives for 2 hours 30 minutes at an average speed of 36 mph.

How far does Reggie drive?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 9 July
subject: Maths
answer: 90 miles — 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, and 2.5 × 36 = 90.

html: Expand   5(x − 2)
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 9 July
subject: Maths
answer: 5x − 10 — multiply each term in the bracket by 5.

html:
Figure: a coordinate grid from −6 to 6 across and −5 to 5 up. Rectangle B has corners (3, 2) and (6, 3); rectangle A has corners (−2, −2) and (1, −1).

Write down the translation vector that would take B to A.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 9 July
subject: Maths
answer: (−5 over −4), written as a column vector — B's bottom-left corner (3, 2) moves to A's (−2, −2): 5 left and 4 down.

html:
Figure: an L-shaped chicken enclosure. The top side is 12m, the right side goes down 5m, then the edge goes 8m in to the left, then 6m down; the left side runs the full height.

Tim wants to build a new fence around the chicken enclosure.
Each metre of fencing will cost £7.99

Work out the cost of the new fence.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 9 July
subject: Maths
answer: £367.54 — the left side is 5 + 6 = 11m and the bottom is 12 − 8 = 4m, so the perimeter is 12 + 5 + 8 + 6 + 4 + 11 = 46m, and 46 × £7.99 = £367.54.

html: “My number is 200 to the nearest 10, but is not 200. What could my number be?”
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 July
subject: Maths
answer: Any number from 195 up to (but not including) 205, other than 200 — e.g. 195, 197, 201 or 204.

y751

html: Share £420 in the ratio 2:3

subject: Maths

html: How much is the smaller share (the 2 parts)?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 July
subject: Maths
answer: £168 — 2 + 3 = 5 parts, £420 ÷ 5 = £84 a part, and 2 × £84 = £168.

html: How much is the larger share (the 3 parts)?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 July
subject: Maths
answer: £252 — £420 ÷ 5 = £84 a part, and 3 × £84 = £252.

html:
The mean of four numbers is 5.

Three of the numbers are 2, 3 and 8.

Work out the fourth number.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 10 July
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — the four numbers total 4 × 5 = 20, and 2 + 3 + 8 = 13.

html:
Shown is a parallelogram

Figure: a parallelogram leaning to the right, with arrows marking the two pairs of parallel sides. The acute angle at the top left is 38°; x is the angle at the bottom right, y the angle at the bottom left and z the angle at the top right.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths

html: Find x
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: x = 38° — opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and x is opposite the 38° angle.

html: Find y
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: y = 142° — neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add to 180°: 180 − 38 = 142.

html: Find z
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: z = 142° — z is next to the 38° angle too (and opposite y): 180 − 38 = 142.

html: Solve   2w + 5 = 37
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: w = 16 — take 5 to get 2w = 32, then halve.

What type of correlation is shown?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: Negative correlation — as the age goes up, the value goes down.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: £132 — 6 + 1 + 8 = 15 parts, £330 ÷ 15 = £22 a part, and John has 6 parts: 6 × £22.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: £22 — £330 ÷ 15 = £22 a part, and Filip has 1 part.

html: How much does Cleo get?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 July
subject: Maths
answer: £176 — £330 ÷ 15 = £22 a part, and Cleo has 8 parts: 8 × £22.

html: Explain why 8028 is not a term in this sequence.
answer: 8028 is even, and every term is odd — an odd number times 3 is always odd, so no term can be even (the terms also jump from 6561 straight to 19683).

html:
A taxi journey costs £3 for 5 miles.

How much is the cost for a 90 mile journey?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 12 July
subject: Maths
answer: £54 — 90 miles is 18 lots of 5 miles, and 18 × £3 = £54.

html:
Make w the subject of the formula

y = 7w + a
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 12 July
subject: Maths
answer: w = (y − a) ÷ 7 — subtract a from both sides, then divide by 7.

html:
The ratio of green to blue counters in a bag is 3:5.

There are 9 green counters.

How many counters are in the bag?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 12 July
subject: Maths
answer: 24 — 3 parts are 9 counters, so a part is 3; the bag holds 8 parts, 8 × 3.

answer: 30 — 50% is a half, and half of 60 is 30.

answer: 40 — 25% is a quarter, so the number is 4 × 10.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 July

answer: 12⁄35 — multiply the tops and the bottoms.

subject: Maths

answer: 7⁄10 — flip the second fraction and multiply: 3⁄5 × 7⁄6 = 21⁄30 = 7⁄10.

html:
A red light flashes every 3 seconds.
A yellow light flashes every 4 seconds.
A green light flashes every 5 seconds
They all flash at the same time.

After how many seconds will they next all flash at the same time?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 July
subject: Maths
answer: 60 seconds — the lowest common multiple of 3, 4 and 5 is 3 × 4 × 5 = 60.

html: What number is on the 2nd card?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 September
subject: Maths
answer: 5 — the cards total 5 × 7 = 35, so the 2nd and 4th add to 35 − 5 − 8 − 9 = 13; the 2nd is at least 5 and the 4th at most 9, so they are 5 and 8.

html: What number is on the 3rd card?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 September
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — the median of five cards in order is the middle (3rd) card.

html: What number is on the 4th card?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 11 September

Figure: a number line with equally spaced marks. One mark is labelled 9 and the mark two places to its right is labelled 12. An arrow points to the mark five places to the right of the 12.

What number is the arrow pointing to?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 2 October
subject: Maths
answer: 19.5 — two gaps span 3, so each gap is 1.5, and 12 + 5 × 1.5 = 19.5.
examiner_note: The number line was read off the rendered page.

html:
The small bottle holds 250ml. The large bottle holds 2L.

How many times larger is the large bottle?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 3 October
subject: Maths
answer: 8 times — 2L = 2000ml, and 2000 ÷ 250 = 8.

html:
The perimeter of a square grass field is 60m. In the field, there is a triangular pond.

Figure: the triangular pond has a base of 5m and a perpendicular height of 7m.

Find the area of the field that is grass.
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 3 October
subject: Maths
answer: 207.5 m² — each side is 60 ÷ 4 = 15m, so the field is 225 m²; the pond is ½ × 5 × 7 = 17.5 m²; 225 − 17.5 = 207.5.

Small pack: 4 batteries for £1.80
Large pack: 6 batteries for £2.76

Which is better value for money?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 October
subject: Maths
answer: the small pack — £1.80 ÷ 4 = 45p a battery, against £2.76 ÷ 6 = 46p a battery in the large pack.

html:
Complete the table of values for y = 2x − 3

x−10123
y(i)−3−1(ii)(iii)

What is y when x = −1?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 October
subject: Maths
answer: −5 — 2 × (−1) − 3 = −2 − 3 = −5.

html: What is y when x = 2?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 October
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — 2 × 2 − 3 = 4 − 3 = 1.

html: What is y when x = 3?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 4 October
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — 2 × 3 − 3 = 6 − 3 = 3; the y values go up by 2 each time.

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 27 November
subject: Maths

name: 5-a-day Foundation — 27 November
subject: Maths

subject: Maths
answer: 35⁄50 = 7⁄10 — 50 − 15 = 35 of the sweets are red.

subject: Maths

What fraction of the sweets are red?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 29 November
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄7 — there are 2 + 5 = 7 parts and 2 of them are red.

html:
Natalie, Olivia and Hugo share 240 sweets in the ratio 3:5:4

How many more sweets does Olivia have than Hugo?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 29 November
subject: Maths
answer: 20 — 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 parts, so one part is 20; Olivia has one more part than Hugo.

subject: Maths
answer: 82⁄11 — 11 goes into 90 eight times (88) with 2 left over.

subject: Maths

subject: Maths

A bus leaves Derby Bus Station every 10 minutes. A train leaves Derby Train Station every 16 minutes.

At 9am a bus and a train leave the stations at the same time.

When is the next time that a bus and train leave at the same time?
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 1 December
subject: Maths
answer: 10:20am — the LCM of 10 and 16 is 80 minutes, and 80 minutes after 9am is 10:20am.

subject: Maths

Here are the nth terms of 4 sequences.

Sequence 1: 3n + 1

subject: Maths

html: Sequence 1:  3n + 1
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 December
subject: Maths
answer: S, sometimes — 3n + 1 gives 4, 7, 10, 13, …: 10 is a multiple of 5, 4 is not.

html: Sequence 2:  5n + 10
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 December
subject: Maths
answer: A, always — 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2), always a multiple of 5.

html: Sequence 3:  10n
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 December
subject: Maths
answer: A, always — 10n = 5 × 2n, always a multiple of 5.

html: Sequence 4:  5n − 1
name: 5-a-day Foundation — 13 December
subject: Maths
answer: N, never — 5n − 1 is always one less than a multiple of 5.

A pencil is weighted with a thin coil of wire. The volume of the wire is negligible. Figure 14 shows the pencil and wire floating upright in equilibrium in water, with a length l of the pencil below the surface. Figure 15 shows it pushed down a further distance y, with an upward force F acting on it.

In Figure 14 the combined weight of the pencil and wire is equal to an upwards force called the buoyancy force. The length of the pencil that is submerged is l. A student pushes the pencil down through a displacement y as shown in Figure 15. The buoyancy force is now greater than the weight.

There is a resultant upward force F acting on the pencil when the student releases it. The magnitude of F for any value of y is given by

html: State and explain which interaction is involved in this decay.
answer: The weak interaction (1); because strangeness changes in this decay — from −1 to 0 — and strangeness can only change in a weak interaction (1). "Strangeness is not conserved (in this decay)" is accepted and "strangeness is lost" condoned. Negative arguments ("strangeness is conserved in a strong interaction") and the idea that strangeness ALWAYS changes in a weak interaction are rejected; a general statement about strangeness in the weak interaction on its own is not enough.

subject: Physics

Peer review is neutral (it argues for independent teams); "avoids bias" and "reproducibility" are not accepted.

Determine the kinetic energy of the car at its maximum acceleration.

kinetic energy = ______ J
answer: 6.6 × 10⁸ J — Speed read from the graph at 5600 m: 450 m s⁻¹ (445 to 455 accepted) (1); then ½mv² with their speed giving a consistent answer — ½ × 6.50 × 10³ × 450² = 6.6 × 10⁸ J (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
At any point on the graph in Figure 1, the acceleration is given by:

acceleration = speed × gradient of line

When the car is at its maximum acceleration, the power input to the jet engines is 640 MW.

Calculate the percentage of the input power used to accelerate the car at its maximum acceleration.

percentage of input power = ______ %
answer: Between 16% and 17%. MAX three marks from: using the graph to find the gradient — <sup>450</sup>⁄<sub>5600</sub> = 0.080(4) s⁻¹; speed × gradient for the acceleration — 450 × 0.08 = 36(.2) m s⁻²; F = ma for the resultant force — 2.35 × 10⁵ N; P = Fv for the power — 450 × 2.35 × 10⁵ = 106 MW. Final answer between 16% and 17% for the fourth mark. Error carried forward from 02.2 is allowed; a power calculated assuming a constant speed is rejected.

subject: Physics

Deduce whether the average deceleration is less than 3g.
answer: Yes: from about 470 m s−1 to rest over 7000 to 7600 m, a = v2⁄2s ≈ 15 m s−2, less than 3g — Identifies the distance over which the car decelerates (7000 m to 7600 m allowed) AND the maximum speed, 470 ± 5 m s⁻¹ (1); uses suvat to get a deceleration of about 15 m s⁻² (an answer consistent with their distance that rounds to 15 or 16), which is less than 3g, so yes (1). Full credit for showing that 3g would stop the car in a much shorter distance, so the actual deceleration must be much less than 3g. For the second mark, gradient × average speed giving 15 m s⁻² is also allowed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
In Figure 2 the cell has emf ε and internal resistance r.

The current in the circuit is I.

The potential difference (pd) across R1 is V1 and the pd across R2 is V2.

Explain how the law of conservation of energy applies in this circuit. You should consider the movement of one coulomb of charge around the circuit.
answer: Each coulomb gains ε J in the cell and transfers it all in R1, R2 and r: ε = IR1 + IR2 + Ir — One of: 1 C of charge gains ε J passing through the cell; OR the energy transferred by 1 C in R₁ is V₁ J; OR in R₂ is V₂ J; OR in r is Ir J (1). For conservation of energy, ε = IR₁ + IR₂ + Ir (1) — or ε = V₁ + V₂ + Ir provided the first mark is awarded. "Dissipated" and "work done" are accepted; "lost volts" is accepted for Ir but "voltage across r" is rejected. If nothing else scores, one mark for a definition of emf in terms of energy transfer.

html:
Figure 3 shows a variable resistor made with a thin conducting layer on an insulating base.

The conducting layer has constant width and thickness and has connections at the ends A and B.

C is a sliding contact that can move along the surface of the conducting layer between A and B.

Figure 4 shows a circuit that uses the variable resistor as a potential divider.

The variable resistor is connected to a battery of emf 3.00 V and internal resistance r.

The resistance of the conducting layer between A and B is 125 Ω.

The sliding contact C is moved to end B of the variable resistor. The switch is closed.

The digital voltmeter reads 2.89 V.

Show that r is approximately 4.8 Ω.
answer: Equates the emf to Ir + 2.89 in some form (1); calculates I = 2.89 ÷ 125 = 0.02312 A (1); giving r = 4.76 Ω — at least 3 sf must be seen and it must round to 4.76 (1). Alternatives: lost volts = 0.11 V (1) and the potential-divider equation 0.11 ÷ 2.89 = r ÷ 125, or 3 ÷ (125 + r) = 2.89 ÷ 125 (1). If nothing else scores, one mark for using the emf value.

html:
Figure 5 shows a variable resistor similar to the one shown in Figure 3 but with the following three manufacturing faults:

  • at P the conducting layer changes in thickness so that AP is thinner than PB
  • at Q there is a scratch into the surface of the conducting layer and across its full width
  • from R to B the conducting connector is laid over the conducting layer.

The width of the conducting layer is constant.

A pd of 3.0 V is applied across A and B.

C is moved from A to B.

Sketch, on the axes in Figure 6, a graph to show how the pd between A and C varies as C is moved from A to B.
answer: 0 V at A rising to P, shallower to Q, a step at Q, shallow to R, then flat at 3.0 V to B — Any four of: a straight line from 0 V at A to P; a less steep, non-zero gradient from P to Q; a short steep increase at Q (no wider than the Q label on the axis); Q to R at about the same non-zero gradient as P to Q; a horizontal line from R to B at 3.0 V. A graph sketched from 3 V at A down to 0 V at B scores max 2 (the P–Q and Q–R marks); a single diagonal straight line from 0 V at A to B scores 1 only; a straight line from 0 V at A to R then horizontal to B scores max 2.

name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Show that the glass used to make the prism has a refractive index of about 1.5
answer: Uses sin c = 1/n, so n = 1/sin 41.5° = 1.51. Relevant working must be seen, with at least 3 sf.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Explain why the ray emerges parallel to the incident ray.
answer: It reflects totally at 45° twice, then leaves along the normal — Each angle of incidence at the second and third surfaces is 45°, which is greater than the critical angle, so total internal reflection occurs (1); the angle of incidence as the ray leaves the block is 0° — it leaves along the normal (so it emerges parallel to the incident ray) (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
Figure 8 shows a ray of light entering the prism at an angle of incidence θ and reflecting off one of the shorter sides.

θ is the largest angle of incidence for which all of the light leaves through the longest side.

Draw on Figure 8 the path of the ray of light as it continues inside the prism and emerges from the longest side.
answer: Totally internally reflected at the second boundary, leaving parallel to the incident ray — Only a (totally internally) reflected ray at the second reflecting boundary (1); the reflected ray parallel to the first refracted ray, by eye (1); the ray leaving parallel to the initial ray, by eye (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
When the angle of incidence is greater than θ, some of the light escapes the prism through one of the shorter sides.

Assume that the refractive index is 1.5 and the critical angle is 41.5°.

Show that θ is about 5°.

You can use Figure 8 in your answer.
answer: θ = 5.3° — Angle of incidence at the second reflecting boundary = 41.5° (1); angle of reflection at the first reflecting boundary = 90° − 41.5° = 48.5° (1); angle of refraction at entry = 90° − 45° − 41.5° = 3.5° (1); n = 1.5 and Snell’s law give θ = 5.3° to at least 2 sf (1). Writing 90° − 41.5° = 48.5° on its own does not get a mark; the angles can be identified from the working or the diagram.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A manufacturer wants to make a prism with a larger value of θ.

Two alternative changes to the original design of the prism are suggested:

  1. use a prism of the original glass in the shape of an equilateral triangle, as shown in Figure 9
  2. use a prism of the original shape made from glass with a smaller refractive index, as shown in Figure 10.

Discuss whether either of the two suggestions would work.
answer: Neither: the 60° prism lets light escape at the second face; a smaller n raises the critical angle, reducing θ — The 60° prism (Figure 9): light would not leave the prism at the original angle (1); light will escape at the second reflection — it is no longer totally internally reflected, the angle of incidence there now being less than the critical angle (1). A smaller n (Figure 10): a larger critical angle (1), which would reduce the value of θ (1). Suggesting that a design would work limits the marks for that design to max 1.

Determine, using Figure 11, the Young modulus of the metal.

Young modulus = ______ Pa
answer: 1.38 to 1.42 × 10¹¹ Pa (2 sf 1.4 × 10¹¹ Pa allowed), with evidence the graph is used — e.g. 105 × 10⁶ ÷ 7.5 × 10⁻⁴: a point on the line between 75 MPa and 125 MPa, a point on the extended straight line, or a triangle using more than half of the linear section.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Explain how the graph shows that this metal is brittle.
answer: There is very little extra strain beyond the linear section before it fractures — The idea that there is only a (very) small increase in strain beyond the linear section before fracture ("extension" or "(plastic) deformation" condoned for strain). Also accepted: no "necking" before fracture; fracture occurs very near the limit of proportionality; a particular value of strain, e.g. 9 × 10⁻⁴ to 12.7 × 10⁻⁴. The idea that there is NO increase in strain is rejected.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
Figure 12 shows a uniform rigid lighting beam AB suspended from a fixed horizontal support by two identical vertical steel wires, one at each end, 2.00 m apart. A lamp is attached to the midpoint of AB.

The unloaded length of each steel wire was 1.20 m before it was attached to AB. AB is horizontal.

mass of AB = 4.4 kg
mass of lamp = 16.0 kg
distance between wires = 2.00 m
diameter of each wire = 0.800 mm
Young modulus of steel = 2.10 × 1011 Pa

Calculate the extension of each wire.

extension = ______ m
answer: 1.1(4) × 10⁻³ m — Total load = (4.4 + 16.0) × 9.8(1) = 200(.1) N, halved to 100 N on each wire (1); uses ΔL = FL/(AE) with A = 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m² (1; a power-of-ten error condoned, and using d for the cross-sectional area condoned); ΔL = 1.1(4) × 10⁻³ m (1). Separate σ = F/A, E = σ/strain and strain = ΔL/L are fine.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
The right-hand steel wire is removed and replaced with an aluminium wire of diameter 1.60 mm. The unloaded length of the aluminium wire is the same as that of the original steel wire.

When the lamp is at the midpoint of AB, one of the wires extends more than the other so that AB is not horizontal. To make AB horizontal the lamp has to be moved to a distance x from A (the end with the steel wire). Figure 13 shows the new arrangement.

The beam, the lamp and the wires are as in 05.3: mass of AB = 4.4 kg, mass of lamp = 16.0 kg, wires 2.00 m apart, steel wire diameter 0.800 mm, Young modulus of steel = 2.10 × 1011 Pa.

The Young modulus of aluminium is 7.00 × 1010 Pa.

Deduce distance x.

x = ______ m
answer: x = 1.18 m — The extension (strain) in each wire is the same, so {FL/AE} for steel = {FL/AE} for aluminium, i.e. F/(d²E) is the same (1); substituting, Fs/(0.8² × 210) = Fa/(1.6² × 70), so Fa = 1.33 Fs (or Fs = 0.752 Fa) (1); 1.33 Fs + Fs = 200 N gives Fs = 86 N and Fa = 114 N (1); an attempt at a moment equation about A, B or another suitable point — expect 16.0g x = 228 − 4.4g (1); x = 1.18 m (1). An answer of 1.14 m comes from ignoring the weight of the beam and scores max 4.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Show that the pencil moves with simple harmonic motion.
answer: Shown: a = −(Aρg/m)y, proportional to y and opposite to it — Equates the resultant force to ma and shows that a is proportional to y, since A, ρ, m and g are all constant: F = ma = −Aρyg, so a = −(Aρg/m)y (1; missing minus signs condoned here); the minus sign included and explained — the (restoring) force/acceleration is directed towards the centre of oscillation, opposite to y (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
The time period T of the vertical oscillations is given by

T = 2π√(l/g)

The measured value of l in Figure 15 is 85 mm. The pencil is pushed down 5.0 mm and released.

Calculate the maximum acceleration of the pencil.

maximum acceleration = ______ m s−2
answer: 0.58 m s⁻² — T = 2π/ω so ω = √(g/l) = 10.74 rad s⁻¹ (1; or the period 0.58(5) s then ω from it); a_max = ω²y_max = (9.81 ÷ 0.085) × 0.005 = 0.58 m s⁻², from some correct working (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A ship floating in the sea can be modelled by the pencil floating in water. The ship can oscillate vertically. These oscillations are called heave oscillations.

Wave motion causes forced oscillations of the ship. Under certain conditions, heave resonance may then occur.

Explain what is meant by resonance.
answer: The driving frequency equals the natural frequency, so the amplitude is a maximum — The frequency of the forced vibrations equals the natural (resonant) frequency (1); the amplitude of the oscillations is at a maximum (1). A fully labelled graph of amplitude against driving frequency with the resonant frequency labelled and an amplitude peak is accepted. "Wave frequency" is condoned for driving frequency; references to phase are ignored.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A ship floating in the sea can be modelled by the pencil floating in water. The ship can oscillate vertically. These oscillations are called heave oscillations.

Wave motion causes forced oscillations of the ship. Under certain conditions, heave resonance may then occur.

Figure 16 shows a ship moving through continuous waves of wavelength 118 m and velocity 14.2 m s−1.

The ship is moving steadily at 8.0 m s−1 relative to the seabed in the same direction as the waves.

The natural frequency of heave oscillations of the ship is 0.13 Hz.

A crew member needs an emergency operation. The ship’s doctor is confident that she can do the operation if the ship remains fairly steady.

There are two options:

  • stop the ship’s motors and loosely anchor the ship to the seabed
  • continue to sail the ship at 8.0 m s−1 in the same direction.

Deduce which is the better option.

Support your answer with a calculation.
answer: Keep sailing: stopped, the forcing frequency is 14.2 ⁄ 118 = 0.12 Hz, near the natural 0.13 Hz; sailing, it is 0.05 Hz — Stopped, the wave frequency is v/λ = 14.2/118 = 0.12 Hz (1; a bald "0.12 Hz" is rejected); moving at 8.0 m s⁻¹ the forcing frequency is further from the resonant frequency — or calculated, (14.2 − 8.0)/118 = 0.05 Hz (1; an incorrect calculation adding the speeds is accepted with a comment that it is further from the resonant frequency); moving is the better option with a reason — stopped, the forcing frequency is very close to the natural frequency so the amplitude will be high, or moving, resonance does not occur (1). An answer that damping will probably keep the amplitude low enough is allowed for the third mark.
topics: Circular & Periodic Motion, Progressive & Stationary Waves

The diagram represents a quark change in which an electron antineutrino is produced. Particle E comes in to a vertex and leaves it as particle F; an exchange particle (a wavy line) runs from that vertex to a second vertex, from which particle G and the electron antineutrino νe go out.

What are E, F and G?

EFG

answer: C: 2.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> — 2.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

html:
Electrons with a certain kinetic energy pass through a powdered crystalline sample and are incident on a fluorescent screen.

The first sketch shows the diffraction pattern produced: a bright centre surrounded by concentric rings.

A change is made and this second pattern is produced: the same concentric rings, each with a larger radius.

Which change could produce the second pattern?
answer: A — decreasing the kinetic energy of the electrons.
choices: decreasing the kinetic energy of the electrons | replacing the electrons with protons with the same kinetic energy | using a crystalline sample with a wider spacing between its atoms | moving the screen closer to the crystalline sample

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A string with a length of 1.2 m vibrates at its second harmonic.

The diagram shows the displacement–time graph for a point on the string.

What are the wavelength and frequency of the wave on the string?

Wavelength / mFrequency / kHz
A0.60.17
B0.60.34
C1.20.17
D1.20.34
answer: C — wavelength 1.2 m, frequency 0.17 kHz.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A standing wave is created on a string.

Which statement about the two waves that create the standing wave is not correct?
answer: B — they have a constant phase relationship.
choices: They have the same frequency. | They have a constant phase relationship. | They travel in opposite directions. | They have the same speed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A double slit with a separation s is illuminated by light of wavelength λ.

Fringes with spacing w are produced on a screen placed a distance D from the slits.

The distance from the slits to the screen is changed to D⁄2.

Which combination of slit separation and wavelength produces a fringe spacing of 1.5w on the screen?

Slit separationWavelength
A0.22s0.66λ
B0.50s0.75λ
C0.60s1.20λ
D1.20s0.40λ
answer: A: 0.22s and 0.66λ — 0.22s and 0.66λ.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A single narrow slit is illuminated with monochromatic light and a diffraction pattern is produced.

The slit width is increased.

What happens to the width and brightness of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern?

Width of central maximumBrightness of central maximum
Aincreasesincreases
Bincreasesdecreases
Cdecreasesincreases
Ddecreasesdecreases
answer: C — the width decreases and the brightness increases.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A ball is kicked from point P on level ground. The ball initially travels at 45° to the horizontal.

The ball reaches its maximum height after a time of 2.0 s.

Air resistance can be ignored.

What is the displacement of the ball from P when at its maximum height?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
An object is moving in a straight line. A graph is plotted to show the variation of the momentum of the object with time.

Which quantities can be calculated from the gradient of the graph and the area under the graph?

Gradient of graphArea under graph
Apowermass × displacement
Bforcework done × time
Cpowerwork done × time
Dforcemass × displacement
answer: D — gradient: force; area: mass × displacement.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Which is a pair of vectors?
answer: C: displacement and momentum — displacement and momentum.
choices: weight and work | force and energy | displacement and momentum | acceleration and power

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html: Which statement about a superconducting metal is correct?
answer: B — a current in it causes no heating effect.
choices: Its resistivity is small but not zero. | A current in it causes no heating effect. | Its critical temperature is independent of the metal it is made from. | Keeping it cold makes it too expensive to use.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A heavy uniform trapdoor is hinged to the floor. It is held open by a rope as shown: the trapdoor leans up and away from a wall at about 45°, and the rope runs from its top edge back to the wall, sloping upwards. Four arrows A to D are drawn from the hinge: A points up and away from the trapdoor, towards the wall side; B points up to the right, steeper than the trapdoor; C points horizontally, away from the wall; D points away from the wall and slightly downwards.

Which arrow shows the direction of the reaction force of the hinge on the trapdoor?
answer: B.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A sphere of mass m falls with speed v.

The resistive force on the sphere is kv, where k is a constant.

What is the terminal speed of the sphere?
answer: A — mg/k.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A trolley moves down a slope with constant acceleration.

The mass of the trolley is doubled and the trolley moves down the same slope again.

Air resistance and friction are negligible.

Which is correct?
answer: C — the acceleration is unchanged.
choices: The accelerating force is unchanged. | The accelerating force is halved. | The acceleration is unchanged. | The acceleration is halved.

The graph shows the variation of F with t.

What is the speed of the object when t = 1.0 s?
answer: C: 7.50 m s<sup>−1</sup> — 7.50 m s⁻¹.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A heavy cable is attached to a fixed support at J and carries a load at its lower end K.

The weight of the cable is not negligible.

The cable has constant cross-sectional area and density.

Which graph shows the variation of tensile stress σ in the cable with distance d from J to K?

The four graphs, each of σ against d from J to K, are all straight lines: A falls from a value at J to zero at K; B rises from a non-zero value at J to a larger value at K; C is constant; D falls from a value at J to a smaller, non-zero value at K.
answer: D.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A box with four terminals is connected to a cell and two ammeters. The top left terminal is X. The cell and the first ammeter are connected between X and the bottom left terminal; the second ammeter is connected between the top right and bottom right terminals.

Each of the boxes A to D is connected into the circuit in turn. All the resistors have equal resistance.

  • A: a resistor from X to top right; a resistor from X to bottom left; a wire from bottom left to bottom right.
  • B: a resistor from X to top right; a wire from X to bottom left; a wire from top right to bottom right.
  • C: a resistor from X to top right; a resistor from X to bottom left; a resistor from bottom left to bottom right.
  • D: a resistor from X to top right; a wire from bottom left to bottom right.

Which box gives the same reading on both ammeters?
answer: D.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
Two circular discs made of card rotate at constant speed on a common axle.

The discs are 2.00 m apart.

An air-gun pellet is fired parallel to the axle. The pellet makes holes in the discs.

The holes are separated by an angle of 45°.

The speed of the pellet between the discs is 300 m s−1.

How many revolutions does each disc complete in one second?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A resistor dissipates 100 W when connected across a 25 V supply with negligible internal resistance.

The supply output is reduced to 20 V and the resistor is replaced so that the power dissipated is still 100 W.

What is the percentage decrease in resistance?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
When an aircraft turns in a horizontal circular path, it banks at an angle θ. The lift force acts at θ to the vertical, the weight mg acts vertically down, and the centre of the circular path is a distance r away horizontally.

The aircraft has mass m and travels at constant speed v in a horizontal circular path of radius r. The lift force acts at the angle θ.

What is tan θ?
answer: D — v²/rg.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2023
html:
A mass, attached to two springs, oscillates horizontally on a smooth surface between P and Q. The motion of the system is simple harmonic.

Which quantity has its magnitude at a minimum value when the mass is at Q?
answer: B: the kinetic energy of the mass — the kinetic energy of the mass.
choices: the acceleration of the mass | the kinetic energy of the mass | the potential energy of the mass–spring system | the resultant force of the springs on the mass

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: State the names of the four fundamental interactions.
answer: Gravity, weak (nuclear), strong (nuclear), electromagnetic — in any order, all four needed. "Interaction" or "force" and "gravitational" are condoned; "electrostatic", "gravitational potential", "em" and "EM" are not accepted.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: State the products of the decay of a free neutron.
answer: A proton, a beta-minus particle (electron, e, e⁻, β⁻) and an (electron) antineutrino — all three needed. "Anti electron neutrino" is condoned.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain which of the fundamental interactions is responsible for the decay of the neutron.
answer: The weak interaction: a quark changes flavour, d to u — The weak (nuclear) interaction (1); because it involves leptons, which do not experience the strong interaction, or because there is a change in quark flavour — a d quark changes to a u quark (1). A reference to the W⁻ (or W) together with the transfer of charge from the neutron is also accepted. The second mark depends on the first.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The forces between two moving electrons cause their paths to change.

Explain, using the concept of exchange particles, why the electron paths change.
answer: They exchange virtual photons, which carry momentum and so change the electrons’ momentum — The exchange particle is a (virtual) photon (1); (virtual) photons / the exchange particles carry momentum (1); conservation of momentum means the photon interchange changes the electrons' momentum and so their paths (1). γ is accepted for photon.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A positive pion collides with a neutron and the following interaction is observed:

π+ + n → K+ + Σ0

Σ0 is a neutral sigma particle with a strangeness of −1

The interaction can be used to deduce the classifications of the Σ0.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Identify the classifications of each particle in the interaction.

Which classifications apply to the π+? Tick (✓) the appropriate boxes.
answer: Hadron and meson — the π+ is made of a quark and an antiquark (u d̅), which makes it a meson, and every meson is a hadron.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which classifications apply to the n (neutron)? Tick (✓) the appropriate boxes.
answer: Baryon and hadron — the neutron is made of three quarks (udd), which makes it a baryon, and every baryon is a hadron.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which classifications apply to the K+? Tick (✓) the appropriate boxes.
answer: Hadron and meson — the K+ is a quark and an antiquark (u s̅): a meson, and so a hadron.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Which classifications apply to the Σ0? Tick (✓) the appropriate boxes.
answer: Baryon and hadron — the Σ0 is made of three quarks (uds): a baryon, and so a hadron.
examiner_note: The paper gives 2 marks for the four rows together, so both sit on this last row: all four rows right for 2 marks, and any two rows right for 1.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A conservation rule predicts that the following interaction cannot occur:

π− + n → K− + Σ0

State the conservation rule.

Go on to explain your answer.
answer: Conservation of strangeness: K⁻ and Σ<sup>0</sup> each have strangeness −1, so it is 0 on the left but −2 on the right — K⁻ and Σ⁰ each have strangeness −1 (1). The strangeness is 0 + 0 on the left and −1 + (−1) = −2 on the right, so it is not conserved (1 — must show the two sides unequal AND the left-hand side zero). No first mark for saying some other quantum number is not conserved.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
One way in which neutral pions decay is

π0 → γ + e+ + e−

Compare the rest energies of the particles involved in this decay.
answer: The π⁰ (135 MeV) has more rest energy than the e⁺, e⁻ (0.511 MeV each) and photon (0) together — Each particle given its correct rest energy, including the photon (1): π⁰ 134.972 MeV, the electron and the positron 0.510999 MeV each, the photon zero (rounded values allowed). The rest energy on the left is greater than the total on the right (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The decay of the neutral pion leads to the production of further gamma photons.

Explain why.
answer: The positron annihilates with an electron. Answers such as "elimination" are not allowed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The Standard Model is a theory that classifies elementary particles.

Evidence for the theory has been collected since about 1950. However, the term Standard Model has only been used since 1973.

Suggest why progress in particle physics is slow.
answer: It needs international collaboration and very expensive equipment — International collaboration / co-operation / verification is required, OR (investment in) expensive equipment, hardware or infrastructure is required. The idea that people with particular specialist talents, technology or infrastructure must be in place is accepted. Peer review and vague statements ("it takes a long time", "the research is expensive") are ignored.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The block is used with a telescope to investigate stars.

The block can be replaced with a diffraction grating.

Describe one non-astronomical application of a diffraction grating.
answer: For example, measuring a light source’s wavelength, or analysing a sample’s composition — An appropriate application with how the grating is used described, e.g. used to determine the wavelength of a named light source; to identify elements in / analyse the chemical composition of a sample; to stabilise or filter laser light; to provide a monochromatic source / select a particular wavelength; in optical encoders for high-precision motor control; to spread the light evenly in e-readers. Condoned: identifying authentic bank notes; light shows or diffraction glasses; analysing light from the Sun.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Figure 2 shows a spectrum of light. Two lines in the spectrum are labelled X and Y.

The light passes at normal incidence through a diffraction grating. The number of lines per metre for the grating is G.

The first-order diffraction angle of X is at 28.2° to the normal.

Calculate G.

G = ______ m−1
answer: G = 1.2 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ — Any two of: λ of X read from the spectrum as 380 nm (377.5 to 382.5 nm accepted); use of d sin θ = nλ (n = 1 assumed if not seen), giving d = 8.04 × 10⁻⁷ m; use of G = 1/d to give 1.2 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ (3 marks). Calculator values 1.2358 to 1.2518 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ (1.2436 × 10⁶ for 380 nm). A power-of-ten error is ignored in the first two marks.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A scientist wants to obtain an accurate value for the difference in wavelength between line X and line Y (Figure 2).

She has two options:

  • option 1: to analyse the second-order spectrum from the original grating
  • option 2: to analyse the first-order spectrum from a grating with 2G lines per metre.

Discuss which option she should choose.
answer: Option 2: the separations are the same, but a second-order spectrum can overlap other orders — An argument using sin θ = nGλ (or equivalent) comparing the effect of n = 2 with G′ = 2G (1); the angular separations are the same for both options (1); option 2 (the 2G grating) should be used because the n = 2 spectrum could overlap with other orders, obscuring lines — or because its maxima are better defined, or because the second-order spectrum would be dimmer (first order with 2G brighter) (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The deuterium–tritium (D–T) reaction is a nuclear reaction between two isotopes of hydrogen. The D–T reaction is

21H + 31H → 42He + n

The energy from this reaction is transferred to the kinetic energy of the helium nucleus and the kinetic energy of the neutron.

Assume that the kinetic energies of the hydrogen nuclei are zero just before the reaction occurs.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Show that the kinetic energy of the neutron represents approximately 80% of the total energy transferred.
answer: Shown: equal momenta and a mass ratio of 4 give the neutron <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of the energy — Either: the mass of He is 4 × the mass of the neutron, OR the neutron and the He nucleus have equal and opposite momenta (1); combining the momentum and kinetic energy equations, KE = p²/2m, so with the same p the KE is inversely proportional to m, and the KE of the neutron is 4 × the KE of the helium nucleus — <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> = 80% of the total (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The combined kinetic energy of the helium nucleus and the neutron is 2.82 × 10−12 J.

Calculate the initial speed of the neutron.

initial speed = ______ m s−1
answer: v = 5.2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ — KE of the neutron = 80% × 2.82 × 10⁻¹² = 2.26 × 10⁻¹² J, used with the neutron mass 1.67(5) × 10⁻²⁷ kg in ½mv² (1); v = 5.2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (1). 5.18 × 10⁷ and 5.19 × 10⁷ are also accepted. Using 2.82 × 10⁻¹² J as the neutron's KE is not allowed.

html:
Figure 4 is a force diagram drawn to scale. It represents the magnitudes and directions of the tensions T1 and T2 in the cable when O is at rest in the position shown in Figure 3. At this position, resistive forces are zero.

Complete the force diagram.

Go on to determine, using your diagram, the magnitudes of T1 and T2.

T1 = ______ N
T2 = ______ N
answer: T₁ = 480 N and T₂ = 400 N (T₁ 470–490 N and T₂ 390–410 N accepted) — Complete a parallelogram or triangle to draw W (1); use the drawn W (350 N) to find the scale — on the printed paper 350 N ↔ 35 mm, 10 N mm⁻¹ (1); use the scale to get T₁ and T₂ — about 48 mm and 40 mm (1); the values (1). Alternative: measure the angles, (34–35)° and (11–12)° to the horizontal (1), then resolve: T₁ sin 34° + T₂ sin 11° = 350 and T₁ cos 34° = T₂ cos 11° (1), giving the values (1). The sine or cosine rule applied correctly is also allowed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
In a second test, pulley P with O attached is released from A. P and O move along the cable to B.

The change in height of the centre of mass of O between A and B is 4.5 m. The distance travelled along the cable is 18 m. The speed of O when it reaches B is 6.5 m s−1.

Calculate the average resistive force on O and P as they move from A to B.

average resistive force = ______ N
answer: 46 N — Max 4 from: m = 350/g = 36 kg; their m in KE with v = 6.5 m s⁻¹ at B (754 J); 350 N and 4.5 m in the GPE equation (1575 J); ΔGPE − ΔKE = work done against friction (821 J); friction force = work done ÷ 18. Then the average force = 46 N (1). Alternative (with a labelled diagram): m = 350/g; suvat gives a = 1.17 m s⁻²; F = ma for the resultant force; the effective component of weight 350 × (4.5 ÷ 18); subtract the resultant from that component. Answers that round to 46 N are accepted.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
O contains a fragile item packed in suitable material.

Explain how the material can prevent damage to the fragile item when O stops suddenly at B.
answer: It makes the stopping time longer, so the same change in momentum needs a smaller force — The contact time, or the distance travelled during contact, is increased (1); then a physical principle (1) and its application to why the force is reduced (1), by any one of: momentum — force is the rate of change of momentum, and the change in momentum (impulse, F × Δt) is constant, so the force decreases; energy — force × distance = change in KE (work done), which is constant, so the force is reduced; Newton's second law — F = ma, and the change in velocity is constant, so the acceleration and hence the force are reduced.

name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Calculate the resistance of the variable resistor.

resistance = ______ Ω
answer: 190 Ω (calculator 191.67 Ω). Appropriate use of V = IR (1) — e.g. total resistance 6.5 / 0.012 = 542 Ω, or a pd of 2.3 V across the resistor — then 190 Ω (1). A power-of-ten error is condoned in the first mark.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
The resistance R of the thermistor at temperature θ in K is given by:

R = R0 eB(1/θ − 1/θ0)

where R0 is the resistance at the initial temperature θ0 in K, and B is a constant.

The temperature of the thermistor is increased to 318 K. The variable resistor is adjusted so that the circuit current is again 12 mA. The potential difference across the thermistor is now 3.2 V.

Determine B.

State an appropriate unit for your answer.

B = ______   unit = ______
answer: B = 1110 K — 22 °C converted to kelvin, 295 K (1); R = 3.2 / (12 × 10⁻³) = 267 Ω (1); use of ln(R/R₀) with their values (1); B = 1110 (1 — 1100, and answers that round to 1110 or 1120, accepted); unit K (1 — "k" is not accepted). R₀ = 190 Ω is condoned in the third mark.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: Explain why the current in the thermistor needs to be controlled.
answer: The current heats the thermistor, which lowers its resistance — The current causes the thermistor's temperature to change (it heats it) (1); the thermistor's resistance decreases as its temperature increases (1). A clear description of thermal runaway gets both marks.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Explain how ammeters and voltmeters can be used in the circuit in Figure 5 to demonstrate the conservation of charge and the conservation of energy.

Refer to points X, Y and Z in your answer.
answer: Equal currents at X, Y and Z show charge conserved; the p.d.s adding to 6.5 V show energy conserved — Ammeter(s) in series show the current at X = the current at Y = the current at Z, OR voltmeter(s) show the emf / terminal pd (6.5 V) = pd across XY + pd across YZ (1); the current readings are linked to conservation of charge AND the pd readings to conservation of energy (1). "Currents across" is not allowed; "battery pd" only if it is clearly measured.

Figure 6 shows the variation of displacement with distance from one end of the string at time t = 0. At this time all points on the string have their maximum displacement. S is one point on the string.

Figure 6

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Deduce the amplitude of one of the progressive waves.

amplitude = ______ mm
answer: 3.5 mm (3.4 to 3.6 accepted).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Determine, in m s−1, the speed of one of the progressive waves.

speed = ______ m s−1
answer: 440 m s⁻¹ — Use of v = fλ with 625 Hz (1); wavelength 0.7 m giving 440 m s⁻¹ (1). λ from 0.68 to 0.72 m, and speeds 425 to 450 m s⁻¹, are accepted.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html: State the phase relationship between the two waves when t = 0
answer: In phase, or a phase difference of 0 (2π, 360° and multiples accepted).

html: Sketch, on Figure 7, a graph to show how the displacement of S varies with t.
answer: A sinusoidal wave starting at displacement = 4 mm (1); amplitude 4 mm (1); period (625⁻¹) = 1.6 ms (1) — Tolerance half a square; the shape is judged on the first complete cycle, and a line with no complete cycle must cover the width of the grid.

Monochromatic light is incident on a metal surface in a vacuum and photoelectrons are emitted from the surface. The photoelectric current I is the rate of flow of charge from the surface.

The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is Ek(max).

Ek(max) and I are measured.

The frequency of the light is then increased. There is no change to the rate at which energy is incident on the surface.

What happens to Ek(max) and I when the frequency is increased?

Ek(max)I
Aincreasesdecreases
Bincreasesno change
Cno changeno change
Dno changedecreases
answer: A: Ek(max) increases, I decreases — Ek(max) increases, I decreases.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
Monochromatic light is used in a Young's double-slit interference experiment after passing through a single slit. The resulting fringe pattern is observed on a screen.

The separation of the fringes can be increased by
answer: A — using monochromatic light of lower frequency.
choices: using monochromatic light of lower frequency. | decreasing the width of the single slit. | increasing the separation of the double slits. | decreasing the distance between the double slits and the screen.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A force of magnitude F acts on a box of mass m that moves along a frictionless slope. The slope is at an angle α to the horizontal and the force acts at an angle β to the slope.

What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the block along the slope?
answer: B: (F/m) cos β − g sin α — (F/m) cos β − g sin α.

The weight of a uniform bar is W.

An object also of weight W is attached to one end.

The bar is pivoted at the other end and held horizontal by a rope attached to its centre.

The tension in the rope is 4W.

What is angle θ?
answer: A — 41°. (Moments about the pivot: 4W cos θ × L/2 = W × L/2 + W × L, so cos θ = 0.75.)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A projectile is fired from ground level over horizontal ground.

Its initial velocity is u at an angle θ to the horizontal.

The range of the projectile is d.

A second projectile is fired with a velocity 2u at the same angle.

What is the range of this projectile?

Assume that air resistance is negligible.
answer: D — 4d (the range is proportional to u²).

A particle travelling horizontally at 1.0 × 107 m s−1 enters a region where it has a constant vertical acceleration of 4 × 1014 m s−2.

What is the horizontal distance the particle has travelled in the region when its vertical displacement is 8 × 10−2 m?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A man has a mass of 75.0 kg.

He stands on weighing scales in a lift that accelerates upwards at 2.60 m s−2.

What is the reading on the scales during the acceleration?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
An average force of 42 kN acts on the air passing through a jet engine. This force causes the speed of the air to increase by 540 m s−1.

What mass of air passes through the engine in one minute?

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A uniform wire is stretched by a load F.

The elastic strain energy stored in the wire is E.

The load is increased from F to 2F.

The wire obeys Hooke's law.

What is the increase in the elastic strain energy stored in the wire?
answer: C — 3E (the energy rises to 4E).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A spring is compressed by a force F. The spring has stiffness k and its length changes by ΔL during the compression. When the force is removed the spring returns to its original length in time t.

What is the average power developed by the spring as it returns to its original length?
answer: C: k(ΔL)2/2t — k(ΔL)²/2t.
choices: kΔL2t | kΔLt | k(ΔL)22t | k(ΔL)2t

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A 12 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals of a battery of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 4.0 Ω.

What is the pd across the resistor?

The mass remains at rest relative to the turntable.

What is the direction of the frictional force on the mass at the instant shown?
answer: A — from P to O (friction provides the centripetal force).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A particle of mass m moves in a circle of radius r. The number of revolutions completed per second is f.

What is the kinetic energy of the particle?
answer: B — 2π²mf²r². (½m(2πfr)².)

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A body is in simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.60 m and period 2π seconds.

What is its speed when its displacement is 0.20 m?
answer: B: 0.57 m s<sup>−1</sup> — 0.57 m s⁻¹. (ω = 1 rad s⁻¹; v = ω√(0.60² − 0.20²).)
choices: 0.32 m s<sup>−1</sup> | 0.57 m s<sup>−1</sup> | 0.63 m s<sup>−1</sup> | 22 m s<sup>−1</sup>

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
When a mass M is suspended from a spring, the spring extends by a distance x. M is displaced vertically and, when released, it oscillates with a period T.

M is removed and suspended from a different spring. The spring extends by a distance x2.

M is again displaced vertically and released.

What is the new period of oscillations of M?
answer: B — T/√2 (the new spring is twice as stiff).
choices: T2 | T√2 | T√2 | 2T

subject: Physics
name: Paper 1 — June 2024
html:
A mass–spring system and a simple pendulum have identical periods of oscillation T when at the surface of the Earth.

Both are taken to planet X where the acceleration due to gravity is g2.

What are the periods of the mass–spring system and the simple pendulum on X?

Period of mass–spring systemPeriod of simple pendulum
AT2T√2
BT2T
CTT√2
DT√2T
answer: C — the mass–spring period is still T; the pendulum's is T√2.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html: State what is meant by the internal energy of an ideal gas.
answer: The total kinetic energy of the particles. "Molecules" or "atoms" are condoned for particles — The mean kinetic energy, or the kinetic energy of a single particle, is not accepted, and neither is any answer implying potential energy (or any other energy) is added to the kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
Figure 1 (01.2): particle P, mass m, velocity c perpendicular to side W of a cube of side length l and volume V.

P collides repeatedly with W.

Show that the frequency f of collisions is c⁄2l.
answer: The time between collisions with W is T = 2l / c (the particle travels 2l at speed c), so f = 1/T = c / 2l — There must be evidence of a time calculation using distance and speed; any attempted use of v = fλ is not allowed.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
The mass of the wheel is measured when the gas in the tyre is at a pressure of 1.01 × 105 Pa.

More of the same gas is added to the tyre and the mass of the wheel is measured again.

Table 1 shows the pressure in the tyre and the mass of the wheel before and after the addition of the extra gas.

The gas is kept at a constant temperature of 100 °C.

Pressure in tyre / PaMass of wheel / kg
Before1.01 × 10514.897
After2.11 × 10514.991

Determine, in kg mol−1, the molar mass of the gas.

molar mass = ______ kg mol−1
answer: 0.028 kg mol⁻¹ — Volume of gas = πhd²/4 for the outer cylinder minus the rim: π × 0.370 × 0.660²/4 = 0.1265 m³ and π × 0.370 × 0.330²/4 = 0.0316 m³ (1, an attempt at either volume; power-of-ten errors condoned), so V = 0.1265 − 0.0316 = 0.0949 m³ (1). n = pV/RT at T = 373 K: 1.01 × 10⁵ × 0.0949 / (8.31 × 373) = 3.09 mol, or 2.11 × 10⁵ × 0.0949 / (8.31 × 373) = 6.46 mol (1); Δn = 6.46 − 3.09 = 3.37 mol (1); molar mass = (14.991 − 14.897)/3.37 = 0.094/3.37 = 0.028 kg mol⁻¹ (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
Motorsport regulations specify a minimum amount of gas in the tyre.

The amount of gas in the tyre is checked by measuring the pressure before the wheel is put onto the car. The regulations also specify a maximum temperature for the tyre when making this measurement.

Explain why a maximum temperature is specified.
answer: A hotter tyre has a higher pressure, so it could pass the check with less gas in it — Carrying out the check at a higher temperature increases the pressure in the tyre (1 — linking pressure to temperature; p ∝ T is condoned); so the tyre could pass the check with a smaller amount of gas in it — when the tyre is hot the same pressure is reached with less gas (1).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html: Describe two properties of a radial gravitational field.
answer: A mass feels an attractive force towards the centre, and it varies as 1/r2 — One general point (1): a region in which a mass experiences a force due to another mass; OR the field is conservative, so any change in potential energy depends only on the initial and final positions and not on the path; OR the force is always attractive / the field lines point to the (centre of) mass / the equipotential surfaces are spherical about the (centre of) mass; OR it is a non-contact force. AND the point specific to a radial field (1): the field strength (force) has an inverse-square variation with distance. "The force is attractive" alone is insufficient; "force" and "mass" must be used rather than words like "effect", "gravity" or "object".

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
A space probe is launched from the Earth’s surface.

Figure 3 shows how the gravitational force acting on the space probe varies with height above the Earth’s surface.

State the physical significance of the shaded area in Figure 3.
answer: The energy needed to lift the probe from the surface to 8 × 10<sup>6</sup> m — The (minimum) energy needed / work done to launch the space probe to a height of 8 × 10⁶ m; OR the change in gravitational potential energy of the probe when it is moved from the Earth’s surface to a height of 8 × 10⁶ m.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
At the Earth’s surface,

  • the gravitational field strength of the Sun is gS
  • the gravitational field strength of the Earth is gE.

Calculate gS⁄gE.

distance from the Earth to the Sun = 1.50 × 1011 m

gS⁄gE = ______
answer: 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ (or 0.060%) — g<sub>S</sub> = GM<sub>S</sub>/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.99 × 10³⁰ / (1.50 × 10¹¹)² = 5.90 × 10⁻³ N kg⁻¹, or a substitution into a valid equation (1); g<sub>S</sub>/g<sub>E</sub> = 5.90 × 10⁻³ / 9.81 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ (1). Alternatively the ratio (M<sub>Sun</sub>/M<sub>Earth</sub>) × (r<sub>Earth</sub>/r<sub>Sun</sub>)² may be used. The answer must be given to at least 2 s.f.; if 3 or more are seen it must round to 6.01 or 6.02 × 10⁻⁴.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
At the Earth’s surface,

  • the gravitational field strength of the Sun is gS
  • the gravitational field strength of the Earth is gE.

Explain why gS is more important than gE in predicting the motion of the space probe as it escapes from the Solar System.
answer: The Sun’s far larger mass makes its pull dominate once far from Earth — The force from the Earth, because of its smaller mass, is less than the force from the Sun at a similar distance; OR the total work done in moving a long way from the Sun is much greater than that in moving a long way from the Earth, because m<sub>E</sub> ≪ m<sub>S</sub>. "Edge of the Solar System" is condoned for "a similar distance".

name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
The space probe eventually reaches a point where the gravitational influence of the Solar System is negligible.

The probe is unpowered as it approaches an isolated interstellar body X.

The gravitational field of X changes the kinetic energy of the space probe.

Table 2 shows the distance of the space probe from the centre of mass of X and the speed for two positions A and B of the space probe.

Distance of space probe from centre of mass of X / 106 mSpeed of space probe / 103 m s−1
A6.01.1
B0.171.3

The space probe has a mass of 4.9 × 104 kg.

Calculate the mass of X.

mass of X = ______ kg
answer: 6.3 × 10²⁰ kg — Change in kinetic energy (or per unit mass) formulated: ½m(v<sub>B</sub>² − v<sub>A</sub>²) = 1.18 × 10¹⁰ J, i.e. m × 2.40 × 10⁵ J (1; 2 s.f. allowed). Change in gravitational potential energy formulated: ΔE<sub>p</sub> = GMm(1/1.7 × 10⁵ − 1/6.0 × 10⁶) = GMm × 5.72 × 10⁻⁶ (1). Evidence of the intention to equate ΔE<sub>k</sub> and ΔE<sub>p</sub>, e.g. ½(v<sub>B</sub>² − v<sub>A</sub>²) = GM/r<sub>B</sub> − GM/r<sub>A</sub>, with data substituted (1; ecf allowed); mass of X = 6.3 × 10²⁰ kg (1).

html:
An alpha particle passes through the mesh.

The alpha particle ionises an argon atom at P on Figure 5, releasing one electron.

The electron and the argon ion have no kinetic energy at P.

The electron then travels to the wire and the argon ion travels to the mesh.

Calculate the ratio speed of electron when it reaches the wire⁄speed of argon ion when it reaches the mesh.

Assume that the air has no effect on the motion of the electron or on the motion of the argon ion.

mass of argon ion = 6.64 × 10−26 kg

ratio = ______
answer: 270 — A statement that the (kinetic) energy gained is the same, or a correct substitution of data into the equation or ratio (1); ratio = √(6.64 × 10⁻²⁶ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 270 (1). Factors that cancel, such as ½, may be absent.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
An alpha particle passes through the mesh.

The alpha particle ionises an argon atom at P on Figure 5, releasing one electron.

The electron and the argon ion have no kinetic energy at P.

The electron then travels to the wire and the argon ion travels to the mesh.

In practice, the air does affect the motion of the electron and the motion of the argon ion.

Suggest how the presence of air between the mesh and the wire changes the ratio in Question 04.2.

No numerical detail is required.
answer: The ratio is larger: in collisions with the air the argon ion loses more energy than the electron — because, due to collisions, the argon ion loses more energy / speed / momentum than the electron; OR the argon ion is more ionising than the electron (the electron is less ionising). The mark is for the explanation. "The argon ion has a higher probability of collision" is accepted, as are reverse arguments; answers suggesting the particles travel different distances, or referring to air resistance, are not.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
The alpha source in Figure 4 is moved to different heights h above the mesh.

Figure 7 shows how the number of sparks N produced in 10 minutes varies with h.

No sparks are produced when the source is not present.

Student A suggests that the spark rate obeys an inverse-square law.

Student B suggests that the spark rate decreases exponentially with h.

Determine whether either student is correct.
answer: Neither: Nh2 is not constant (10, then 7.18), and N does not halve in equal steps of h (0.25 cm, 0.31 cm) — Evidence of a suitable test of A’s suggestion using 2 or more data points, e.g. Nh² = constant (1): 10 × 1.0² = 10 but 4 × 1.34² = 7.18, so Nh² is not constant. Evidence of a suitable test of B’s suggestion using 2 or more sets of data (1): N should halve in equal intervals of h (or N eh constant for N = k e−h; log/ln tests accepted) — but N falls from 10 to 5 in 0.25 cm and from 5 to 2.5 in 0.31 cm. Both tests performed AND both suggestions rejected with reasons (1). An answer accepting B is allowed if it refers to experimental error and the difference is small.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html: Show that the time taken for the capacitor to charge from 2.0 V to 4.0 V is approximately 0.7R1C.
answer: Shown: t2 − t1 = R1C[ln(2⁄3) − ln(1⁄3)] = R1C ln 2 = 0.69R1C — Time to charge to 4.0 V: t2 = −R1C ln(1 − 4⁄6); or to 2.0 V: t1 = −R1C ln(1 − 2⁄6) (1; can be t2 = 1.10R1C or t1 = 0.41R1C). t2 − t1 = R1C[ln(2⁄3) − ln(1⁄3)] = R1C ln 2 = 0.69R1C, or (1.10 − 0.41)R1C = 0.69R1C (1 — 0.69R1C must be seen, from a time difference). Finding the time to charge to 2 V from a 4 V supply gains only the first mark; a solution using the discharge equation scores 0.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
The capacitor is fully discharged.

The capacitor is then charged until the potential difference (pd) across it is 4.0 V.

Figure 9 shows the variation with time of the ammeter reading as the capacitor is charged.

Show that the capacitance of the capacitor is about 1 × 10−4 F.
answer: C = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F — Method 1 (area): an attempt at the area under the I–t graph by counting squares (1); one 1 cm square (1 s × 0.5 × 10⁻⁵ A) is a charge of 0.5 × 10⁻⁵ C (1); about 80 squares (78 to 82), so Q = (3.9 to 4.1) × 10⁻⁴ C (1); C = Q/4 = a value that rounds to 1 × 10⁻⁴ F to 2 or more s.f. (1). Method 2 (data points): with the capacitor at 4 V the resistor has 2 V across it at I = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ A (or 6 V at 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ A at the start) (1), so R<sub>1</sub> = 1.0 × 10⁵ Ω (1); the charging time constant R<sub>1</sub>C = 10(.0) s, e.g. from I = I<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−t/R₁C</sup> with I = 2 × 10⁻⁵ A, I<sub>0</sub> = 6 × 10⁻⁵ A, t = 11 s (1); C = 10.0 / 1.0 × 10⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F (1). Estimating an average current by sight and using C = IT/V scores 1 mark at most.

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
When the pd reaches 4.0 V the switch is immediately set to discharge the capacitor.

When the pd reaches 2.0 V the switch is immediately set to charge the capacitor.

Figure 10 shows how the pd across the capacitor varies with time.

Determine the value of R2.

R2 = ______ Ω
answer: 2.0 × 10⁵ Ω — Reading relevant discharge data from Figure 10, e.g. the time to fall to half: 4.0 V to 2.0 V in (32 − 11) s (1). A valid substitution to find R<sub>1</sub> or R<sub>Total</sub>: t<sub>½</sub> = 0.69R<sub>Total</sub>C (0.7RC allowed) gives R<sub>Total</sub> = 3.0 × 10⁵ Ω; R<sub>1</sub> = 1.0 × 10⁵ Ω from Figure 9 (6.0 to 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ A in 6.8 s) or from 05.2 (1). R<sub>2</sub> = R<sub>Total</sub> − R<sub>1</sub> = 2.0 × 10⁵ Ω (1; one error carried forward allowed from R<sub>Total</sub> or R<sub>1</sub>).

subject: Physics
name: Paper 2 — June 2023
html:
Nuclear radii can be estimated using either alpha particles or high-energy electrons.

State two advantages of using high-energy electrons rather than alpha particles for this estimate.
answer: Any two: better resolution, no repulsion, less recoil, easier to accelerate, no strong force — Any two: electrons give greater resolution (the wavelength can be made very small); electrons can get closer to the nuclei (no electrostatic repulsion); electrons have less recoil (their mass is small compared with the nucleus); free electrons are easier to accelerate / give energy to (higher charge-to-mass ratio); electrons are easier to produce; the scattering distributions are easier to interpret / the strong nuclear interaction is not involved; alpha particles only give the distance of closest approach (an upper limit to the radius). Reverse arguments are allowed.
